### 23. Mardi Gras

**Port:** New Orleans
**Date:** Tue Feb 9
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Fat Tuesday; the climax of a 35-day Carnival season that begins at Twelfth Night on Jan 6. Parades start three weekends earlier with Krewe du Vieux’s satirical march through the Marigny in late January, then build through the family krewes, Endymion’s super-krewe on Saturday Feb 6, Bacchus on Sunday, Proteus and Orpheus on Lundi Gras night. On Mardi Gras Day: Zulu rolling at 8 a.m. with the hand-decorated coconuts, Rex following at 10, the Society of St. Anne walking from the Bywater through the Quarter by noon in homemade finery, the Mardi Gras Indians out in full-suit splendor in the Tremé, the truck parades all afternoon, the Quarter cleared on horseback at midnight when the season ends. King cakes from Twelfth Night through Ash Wednesday, Manny Randazzo, Dong Phuong, Haydel’s, and yours. Red beans on Lundi Gras. Whatever’s left in the kitchen on Tuesday night, because the fast starts in the morning.

**The Berth.** The Pontchartrain on St. Charles; the Hotel Monteleone in the French Quarter for the Carousel Bar; the Roosevelt for old grandeur. Maison de la Luz on Carondelet, Atelier Ace boutique, the Library bar for the Lundi Gras nightcap; Henry Howard Hotel on Prytania, Garden District boutique in 1867 Italianate, walks to the St. Charles parade route.

**The Galley.** Commander’s Palace in the Garden District; Antoine’s on Rue St. Louis since 1840; Café du Monde for beignets; Cochon for whole-pig; Galatoire’s on Bourbon for the Friday- afternoon ritual. Compère Lapin in the Old No. 77 Hotel, Nina Compton’s flagship Caribbean-Creole; Saba on Magazine Street, Alon Shaya’s Israeli, the post-parade Saturday morning shakshuka.

**The Bearings.**

1. *St. Louis Cathedral* (New Orleans, Louisiana, USA). The three-spired cathedral facing Jackson Square, oldest continuously active in the United States, founded 1727; the Mississippi swings past at her shoulder and Andrew Jackson rides bronze out front
2. *Garden District & Lafayette Cemetery No. 1* (New Orleans, Louisiana, USA). The mid-nineteenth-century American quarter of broad oak streets and white-pillared mansions, the brick-walled cemetery with its above-ground tombs at the heart; Anne Rice's vampires walk here

### 24. Patrino Karnavali

**Port:** Patras, Peloponnese, Greece
**Date:** Sun Jan 17 – Mon Feb 8
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Opening on St. Anthony’s Day Jan 17, climax on the Sunday and Clean Monday before Lent, the largest Carnival in Greece and one of the largest in Europe, dating to 1829. Three weeks of treasure hunts, masked balls (the historic Bourboulia women’s masquerade ball dating to 1872), the children’s parade, and the spectacular Saturday-night Illuminated Parade and Sunday afternoon Grand Parade with 50,000+ costumed participants, satirical floats built year-round in the municipal carnival workshops, and the closing-night ritual burning of the Carnival King at the St. Nikolaos Street pier in the harbour, broadcast nationally. Tiganites and traditional carnival foods at every taverna; bouzouki music until dawn. 3.5 hours west of Athens by car or train.

**The Berth.** Athens: Hotel Grande Bretagne on Syntagma; Electra Metropolis for the rooftop view; or AthensWas in Plaka for the boutique. Crete: Domes of Elounda; Blue Palace. In Patras: Astir Hotel Patras on the downtown waterfront, walking distance to the parade route; in Nafplio (1.5 hours back toward Athens): Nafplia Palace on the cliff above the old town, the post-Carnival Peloponnese stop.

**The Galley.** Athens: Funky Gourmet for the modern Michelin (when open); Spondi for the canonical contemporary; Diporto in the central market for the canonical kafeneio; Karamanlidika for the deli-restaurant. In Patras: Ouzeri Manolis for canonical Patrino mezedes and tsipouro; in Athens en route: To Mavro Provato in Pangrati for the all-day mezedopoleio and the lamb-on-paper.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Ancient Olympia* (Elis, Peloponnese, Greece). The sanctuary of Zeus where the games ran every four years from 776 BCE for a thousand years; the stadium track still measured at six hundred Greek feet, the starting blocks still in the stone
2. *Temple of Apollo Epicurius at Bassae* (Oichalia, Arcadia, Greece). Iktinos's high-altitude temple of 420 BCE at 1,131 metres in the Arcadian mountains, the first ancient site UNESCO inscribed in Greece (1986); now sheltered under a permanent white tent

### 25. Sauti za Busara

**Port:** Stone Town, Zanzibar
**Date:** Feb 11–14
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

Four-day East African music festival in Stone Town, Zanzibar, held annually in mid-February at the Old Fort (Ngome Kongwe) on the seafront, founded 2004 to showcase live African music from across the continent. ’Sauti za Busara’ means ’Sounds of Wisdom’ in Swahili. 400+ artists across the four nights from Tanzania, Kenya, Uganda, Mozambique, Madagascar, the DRC, and the broader African diaspora, taarab, bongo flava, kwasa-kwasa, mbalax, and the experimental electronic-meets-traditional fusion that defines contemporary East African music. Pair with a daytime Stone Town walking tour and a sunset dhow cruise.

**The Berth.** Park Hyatt Zanzibar on the seafront; Emerson Spice in the converted merchant’s palace; or Jafferji House & Spa for the boutique. Zuri Zanzibar on the Kendwa northwest coast for the post-festival beach decompression; &Beyond Mnemba Island on the private island off the northeast coast for the splurge.

**The Galley.** Forodhani Gardens night market for the seafood skewers; The Tea House at Emerson Spice for the rooftop tasting; Lukmaan for canonical Zanzibari biryani; Stone Town Café for breakfast. 6 Degrees South Grill & Wine Bar on Shangani for the rooftop sunset over the Indian Ocean; The Rock Restaurant on the offshore boulder near Pingwe, the iconic island restaurant, wade out at low tide, boat across at high.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Stone Town of Zanzibar* (Zanzibar City, Tanzania). The labyrinth of coral-stone alleys facing Mombasa across a hundred kilometres of Indian Ocean, the brass-studded carved doors of Omani merchants on every corner; UNESCO 2000, the slave market in the centre
2. *Ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani* (Kilwa, Lindi Region, Tanzania). The thirteenth-century Swahili sultanate ruined on its mangrove island, the Great Mosque's domed roofs still standing on coral piers; UNESCO 1981, Ibn Battuta praised it as one of the world's most beautiful

### 27. Salon du Chocolat Brussels

**Port:** Tour & Taxis, Brussels, Belgium
**Date:** Fri–Sun Feb 12–14
**Flags:** FOOD, ART

The 13th annual Brussels edition; Belgium’s flagship chocolate festival, the most internationally important chocolate event in Europe, gathering 2,000+ chocolatiers, pastry chefs, confectioners, and cocoa-producers into a single three-day temple of the cacao bean. The flagship Paris edition launched 1994 by Sylvie Douce and François Jeantet; the Brussels edition launched 2015 to give Belgian chocolatiers their own dedicated platform on home soil. The Brussels venue, the spectacular Tour & Taxis complex, is itself a destination, the magnificently restored 19th-century railway-and-customs station along the canal in northwest Brussels, with cathedral-like industrial architecture (vast iron-and-glass roofs over former goods halls), now Brussels’s premier event venue.

**The Berth.** Hotel Amigo (Rocco Forte’s flagship behind the Grand Place); Warwick Brussels (next to the Sablon chocolate quarter); Rocco Forte Brussels or Steigenberger Wiltcher’s on Avenue Louise. The Dominican, boutique in a former 15th-century Dominican monastery near the Grand-Place; 9 Hotel Sablon, small design hotel inside the Sablon antiques quarter, walk to Pierre Marcolini.

**The Galley.** Comme Chez Soi on Place Rouppe for the splurge; Chez Léon for canonical moules- frites; Friterie Tabora for the late-night cone. Mary Chocolatier for the boutique Belgian since 1919, royal warrant; Pierre Marcolini in Sablon for the modern artisan flagship, the bean-to-bar tasting flight is the right post-Salon move.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Grand-Place / Grote Markt* (Brussels, Belgium). The square framed by the Gothic Town Hall and the late-baroque guildhouses rebuilt after the 1695 French bombardment; chocolatiers along the surrounding lanes have made the city the cocoa capital of Europe
2. *Atomium* (Brussels, Belgium). André Waterkeyn's 102-metre stainless-steel iron crystal magnified 165 billion times, built for Expo 58 and kept as the city's twentieth-century landmark; the lighting changes through the night

### 28. Jorvik Viking Festival

**Port:** York, UK
**Date:** Sat–Sun Feb 13–21
**Flags:** VIKING, CASTLE

Europe’s largest Viking festival, in its 41st year, built around the Jorvik Viking Centre and the actual Coppergate excavation site of the 10th-century Viking city, 50,000+ attendees over nine days for combat reenactments in the Eye of York, longship races on the Ouse, the spectacular finale Strongest Viking competition, plus medieval markets, sagas read in the Minster, and the Viking Eve Walk by torchlight.

Middlethorpe Hall outside the city, 17th-century William and Mary country house, walled garden, the post- festival countryside stay; The Principal York on Station Rise (the renamed Royal York), the dependable old grand hotel by the train station.

Roots York on Marygate, Tommy Banks’ York outpost, the seasonal Yorkshire tasting menu; The Whippet Inn on North Street for the casual gastropub and the regional ale list.

1. *York Minster* (York, North Yorkshire, England, UK). The Gothic cathedral built across two and a half centuries between 1220 and 1472, the Great East Window the size of a tennis court the largest expanse of medieval stained glass on Earth; the Roman fortress still under the crypt
2. *Hadrian's Wall* (Northumberland, England, UK). The Roman frontier wall of 122 CE, eighty miles of stone running coast to coast across northern Britain; UNESCO 1987, the milecastles and turrets still standing on the windy ridges of Whin Sill

### 29. Basel Fasnacht

**Port:** Basel, Switzerland
**Date:** Mon Feb 15 – Thu Feb 18 at 4:00 a.m.
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

A 72-hour run from Morgestraich at 4 a.m. Monday to Endstraich at 4 a.m. Thursday; Switzerland’s largest carnival, the only major Protestant carnival in the world, and UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage since 2017. Locals call it ’Die drey scheenschte Dääg’, the three most beautiful days, and the carnival itself is personified as ’Dame Fasnacht.’ The defining moment is the opening Morgestraich: at the fourth chime from St Martin’s Church at exactly 4:00 a.m., the city utility extinguishes every streetlight in the Old Town, plunging the medieval Altstadt into total darkness. The drum majors give the command ’Morgestraich, vorwärts marsch!’ and hundreds of Cliques begin marching slowly through the cobblestoned streets in absolute concentration, playing the archaic Morgestraich tune on piccolos and the distinctive Basler snare drums.

**The Berth.** Les Trois Rois on the Rhine, the 1681 grand dame on the Münsterplatz, Basel’s canonical luxury and the building from whose balcony the Morgestraich is best viewed; Hotel Krafft on the Kleinbasel side of the Rhine, the 1873 boutique with the river-terrace breakfast; Der Teufelhof Basel for the design-set boutique built inside a stretch of the medieval city wall.

**The Galley.** Basler Mehlsuppe (the dark roasted-flour soup, the Fasnacht specialty), Zwiebelwähe (Basel’s onion tart) and Käsewähe (cheese quiche) at every wirtshaus; Fasnachtskiechli (large thin fried- dough biscuits dusted with sugar). Volkshaus Basel for the contemporary Herzog & de Meuron-renovated brasserie; Stucki Basel for Tanja Grandits’ Michelin two-star at Bruderholz, the post-Endstraich dinner.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Strasbourg Cathedral* (Strasbourg, France). The pink Vosges-sandstone cathedral whose single spire reached 142 metres in 1439 and held the record as the world's tallest building for 227 years; Victor Hugo called it a prodigy of the gigantic and the delicate
2. *Old City of Berne* (Berne, Switzerland). The medieval Swiss capital on its sandstone peninsula in a bend of the Aare, six kilometres of arcaded sandstone houses, the Zytglogge clock tower at the centre; UNESCO 1983

### 31. Battle of Olustee Civil War Reenactment

**Port:** Olustee Battlefield, FL
**Date:** Sat–Sun mid-February
**Flags:** CULTURE

Annual late-February reenactment of the February 20, 1864 Battle of Olustee at Olustee Battlefield Historic State Park, 80 km west of Jacksonville, Florida, the largest Civil War battle fought in Florida, a Confederate victory that halted the Union advance into the state’s interior. 1,500+ reenactors representing both armies refight the battle across three afternoons, with cavalry charges through the pine flatwoods, infantry advances, and artillery duels. The battle is notable for the participation of the 54th Massachusetts (the regiment of Glory) on the Union side. Living-history camps, sutler row, and period civilian impressions fill the surrounding park.

**The Berth.** Stay in Jacksonville (60 km east): Marriott Jacksonville Downtown; or the Cumberland Island Greyfield Inn for the historic island option. In St. Augustine, 70 km east: Casa Monica, the 1888 Henry Flagler hotel in the Spanish Colonial centre; in Gainesville, 60 km south: Hotel Eleo at the University of Florida for the design-set option.

**The Galley.** Jacksonville: Bistro Aix for the modern American; Black Sheep Restaurant in Riverside; Maple Street Biscuit Company for breakfast. TacoLu Baja Mexicana in Jacksonville Beach for the canonical post-battlefield tacos and tequila list; in St. Augustine en route: Catch 27 for canonical Florida seafood, Mayport shrimp and Atlantic flounder.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Castillo de San Marcos* (St. Augustine, Florida, USA). The Spanish star fort of 1672 cut from coral-stone coquina, the soft rock that absorbed British cannonballs like a sponge; the oldest masonry fort in the continental United States, never taken by force
2. *Andersonville National Historic Site* (Andersonville, Georgia, USA). The Confederate prisoner-of-war stockade where 13,000 Union soldiers died in fourteen months of 1864 and 1865, the deadliest ground of the Civil War; now also the National Prisoner of War Museum

### 32. Houston Rodeo

**Port:** NRG Park, Houston, TX
**Date:** Thu Feb 25 – Sun Mar 21, ~25 days
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo, known to Texans simply as RodeoHouston, the world’s largest livestock show and rodeo, runs three weeks each late February through mid-March. The official kickoff is the Bar-B-Que Cookoff over the three days preceding opening night, the largest and most prestigious barbecue competition in the United States, hosting 250+ teams across the parking lots and grounds of NRG Park, by some measures the largest barbecue gathering on Earth. Launched 1974 in the original Astrodome parking lot with 17 teams; the rule from day one remains: minimum 10 pounds of barbecue, cooked over a wood fire only, no electric or gas. 90% of teams compete by invitation-only and most have wait lists measured in years. Once the Cookoff ends, the main rodeo begins with daily competitions across all eight rodeo events plus headline country concerts at NRG Stadium every evening.

**The Berth.** The Houstonian at Memorial; the Post Oak Hotel Uptown, the Forbes Five-Star in the Galleria district; the C. Baldwin Marriott downtown. La Colombe d’Or in Montrose, the Old World boutique in a 1923 mansion on Montrose Boulevard; Hotel Saint Augustine in the Museum District, Bunkhouse Group’s Texas-modern, walking distance to MFA Houston.

**The Galley.** Truth BBQ on Washington Avenue for the James Beard-nominated brisket; Pinkerton’s Barbecue downtown; Killen’s Barbecue in Pearland; Goode Co. Barbeque since 1977; Ninfa’s on Navigation for the original 1973 fajitas. Crawfish & Noodles in Bellaire for Trong Nguyen’s Viet-Cajun crawfish, the Bourdain pilgrimage; Theodore Rex in EaDo for Justin Yu’s contemporary American, the post-rodeo Sunday-night dinner.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Space Center Houston / Johnson Space Center* (Houston, Texas, USA). The Mission Control that has spoken to every American astronaut since Gemini IV in 1965, the Saturn V on display lying on its side under a hangar roof; Houston, the first word from the moon
2. *San Jacinto Monument* (La Porte, Texas, USA). The 173-metre Art Deco obelisk topped by a 220-ton star, marking the eighteen-minute battle of 1836 where Texas independence was won; the tallest stone column monument in the world

### 33. Mobile Mardi Gras

**Port:** Mobile, Alabama
**Date:** Carnival season through Tue Feb 9
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

The oldest organized Carnival celebration in the United States, established 1703 by the French Catholic settlers of La Mobile, fifteen years before they founded La Nouvelle-Orléans. Every Mardi Gras tradition that New Orleans claims as its own, the mystic societies, the masked balls, the parades with throws, the king cakes, the marching brass bands, originated here on the Mobile Bay. The Order of Myths, founded 1868, is the oldest mystic society in the country and still parades on Fat Tuesday night carrying its iconic Folly and Death emblems. Joe Cain Day (Sunday before Mardi Gras) is the people’s parade, named for the merchant who revived the festival after the Civil War. The Comic Cowboys throw satirical placards. The MoonPies, pulled from the parades since 1956, are the essential throw, not the beads. Mobile’s celebration is family-oriented, less commercial, and unapologetically older than the New Orleans version that overshadows it nationally.

**The Berth.** The Battle House Renaissance Mobile on Royal Street, the 1908 grand-dame hotel two blocks from the parade route; Fort Conde Inn, the converted 1836 antebellum Creole townhouse for the heritage boutique stay in the De Tonti Square historic district.

**The Galley.** Wintzell’s Oyster House on Dauphin Street, since 1938, for the dozen on the half-shell and the canonical fried Gulf oysters; The Noble South in downtown Mobile for the modern Southern coastal kitchen, the shrimp and grits, the Conecuh sausage, the local Royal Reds.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Fort Morgan* (Gulf Shores, Alabama, USA). The brick five-bastion Third System fort at the mouth of Mobile Bay, completed 1834, the keystone of Farragut's damn-the-torpedoes battle of August 1864; the masonry still pocked by Union cannon
2. *USS Alabama* (Mobile, Alabama, USA). The South Dakota-class battleship that earned nine battle stars across the Pacific and is now moored at Mobile Bay, opened as a memorial in 1965; 680 feet of war-grey steel and teak

### 34. Hadaka Matsuri

**Port:** Saidaiji Kannon-in Temple, Okayama, Japan
**Date:** 3rd Saturday of February
**Flags:** CULTURE

The Naked Man Festival at the Saidaiji Kannon-in Temple in Okayama, one of Japan’s three great kisai (eccentric festivals) and the largest of the country’s many hadaka matsuri traditions, observed continuously since 1510. Ten thousand Japanese men strip down to white fundoshi loincloths and assemble inside the temple courtyard in freezing February rain, jostling and shoving in a single seething crowd. At precisely midnight, the temple’s priests cast two shingi (lucky wooden batons, approximately 20 cm long) into the crowd from the temple balcony. The men battle for the batons with the ferocity of an NFL goal-line scrimmage, the men who escape the crowd with a shingi held aloft become fuku-otoko (lucky men) and are believed to enjoy a year of prosperity. The temple sprays the participants with cold water throughout the buildup as a purification rite. The event lasts approximately ten minutes and is over by 12:15 a.m. The post-festival oden at any cart still steaming in the lanes around the temple is the meal.

**The Berth.** Hotel Granvia Okayama, directly above Okayama Station for the 15-minute train to Saidaiji and the dependable post-festival hot bath; Korakuen Hotel across from the famous Korakuen garden, walking distance to the castle for the daytime side trip.

**The Galley.** Aji Tasuke Okayama for the canonical Okayama-style okonomiyaki with mochi and squid; Sushi Ninja in the Omotecho arcade for the sleeper omakase, the local Setouchi-Sea seasonal fish, the toro from the Inland Sea bluefin.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Himeji Castle* (Himeji, Hyōgo, Japan). The seventeenth-century White Heron castle, six storeys of brilliant white plaster on a stone base, surviving WWII firebombing and the 1995 Kobe earthquake; UNESCO 1993, the finest example of Japanese castle architecture
2. *Kōraku-en* (Okayama, Japan). One of the Three Great Gardens of Japan, laid out by the lord of Okayama between 1687 and 1700, the kaiyū-style stroll garden with borrowed views of Okayama Castle across the Asahi River

### 35. Berlinale

**Port:** Berlin, Germany
**Date:** Thu–Sun mid-February, 11 days
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

Europe’s first major film festival of the year and one of the ’Big Three’ alongside Cannes and Venice, founded 1951 as a Cold War-era cultural statement in the divided city, scheduled around Potsdamer Platz, the no-man’s-land between East and West. The Golden Bear for best film is awarded in the closing gala at the Berlinale Palast. Eleven days of programming across Competition, Encounters (experimental work), Berlinale Special (the auteur retrospective), Generation (films for and by young people), Panorama (international independent), and the European Film Market parallel trade fair. The festival’s atmospheric register is deep Berlin winter, snow, leather, schnapps, the late-night receptions at Soho House and the Adlon. Eat at one of Berlin’s hundred-plus excellent restaurants between screenings; the city is the most underrated food capital in Europe.

**The Berth.** Soho House Berlin in the Bauhaus-era 1928 Jewish department store on Torstrasse for the design-set member-style boutique; Hotel de Rome on Bebelplatz, the converted 1889 Dresdner Bank for the heritage luxury with the rooftop view of the Brandenburg Gate.

**The Galley.** Nobelhart & Schmutzig in Mitte for Billy Wagner’s vor-Ort ten-course tasting menu, only ingredients from a 200-km radius; Curry 36 in Kreuzberg at 3 a.m. for the canonical currywurst and the corrective to ten days of festival receptions.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Reichstag* (Berlin, Germany). Wallot's 1894 imperial parliament building burned in 1933 and shelled in 1945, restored under Foster's glass dome in 1999; the spiral walkway inside lets visitors look down on the Bundestag debating below
2. *Berlin Wall Memorial & East Side Gallery* (Berlin, Germany). The Bernauer Strasse section preserved as memorial, the death strip kept open above the foundations of the demolished houses; on the Spree the 1.3 km of painted Wall is the largest open-air gallery in the world

### 36. Carnival of Tenerife

**Port:** Santa Cruz de Tenerife, Canary Islands, Spain
**Date:** Sat–Tue Feb 6–9 with the festival weeks adjacent
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

The second largest Carnival on Earth after Rio, and the most distinctive Carnival in Europe, held in Santa Cruz de Tenerife under the African winter sun (the Canary Islands sit at the latitude of southern Morocco). The festival has its modern form since the 1980s, declared a Fiesta of International Tourist Interest by Spain and proposed as UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage. The opening parade (Cabalgata Anunciadora) on the first Friday launches three weeks of programming. The Election of the Queen of Carnival is the marquee gala in the Plaza de la Candelaria, with contestants in costumes weighing 100+ kg, mounted on wheels and pulled through the plaza. The Carnival Coso Apoteosis parade on Shrove Tuesday is the climax, hundreds of comparsas and murgas through the city’s main avenues. The festival closes Ash Wednesday with the Entierro de la Sardina, the burial of a giant papier-mâché sardine, processioned with mock weeping widows, burned at midnight in the harbor.

**The Berth.** Iberostar Grand Mencey on Calle Méndez Núñez, the heritage 1950s grand hotel in Santa Cruz centre, walking distance to the parade route; Hotel Botánico in Puerto de la Cruz, 45 minutes north for the post-Carnival sub-tropical garden escape and the Mount Teide views.

**The Galley.** Tasca El Callejón on Calle Bethencourt Alfonso for canonical Canarian, the papas arrugadas with mojo rojo and mojo verde, the cabrito al horno; Kazan Restaurant on Calle Milicias de Garachico, the sleeper Japanese in Santa Cruz, Michelin-starred, the Canarian-Japanese fusion that nobody outside the islands talks about.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Teide National Park* (Tenerife, Canary Islands, Spain). The 3,718-metre volcano at the centre of Tenerife, Spain's highest peak and the third-tallest volcano on Earth measured from its ocean floor; UNESCO 2007, lunar lava-rock cirques above the cloud line
2. *San Cristóbal de La Laguna* (Tenerife, Canary Islands, Spain). The grid-plan colonial town of 1496 in the green hills above Santa Cruz, the model for every Spanish American city that followed; UNESCO 1999, the first unwalled colonial town designed from scratch

### 37. Festa de Iemanjá

**Port:** Salvador da Bahia, Brazil
**Date:** Tue Feb 2
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

The annual offering to Iemanjá, the Afro-Brazilian Candomblé orixá of the sea, mother of all life, syncretized with the Virgin Mary in the Catholic-Yoruba blend that defines Brazilian Bahia. Observed on February 2, the feast day of Nossa Senhora dos Navegantes (Our Lady of Seafarers), at the Praia do Rio Vermelho beach in Salvador, where the morning begins with the procession of the orixá’s image from the Casa de Iemanjá temple to the sand. Devotees in white robes carry baskets of offerings, flowers (especially white roses), perfumes, jewelry, mirrors, sweet cakes, and handwritten prayers, that are loaded into small wooden boats by the local fishermen and rowed out beyond the breakers to be cast on the swell as gifts to the goddess. Whatever sinks is accepted; whatever washes back is rejected. The afternoon and night continue with public celebration along the beach, drum circles, capoeira, and street feasts of acarajé and vatapá made by the Bahian baianas in white headwraps and lace. The festival is older than every cathedral in Brazil.

**The Berth.** Fasano Salvador in the historic 1933 Palácio da Associação Comercial in the Comércio district for the contemporary luxury; Villa Bahia on Largo do Cruzeiro de São Francisco in the Pelourinho UNESCO old town for the colonial-era heritage boutique.

**The Galley.** Casa de Tereza in Rio Vermelho for canonical Bahian moqueca and the post-festival sunset table near the beach; Acarajé da Dinha on Largo de Santana, the canonical street-cart acarajé stand of Dona Dinha (now run by her daughters), the festival’s traditional snack of black-eyed pea fritters split open and stuffed with shrimp, vatapá, and caruru.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Pelourinho Historic Centre* (Salvador da Bahia, Brazil). The pastel colonial quarter on the upper bluff above the Bay of All Saints, gilded baroque churches above and the slave-port docks below; UNESCO 1985, the cradle of Afro-Brazilian Brazil
2. *Recôncavo Baiano & Cachoeira* (Cachoeira, Bahia, Brazil). The sugar-and-tobacco hinterland of Salvador, the 1693 colonial river-port of Cachoeira preserved whole with its blue-and-white tiled churches; the Sisterhood of the Boa Morte still parades the August streets

### 38. Maslenitsa

**Port:** Moscow & the Russian Federation
**Date:** Mon–Sun week before Orthodox Lent (mid-Feb to early March)
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

The seven-day pre-Lenten festival in the Russian Orthodox tradition, observed since pre-Christian Slavic times as the provody zimy, the seeing-off of winter, and continued under the Orthodox Church as the last week before the Great Fast. The festival’s central image is the blin, the thin Russian buckwheat pancake, eaten throughout the week with caviar, salted fish, smetana, honey, butter, and jam, symbolising the round sun returning. Each day of Maslenitsa has its own name and ritual: Monday is Vstrecha (the meeting); Wednesday is Lakomka (the gourmand) when mothers-in-law cook for sons-in-law; Friday is Tyoshchiny Vechorki (the mother-in-law’s evening); Saturday is Zolovkiny Posidelki (the sister-in-law’s gathering); Sunday is Proshchyonoye Voskresenye (Forgiveness Sunday) when Russians ask forgiveness from family and friends for the year’s offenses, and the great straw effigy of Lady Maslenitsa is burned at sunset in town squares across the country to mark the end of winter. Snowball fights, troika rides, ice skating, fistfights traditionally between villages, the festival predates the Tsars and has outlasted everyone since.

**The Berth.** Moscow: Hotel Metropol Moscow, the 1905 Art Nouveau grand-dame on Teatralnaya Square, two minutes’ walk from Red Square; Four Seasons Hotel Moscow on Okhotny Ryad for the modern luxury with Kremlin views across the gardens.

**The Galley.** Café Pushkin on Tverskoy Boulevard for the canonical Russian aristocratic kitchen in the recreated 18th-century apothecary mansion, the blini with caviar, the vareniki, the borscht; Teremok, the chain of street kiosks across Moscow for the canonical workers’ blini with every classical filling, eaten standing in the cold for two hundred rubles.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Saint Basil's Cathedral & the Kremlin* (Moscow, Russia). The nine onion-domed cathedral on Red Square ordered by Ivan the Terrible in 1555, painted in primary colours in the seventeenth century; the red-brick Kremlin walls and towers behind, UNESCO since 1990
2. *Trinity Lavra of Saint Sergius* (Sergiyev Posad, Moscow Oblast, Russia). The fourteenth-century monastery founded by Sergius of Radonezh, the spiritual heart of Russian Orthodoxy 70 km north of Moscow; UNESCO 1993, Andrei Rublev painted his Trinity icon for this iconostasis

## Chart III. March

*29 voyages charted.*

> Our life is March weather, savage and serene in one hour
> *Ralph Waldo Emerson*

### 1. Arkansas Viking Festival

**Port:** Hot Springs, Arkansas
**Date:** Sat–Sun first weekend of March
**Flags:** VIKING

Three-day Viking festival in early March at the Garland County Fairgrounds in Hot Springs, Arkansas, the oldest Viking festival in the American South, founded 2010, drawing 200+ reenactors from across the Mid-South. Authentic 9th–10th century period camp, weapons demonstrations, longship-building workshops, blacksmithing, and the standard evening mead hall with skaldic poetry and saga readings. Smaller and more focused than the big East Coast Viking events; the friendliness is South-of-the-Mason-Dixon.

**The Berth.** The Arlington Resort Hotel on Central Avenue since 1875; Hotel Hale in the converted Bathhouse Row hotel; or the Park Hotel for the historic option. The Waters Hot Springs, boutique on Central Avenue in the renovated 1913 Thompson Building; Embassy Suites by Hilton Hot Springs, the modern dependable, walk to Bathhouse Row.

**The Galley.** Belle Arti Ristorante for Italian; Rolando’s for Caribbean-Latin; The Pancake Shop since 1940 for breakfast; Superior Bathhouse Brewery, the only brewery inside a US National Park. Steinhaus Keller for the canonical Hot Springs Bavarian, schnitzel and dark lagers since 1976; Mio Italia on Central Avenue for the contemporary Italian and the chef’s pasta tasting.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Hot Springs National Park* (Hot Springs, Arkansas, USA). The Bathhouse Row of eight 1912-and-on stone-and-brick spas along Central Avenue, the thermal waters of the Ouachitas rising 143°F into the marble plunges; protected as a federal reservation since 1832
2. *Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art* (Bentonville, Arkansas, USA). Moshe Safdie's bridge-shaped pavilions stitched across a wooded Ozark ravine, opened 2011, free admission for life; American art from the colonial to the contemporary held in eight glass-roofed galleries

---

### 2. PAX East

**Port:** Boston Convention and Exhibition Center
**Date:** Thu–Sun first weekend of March
**Flags:** GAME

America’s largest East Coast gaming convention, held annually in early March at the Boston Convention and Exhibition Center, three days, 100,000+ attendees, the East Coast installment of Penny Arcade’s PAX series. AAA publisher booths (Bethesda, Square Enix, Riot, Sega historically), the indie-game pavilion is the largest on the East Coast, esports tournaments, the Omegathon, and the Saturday-night live-music concert. Pair with the Boston Tea Party Ships Museum a short walk from the BCEC, or the Children’s Museum next door.

**The Berth.** The Boston Harbor Hotel on Rowes Wharf; The Liberty in the converted Charles Street Jail; or XV Beacon for the boutique on Beacon Hill. Four Seasons One Dalton, the modern tower in Back Bay with Zuma on premises; The Verb Hotel in Fenway, music- themed boutique near the convention shuttle and Fenway Park.

**The Galley.** Neptune Oyster in the North End for the lobster roll; Mamma Maria for canonical North End Italian; Townsman for the modern New England; Mike’s Pastry for the cannoli pilgrimage. Menton in Fort Point, Barbara Lynch’s contemporary New England tasting; Saltie Girl on Newbury Street for the seafood-bar and the tinned-fish menu.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Faneuil Hall* (Boston, Massachusetts, USA). Peter Faneuil's 1742 brick market-and-meeting-hall on the harbor, the Cradle of Liberty where Samuel Adams and James Otis argued the Revolution into being; the grasshopper weathervane still turns over Quincy Market
2. *Old North Church* (Boston, Massachusetts, USA). Boston's oldest standing church, 1723, the steeple from which two lanterns hung on the night of April 18, 1775 sent Paul Revere riding into legend; the pews still numbered to their colonial families

---

### 3. Emerald City Comic Con

**Port:** Seattle Convention Center
**Date:** Thu–Sun first weekend of March
**Flags:** GAME

The Pacific Northwest’s largest pop-culture convention, held annually in early March at the Seattle Convention Center, four days, 95,000+ attendees, the major West Coast comics convention apart from San Diego. Strong tradition of comics-creator focus (the Eisner Award nominees are heavily represented), dedicated film/TV celebrity programming (regular Marvel, DC, and HBO presence), and the unique Seattle indie-game and tabletop RPG presence (Wizards of the Coast and Magic: The Gathering are headquartered nearby in Renton). Pair with Pike Place Market a short walk away.

**The Berth.** Fairmont Olympic on University Street; The Edgewater on the harbour; or Pan Pacific Seattle in South Lake Union. The Inn at the Market at Pike Place, the boutique market- side stay with rooftop deck; Thompson Seattle in Belltown for the design-set with Olympic Mountains views from the rooftop bar.

**The Galley.** Canlis on the bluff for the Pacific Northwest classic; The Walrus and the Carpenter in Ballard for the oysters; Pike Place Chowder; Salumi for the cured meats and the porchetta sandwich. Sushi Kashiba in Pike Place Market for Shiro Kashiba’s omakase, the godfather of Seattle sushi; Spinasse in Capitol Hill for canonical Piedmontese, the tajarin pasta is the city’s calling card.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Pike Place Market* (Seattle, Washington, USA). The 1907 farmer's-and-fishmonger's market hanging off the bluff above Elliott Bay, the original neon clock still keeping time over Pike Place; the salmon still thrown from ice to scale
2. *Space Needle* (Seattle, Washington, USA). John Graham's 184-metre saucer-on-a-tripod built in 400 days for the 1962 World's Fair, the tallest in the western United States the day it opened; the rotating Loupe deck added in 2018

---

### 4. South by Southwest

**Port:** Austin, Texas
**Date:** Fri–Sun mid-March, 10 days
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

Ten days; the convergence festival of music, film, technology, and culture, founded 1987. Music Week showcases 2,000+ acts across every Austin venue large and small; the Film & TV Festival premieres next year’s indie breakouts; Interactive draws every major tech announcement of the spring (Twitter and Foursquare both launched here). The Conference badges are tier-priced; many of the music showcases are free with RSVP. The festival has, for better or worse, set the agenda for the American creative-technology calendar for nearly four decades.

**The Berth.** Hotel Saint Cecilia in South Congress; the Hotel Van Zandt downtown; or Hotel Magdalena in South Congress for the design-set choice. Austin Proper Hotel on Bowie Street for the Kelly Wearstler interiors; South Congress Hotel, the boutique heart of SoCo with the Café No Sé all-day kitchen.

**The Galley.** Franklin Barbecue for the brisket queue; Uchi for the modern Japanese; Loro for Asian smokehouse; the East Austin food trucks; Salt Traders Coastal Cooking when downtown. Suerte on East Cesar Chavez for the modern Oaxacan masa work; Olamaie in Allandale for the heritage Southern and the cathead biscuits that have ruined the Southern-biscuit landscape elsewhere.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Texas State Capitol* (Austin, Texas, USA). Elijah Myers's 1888 pink-granite Renaissance Revival statehouse, 92 metres tall, fifteen feet taller than the US Capitol on purpose; the Goddess of Liberty on the dome lifts a gilded lone star
2. *LBJ Presidential Library* (Austin, Texas, USA). Gordon Bunshaft's eight-storey travertine cube on the UT campus, opened 1971, holding 45 million pages of the Johnson White House; the Great Society scrolled across the walls of the great hall

---

### 5. Honolulu Festival

**Port:** Waikīkī, Honolulu, Oahu, Hawaii
**Date:** Fri–Sun Mar 12–14
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART, FOOD

The 31st edition; Hawaii’s premier cultural exchange festival and the largest Pacific-Rim cultural-diplomacy event in the United States, founded 1995 as a deliberate vehicle for what its founders called ’pacific harmony’, building cultural and economic ties across the Pacific basin in the post-Cold War era. Anchored by sister-city ties between Honolulu and several Japanese municipalities (Hiroshima, Nagaoka, Okinawa, Uwajima). The programming has expanded across three decades to encompass Tahiti, Fiji, Samoa, Aotearoa New Zealand, Australia, the Philippines, Taiwan, the Republic of Korea, and the Pacific-facing United States. Three-day three-island programming runs across Waikīkī, the Hawaii Convention Center, Ala Moana Center, the International Market Place, and the Waikīkī Beach Walk, continuous performance stages of traditional Japanese taiko, bon odori, Okinawan eisa, Polynesian hula, Tahitian ori, Filipino pangalay, Korean samul-nori, and Hawaiian halau in both kahiko and auana hula.

**The Berth.** The Royal Hawaiian, the Pink Palace on Waikīkī Beach since 1927; Halekulani next door for the ocean wing; or The Modern Honolulu for the design-boutique. The Surfjack Hotel & Swim Club for the design-set retro-cool boutique; Espacio The Jewel of Waikiki for the all-suite luxury on Kalakaua Avenue.

**The Galley.** Poke at Maguro Spot or Foodland; loco moco at Rainbow Drive-In; kalua pig at Helena’s Hawaiian Food (James Beard America’s Classic, 1946); shave ice at Matsumoto in Haleiwa; the Pig & the Lady for modern Vietnamese-Hawaiian. MW Restaurant on Kapahulu, Wade Ueoka and Michelle Karr-Ueoka for canonical contemporary local- Hawaiian; Mitsu-Ken Okazu in Kalihi for the local-style Hawaiian plate-lunch standard.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Diamond Head / Lēʻahi* (Honolulu, Oahu, Hawaii, USA). The 232-metre tuff-cone crater rising at the east end of Waikīkī, formed in a 300,000-year-old eruption; the trail to the rim ends at a 1908 coastal-defense bunker with the city laid out below
2. *USS Arizona Memorial* (Pearl Harbor, Oahu, Hawaii, USA). Alfred Preis's white concrete saddle straddling the sunken battleship of December 7, 1941, 1,177 sailors and marines still aboard her; bunker oil still wells up through the harbor in occasional black tears

### 6. Vinland Viking Event

**Port:** Cohanzick Zoo Park, Bridgeton, New Jersey
**Date:** Sat–Sun mid-March
**Flags:** VIKING

One of the largest Viking events in the Mid-Atlantic, in its 14th year, three full-contact steel-combat tournaments per day, longship rowing on the Cohansey River, period encampments with Norse craft demonstrations, Norse music and storytelling, plus the traditional Mead Hall feast on Saturday night.

**The Berth.** Stay in Cape May, NJ (90 minutes south): Congress Hall since 1816; or in Philadelphia (90 minutes northwest): The Rittenhouse; Hotel Monaco. Inn of Cape May for the Victorian heritage stay on the boardwalk; in Bridgeton itself: Hotel Wilbur, the small- town dependable for festival-base proximity.

**The Galley.** Cape May: The Ebbitt Room at The Virginia Hotel; Lobster House for seafood. Philadelphia: Vetri Cucina; Zahav. In Bridgeton: Mortellito’s Italian Bistro for canonical South Jersey Italian; in Philadelphia: Royal Boucherie in Old City for the modern French-American.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Independence Hall* (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA). The red-brick Pennsylvania State House where the Declaration was signed in 1776 and the Constitution drafted in 1787, the Assembly Room still set with the rising-sun chair Washington took; UNESCO 1979
2. *Liberty Bell* (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA). The 2,080-pound bronze bell cast in London in 1752 for the Pennsylvania State House, cracked beyond use by the 1840s and kept exactly so; Proclaim Liberty throughout all the land cast around the crown

---

### 7. Vancouver International Wine Festival

**Port:** Vancouver Convention Centre East, British Columbia
**Date:** Wed Feb 24 – Sat Mar 6, ~10 days
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The 50th annual edition; VanWineFest, Canada’s #1 wine show, widely considered the best wine event in North America. Six days each March, 25,000+ attendees converge on the LEED-Platinum Vancouver Convention Centre on Burrard Inlet, the ’living roof’ building with floor-to-ceiling windows facing Stanley Park, the Coal Harbour seaplane docks, and the North Shore mountains. Over 1,000 wines poured by 100+ wineries from 14–17 countries across the festival week, paired with masterclass seminars, winemaker dinners, vintage tastings, gala events, and trade competitions. The cornerstone of the British Columbia wine-and-food scene, and one of the most sophisticated public-and-trade wine experiences anywhere in the world.

**The Berth.** Fairmont Pacific Rim in Coal Harbour; the Rosewood Hotel Georgia downtown; or the Sylvia Hotel on English Bay for the heritage budget. The Loden Vancouver, boutique luxury in Coal Harbour two blocks to the festival; The Burrard, the design-set mid- century motor-inn renovation in the West End.

**The Galley.** St. Lawrence in Railtown for Québec-Vancouver; Bao Bei in Chinatown for the modern Chinese; Vij’s on Cambie for the modern Indian; Joe Fortes for the canonical Vancouver oyster lunch. Hawksworth at Rosewood Hotel Georgia for canonical Vancouver fine dining and the festival-week winemaker dinners; Anh and Chi on Main Street for the modern Vietnamese family table.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Stanley Park & Totem Poles* (Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada). The thousand-acre rainforest peninsula reaching into Burrard Inlet, the seawall a 10-km promenade with Lions Gate Bridge spanning the gap to the North Shore mountains; the nine carved totems at Brockton Point the most-visited cluster in British Columbia
2. *Capilano Suspension Bridge* (North Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada). The 137-metre cedar-plank-and-hemp footbridge swinging 70 metres above the Capilano River since 1889, the cables since replaced in steel; treetops walk on either bank, North Shore mountains beyond

### 8. Cheltenham Festival

**Port:** Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, UK
**Date:** Tue–Fri Mar 16–19
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Britain’s premier National Hunt (jumps) racing festival, held over four days in mid-March at Cheltenham Racecourse, the Olympics of jumps racing, with the Cheltenham Gold Cup the highest prize in the sport since 1924. 250,000 attendees across four days, a quarter of them Irish (the festival coincides with St Patrick’s Day; Wednesday is traditionally Ladies’ Day). The Champion Hurdle on Tuesday, the Queen Mother Champion Chase on Wednesday, the Stayers’ Hurdle on Thursday, the Gold Cup on Friday, and the Guinness Village outside the grandstand becomes a contained Irish republic for the week.

**The Berth.** London anchored: The Connaught, The Beaumont, The Zetter Townhouse, or the Hoxton. Country: Heckfield Place, The Pig hotels, or Soho Farmhouse. In Cheltenham itself: No.131 The Promenade, the boutique on Imperial Square; Ellenborough Park, the Tudor manor on the Cleeve Hill racecourse approach with views over the Cotswold escarpment.

**The Galley.** London: St. John, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers in Marlow; L’Enclume in Cumbria; or the canonical local gastropub. In Cheltenham: The Daffodil for the canonical Cheltenham table in the 1922 Art Deco cinema; Coal Kitchen at the Brewery Quarter for the wood-fire grill.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Stratford-upon-Avon* (Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire, England, UK). The Tudor market town on the slow Avon where Shakespeare was born in 1564 and died in 1616, his birthplace on Henley Street, his grave at Holy Trinity by the river; the RSC's two theatres on the bank
2. *Roman Baths* (Bath, Somerset, England, UK). The thermal sanctuary the Romans built around the hot spring of Sulis Minerva from 60 CE, the Great Bath still filled with steaming green water; UNESCO 1987 with the Georgian Royal Crescent above

---

### 9. Las Fallas

**Port:** Valencia, Spain
**Date:** Mar 15–19
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage since 2016, Valencia’s five-day fire festival (March 15–19) celebrating Saint Joseph, in which 800+ massive papier-mâché sculptures (fallas), some 30 metres tall, are erected in neighbourhood squares across the city. On the night of March 19, the Nit del Foc, every single one is set ablaze in a coordinated city-wide pyromaniac spectacle. Daily Mascletà firework displays in the Plaza del Ayuntamiento at 2 p.m., the Ofrenda de Flores procession to the Virgin of the Forsaken, the Cabalgata del Fuego on March 18 night.

**The Berth.** Madrid: The Westin Palace; The Ritz; NH Collection on Atocha. Barcelona: Hotel Casa Fuster; El Palace. San Sebastián: Hotel María Cristina. In Valencia itself: Caro Hotel in the historic centre, built into a Moorish-and-Roman wall ruin discovered during construction; The Westin Valencia in the converted 1917 cotton mill on Avenida Amadeo de Saboya.

**The Galley.** Madrid: Casa Lucio; Sobrino de Botín; DiverXO. Barcelona: Disfrutar; Tickets; Bar Cañete; Quimet i Quimet. San Sebastián: Arzak; Akelaŕe; pintxo bars in the Parte Vieja. In Valencia: Casa Carmela on Malvarrosa Beach for the canonical original paella valenciana over orange-wood embers; Lavoe on Calle Conde de Altea for the contemporary Mediterranean kitchen.

**The Bearings.**

1. *La Lonja de la Seda* (Valencia, Spain). The late-fifteenth-century Gothic silk exchange of Valencia, the Sala de Contratación a vault of spiral pillars rising like palm trees; UNESCO 1996, the most extravagant secular Gothic civic building in Europe
2. *City of Arts and Sciences* (Valencia, Spain). Calatrava and Candela's white biomorphic complex in the drained Turia riverbed, the Hemisfèric like a half-closed eye, the Palau de les Arts like a sailing ship; built 1998–2009 along the diverted river

---

### 10. St Patrick’s Festival

**Port:** Dublin, Ireland
**Date:** Wed Mar 17
**Flags:** CULTURE

Feast day of Ireland’s patron saint; the official five-day festival runs Sat–Wed surrounding the date. The Saturday parade through Dublin city centre is the largest in Ireland, the Skyline Climb of Croke Park, the festival concert at Smithfield Square, and the entire city’s pubs running pre-1916 traditional music sessions. Pair the Wednesday with a pint of Guinness at the Gravity Bar at the brewery storehouse.

**The Berth.** The Merrion on Upper Merrion Street; The Westbury off Grafton Street; or The Wilder for the boutique-budget option. The Shelbourne on St Stephen’s Green, the canonical 1824 grand-dame where the Irish constitution was drafted; The Devlin in Ranelagh, the design-set budget boutique south of the Grand Canal.

**The Galley.** Chapter One for the modern Irish splurge; The Pig’s Ear on Nassau Street; Mulligan’s of Poolbeg for the after-show pint. Variety Jones on Thomas Street for the Michelin- starred contemporary Irish; Hugo’s in Merrion Row for the family-run Irish bistro and the canonical fish-and-chips.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Trinity College & the Book of Kells* (Dublin, Ireland). Elizabeth I's college of 1592, the Long Room of the Old Library lined with two hundred thousand books and the marble busts of philosophers; the four illuminated gospel-books of c. 800 CE in glass below
2. *Newgrange* (Brú na Bóinne, County Meath, Ireland). The 5,200-year-old passage tomb on a low hill above the Boyne, older than Stonehenge or the Pyramids, its inner chamber lit by the winter solstice sun for seventeen minutes a year; UNESCO 1993

### 11. Paro Tshechu

**Port:** Rinpung Dzong, Paro Valley, Kingdom of Bhutan
**Date:** Thu–Mon Mar 18–22
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

Projected from the lunar calendar, the festival begins on the 10th day of the second Bhutanese month, one of the most spiritually significant and visually transcendent festivals on Earth and arguably the most beautiful religious event in Asia. The tshechu (’tenth day’ in Dzongkha) is held in honor of Guru Padmasambhava, the 8th-century Indian tantric master who introduced Vajrayana Buddhism to the Himalayan region, regarded across the Himalayan Buddhist world as the second Buddha. Tshechus are held annually at the Dzong of every Bhutanese district on auspicious days correlating to specific moments in Guru Rinpoche’s life. Among them, Paro Tshechu is the largest, the most-attended by international visitors, and the spiritual peak of Bhutan’s annual festival calendar. Held at the magnificent Rinpung Dzong (’Fortress on a Heap of Jewels’), the 17th-century whitewashed fortress-monastery built in 1646 that sits on a promontory above the Paro River with snow-capped Himalayan peaks rising behind. Across five days the inner courtyard becomes a spiritually charged living theatre of masked cham dance.

**The Berth.** Amankora Paro (Aman’s Bhutan flagship, 24 suites in a forested estate at Drukgyel Valley); Uma Paro (COMO Hotels’ design property); Zhiwa Ling Heritage Hotel (Bhutanese-owned, working temple within the property). Six Senses Bhutan Paro Lodge in the pine forest above the Paro valley; Le Méridien Paro riverside for the modern dependable option.

**The Galley.** Ema datsi (the Bhutanese national dish, chili peppers slow-cooked in yak-milk cheese, served over red rice), kewa datsi (potato variation), shamu datsi (mushroom variation), jasha maroo (spicy minced chicken). Bukhari Restaurant at Uma Paro for the elevated Bhutanese tasting; Sonam Trophel Restaurant in Paro town for the canonical festival-week local table.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Tiger's Nest / Paro Taktsang* (Paro Valley, Bhutan). The cluster of white temples clinging to a granite cliff 900 metres above the Paro Valley, founded 1692 on the cave where Guru Rinpoche meditated for three months; reached only by a steep two-hour climb
2. *Punakha Dzong* (Punakha, Bhutan). The seventeenth-century fortress-monastery at the confluence of the Mo and Pho rivers, the Palace of Great Happiness, jacaranda blooming purple along its whitewashed walls each spring

---

### 12. Semana Santa de Sevilla

**Port:** Sevilla, Andalusia, Spain
**Date:** Sun–Sun Mar 21–28
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART, FOOD

Palm Sunday through Easter Sunday; the most famous Holy Week observance in the Catholic world, the spiritual and cultural high point of the Sevillano year, and one of the great living religious-artistic traditions on Earth, a centuries-old fusion of Counter-Reformation Catholic theology, Andalusian folk Catholicism, baroque polychrome sculpture, and the unique cofradía (brotherhood) civic structure that has organised the procession of penitents through the streets of Sevilla every spring since at least the late Middle Ages, with documented brotherhood foundation dates as early as 1340 (la Hermandad del Silencio, the oldest existing brotherhood). Across eight days from Palm Sunday (Domingo de Ramos) through Easter Sunday (Domingo de Resurrección), 71 brotherhoods process through the historic centre carrying nearly 120 pasos, the float-mounted polychrome wood-and-silver ensembles depicting Christ’s Passion and the grieving Virgin Mary, accompanied by 50,000 nazarenos in hooded penitential robes and 5,000+ costaleros (the bearers who carry the multi-tonne pasos on the back of their necks from inside the float, making the pasos appear to glide impossibly through narrow streets).

**The Berth.** Hotel Alfonso XIII (the iconic 1929 Mudéjar-Revival landmark adjacent to the Cathedral); Hotel Colón Gran Meliá; Hotel Casa 1800 Sevilla in the Santa Cruz quarter; Hotel Casa del Poeta in the Jewish Quarter. Mercer Sevilla in the historic Casa Castelar palace for the design-set boutique; EME Catedral Mercer opposite the Cathedral for the modern Andalusian luxury with the rooftop view of the Giralda tower.

**The Galley.** In Sevilla: Cañabota on Calle Orfila for Michelin-starred contemporary Andalusian seafood; Bodega Santa Cruz (’Las Columnas’) in the Santa Cruz quarter for canonical Sevillano tapas, montaditos and fino sherry at the marble counter; Pelayo for the canonical post-cofradía late-night chocolate con churros after the midnight processions.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Real Alcázar of Seville* (Seville, Andalusia, Spain). The Mudéjar royal palace begun in the tenth century and rebuilt across the centuries, plasterwork stalactites in the Hall of Ambassadors, orange trees in the Patio de las Doncellas; UNESCO 1987
2. *Seville Cathedral & the Giralda* (Seville, Andalusia, Spain). The largest Gothic cathedral in the world built on the foundations of the Almohad mosque, the Giralda its old minaret turned bell-tower; Columbus's tomb borne on the shoulders of four bronze kings

### 13. Melbourne Food and Wine Festival

**Port:** Melbourne, Victoria, Australia
**Date:** Fri–Sun Mar 19–28
**Flags:** FOOD, ART, CULTURE

The 35th annual edition; Australia’s preeminent culinary festival and the founding charter document of Melbourne’s identity as ’the food and wine capital of Australia.’ Founded 1993 with a modest 12-event program, the festival has grown across three decades into a massive month-bridging celebration that now spans 200+ events and draws 350,000+ attendees per edition. The festival’s official charter is to promote the produce, talent, and lifestyle of Melbourne and Victoria; the food critic Matt Preston served as creative director through 2009. The festival has hosted some of the most significant chef-and-winemaker visits in Australian culinary history, Heston Blumenthal of The Fat Duck, Thomas Keller of The French Laundry and Per Se, René Redzepi of Noma, and the winemakers Michel Chapoutier of the Rhône and Sophie and Pierre Larmandier of Champagne, all came to Melbourne for the festival across the late 2000s and 2010s.

**The Berth.** QT Melbourne on Russell Street for the design hotel; the Hotel Windsor opposite Parliament for the grand-dame heritage; Rydges Melbourne for festival-central; Adelphi for the CBD rooftop pool. The Olsen in South Yarra for the design-set art-themed boutique on Chapel Street; United Places in South Yarra for the small-luxury all-suite with the day-kitchen breakfast.

**The Galley.** Cumulus Inc. on Flinders Lane; Chin Chin for the canonical Thai; Attica in Ripponlea for the splurge. Vue de Monde atop the Rialto Tower for the modern Australian fine- dining with the bird’s-eye Melbourne view; Tipo 00 in CBD for the canonical Italian pasta-bar.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Royal Exhibition Building & Carlton Gardens* (Melbourne, Victoria, Australia). Joseph Reed's 1880 dome-and-nave palace of glass and iron in its formal garden frame, host to the first parliament of federated Australia in 1901; UNESCO 2004, the only surviving Great Exhibition building still in use
2. *Flinders Street Station* (Melbourne, Victoria, Australia). The dome-and-clock-faced Edwardian terminus opened 1909, eleven yellow-and-black-stripe clocks on the front showing the next departure times for every line; Meet me under the clocks the city's oldest assignation

### 14. Alamo Commemoration & Reenactment

**Port:** San Antonio, Texas
**Date:** Sat–Sat Feb 27 – Mar 6
**Flags:** CULTURE

Annual March commemoration at the Alamo Mission in San Antonio, observing the March 6, 1836 fall of the mission and the deaths of all 187–257 Texan defenders (including Davy Crockett, James Bowie, and William B. Travis) after a 13-day siege by Santa Anna’s army during the Texas Revolution. The Texas Cavaliers’ River Parade and the Battle of the Flowers Parade run earlier in March; the Alamo itself hosts a Dawn at the Alamo ceremony on March 6 with a wreath-laying and the reading of Travis’s letter. The site is a registered Texas State Antiquity Landmark.

**The Berth.** Hotel Emma in the Pearl Brewery historic district; The St. Anthony Hotel since 1909 on Travis Park; or the Mokara on the Riverwalk. Hotel Havana on the River Walk, Cuban- themed boutique in the 1914 mansion of the Havana Cigar magnate; The Westin Riverwalk for the festival-route dependable luxury.

**The Galley.** Mixtli for the modern Mexican tasting; Cured at the Pearl for the canonical Texas charcuterie; Mi Tierra in Market Square (open since 1941, never closes) for canonical Tex-Mex; The Esquire Tavern on the Riverwalk. Botika at The Pearl for the Latin-Asian fusion; La Gloria at The Pearl for Mexico-City street food, esquites and tacos al pastor.

**The Bearings.**

1. *The Alamo* (San Antonio, Texas, USA). The Mission San Antonio de Valero, founded 1718 and abandoned as a mission by 1793, the chapel and long barrack remembered as the sanctuary where 189 Texians died March 6, 1836; the most visited site in Texas
2. *San Antonio Missions* (San Antonio, Texas, USA). The four other eighteenth-century Spanish missions threaded down the river south of the Alamo, Concepción and San José and San Juan and Espada, still active parishes; UNESCO 2015 with the Alamo at the head

---

### 15. Fiesta Nacional de la Vendimia

**Port:** Mendoza, Argentina
**Date:** Wed–Sat early March, ~10 days
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD, ART

First weekend of March, dating to 1936, the National Wine Harvest Festival, declared ’one of the world’s most important harvest festivals’ by National Geographic. Mendoza produces 70% of Argentine wine and almost all the world’s Malbec; the festival celebrates the end of the grape harvest with three weeks of pre-events across the wine valleys (Bendición de los Frutos, Vía Blanca de las Reinas, Carrusel) culminating in the central Acto Central in the open-air Frank Romero Day Greek Theatre carved into the side of Cerro de la Gloria, 25,000 attendees over three nights of choreographed historical pageantry, traditional Cuyana folk music, and the crowning of the new Reina Nacional de la Vendimia. Asado, empanadas mendocinas, and Malbec at every winery’s open-house weekend; book a Luján de Cuyo or Uco Valley winery tour ahead.

**The Berth.** Buenos Aires: Faena, Alvear Palace, Palacio Duhau, or Casa Lucía. Mendoza: Cavas Wine Lodge or The Vines Resort & Spa for the wine country. In Mendoza city: Park Hyatt Mendoza on Plaza Independencia, the heritage 1907 grand-dame; Entre Cielos in Vistalba, wine-country hammam-and-spa option with vineyard views.

**The Galley.** Buenos Aires: Don Julio in Palermo for the canonical parrilla; El Preferido for the bodegón; Tegui for contemporary. Mendoza: 1884 Restaurante Francis Mallmann at Bodega Escorihuela. Azafrán in Mendoza city centre for canonical regional Argentine; Anna Bistro on Calle Belgrano for the wine-country chef’s tasting and the natural-wine list.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Aconcagua* (Mendoza Province, Argentina). The 6,961-metre stone wall of the Andes rising on the Chilean border, the highest mountain outside Asia; the Cementerio de los Andinistas at its foot holds climbers from a dozen countries
2. *Cristo Redentor de los Andes* (La Cumbre Pass, Mendoza Province, Argentina). The seven-metre bronze Christ raised in 1904 on the 3,832-metre Argentina-Chile border pass, his hand on a cross, sworn to keep the peace; a treaty stands on each side, his back to neither

### 16. Holi Festival of Colors

**Port:** Mathura & Vrindavan, Uttar Pradesh, India
**Date:** Mon Mar 22
**Flags:** CULTURE

Holi, the Festival of Colors, marks the arrival of spring and the triumph of good over evil; observed by Hindus on the full moon of Phalguna. The flagship celebration is in the Braj region of Uttar Pradesh, Krishna’s mythological homeland, where Holi originated and runs an entire week with a depth found nowhere else on Earth. The Braj rhythm: Lathmar Holi at Barsana (Radha’s village) eight days before, where women playfully beat shield-bearing men from Nandgaon with bamboo staves; Lathmar at Nandgaon the next day, roles reversed; Phoolwali Holi at the Banke Bihari Temple in Vrindavan, when priests rain flower petals down instead of color; Widow’s Holi at the Pagal Baba and Gopinath temples, a moving recent tradition that broke centuries of taboo; Holika Dahan bonfires at every village crossroads at moonrise the night before; and the main morning at Banke Bihari, where priests open the doors at 9 a.m. and tons of dry color and water shower the crowd until the entire town is dyed pink, green, yellow, and indigo. Plan with white wardrobes you’ll throw away, mineral oil for the skin, sunglasses, and a waterproof phone bag.

**The Berth.** Most travellers base in Agra for the refined hotels and day-trip into Braj: The Oberoi Amarvilas in Taj Ganj for the Taj-view luxury; the ITC Mughal; or the Trident Agra. Closer in: the Brijwasi Lands Inn in Mathura, or the Radha Ashok Boutique Hotel in Vrindavan. Delhi anchors: The Imperial on Janpath; The Oberoi; or The Lodhi. Taj Hotel & Convention Centre Agra for the modern luxury near the Yamuna; Ras Resorts Mathura for the closer-in spiritual retreat near the temples.

**The Galley.** Vrindavan and Mathura: Brijwasi Mithai for canonical Mathura pedha (the city’s signature milk- fudge sweet since 1864); Govinda’s at ISKCON Mathura for the Krishna satvik thali; MVT Restaurant in Vrindavan for the international vegetarian pilgrim crowd. Agra: Esphahan at Oberoi Amarvilas; Peshawri at ITC Mughal; Joney’s Place. Delhi: Bukhara; Indian Accent; Karim’s in Old Delhi behind Jama Masjid for canonical Mughlai since 1913. Tajview Restaurant at Trident Agra for the rooftop Taj-view dining; Brijwasi Royal in Mathura for canonical festival-week sweet-shop standing.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Taj Mahal* (Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India). Shah Jahan's white-marble mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal, twenty thousand workers over twenty years, the inlaid pietra dura still tight after 370 monsoons; UNESCO 1983, the dome a different colour at every hour
2. *Fatehpur Sikri* (Agra District, Uttar Pradesh, India). Akbar's red-sandstone capital of 1571, abandoned within fifteen years for lack of water but left whole; UNESCO 1986, the Buland Darwāza gate of 54 metres still the tallest in India

### 17. Tolkien Reading Day

**Port:** Oxford, England
**Date:** Thu Mar 25
**Flags:** FANDOM

March 25, the date Sauron fell, observed annually since 2003 by the Tolkien Society as a global reading day for J.R.R. Tolkien’s works. The flagship celebration is in Oxford, where Tolkien lived, taught for 34 years, wrote The Hobbit and most of The Lord of the Rings, and is buried. The day follows a three-part Oxford rhythm: morning at Pembroke College, where Tolkien was Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon from 1925 to 1945, or at Exeter College, his undergraduate college from 1911, for academic readings from the Silmarillion’s high-language passages; midday at the Eagle and Child on St Giles’ (the Bird and Baby), the pub where the Inklings, Tolkien with C.S. Lewis, Charles Williams, Owen Barfield, and Hugo Dyson, met every Tuesday morning from 1933 to 1962; the back-room Rabbit Room is the classic setting for the afternoon reading-aloud of chapters; late afternoon pilgrimage to Wolvercote Cemetery on the Banbury Road two miles north, where Tolkien lies under a single grey granite headstone with his wife Edith, inscribed with the Beren and Lúthien names from the Silmarillion. Devotees bring stones, leaves, and the occasional pipe-weed.

**The Berth.** Old Parsonage Hotel on Banbury Road for the boutique-historic stay in the converted 1660 manor; the Randolph (now Graduate Oxford) on Beaumont Street; the Macdonald Eastgate near Magdalen Bridge; or the Old Bank Hotel on the High Street. The Vanbrugh House Hotel for the boutique heritage on St Michael’s Street; Malmaison Oxford in the converted Victorian prison for the design-set heritage with cells-as-suites.

**The Galley.** The Eagle and Child on St Giles’ for the canonical Inklings pint in the Rabbit Room; The Trout Inn at Wolvercote for the riverside lunch in the 17th-century thatched inn (the Inspector Morse local); Cherwell Boathouse for the punt-launch riverside Oxford classic; Quod Brasserie on the High; Magdalen Arms in Iffley for the Sunday roast; Brown’s Café on Market Street for the canonical Oxford full English since 1872. Gee’s Restaurant in the conservatory glasshouse on Banbury Road for the canonical Oxford garden dining; Pierre Victoire on Little Clarendon Street for the canonical Oxford bistronomy.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Bodleian Library & Radcliffe Camera* (Oxford, England, UK). The university library founded 1602 around Duke Humphrey's older reading room, the circular Radcliffe Camera of 1748 the third-oldest library in England still in daily use; every book printed in Britain comes here by law
2. *Blenheim Palace* (Woodstock, Oxfordshire, England, UK). Vanbrugh and Hawksmoor's English-baroque seat granted to the first Duke of Marlborough for the 1704 victory, Churchill born here November 1874; UNESCO 1987, the only non-royal English country house called a palace

### 18. Fête du Jambon de Bayonne

**Port:** French Basque Country
**Date:** around Mar 24–28
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

Bayonne’s four-day Easter ham fair, running Holy Thursday through Easter Monday since 1462, among the oldest continuously-held food fairs in France, dedicated to jambon de Bayonne, the dry-cured Basque ham aged a minimum of nine months in the salt-laden Atlantic air of the lower Adour valley. Over 150 producers, the Carrousel des Saveurs daily tasting, the Saturday-morning election of the year’s queen of ham, and the Sunday confraternity procession in red berets and aprons through the cobbled streets of Petit Bayonne. Pair with Espelette pepper from the village 25 km south.

**The Berth.** Biarritz: Hôtel du Palais on the seafront; Hôtel des Basses Pyrénées Bayonne in central Bayonne; or Brindos Lac & Châteaux on the lake. Les Sources de Caudalie in Martillac for the post-festival vinotherapy spa weekend; Hôtel Villa Koegui Bayonne in central Bayonne for the boutique-budget two minutes from the cathedral.

**The Galley.** Le Chistera or Bar du Marché in Bayonne; Bistrot Berria in Bayonne; in Biarritz: Le Bistrot Saint Charles; in Saint-Jean-de-Luz: Le Kaiku. L’Auberge Basque in Saint-Pée- sur-Nivelle, Cédric Béchade’s canonical Basque-mountain cooking, the axoa de veau, the gâteau basque; L’Atelier de Pintxos in Bayonne for the canonical Spanish-style tapas across the festival days.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Citadelle de Bayonne* (Bayonne, French Basque Country). Vauban's seventeenth-century star-fort guarding the confluence of the Nive and the Adour where Bayonne ham has been cured in the cold ocean air for at least a thousand years; still an active French military base
2. *Guggenheim Bilbao* (Bilbao, Basque Country, Spain). Frank Gehry's titanium-clad ship of a museum, opened 1997, the building that taught the world an outpost art museum could resurrect a steel city; Jeff Koons's Puppy in flowers stands guard outside

**Port:** McDade, Texas

Largest Renaissance fair in central Texas, themed around the Sherwood Forest of Robin Hood, 25 acres of permanent-build village 45 minutes east of Austin, with a fully built tournament joust field, a King’s Highway lined with shops, multiple food and ale houses, daily Robin Hood vs. Sheriff of Nottingham staged combat, and the Friday late-night adult-only Pirate Pubcrawl events.

### 20. Ultra Music Festival

**Port:** Bayfront Park, Downtown Miami
**Date:** Fri–Sun Mar 26–28
**Flags:** ART

The 29th annual edition; the most influential electronic-music festival in North America and the spiritual cathedral of mainstream EDM, the festival that, more than any other event, took electronic dance music from the European underground to global pop dominance across the 2010s. Founded 1999 by Russell Faibisch, Ray Navarro, and Alex Omes, named for Depeche Mode’s 1997 album Ultra. The first festival ran a single day on the sand at Collins Park in Miami Beach on March 13, 1999, with Paul van Dyk, Rabbit in the Moon, Josh Wink, and DJ Baby Anne, ~10,000 attendees and a $10,000–$20,000 loss. The 2001 edition moved across the bay to Bayfront Park in Downtown Miami, the spectacular waterfront park between Bayside Marketplace, the Intercontinental Hotel, and Biscayne Bay, where the festival has been anchored ever since.

**The Berth.** The InterContinental Miami adjacent to Bayfront Park (roll out of bed and into the festival); EAST Miami and W Miami in Brickell for the sleek high-rise; Kimpton Surfcomber on South Beach for the Art Deco. The Standard Spa Miami Beach for the wellness-set boutique on Belle Isle; Mondrian South Beach for the design-set Marcel Wanders interiors and the Biscayne Bay rooftop.

**The Galley.** Joe’s Stone Crab on Washington Avenue (in season Oct–May); Versailles in Little Havana for the Cuban; The Bazaar by José Andrés at SLS South Beach; Mandolin Aegean Bistro in the Design District. Stiltsville Fish Bar in Sunset Harbour for the modern Florida-coastal seafood; Coyo Taco in Wynwood for the late-night festival- energy taqueria, open till 5 a.m.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Freedom Tower* (Miami, Florida, USA). Schultze & Weaver's 1925 Mediterranean Revival tower on Biscayne Boulevard, modelled on the Giralda of Seville, the place where Cuban refugees were processed from 1962 to 1974; the Ellis Island of the South
2. *Pérez Art Museum Miami* (Miami, Florida, USA). Herzog & de Meuron's hanging-garden museum on a stilted concrete platform over Biscayne Bay, opened 2013, the city's contemporary collection beneath dripping vines of hanging gardens

### 21. AnimeJapan

**Port:** INTEX Osaka, Suminoe Ward, Osaka, Japan
**Date:** Sat–Sun Mar 27–28 (Public Days)
**Flags:** FANDOM, GAME

The 14th edition and the first ever outside Tokyo since the festival’s 2014 founding, the largest and most important anime industry convention on Earth, the global epicentre of Japanese animation, and the calendar moment when every major studio reveals next year’s slate to 150,000+ fans across two days. Born in 2014 from the merger of two predecessor events, the Tokyo International Anime Fair (the long-running Tokyo Metropolitan Government showcase founded in 2002) and the Anime Contents Expo (the rival fan-facing event launched in 2011 after a 2010 controversy split the original fair), AnimeJapan reunified the entire industry under one banner and has grown each year since. Run by the AnimeJapan Executive Committee, a coalition of 19 major companies. The 2026 edition (the 13th, at Tokyo Big Sight on Mar 28–29) drew a record 156,000 attendees over two public days with 130+ exhibitor booths, the largest in the festival’s history, and immediately announced the historic relocation: AnimeJapan will hold its next two editions at INTEX Osaka in the Suminoe Ward, the first venue outside Tokyo in the festival’s history.

**The Berth.** Conrad Osaka at the Festival Tower; or the Imperial Hotel on Tenma. The St. Regis Osaka on Honmachi for the modern luxury with the butler service; Hotel Nikko Osaka in Shinsaibashi for the dependable mid-luxury, walking distance to Dōtonbori.

**The Galley.** Mizuno for the canonical okonomiyaki in Dōtonbori; Sushi Nakamura for Edo-style nigiri; Hajime in Hommachi for the four-Michelin-star modern tasting; Kashiwaya in Senriyama for the three-Michelin-star kaiseki in the converted private home; and Akakara Yakiniku in Shinsaibashi for the canonical Kansai yakiniku post-convention dinner.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Tōdai-ji* (Nara, Japan). The Great Eastern Temple founded 752, its Daibutsuden the largest wooden building in the world for a thousand years, the 15-metre seated bronze Buddha at its centre; UNESCO 1998, sika deer free to roam the grounds
2. *Osaka Castle* (Osaka, Japan). The five-tiered gold-trimmed donjon Toyotomi Hideyoshi raised in 1583 as the capital of his unifying ambition, twice burned and twice rebuilt; the modern concrete inside, the moats and stone footings as they were

**Port:** Anaheim Convention Center, California
**Date:** Fri–Sun last weekend of March
**Flags:** GAME

California’s spring comic-con, held annually in late March at the Anaheim Convention Center, the smaller, more focused younger sibling of San Diego Comic-Con, founded 1987, drawing 65,000 attendees. The convention’s identity sits at the intersection of comics (the panels are heavily comics-anchored, with strong DC, Marvel, and indie creator presence), animation, and tabletop gaming. Grand Californian Hotel at Disneyland Resort for the Arts & Crafts-style on-property luxury; JW Marriott Anaheim Resort for the modern convention-center dependable.

GG’s Bistro in Old Towne Orange for canonical Italian-French in a historic plaza setting; Mahmoud’s Brick & Stone Oven Pizza for the family-run Lebanese-pizza standout, the lahmajun is the move.

### 23. Hanami

**Port:** Kyoto, Japan
**Date:** late March through early May
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD, ART

The most beloved annual ritual in Japanese culture and one of the most photographed natural phenomena on Earth, the centuries-old practice of viewing the sakura cherry blossom at peak bloom, a moment in the natural calendar so spiritually weighted in Japanese aesthetics that it has its own grammar, its own vocabulary, its own seasonal cuisine, its own particular emotional register. The word hanami literally means ’flower viewing’ (hana = flower, mi = look/see); the term refers narrowly to the cherry blossom. The practice traces to the imperial Heian court of the 8th–9th centuries, the oldest documented hanami banquet was hosted by Emperor Saga in 812 CE in the Shinsen-en imperial garden in Kyoto. The contemporary public hanami festival was firmly established in the Edo period (1603–1868) when the eighth Tokugawa shogun Yoshimune planted thousands of cherry trees in Asukayama, Sumida, and the Koganei Embankment in 1720s Edo to make hanami accessible to commoners.

**The Berth.** The Ritz-Carlton Kyoto on the Kamogawa for the riverside-cherry luxury anchor; Four Seasons Hotel Kyoto in Higashiyama for the 800-year-old Ikeniwa pond-garden; Aman Kyoto in the Takagamine forest for the secluded mountain-cherry retreat near Kinkaku-ji; Hoshinoya Kyoto in Arashiyama for the riverside ryokan accessible by private boat. The historic ryokan circuit: Tawaraya in central Kyoto for the 300-year-old canonical stay; Hiiragiya next door for the alternative heritage option (Matsuo Bashō, Yukio Mishima, and Charlie Chaplin all slept here).

**The Galley.** Sakura-flavored everything, the seasonal explosion of cherry-blossom flavor that takes over Japanese commerce for six weeks: hanami dango (the iconic three-color rice-flour dumplings on a skewer); sakura-mochi at Tsuruya Yoshinobu and Toraya Karyo for the canonical Kyoto wagashi houses. Kikunoi Honten in Higashiyama for the three-Michelin-star kaiseki; Hyotei at the entrance to Nanzen-ji Temple for the 400-year-old kaiseki where samurai once stopped for tea; Wakuden near Kodai-ji for the walk-to-Maruyama dinner; and Pontocho Alley along the Kamogawa for yakatabune lantern-boat dining under riverside cherry trees.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Kinkaku-ji* (Kyoto, Japan). The fourteenth-century Golden Pavilion floating above its mirror-pond in the northwest of Kyoto, burned by a deranged novice in 1950 and rebuilt within five years; UNESCO 1994, two upper storeys in gold leaf
2. *Fushimi Inari Shrine* (Kyoto, Japan). Ten thousand vermilion torii gates winding up Mount Inari from the foot, each one donated by a Japanese business; the small fox messengers in stone at every shrine, the climb a quiet ascent of two hours

### 24. Battle of Towton Reenactment

**Port:** Towton, North Yorkshire, UK
**Date:** Sun nearest Mar 29
**Flags:** CASTLE

Annual Palm Sunday weekend reenactment near Towton, North Yorkshire, of the March 29, 1461 Wars of the Roses battle that may have been the bloodiest day of fighting on English soil, with 28,000+ killed in a single day’s combat in driving snow. The Towton Battlefield Society organises the modern commemoration: a guided battlefield walk, a memorial service at the Towton Cross, and a 100-strong reenactment of the Yorkist and Lancastrian forces clashing across the snowy plateau. The Crooked Billet Inn at Saxton hosted the wounded and the dead in 1461 and still serves the modern reenactors today.

**The Berth.** London anchored: The Connaught, The Beaumont, The Zetter Townhouse, or the Hoxton. Country: Heckfield Place, The Pig hotels, or Soho Farmhouse. In York, 30 minutes from the battlefield: The Grand York at Station Rise for the heritage luxury; Middlethorpe Hall outside the city walls in the 17th-century William and Mary country house, walled-garden and Wars-of-the-Roses-era oaks.

**The Galley.** London: St. John, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers in Marlow; L’Enclume in Cumbria; or the canonical local gastropub. Skosh on Micklegate in York for the small-plate seasonal Yorkshire kitchen; The Crooked Billet Inn at Saxton near the battlefield for the canonical post-reenactment pint, the very inn that received the wounded in 1461.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Fountains Abbey & Studley Royal* (Ripon, North Yorkshire, England, UK). The largest Cistercian ruin in England, founded 1132 and dissolved 1539, the great church a roofless skeleton in a Georgian water garden; UNESCO 1986, deer parks and cascading mirror ponds below
2. *Castle Howard* (York, North Yorkshire, England, UK). Vanbrugh's first house, begun 1699 for the third Earl of Carlisle in the rolling Howardian Hills, the great hall topped by a painted dome; Evelyn Waugh's Brideshead on screen, still the home of the Howards
