### 25. Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race

**Port:** Anchorage to Nome, Alaska
**Date:** Sat Mar 6 (ceremonial start) and onward
**Flags:** CULTURE

A thousand-mile sled-dog race across Alaska from Anchorage to Nome, observed annually since 1973 on the first Saturday of March, commemorating the 1925 serum run to Nome, when 20 mushers and 150 dogs relayed diphtheria antitoxin 674 miles in five and a half days to stop an outbreak. The modern race takes 8 to 15 days across the southern Alaska Range, the Yukon River basin, the Bering Sea coast, and the final ice runs into Nome under the burled-arch finish line on Front Street. The ceremonial start is on Fourth Avenue in downtown Anchorage on Saturday; the official restart in Willow on Sunday. 70+ mushers compete with teams of 14 dogs. Iditarod has fielded champions including Rick Swenson (the only five-time winner), Susan Butcher (the only four-time woman champion), and Dallas Seavey (six-time, the all-time wins record). Every musher carries the equipment to survive 60-below temperatures, blizzards, river overflow, and the long sections without checkpoints. The dogs are the athletes. The mushers are the support crew.

**The Berth.** In Anchorage: The Hotel Captain Cook downtown for the dependable luxury, walking distance to the Fourth Avenue ceremonial start; The Lakefront Anchorage on Lake Spenard for the seaplane-base-side dependable. In Nome for the finish: Aurora Inn, the in-town Nome stay, the closest dependable option to the burled arch on Front Street.

**The Galley.** In Anchorage: Crow’s Nest atop the Hotel Captain Cook for canonical Anchorage fine- dining with Cook Inlet views; Humpy’s Great Alaskan Alehouse on West 6th Avenue for canonical Anchorage seafood-and-beer, the Alaskan king crab, the smoked salmon dip, and the 60-tap Alaskan beer list.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Denali* (Denali National Park, Alaska, USA). The 6,190-metre granite massif rising from the Alaskan tundra, North America's highest peak, the Athabaskan name returned in 2015 after a century of McKinley; visible only one day in three through its own weather
2. *Glacier Bay National Park* (Gustavus, Alaska, USA). The 1.3-million-hectare wilderness on the Inside Passage, the tidewater glaciers calving into water that was solid ice when Captain Vancouver charted it in 1794; UNESCO 1992, brown bears on the shore, humpbacks in the bay

### 26. Vasaloppet

**Port:** Sälen to Mora, Dalarna, Sweden
**Date:** Sun first Sunday of March
**Flags:** CULTURE

The world’s largest, oldest, and longest cross-country ski race, 90 kilometres of forest and lake trail run annually on the first Sunday of March from Sälen to Mora in Dalarna, Sweden, commemorating the legendary 1521 flight of the future King Gustav Vasa from Danish soldiers, who was famously chased on skis by two villagers from Mora to Sälen to convince him to return and lead the rebellion that founded modern Sweden. Founded 1922, the race now hosts 15,800+ skiers across an entire Vasaloppsveckan (’Vasa Week’) of associated events including the half-distance Halvvasan, the Tjejvasan women’s race, and the elite Open Track. The starting gun fires at 8 a.m. with skiers funneling into the woods through narrow tracks, the elite contenders finishing the 90 km in around three and a half hours. Every checkpoint serves the traditional blåbärssoppa (warm Swedish blueberry soup) and bread. The race ends in the centre of Mora at the Vasaloppet finish gate; the Kranskulla, the wreath-laying maiden, places the laurel wreath on the winner’s head. The festival is the centrepiece of the entire Dalarna winter cultural calendar.

**The Berth.** In Mora at the finish: Mora Parken Hotell for the canonical race-week base on Strandgatan; Hotell Mora in the town centre for the dependable mid-range. In Sälen at the start: Sälen Högfjällshotell for the slope-side luxury stay before the morning’s start.

**The Galley.** In Mora: Wasa Hotell Restaurant for the canonical Swedish post-race kötbullar with lingonberries and gravlax dinner; Vasaloppshuset Restaurant in the official race headquarters for the festival-week cafeteria-counter blåbärssoppa, the cinnamon buns, and the morning kanelbullar.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Falun Copper Mine* (Falun, Dalarna, Sweden). The Great Pit of Falun where copper was mined for a thousand years, collapsed into a 100-metre-deep crater on Midsummer's Day 1687 with no one killed; UNESCO 2001, the red iron oxide of the slag still paints every Swedish cottage
2. *Zorn Museum & Mora Church* (Mora, Dalarna, Sweden). Anders Zorn's red-wood lakeside studio kept exactly as he left it in 1920, his nudes and his portraits of three American presidents still on the walls; the white onion-domed church on the lake holds the finish line of the Vasaloppet

### 27. Sandhill Crane Migration

**Port:** Platte River, central Nebraska
**Date:** mid-February through early April, peak mid-March
**Flags:** CULTURE

The annual staging of 600,000 sandhill cranes (Antigone canadensis) on a 50-mile stretch of the central Platte River in Nebraska, between mid-February and early April, with peak numbers from mid-March to early April. The cranes, North America’s oldest living bird species, with a fossil record dating back 2.5 million years, pause here for six weeks to fatten on waste corn from the surrounding farmland before continuing their northward journey to nesting grounds in Canada, Alaska, and Siberia. Dawn lift-off and dusk return are the iconic moments: the entire river roosts at sunset, and at first light tens of thousands of cranes rise simultaneously in a roar of wings and bugling calls, a sound and sight available almost nowhere else on Earth. The Audubon Society’s Rowe Sanctuary near Gibbon and the Crane Trust near Wood River operate dawn and dusk viewing blinds, small camouflaged shelters at the riverbank, reserved months in advance. Stay in Kearney or Grand Island. Eat at any small-town Nebraska café. Tip your hat to the cranes; they were here long before us.

**The Berth.** In Kearney: Holiday Inn Kearney Resort on East 25th Street for the dependable mid- range, closest to the Rowe Sanctuary; Comfort Inn Kearney for the budget option, fifteen minutes from the river. In Grand Island, 35 minutes east: Riverside Inn on the South Platte for the closer-in-to-the-river stay.

**The Galley.** In Kearney: The Local on East 23rd Street for canonical Kearney American with the local Nebraska beef from the surrounding ranches; Wagner’s Bistro on West 24th Street for the modern American, the bison meatloaf, the Nebraska prime rib, the dependable evening table after the dusk blind.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Chimney Rock* (Bayard, Nebraska, USA). The 100-metre spire of Brule clay and Arikaree sandstone rising from the high plains, the most mentioned landmark in pioneer diaries of the Oregon Trail; National Historic Site 1956, the spire still narrowing year by year
2. *Carhenge* (Alliance, Nebraska, USA). Jim Reinders's 1987 stone-circle replica built from thirty-nine grey-spray-painted American cars half-buried nose-down in the high plains; the precise proportions of Stonehenge in 1980s sedans and pickups

### 28. St. Joseph’s Day Altars

**Port:** Salemi, Trapani Province, Sicily
**Date:** Fri Mar 19
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

The Sicilian tradition of building elaborate three-tiered altars (altari di San Giuseppe) on March 19, the feast day of St. Joseph, patron saint of workers, fathers, and the dying. The custom originated in medieval Sicily during a great famine, when peasants prayed to St. Joseph for relief and promised a feast of thanksgiving when the rains returned; when the fava bean crop saved the island from starvation, the altars became a permanent annual rite. The flagship celebration is in Salemi, the hill town in western Sicily where the tradition reaches its most spectacular form. Salemi families spend weeks shaping elaborate bread sculptures into religious symbols (the lamb of God, the cross, the hand of God, the dove, the staff of Joseph), building entire altar facades that fill the front rooms of participating homes. The altars are loaded with citrus fruit pyramids, candied biscotti, almond cookies, frittedda (artichoke-fava-pea stew), pasta con sarde, sfincia di San Giuseppe (cream-filled fritters), and twelve vegetarian dishes, one for each apostle (no meat is served because Lent is still in progress). The altars open to the public; families serve plates to anyone who knocks. Eat what you’re offered. Leave a donation. Take a fava bean, it is said the one in your pocket will never let you go hungry.

**The Berth.** Baglio Oneto Resort Wines in Marsala (24 km west of Salemi) for the converted 17th-century baglio wine estate with Egadi Islands views; Donnafugata Golf Resort & Spa near Mazara del Vallo for the modern luxury anchor; Foresteria Planeta in Menfi for the working-winery estate experience; Verdura Resort (Rocco Forte) in Sciacca for the world-class luxury anchor on the southwestern coast. Or stay in Salemi itself at Antiche Mura, the small heritage guesthouse in the medieval old town.

**The Galley.** Antichi Sapori in Salemi for the local Salemitano kitchen and the pani di San Giuseppe; Cantina Siciliana in Trapani for cous cous trapanese (the signature North-African-influenced Sicilian fish couscous); Cantina Florio in Marsala for the historic 1833 wine cellar with paired tastings; Pierrot in Marsala for the canonical caponata and pasta con le sarde. And any village trattoria in Salemi with the family altar opened in the front room.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Selinunte* (Castelvetrano, Sicily, Italy). The largest archaeological park in Europe, the Greek city founded 628 BCE on the south coast of Sicily and destroyed by Carthage in 409; eight temples toppled by earthquake, the columns still lying where they fell
2. *Segesta* (Calatafimi, Sicily, Italy). The lone unfinished Doric temple of the Elymians, built around 420 BCE in the hills above the western Sicilian plain, the columns never fluted because the city fell first; a Greek amphitheatre cut into the next ridge

---

### 29. Hokitika Wildfoods Festival

**Port:** Hokitika, West Coast, South Island, New Zealand
**Date:** Sat second Saturday of March
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

An annual festival in the small West Coast town of Hokitika on the South Island of New Zealand, established 1990 by the local Lions Club as a deliberate exercise in eating things that should not be eaten. Held on the second Saturday of March on the foreshore beside the Tasman Sea. The festival rules permit only foods sourced from the New Zealand wild, but interprets that broadly. Recent menu items: huhu grubs (the wood-boring larvae of the huhu beetle, eaten alive or sautéed with garlic, with the texture of butter); mountain oysters (sheep’s testicles); fish-eye sushi; gorse-flower wine; whitebait fritters from the Hokitika River (the festival’s only conventional offering); worm and grasshopper truffles; possum pâté; deer-velvet smoothies; sea urchin ice cream. The festival draws 12,000 visitors per year, capping ticket sales to keep the experience close. The Glow-in-the-Dark Stomp Wild Foods Trail Marathon runs the morning of the festival; the night-time Feastival Ball follows on Saturday night.

**The Berth.** In Hokitika: The Beachfront Hotel Hokitika on the Tasman seafront, the canonical festival-base stay; Stations Inn in the converted 1879 Hokitika railway station for the heritage boutique. In Franz Josef, 60 minutes south for the glacier: Te Waonui Forest Retreat for the eco-luxury rainforest stay.

**The Galley.** In Hokitika: Stations Inn Restaurant for the canonical West Coast dinner, the local whitebait, the West Coast venison, the Greenstone Pale Ale on tap; Pure Café on Revell Street for the canonical morning post-festival recovery flat white.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Aoraki / Mount Cook* (Mackenzie Basin, South Island, New Zealand). The 3,724-metre snow pyramid sacred to Ngāi Tahu, the cloud-piercer at the centre of the Southern Alps; part of the Te Wāhipounamu UNESCO South West New Zealand site since 1990, Edmund Hillary trained on its ridges
2. *Franz Josef Glacier* (Westland District, South Island, New Zealand). The Te Moeka o Tūawe ice river descending nearly to sea level through temperate rainforest, twelve kilometres of glacier meeting tree fern within a single valley; one of three coastal glaciers in the temperate world

*36 voyages charted.*

### 1. Scira Sheringham Viking Festival

**Port:** Sheringham, Norfolk, UK
**Date:** Sat–Sun first weekend of April
**Flags:** VIKING

Largest Viking festival in East Anglia, themed around the Anglo-Saxon-Viking settlement of Scira on the Norfolk coast, full Viking encampment on the seafront, three combat tournaments per day, Saturday-night longship build culminating in the iconic beach boat-burning at sunset, kids’ rune workshops, mead and Norse food along the High Street.

**The Berth.** London anchored: The Connaught, The Beaumont, The Zetter Townhouse, or the Hoxton. Country: Heckfield Place, The Pig hotels, or Soho Farmhouse. Far better: stay in Norfolk itself. The Pheasant Hotel at Kelling Heath, the boutique inn 15 minutes west; No. 1 The Drive in Sheringham, the Edwardian boutique B&B walking distance to the seafront and the festival ground.

**The Galley.** London: St. John, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers in Marlow; L’Enclume in Cumbria; or the canonical local gastropub. In coastal Norfolk: No. 1 Cromer for canonical East Anglian fish-and-chips on the Cromer pier; Roger Hickman’s Restaurant in Norwich (40 minutes south) for the contemporary Norfolk fine-dining.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Sutton Hoo* (Suffolk, England, UK). The seventh-century Anglo-Saxon ship burial uncovered in 1939 on the eve of war, the king laid out in a 27-metre oak hull with helm and gold and garnet; the iron rivets still in the sand where the wood rotted
2. *Norwich Cathedral* (Norwich, Norfolk, England, UK). The Norman cathedral begun 1096 of pale Caen stone shipped across the Channel, the second-tallest spire in England, the largest cloister; flint-knapped East Anglian fields all the way to the coast

**Port:** McCormick Place, Chicago
**Date:** Fri–Sun first weekend of April
**Flags:** GAME

The Midwest’s flagship comic and pop-culture convention, founded 2010 by ReedPOP, 90,000+ attendees, comic publisher panels, film and TV celebrity Q&As, the C2E2 Crown Championship cosplay competition, and Artist Alley filling Hall F. The McCormick lakefront setting puts you ten minutes from downtown Chicago for after-hours.

**The Berth.** The Langham on Wacker; the Peninsula on Superior. Soho House Chicago in the West Loop for the design-set boutique with the rooftop pool; Chicago Athletic Association Hotel on Michigan Avenue, the heritage 1893 athletic-club hotel with the Cherry Circle Room and the Game Room.

**The Galley.** Alinea for the splurge; Au Cheval for the burger; Lou Malnati’s for deep-dish; Pequod’s for the caramelized crust. Smyth by John and Karen Shields for the three-Michelin-star contemporary; Kasama in Ukrainian Village, the world’s only restaurant with Michelin stars for both breakfast and dinner.

2. *Willis Tower / Sears Tower* (Chicago, Illinois, USA). The black bundled-tube skyscraper of 1973, 442 metres tall, the highest building in the world for a quarter-century; the Skydeck glass boxes hang out over Wacker 412 metres below

### 3. National Beer Day

**Port:** St. Louis, Missouri
**Date:** Wed Apr 7
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

April 7, the day in 1933 the Cullen-Harrison Act took effect at 12:01 a.m., legalizing the manufacture and sale of 3.2% beer after thirteen dry years of Prohibition, three months before the 21st Amendment fully repealed the Volstead Act. The night of April 6–7 became known across the country as ’New Beer’s Eve.’ The flagship celebration is in St. Louis, where the Anheuser-Busch brewery on the south side of the city (the largest in the United States, in continuous operation at the same Pestalozzi Street site since 1860) sold the first legal case of beer in the nation at the stroke of midnight, then dispatched a Clydesdale-drawn wagon north to deliver a complimentary case to President Franklin Roosevelt at the White House and another to former Governor Al Smith of New York, the wet-Democrat who had championed repeal. The day’s St. Louis program: morning brewery tour at Budweiser (the Clydesdale stables, the limestone lager cellars cut into the Mississippi bluffs, and the original 1885 Brew House with the hop-and-cone copper kettles); midday flight tasting through the modern St. Louis craft canon (Schlafly, 4 Hands, Urban Chestnut, Civil Life, Side Project); afternoon pilgrimage across the river to the Budweiser Clydesdale paddock at Grant’s Farm in Sappington for the closing toast at the Bauernhof beer garden.

**The Berth.** The Last Hotel in the Garment District (converted 1909 International Shoe headquarters with the rooftop pool over the Arch view); The Cheshire on Clayton Road; the Four Seasons St. Louis at Lumière Place on the Mississippi; or the 21c Museum Hotel in the Old Post Office. The Chase Park Plaza in Central West End for the 1922 grand-dame; The Magnolia Hotel St. Louis in the converted Mayfair Hotel for the heritage boutique downtown.

**The Galley.** Pappy’s Smokehouse in Midtown for the Memphis-style ribs (St. Louis-cut, the city’s signature); Tony’s on Market Street for canonical St. Louis Italian since 1946; Sidney Street Café in Benton Park; Schlafly Tap Room; The Civil Life Brewing Co. in Tower Grove South for the working-pub atmosphere; Imo’s anywhere in the metro for canonical St. Louis-style provel-cheese cracker-thin pizza. Vicia in Central West End for the modern American with the chef’s garden; Sugarfire Smoke House for the canonical St. Louis BBQ, the Texas-Carolina-Memphis hybrid.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Gateway Arch* (St. Louis, Missouri, USA). Eero Saarinen's 192-metre stainless-steel catenary on the west bank of the Mississippi, completed 1965 as the memorial to the westward expansion; the tallest man-made monument in the western hemisphere
2. *Cahokia Mounds* (Collinsville, Illinois, USA). The Mississippian city of 1050 CE, larger than London at the time, the 30-metre Monks Mound the largest earthwork pyramid north of Mexico; UNESCO 1982, abandoned by 1350 for reasons not understood

### 4. Original Renaissance Pleasure Faire

**Port:** Santa Fe Dam Recreation Area, Irwindale, California
**Date:** weekends Apr 3 – May 16
**Flags:** CASTLE, PIRATE

The original Renaissance fair in the United States, founded 1963 by Phyllis and Ron Patterson in Agoura Hills, the entire genre traces back to this event. Now seven weekends across 16 acres of fully built Tudor village; the Royal Court of Elizabeth I, full lists jousting tournaments, 200+ artisan vendors, and the iconic Pickle Booth that started the trend of period in-character vendors.

**The Berth.** Stay in Pasadena (15 minutes): The Langham Huntington; Hotel Constance; the Westin Pasadena. Irwindale itself is industrial; sleep in Pasadena. Hotel Bel-Air for the Old Hollywood luxury 45 minutes west; Hotel Casa del Mar in Santa Monica for the canonical Pacific-seafront grand stay.

**The Galley.** Pasadena: Vertical Wine Bistro; Union Restaurant for Italian-Californian; Mijares Mexican; and Pie ’n Burger since 1963 for the Pasadena institution. Bistro 1881 in Old Pasadena, the modern Californian in the 1881 Castle Green building; Roy’s Pasadena for Hawaiian fusion and Roy Yamaguchi’s canonical macadamia-crusted fish.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Mission San Gabriel Arcángel* (San Gabriel, California, USA). The 1771 fourth Franciscan mission of Alta California, the Cordovan-style stone church with capped buttresses, six bells in the campanario; the mother church from which the Los Angeles pueblo was settled in 1781
2. *The Huntington Library* (San Marino, California, USA). Henry Huntington's 1919 estate of 120 acres holding Gutenberg Bibles, the Ellesmere Chaucer, Gainsborough's Blue Boy and Lawrence's Pinkie; the largest Asian garden outside Asia at its centre

### 5. Star Wars Celebration

**Port:** Los Angeles Convention Center
**Date:** Thu–Sun Apr 1–4
**Flags:** FANDOM, GAME

The 50th anniversary of the original 1977 Star Wars film; the official Lucasfilm-hosted convention, held biennially since 1999, major announcements of upcoming films and Disney+ series, surprise actor appearances, the saber-fight choreography demonstrations, a fully built Mos Eisley cantina experience on the show floor, a 501st Legion costume parade through downtown LA, and the largest concentration of Star Wars cosplayers anywhere on Earth.

Bavel in the Arts District by Ori and Genevieve Menashe for the modern Middle Eastern; Howlin’ Ray’s in Chinatown for the canonical LA hot- chicken sandwich, line at dawn.

2. *Getty Center* (Brentwood, California, USA). Richard Meier's white travertine mountain campus opened 1997 above the 405, the museum, research institute, and conservation lab connected by tram to the parking below; Robert Irwin's Central Garden a working sculpture

### 6. Time Warp

**Port:** Maimarkthalle, Mannheim, Germany
**Date:** Sat Apr 3
**Flags:** ART

The 33rd edition of the world’s most respected techno festival, founded November 26, 1994 by the Cosmopop agency at the Walzmühle in Ludwigshafen and held in Mannheim’s Maimarkthalle every year since 1995, the same industrial exhibition hall, every spring, for three decades. The format is a deliberate religious observance: one night, one day, 19 hours of unbroken music from early Saturday evening through Sunday afternoon, across five stages inside the cavernous concrete Maimarkthalle (capacity ~20,000), each with a distinct acoustic character and immersive stage design built fresh each year by an international design team. No headliners-and-supports hierarchy in the conventional sense; the lineup is a 40–50 artist deep cross-section of every era of techno and house, from the founding generation (Sven Väth, Carl Cox, Richie Hawtin, Laurent Garnier, Ricardo Villalobos, most have played essentially every Time Warp since 1994) through the contemporary peak-time tier (Adam Beyer, Charlotte de Witte, Amelie Lens, Nina Kraviz, Marco Carola, Joseph Capriati) to the next generation (Clara Cuvé, Indira Paganotto, KI/KI). Each stage is designed for extended sets, the festival mirrors the four-to-six-hour DJ-set culture of Berghain and Fabric. The signature Time Warp moment is the 5 a.m. shift, when the music turns harder and more hypnotic and the room collectively decides to keep going until daylight comes through the plastic windows.

**The Berth.** Berlin: Hotel Adlon Kempinski; Soho House Berlin; 25hours Bikini. Munich: Bayerischer Hof. Hamburg: The Fontenay. Frankfurt: Roomers. In Mannheim itself: Steigenberger Mannheimer Hof opposite the Schloss for the heritage stay; Hotel Speicher 7 on the Rhine harbour for the design-boutique in the converted grain silo. In Heidelberg (20 minutes south): Heidelberg Marriott on the Neckar for the modern dependable.

**The Galley.** Berlin: Markthalle Neun; Mustafa’s Gemüse Kebap; Lode & Stijn. Munich: Tantris; Hofbräuhaus; Schneider Bräuhaus. Hamburg: Fischmarkt; Bullerei. Frankfurt: Adolf Wagner; Lafleur. In Mannheim: Bootshaus Mannheim for the canonical Wasser-restaurant on the Neckar; Restaurant Marly for the Michelin-recommended contemporary German in central Mannheim.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Heidelberg Castle* (Heidelberg, Baden-Württemberg, Germany). The pink-sandstone Renaissance castle ruined on its wooded slope above the Neckar, struck by lightning in 1764 and never fully rebuilt; the Great Cask in the cellar holds 220,000 litres of wine and has done since 1751
2. *Speyer Cathedral* (Speyer, Rhineland-Palatinate, Germany). The Salian imperial cathedral begun 1030, the largest surviving Romanesque church in the world, eight Holy Roman Emperors buried in the crypt; UNESCO 1981

### 7. Coachella Music Festival

**Port:** Empire Polo Club, Indio, California
**Date:** Fri–Sun weekends Apr 9–11 & Apr 16–18
**Flags:** ART

The second-largest music festival in North America by attendance, 125,000 per day across both weekends, eight stages, headliner-tier mainstream acts plus desert-house DJs running the Yuma tent until dawn; the Sahara tent for electronic music, the Outdoor Theatre for indie, and the Mojave for emerging acts. Glamping and camping options for those without a Palm Springs Airbnb. Stagecoach country festival follows the next weekend on the same grounds.

Two Bunch Palms in Desert Hot Springs for the mineral-spring spa retreat; Sands Hotel Indian Wells for the design-set Moroccan-themed boutique fifteen minutes from the polo grounds.

**The Galley.** Palm Springs: Sherman’s Deli & Bakery; Workshop Kitchen + Bar; Birba for the Italian; Cheeky’s for the iconic Palm Springs brunch. Tac/Quila in Palm Springs for canonical modern Mexican; Las Casuelas Terraza since 1958 for the canonical Palm Springs Mexican on the Palm Canyon Drive courtyard.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Joshua Tree National Park* (San Bernardino & Riverside Counties, California, USA). The granite-and-yucca high desert where the Mojave meets the Colorado, the namesake Joshua trees the Mormons saw as the prophet's beckoning arms; the dark sky reserve where U2 made an album
2. *Salton Sea & Bombay Beach* (Imperial & Riverside Counties, California, USA). The accidental inland sea of 1905 when a Colorado River canal failed, briefly Southern California's Riviera and now a saline ruin; Bombay Beach kept as outsider-art installation among the salt-encrusted trailers

### 8. Kentucky Derby Festival

**Port:** Churchill Downs and venues citywide, Louisville, Kentucky
**Date:** Sat Apr 17 – Sat May 1, 2 weeks
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE, ART

Two weeks each spring when the Ohio River city of Louisville (population 633,000) becomes the absolute focus of American sporting tradition. Thunder Over Louisville opens on the third-Saturday-before-Derby; the Derby Festival miniMarathon and Marathon run April 24; the Pegasus Parade Sunday April 25 in the new Sunday-on-Broadway tradition; and the 153rd Kentucky Derby anchors Saturday May 1, the most respected thoroughbred horse race in North America and the institutional crown jewel of the festival. One of the largest civic festivals in the United States, the most important annual cultural event in Kentucky, and the heart of Louisville’s identity as a major American city; the central American Mid-South sporting-cultural pilgrimage drawing ~1.5 million attendees across 70+ events and generating $127.9 million in annual economic impact for the city.

**The Berth.** The Brown Hotel since 1923 (home of the Hot Brown sandwich); 21c Museum Hotel for the modern art-and-stay; or Hotel Distil in the converted bourbon distillery. Galt House Hotel on the Ohio River for the heritage waterfront stay; The Seelbach Hilton, the 1905 grand-dame where The Great Gatsby was written and Al Capone hid out in the basement billiard rooms.

**The Galley.** Jack Fry’s since 1933 for canonical Louisville; Mayan Café for Latin-American; Decca for the modern Southern; Lilly’s Bistro; Hot Brown at The Brown Hotel. 610 Magnolia by Edward Lee for the canonical Southern tasting menu; Proof on Main at the 21c Museum Hotel for the modern Kentucky and the canonical bourbon list.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Cave Hill Cemetery* (Louisville, Kentucky, USA). Cave Hill Cemetery on Baxter Avenue, the 1848 garden-cemetery on a Louisville bluff above the Beargrass Creek, Colonel Sanders and Muhammad Ali both buried beneath the limestone bluffs; the city's most spectacular memorial landscape
2. *Mammoth Cave National Park* (Edmonson County, Kentucky, USA). The world's longest known cave system, more than 685 km of mapped passages carved into Kentucky limestone over a hundred million years; UNESCO 1981, the underground rivers still being explored

---

### 9. Peixe Em Lisboa

**Port:** Pavilhão Carlos Lopes, Parque Eduardo VII, Lisbon
**Date:** Sun–Wed Apr 4–14, 11 days
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The 20th annual edition of the Iberian Peninsula’s most prestigious seafood festival, eleven days each early April when Lisbon collectively transforms into a celebration of the Portuguese fishing tradition, drawing 50,000+ visitors to the spectacular early-20th-century Pavilhão Carlos Lopes exhibition hall in Parque Eduardo VII. Founded in 2008, the festival was conceived to promote Portugal’s traditional fish and seafood dishes to the international audience and to support the local fishing industry. The eleven-day programme: tasting stations from 30+ of Portugal’s top chefs (José Avillez, Henrique Sá Pessoa, Vítor Sobral, Alexandre Silva, and the Algarve and Madeira regional ambassadors); the bacalhau showcase (’1001 ways with salt cod’, the national dish); the sardine grill running daily on the outdoor terrace; cataplana, arroz de marisco, polvo à lagareiro, and percebes (goose barnacles); nightly wine pairings from Douro, Alentejo, and Madeira; chef masterclasses; and trade-day conferences on sustainable Atlantic fishing.

**The Berth.** Bairro Alto Hotel on Praça Luís de Camões for the design-boutique heart-of-the-city stay; the Pestana Palace in Alcântara for the 19th-century palacete; the Pestana Pousada de Lisboa in the converted former Banco de Portugal building on Praça do Comércio; the Four Seasons Hotel Ritz Lisbon; or the Lumiares Hotel & Spa in Bairro Alto. Tivoli Avenida Liberdade on the grand boulevard for the heritage dependable; Memmo Alfama Hotel in the Alfama quarter for the rooftop-pool boutique with Tagus views.

**The Galley.** Belcanto by José Avillez (two Michelin stars, the modern-Portuguese flagship in Chiado); Cervejaria Ramiro in Anjos for canonical Lisbon shellfish (prawns, lobster, percebes); Cervejaria Trindade in Bairro Alto; A Cevicheria in Príncipe Real; Time Out Market at Mercado da Ribeira; Pastéis de Belém since 1837 for the original custard tart. Mini Bar by José Avillez at the São Luiz Theatre for the cocktail-tasting cousin of Belcanto; Sea Me in Chiado for the modern peixaria- and-sushi hybrid.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Belém Tower* (Lisbon, Portugal). The 1519 Manueline watchtower on the Tagus mouth, half fortress and half ceremonial gateway, the place from which the caravels sailed to India and Brazil; UNESCO 1983 with the Jerónimos opposite
2. *Jerónimos Monastery* (Lisbon, Portugal). The vast white limestone monastery raised from the pepper-and-spice trade after Vasco da Gama, the Manueline cloister and the long vault held up on six octagonal pillars; Vasco himself buried in the church

### 10. Pyrkon Festival

**Port:** Poznań International Fair grounds, Poznań, Poland
**Date:** mid-to-late April
**Flags:** FANDOM, GAME

Poland’s largest fantasy and sci-fi convention, held annually in late April at the Poznań International Fair grounds, three days, 50,000+ attendees, the largest fan gathering in Central Europe. CD Projekt Red regularly previews Witcher and Cyberpunk content here; the Polish RPG and tabletop scene anchors the programming with a 24-hour gaming hall. The cosplay competition on Saturday night is the hardest-fought in Eastern Europe. The convention bus from Poznań Główny station runs every fifteen minutes.

In Poznań itself: Blow Up Hall 5050 in the Stary Browar art-and-shopping complex for the design-set boutique; Brovaria on the Old Market Square for the heritage stay above the in-house brewery.

**The Galley.** Warsaw: Atelier Amaro; Bibenda for the modern; pierogi at Pierogarnia Mandu. Kraków: Bottiglieria 1881; Pod Aniołami for canonical Polish. In Poznań: Hyćka on the Old Market Square for canonical Wielkopolska regional Polish, the pyzy poznańskie dumplings; Cocorico for the modern Polish in the converted Art Nouveau bakery.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Stary Rynek / Old Market Square* (Poznań, Poland). The square framed by Renaissance burgher houses and the central Town Hall with its mechanical goats butting heads at noon; the heart of one of Poland's three founding cities, rebuilt after 1945
2. *Ostrów Tumski / Cathedral Island* (Poznań, Poland). The river island where Mieszko I was baptized in 966 and Poland began, the Romanesque-into-Gothic cathedral over the founding kings' tombs; the oldest still-standing place of Polish Christianity

### 11. Songkran

**Port:** Chiang Mai, Thailand
**Date:** Tue–Thu Apr 13–15
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART, FOOD

Songkran, the Thai New Year, marks the sun’s astrological passage from Pisces into Aries in the Theravada lunar-solar calendar; observed nationwide April 13–15 with three named days: Wan Sankhan Long (April 13, the great-going-out, the year ending), Wan Nao (April 14, the in-between), and Wan Phaya Wan (April 15, the year beginning). Inscribed on UNESCO’s Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in December 2023. The flagship celebration is in Chiang Mai, the 13th-century Lanna capital, where the rectangular moat around the old city becomes the world’s most photographed water fight. The Phra Buddha Sihing Procession on the morning of April 13 carries the sacred Lanna-era Buddha image (kept in Wat Phra Singh since 1367) on a flower-decorated cart while devotees pour scented jasmine water over the image as it passes; afternoons across all three days, the moat road perimeter becomes a six-kilometre water battle; April 14 the day to build sand stupas (chedi sai) on the temple grounds; April 15 the family ritual of pouring scented water over elders’ hands. Sunset rewards the drive up Doi Suthep to the gold-leaf chedi.

**The Berth.** The Anantara Chiang Mai Resort on the Mae Ping riverside; 137 Pillars House in Wat Ket for the British East India Company era teak heritage; Raya Heritage on the Ping for contemporary Lanna design; or Tamarind Village inside the old city walls. Four Seasons Resort Chiang Mai in Mae Rim for the rice-paddy-pavilion luxury 20 minutes north; Dhara Dhevi in Mae Rim for the temple-architecture grand resort.

**The Galley.** Khao Soi Khun Yai on Si Phum Road for canonical Burmese-Lanna coconut-curry noodle soup since 1980; SP Chicken for the canonical Thai charcoal-roasted gai yang; Huen Phen for the temple-style Lanna khantoke spread; Tong Tem Toh for sai oua and gaeng hung lay; David’s Kitchen for European fine-dining. Issaya Siamese Club Chiang Mai for canonical modern Thai by chef Ian Kittichai; Maha Naga in the Lanna-style teak compound for canonical Thai garden dining.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Wat Phra Singh* (Chiang Mai, Thailand). Chiang Mai's most revered temple, founded 1345 to house a buddha image that may or may not have come from Sri Lanka; the gold leaf flaked on the prayer hall's red lacquer, the chanting at four every morning
2. *Wat Chedi Luang* (Chiang Mai, Thailand). The vast brick stupa raised between 1391 and 1475 to 80 metres before a 1545 earthquake brought the top down, still 60 metres of ruined pyramid in the old city; the Emerald Buddha was kept here for 84 years

---

### 12. BaliSpirit Festival

**Port:** The Yoga Barn & Puri Padi Hotel, Ubud, Bali
**Date:** Wed–Sun Apr 14–18
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART, FOOD

The 18th edition; the largest annual yoga, music, and wellness festival in Southeast Asia and one of the most respected gatherings in the global wellness movement, drawing ~5,000 attendees from 50+ countries to the Balinese highland town of Ubud, the cultural and spiritual capital of the Island of the Gods. Founded in 2008 by an international team rooted in the Ubud expat-and-local hybrid community, the festival was designed to honour and amplify the Balinese Hindu philosophy of tri hita karana, the threefold harmony with the spiritual, social, and natural realms (Parahyangan, Pawongan, Palemahan) that organises every aspect of Balinese village life. The festival is not a wellness retreat parachuted onto Bali but a deliberately Balinese event, organised in dialogue with the local banjar (village council), the surrounding temples, and the Balinese Hindu calendar, committed financially through outreach programs: AYO! Kita Bicara HIV & AIDS (youth sex-ed across Gianyar and Bangli regencies) and Bali ReGreen (mangrove planting, watershed restoration).

**The Berth.** The festival is in Ubud, stay in Ubud, not Nusa Dua. Como Shambhala Estate in Ubud for the wellness-retreat luxury aligned with the festival’s animating premise; Mandapa, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve on the Ayung River for the contemporary Balinese luxury; Bambu Indah in Sayan for the design-eco-pioneer eight-suite boutique by John and Cynthia Hardy. For Nusa Dua-and-Java side trips: Aman Villas at Nusa Dua, the Mulia; in Java, Tugu Yogyakarta or the Phoenix Hotel Yogyakarta.

**The Galley.** Locavore in Ubud for the modern Indonesian; Mama San in Seminyak for the colonial-Asian; the night markets of Sanur. Java: Gudeg Yu Djum in Yogyakarta. Bridges Bali on the Wos River gorge for the canonical Ubud cliff-restaurant Italian-Indonesian; Hujan Locale for the modern Indonesian by chef Will Goldfarb.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Pura Tirta Empul* (Tampaksiring, Bali, Indonesia). The 962 CE water temple built around a sacred spring, twelve carved stone spouts feeding the purification pools where Balinese Hindus still queue to bathe; the green moss of nine hundred rainy seasons on the walls
2. *Jatiluwih Rice Terraces* (Tabanan, Bali, Indonesia). The 600 hectares of stepped paddy ascending Mount Batukaru, watered by the thousand-year-old subak irrigation system run by farmers' temples; UNESCO 2012 as a working cultural landscape

---

### 13. Patriots’ Day Battle Reenactments

**Port:** Lexington Green & Concord's North Bridge, Massachusetts
**Date:** Mon Apr 19
**Flags:** CULTURE

Annual Patriots’ Day (third Monday in April) reenactments at Lexington Green and Concord’s North Bridge in Massachusetts, commemorating the April 19, 1775 “shot heard round the world”, the opening of the Revolutionary War. The Lexington Green dawn reenactment (typically 5:30 a.m.) recreates the Lexington Minutemen confronting British regulars; the Concord North Bridge afternoon reenactment recreates the Minute Men driving the British back. Pair with the Old North Bridge, the Minute Man National Historical Park, the Battle Road Trail walk, and the Boston Marathon (which runs the same day).

**The Berth.** Stay in Boston (25 km east): Boston Harbor Hotel; The Liberty; XV Beacon. Or in Concord: The Colonial Inn since 1716. Boston Park Plaza for the historic 1927 grand- dame in Back Bay; Lenox Hotel on Boylston Street for the heritage Marathon-finish- line proximity, the Patriots’ Day Boston Marathon runs the same morning.

**The Galley.** Concord: The Colonial Inn dining room; 80 Thoreau for the modern. Boston: Neptune Oyster; Mamma Maria; Townsman; Mike’s Pastry. No. 9 Park on Beacon Hill for Barbara Lynch’s canonical New England fine-dining; Coppa in the South End for the modern Italian.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Minute Man National Historical Park* (Concord, Massachusetts, USA). The five-mile Battle Road from Lexington Green to the Old North Bridge where the colonial militia turned the regulars back on April 19, 1775; Daniel Chester French's Minute Man stands above the bridge
2. *Walden Pond* (Concord, Massachusetts, USA). The 25-hectare kettle pond in the second-growth woods where Thoreau lived from July 1845 to September 1847 in a ten-by-fifteen-foot cabin; a cairn of stones grew over the site through Emerson's century

### 14. Mile High 420 Festival

**Port:** Civic Center Park, Denver, Colorado
**Date:** Tue Apr 20
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

The largest 4/20 cannabis celebration in the world, held annually on April 20 at Civic Center Park in downtown Denver since recreational sale took effect across Colorado on January 1, 2014. The date itself has a documented origin: in 1971, five high-school students at San Rafael High School in California, known as ’the Waldos’, used ’4:20’ as a code phrase for their after-school meetings to search for a rumored abandoned cannabis crop near Point Reyes; the code spread through the Grateful Dead’s social network in the 1970s and 1980s, was popularized internationally by High Times magazine in 1991, and is now the universal global cannabis day. Denver is the natural festival anchor: Colorado’s Amendment 64 in 2012 made it (with Washington State) one of the first two U.S. jurisdictions to legalize recreational cannabis. The festival programme is free: live music across multiple stages, cannabis industry exhibitions and education programming (on-site sale is prohibited by state law), art installations and craft markets, food trucks at scale, and the iconic mass observance at exactly 4:20 p.m. Pair with a Red Rocks Amphitheater concert (15 miles southwest), the South Broadway dispensary corridor, and a day-trip up I-70 to Idaho Springs, Georgetown, and Breckenridge.

**The Berth.** The Brown Palace Hotel and Spa, the canonical Denver grand-hotel since 1892 on Tremont Place; Hotel Teatro on 14th Street directly across from Civic Center Park; The Crawford Hotel at Union Station; The Maven Hotel at Dairy Block in LoDo; or The Source Hotel in the RiNo Art District. The Limelight Hotel Denver at Union Station for the modern boutique; The Ramble Hotel in RiNo for the design-set with the in-house Death & Co cocktail bar.

**The Galley.** Tavernetta in Union Station; Mizuna in Capitol Hill; Mister Tuna in RiNo; The Buckhorn Exchange on Osage since 1893 (oldest restaurant in Denver, classic steakhouse with elk-and- buffalo trophies and Liquor License #1); Sushi Den in Platt Park; Cherry Cricket on Second Avenue for the canonical Denver burger since 1945; Snooze on Larimer for breakfast; Linger on Little Raven for the rooftop in the converted Olinger Mortuary; in Boulder, Frasca Food and Wine. Bruto in RiNo for the modern Mexican by Tyler Hill; Hop Alley by Tommy Lee for canonical modern Chinese-American.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Red Rocks Amphitheatre* (Morrison, Colorado, USA). The natural sandstone amphitheatre held between two 90-metre red-rock fins, opened as a venue in 1941; the Beatles played here, U2 filmed here, the acoustics still unrepeated
2. *Denver Art Museum* (Denver, Colorado, USA). Daniel Libeskind's 2006 titanium-clad Hamilton Building leaning out over 13th Avenue in fractured planes, joined to Gio Ponti's 1971 tile-clad fortress next door; an indigenous-art collection of national rank

### 15. Earth Day

**Port:** Worldwide observance, anchored at the National Mall,
**Date:** Thu Apr 22
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

The 58th annual Earth Day; the world’s largest secular civic observance, observed in 192+ countries by ~1 billion participants annually. Founded April 22, 1970 by U.S. senator Gaylord Nelson of Wisconsin in collaboration with Harvard graduate student Denis Hayes (whom Nelson hired as the national coordinator for the inaugural event), in direct response to the catastrophic January 1969 Santa Barbara oil spill, at the time the largest oil spill in U.S. history, releasing three million gallons of crude across 800 square miles of California coastline, killing seabirds, dolphins, sea lions, and seals on a scale the country had never witnessed and that was televised live for two weeks straight. Nelson, having toured the spill aftermath, returned to the Senate convinced that environmental concern was about to become a mass movement, and modeled the new event on the anti-Vietnam War teach-ins of the late 1960s, combining grassroots organizing with a single coordinated national day of environmental education and demonstration. The first Earth Day on April 22, 1970, drew an estimated 20 million Americans into the streets, at the time, the largest organized public demonstration in U.S. history.

**The Berth.** The Hay-Adams across from the White House; Riggs in the converted bank in Penn Quarter; or the Eaton DC for the design-set option. The Jefferson on 16th Street for the European-style boutique with the Smithsonian-adjacent location; The St. Regis Washington DC on K Street for the modern luxury near the White House.

**The Galley.** Minibar by José Andrés for the two-Michelin-star; Old Ebbitt Grill near the White House since 1856; Rasika in Penn Quarter for the modern Indian; Ben’s Chili Bowl on U Street for the half- smoke. Rose’s Luxury on Capitol Hill (James Beard winner) for the canonical Washington American; Pineapple and Pearls next door for the two-Michelin-star fine-dining and the sister restaurant tasting menu.

**The Bearings.**

1. *National Mall* (Washington, DC, USA). The two-mile green spine running from the Capitol dome to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, framed by Smithsonian museums and the Washington Monument's obelisk; Pierre L'Enfant's 1791 plan still visible whole
2. *Yellowstone National Park* (Wyoming, Montana, Idaho, USA). The supervolcano caldera turned into the world's first national park in 1872, half the geysers on Earth concentrated in one basin; UNESCO 1978, the wolves returned in 1995 after seventy years

### 19. Feria de Abril de Sevilla

**Port:** Real de la Feria, Los Remedios, Sevilla
**Date:** Tue–Sun Apr 13–18
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART, FOOD

The 181st annual edition; the most spectacular fair in Spain, the joyous secular bookend to Semana Santa two weeks earlier, and one of the great living folkloric celebrations in Europe, six days and seven nights when the entire city of Sevilla collectively transforms into the most exuberant version of itself. Sevillano society parades through a temporary tent-city of 1,052 casetas in the largest, most elaborate, and most photographed Andalusian celebration on Earth. Founded in 1846 by two Catalan and Basque councillors, Narciso Bonaplata and José María Ybarra, originally proposed to Queen Isabel II as a livestock fair to promote the local economy; the first edition was held April 18–20, 1847 at the Prado de San Sebastián, with 19 livestock dealers and four days of trading. Within a year, festive elements began to transform the trading event, the founding three casetas belonged to the Duke and Duchess of Montpensier, the Seville Town Hall, and the Casino of Seville, and the Feria began its slow evolution from livestock market into the spring social pageant the world knows today.

**The Berth.** Hotel Alfonso XIII (the iconic 1929 Mudéjar-Revival landmark, built specifically for the Ibero- American Exposition that defined the modern Feria aesthetic, $800–2,500/night during Feria with rates doubled from baseline); Hotel Colón Gran Meliá. Mercer Sevilla in the Casa Castelar palace for the design-set boutique; EME Catedral Mercer opposite the Cathedral for the modern Andalusian luxury with the rooftop view of the Giralda.

**The Galley.** In Sevilla, the festival is here, eat here: Cañabota on Calle Orfila for Michelin-starred contemporary Andalusian seafood; Bodega Santa Cruz (’Las Columnas’) in the Santa Cruz quarter for canonical Sevillano tapas at the marble counter, the montaditos and fino sherry; Eslava in San Lorenzo for the tapas-tasting; El Rinconcillo since 1670, the oldest bar in Sevilla.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Plaza de España* (Seville, Andalusia, Spain). The vast tile-and-brick crescent built for the 1929 Ibero-American Exposition, a canal in front and 48 painted azulejo benches for the Spanish provinces; the place where Lawrence of Arabia and Star Wars Episode II both shot
2. *Itálica* (Santiponce, Andalusia, Spain). The Roman city founded 206 BCE on the Guadalquivir, birthplace of Trajan and Hadrian, the third-largest amphitheatre in the empire still complete; nine kilometres from Seville and rarely crowded

### 21. World Gourmet Summit

**Port:** Various five-star hotels and top restaurants across Singapore
**Date:** Mon Apr 12 – Sun May 9, 4 weeks
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE, ART

The 31st annual edition; Asia’s most prestigious culinary festival, the apex event in Singapore’s gastronomic calendar, and one of the great global chef-and-vintner gatherings, the only multi-week festival on Earth where Michelin-starred chefs from every continent come into Singapore in series across nearly a month to cook one-night-only collaborative menus at the city-state’s finest restaurants. Founded in July 1997 by Peter Knipp, the German-born Singapore-based food and beverage consultant, in collaboration with Tan Chin Nam, the legendary CEO of the Singapore Tourism Board, as a deliberate copy of the Saint Moritz Gourmet Festival they had attended together in the Swiss Alps the year before. The founding mission was to plant Singapore as a serious culinary destination on global maps and to give Singaporean chefs a stage on which to host and learn from the world’s finest. Run since the second edition by Peter Knipp Holdings / À la Carte Productions in partnership with the STB. The Summit has grown across nearly three decades into a four-week extravaganza that anchors Singapore’s tourism shoulder season between the Lunar New Year peak and the August National Day rush.

**The Berth.** The Raffles Hotel, the 1887 colonial grand-dame, restored 2019, the home of the Singapore Sling, where Joseph Conrad and Somerset Maugham wrote and where the festival’s most prestigious dinners are held. **The Bearings.**

**Flags:** VIKING

One of the largest Viking-Age living-history events in Scandinavia, in its 26th year, held in the actual Ribe Viking Centre on the site of the 700s trading port, Denmark’s oldest town. 800+ Viking reenactors from across Europe in period dress operating an authentic Viking marketplace; combat displays, longship sailings on the Ribe River, period crafts demonstrations, and traditional Norse food.

**The Berth.** Hotel Dagmar, Denmark’s oldest hotel (1581) on the Torvet; or Hotel Ribe Byferie for the apartment-style stay; or Den Gamle Arrest in the converted prison for the boutique. Hotel Ribe Byferie Resort for the family-style apartment stay 5 minutes from the Viking Centre; Sønderho Kro on Fanø Island (20 minutes by ferry) for the 1722 inn heritage on the Wadden Sea.

**The Galley.** Sælhunden on the Skibbroen for canonical Danish; Kammerslusen for the smørrebrød; Postgaarden in the old post house for the local seasonal; Weiss’ Stue for after the festival. Restaurant Kolvig in Ribe for the Michelin Bib Gourmand canonical Danish; Tre Søstre on the main pedestrian street for the canonical Danish smørrebrød lunch.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Jelling Stones* (Jelling, Denmark). The two carved runestones raised by Gorm and Harald Bluetooth in the tenth century, Denmark's birth certificate in stone, Harald's the larger boasting he made the Danes Christian; UNESCO 1994 with the burial mounds
2. *Roskilde Cathedral* (Roskilde, Denmark). The first Gothic-brick cathedral in Scandinavia, begun by Bishop Absalon in the 1170s and the royal burial church since the fifteenth century; UNESCO 1995, 39 Danish monarchs sleep within

### 29. Walpurgis Night

**Port:** Throughout Sweden, anchored at Uppsala
**Date:** Fri Apr 30
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD, ART

Eve of Saint Walpurga’s feast day; one of Sweden’s most beloved national traditions, marking the symbolic end of winter and welcome of spring with bonfires, choral singing, and a national champagne breakfast. The two great university anchors are Uppsala and Lund. In Uppsala, the day starts before dawn with a champagne-and-strawberry breakfast in city parks; the legendary student orchestra Wijkmanska Blecket performs on the steps of Carolina Rediviva (the university library) at noon; at 3 p.m. exactly, the entire student body, 50,000 strong, performs the Mösspåtagning (the simultaneous donning of the white student cap with the black peak) outside the Carolina Rediviva, the iconic photograph of the Swedish year. Then 120,000 people pour into Ekonomikum Park; the absurdist Forsränningen raft race down the Fyris river (since 1975, with intentionally unseaworthy homemade rafts that are designed to break apart partway through); the Champagnegalopp at the student nations (champagne sprayed not consumed); and the torchlit procession to the Royal Mounds bonfire at Gamla Uppsala at dusk.

**The Berth.** Stockholm: Grand Hôtel on Blasieholmskajen; Ett Hem in Lärkstaden for the boutique; or At Six in Brunkeberg. In Uppsala for the day-of festival access: Best Western Hotell Akademihotellet on Övre Slottsgatan for the historic dependable; Elite Hotel Academia on Suttungs gränd for the modern-boutique walking distance to the Carolina Rediviva and the Forsränningen route.

**The Galley.** Frantzén for the three-Michelin-star; Aira on Djurgården for the Nordic seasonal; Tradition for canonical husmanskost; Östermalms Saluhall for the hall lunch. In Uppsala: Hambergs Fisk on Fyristorg for canonical Swedish fish; Domtrappkällaren in the medieval cellar by the Cathedral for the canonical Uppsala formal dinner since 1953.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Gamla Uppsala* (Uppsala, Sweden). The three great royal burial mounds of pre-Christian Sweden raised over the kings of the Yngling dynasty in the fifth and sixth centuries, the heathen temple of Adam of Bremen's description once standing beside them
2. *Drottningholm Palace* (Lovön, Stockholm, Sweden). Sweden's seventeenth-century baroque royal residence on its lake island, the Court Theatre of 1766 still using its original wood machinery for thunder, waves, and scene-changes; UNESCO 1991

### 30. Greek Orthodox Easter

**Port:** Patmos, Dodecanese, Greece
**Date:** Thu Apr 29 – Sun May 2
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Greek Orthodox Holy Week ending on Pascha Sunday May 2; the most spiritually charged Easter celebration in Greece, on the small Aegean island where John of Patmos received the Book of Revelation in 95 CE. The week opens with the Niptiras Ceremony on Holy Thursday morning in the square outside the Monastery of Saint John the Theologian (UNESCO-listed), where the Abbot ritually washes the feet of twelve monks reenacting the Last Supper, the only place in the world this medieval ceremony is still performed in public. Holy Friday brings the Epitaphios procession through Chora by candlelight; the Saturday-midnight Anastasi (Resurrection) service ends with the cry ’Christos Anesti’ and a fireworks display visible from across the island; Easter Sunday brings the magiritsa soup, lamb on the spit, and the egg-cracking tsougrisma ritual.

**The Berth.** On Patmos itself: Patmos Aktis Suites and Spa in Grikos Bay for the boutique seafront stay near the monastery; Petra Hotel in Grikos for the design-boutique on Petra Beach with the Adelphi-rock view; The 4 Epochs Suites & Apartments in Skala for the heritage-style harbour stay. Athens stop en route: Hotel Grande Bretagne on Syntagma; Electra Metropolis for the rooftop view.

**The Galley.** On Patmos: Vegghera Patmos for the canonical waterside Greek; Pantheon in Skala harbour for the canonical Patmian taverna, slow-cooked goat, ladenia (Patmian flatbread), fresh octopus from the harbour, the local Limnio wine; Tarsanas Studios Restaurant in Grikos for the canonical seaside fresh-catch lunch.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Monastery of Saint John the Theologian* (Chora, Patmos, Greece). The fortified Byzantine monastery raised 1088 by Christodoulos around the cave where John is said to have received the Revelation; UNESCO 1999, the small library still holding the founding chrysobull of Alexios I
2. *Cave of the Apocalypse* (Patmos, Greece). The whitewashed grotto halfway up the road from Skala to Chora where John heard the voice through the rift in the rock that still splits the ceiling into three; the iron grille around the rest-stone he leaned against

### 31. Kanamara Matsuri

**Port:** Kanayama Shrine, Kawasaki, Kanagawa, Japan
**Date:** first Sunday of April
**Flags:** CULTURE

The Shinto festival of the Steel Phallus at Kanayama Shrine in Kawasaki, one of Japan’s three great kisai (eccentric festivals) and the most famous penis festival on Earth. Originated in the Edo period as a healing rite for sex workers in the Kanagawa-juku post-station district along the Tōkaidō highway, who prayed at Kanayama Shrine for protection from sexually transmitted infections; the shrine’s tutelary deities Kanayama-hiko and Kanayama-hime are also the patron kami of metalworkers and smiths, hence the association with iron and steel phallic forms. Three black, pink, and steel-pink mikoshi (portable shrines) carrying carved phalluses are paraded through the streets of Kawasaki, accompanied by women crossdressed in male attire, men crossdressed in female attire, and the iconic Elizabeth-pink-mikoshi carried by drag queens in pink kimono. Phallic-shaped candy (chinpoko-ame), daikon carvings, and the bawdy festival snacks line the food carts. Since 2000, all proceeds have gone to HIV/AIDS research and to sex-worker advocacy organisations. The festival is solemn, joyful, deeply Japanese, and not what you think it is.

**The Berth.** In Kawasaki: Hotel Metropolitan Kawasaki at Kawasaki Station for the dependable festival-side stay. In central Tokyo (20 minutes by JR): Hoshinoya Tokyo in Otemachi for the urban-ryokan luxury with the rooftop onsen.

**The Galley.** In Kawasaki: Yakitori Nakamura in the Kawasaki-juku district for canonical Edo-style yakitori; Saiyū near the Kanayama Shrine approach for the canonical festival-week street snacks, yakisoba, takoyaki, and the seasonal phallic candies sold at every cart.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Kawasaki Daishi* (Kawasaki, Japan). The Heiken-ji temple founded 1128 around a small Kobo Daishi image netted from the sea by a fisherman, the third-most-visited shrine in Japan over New Year's; the candy-cutting craftsmen at the gate selling tonkatsu-ame in beats
2. *Tokyo Skytree* (Sumida, Tokyo, Japan). The 634-metre broadcast tower opened 2012, the tallest in Japan and the second-tallest free-standing structure in the world; the height in metres chosen to read musashi, the old name of the eastern Tokyo plain

### 32. Hùng Kings Temple Festival

**Port:** Nghĩa Lĩnh Mountain, Phú Thọ Province, Vietnam
**Date:** 10th day of the 3rd lunar month (mid-April)
**Flags:** CULTURE

The Vietnamese national ancestor-worship festival, observed on the 10th day of the third lunar month at the Hùng Kings Temple complex on Nghĩa Lĩnh mountain in Phú Thọ province, 100 km northwest of Hanoi. The festival honors the legendary Hùng Vương kings, the eighteen sovereigns of the proto-state of Văn Lang who, according to Vietnamese national mythology, founded the nation in 2879 BCE. The temple complex has been a pilgrimage site since at least the 10th century; the current festival programme dates to a 1917 royal proclamation declaring the day a national holiday. Pilgrims climb the 525 stone steps from the foot of the mountain to the upper temple complex (Đền Thượng) where the sacred well and the eternal incense are kept. The traditional offerings of bánh chưng (the square sticky-rice cakes wrapped in dong leaves, symbolizing earth) and bánh giầy (the round pounded rice cakes, symbolizing sky) are presented at every temple stop. Folk performances in Xoan singing, the Phú Thọ regional folk-song tradition that has been UNESCO-inscribed since 2011, fill the festival ground throughout the week. The country observes a public holiday; expect rural Vietnam at its most authentic.

**The Berth.** In Hanoi (the base for the day-trip north): Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi on Ngô Quyền Street for the canonical 1901 French-colonial grand-dame; Capella Hanoi in the Opera House district for the modern luxury by the Bill Bensley-designed reading rooms.

**The Galley.** In Hanoi: Chả Cá Lã Vọng since 1871 for the canonical Hanoi turmeric-fish dish served at one of two tables on Chả Cá Street; Bun Cha Huong Lien (“Obama Bun Cha”) for the canonical Hanoi grilled pork-and-vermicelli that Anthony Bourdain and President Obama ate together in 2016.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Hung Kings Temple Complex* (Nghĩa Lĩnh Mountain, Phú Thọ Province, Vietnam). The four temples ascending the sacred Nghĩa Lĩnh hill where the legendary Hùng kings, founders of the first Vietnamese state of Văn Lang, are said to be buried; the highest the Thượng temple where Hồ Chí Minh paid respects in 1954
2. *Trang An Landscape Complex* (Ninh Bình Province, Vietnam). The 12,000-hectare karst landscape of jungle-covered limestone karsts and cave-river boats, the tenth-century capital of Hoa Lư at its centre; UNESCO 2014, a mixed cultural and natural site

### 33. Battle of San Jacinto Reenactment

**Port:** San Jacinto Battleground, La Porte, Texas
**Date:** Wed Apr 21
**Flags:** CULTURE

The annual commemoration of the eighteen-minute battle that won Texas independence on April 21, 1836, refought on the actual battlefield under the San Jacinto Monument, at 567.31 feet, the world’s tallest masonry obelisk and twelve feet taller than the Washington Monument by Texas insistence. The reenactment, organized by the San Jacinto Battleground State Historic Site and the San Jacinto Volunteers, runs the third Saturday in April. The 18-minute battle in 1836 ended the Texas Revolution when General Sam Houston’s 910-man Texan army surprised General Santa Anna’s 1,360 Mexican troops during their afternoon siesta on the plains east of present-day Houston. The Texans, shouting ’Remember the Alamo!’ and ’Remember Goliad!’ (referring to the earlier Texan defeats at the Alamo six weeks before and Goliad three weeks before), killed 630 Mexican soldiers and captured Santa Anna himself in the surrounding marsh; the Treaty of Velasco signed by the captive general formally ended the war. Modern reenactors stage the battle in period dress with replica muskets, cannons, and cavalry charges, followed by a wreath-laying at the monument and the reading of Sam Houston’s address to the troops the morning of battle. The Battleship Texas, a WWI-era dreadnought, is moored at the battlefield wharf.

**The Berth.** In Houston (30 minutes west of the battlefield): The Lancaster Hotel in the Theatre District for the heritage 1926 boutique; Hotel ZaZa Memorial City for the design-set with the rooftop pool.

**The Galley.** In Houston: Georgia James by Chris Shepherd for the canonical Houston steakhouse; Xochi by Hugo Ortega for the Oaxacan tasting menu; Killen’s Barbecue in Pearland for the canonical Texas BBQ, book a day ahead, line at dawn.

**The Bearings.**

1. *San Jacinto Monument* (La Porte, Texas, USA). The 173-metre Art Deco obelisk topped by a 220-ton star, marking the eighteen-minute battle of April 21, 1836 in which Texas independence was won from Mexico; the tallest stone column monument in the world
2. *Battleship Texas* (La Porte, Texas, USA). The dreadnought USS Texas, BB-35, commissioned 1914 and the only surviving ship to have served in both world wars; moored beside the San Jacinto battleground since 1948, the country's first museum ship

---

### 34. Frühlingsfest

**Port:** Theresienwiese, Munich, Germany
**Date:** mid-April through early May, 2 weeks
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The “Spring Oktoberfest” on the Theresienwiese, the same massive Munich fair-ground that hosts the quintessential September Oktoberfest, on a smaller, less-touristed scale. Founded 1965 by a Munich businessman as a deliberate spring fair to fill the long Bavarian winter-to-summer gap, the festival has grown across six decades into the second-largest folk festival in Munich and one of the great Bavarian beer-tent events of the year. Two weeks running mid-April through early May: two large beer tents (Hippodrom-Festzelt and Münchner Weißbierkarussell), one Schießzelt (shooting tent), a midway with the Riesenrad ferris wheel and the customary Bavarian fair-ride lineup, and the festival’s signature flea market on the first weekend, the largest in Bavaria. The Frühlingsfest beer pours are the same Munich six (Hofbräu, Löwenbräu, Augustiner, Spaten, Paulaner, Hacker-Pschorr) but in smaller liter Maß mugs and at half the September prices. Hendl roasted whole. Steckerlfisch on the stick. The Bavarians at half-volume, which is still loud.

**The Berth.** Hotel Bayerischer Hof on Promenadeplatz for the canonical Munich grand-dame since 1841; The Charles Hotel by Rocco Forte in Maxvorstadt for the contemporary luxury with the Old Botanical Garden views.

**The Galley.** Tantris in Schwabing for canonical Michelin-starred classical Munich since 1971; Hofbräuhaus am Platzl since 1589 for the canonical Bavarian beer-hall, the Weisswurst breakfast, the pretzel and the Maß of Hofbräu Original on the long oak bench.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Neuschwanstein Castle* (Hohenschwangau, Bavaria, Germany). Ludwig II's white-limestone fairy-tale castle on a Bavarian alpine spur, begun 1869 and unfinished at his mysterious death in 1886; the model for Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle, six million visitors annually
2. *Nymphenburg Palace* (Munich, Bavaria, Germany). The summer palace begun 1664 by the Bavarian elector for his Italian wife's first son, four kilometres of central building and pavilions in formal grounds; the porcelain manufactory in the grounds since 1761

---

### 35. Almadraba Bluefin Tuna Trap

**Port:** Cádiz coast, Andalusia, Spain
**Date:** late April through May, ~4 weeks
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The 3,000-year-old Phoenician trapping method for catching migrating Atlantic bluefin tuna as they enter the Mediterranean to spawn, practiced by four villages on the Cádiz coast of southern Spain: Barbate, Conil de la Frontera, Zahara de los Atunes, and Tarifa. The Almadraba is a vast maze of underwater nets, set in late April each year for the four-week tuna run between Gibraltar and the Spanish coast, that funnels the fish through a series of chambers until they reach the central death-chamber (the copo) where they are harvested by hand in the medieval matanza ritual, the most sustainable bluefin fishery on Earth. The four villages observe the festival together: the Bendición del Mar (blessing of the sea) at the start of the season; the Día de la Almadraba family-feast days at each village; and the closing nights at Zahara de los Atunes where the entire town turns out to eat the fresh bluefin in every cut from snout to tail. The tradition has been a Mediterranean fishing custom since the Phoenicians settled the coast in the 9th century BCE and was codified by Roman fishing law in the 1st century CE. The cuts (ronqueo) follow ancient anatomical terminology: mojama, tarantelo, ventresca, parpatana, contramormo, each a different texture, a different ceremony.

**The Berth.** Parador de Cádiz on the Atlantic seafront in the Bahía de Cádiz for the heritage parador stay; Hotel V de Vejer in Vejer de la Frontera for the design-boutique in the whitewashed hilltop town 15 km from Barbate.

**The Galley.** El Campero in Barbate for the canonical Almadraba tasting, every cut of bluefin from snout to tail, the most respected ronqueo expertise on the coast; Aponiente by chef Ángel León in El Puerto de Santa María for the three-Michelin-star modern Andalusian sea-cooking, ’el chef del mar’ for his work on plankton and overlooked marine ingredients.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Cádiz Old Town* (Cádiz, Andalusia, Spain). The oldest continuously inhabited city in western Europe, founded by the Phoenicians 1100 BCE on a thin spit of land in the Atlantic; the gold-tile cathedral dome rising above the white roofs the city's compass
2. *Doñana National Park* (Huelva & Seville Provinces, Andalusia, Spain). The marshes and dunes at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, half a million migrating birds wintering here each year, the Iberian lynx clinging to thirty square kilometres of cork-oak woodland; UNESCO 1994

### 36. Saint Jordi Day

**Port:** Barcelona & Catalonia
**Date:** Fri Apr 23
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

Catalonia’s patron-saint holiday and de facto national day, celebrated every April 23 across Barcelona and every Catalan town with the most beautiful public-romance ritual on the calendar: men give women roses, women give men books, and Las Ramblas fills end-to-end with thousands of book stalls and rose vendors from morning until past midnight. The day combines the medieval legend of Sant Jordi (Catalonia’s dragon-slaying patron saint, whose spilled dragon’s blood is said to have become the red rose) with the coincidence that April 23 marks the deaths of both Cervantes and Shakespeare in 1616, the basis for UNESCO’s World Book and Copyright Day since 1995. The Generalitat de Catalunya on Plaça Sant Jaume opens its medieval courtyards to the public this one day each year. Catalonia sells roughly half its annual books in 24 hours, and the Catalan flag flies on every Barcelona balcony.

**The Berth.** Hotel Casa Fuster on Passeig de Gràcia for the Domènech i Montaner Modernista landmark within walking distance of the Las Ramblas book route; Cotton House Hotel on Gran Via for the literary-salon atmosphere; The Serras at the Born for the Gothic Quarter and Cathedral Mass proximity. Mercer Hotel Barcelona inside the Roman city walls for the most-atmospheric Gothic-Quarter stay; Hotel Neri inside an 18th-century palace facing Plaça Sant Felip Neri for the literary-residence feel.

**The Galley.** Quimet i Quimet in Poble Sec for the canonical tinned-fish standing-bar montaditos; Bar Pinotxo at La Boqueria for breakfast on the Las Ramblas book route; Tickets and Bodega 1900 by the Adrià brothers for the modern Catalan tapas canon; Disfrutar in Eixample for the El Bulli alumni three-Michelin contemporary Catalan. Can Culleretes in the Gothic Quarter, Barcelona’s oldest continuously operating restaurant, opened 1786, for the canonical Catalan history with the day’s reading; Cervecería Catalana on Mallorca for the bench-seat tapas canon.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Sagrada Família* (Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain). Antoni Gaudí's basilica begun 1882 and still rising today, the three façades of Nativity and Passion and Glory each by a different generation of carvers; UNESCO inscribed in 1984 with six other Gaudí works
2. *Park Güell* (Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain). Gaudí's failed garden-city of 1900 turned public park, the dragon staircase and the serpent bench of trencadís broken-tile mosaic at the heart, Barcelona spread out below to the sea; UNESCO 1984

### 1. Brixham Pirate Festival

**Port:** Brixham, Devon, UK
**Date:** Sat–Mon May 1–3
**Flags:** PIRATE

UK May Bank Holiday; the largest pirate festival in the UK, in its 16th year, over 8,000 fully costumed pirates parading through the historic fishing port of Brixham, the harbour filled with tall ships and replica galleons, three days of cannon-fire demonstrations, sea-shanty performances on multiple stages, fancy-dress competitions, and the Saturday-night Pirate Ball.

Far better, stay in Devon itself: The Berry Head Hotel on the cliff above Brixham harbour for the canonical festival-base; Number Seven Hotel on Brixham harbour for the boutique fishing-village stay across from the marina.

**The Galley.** London: St. John, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers in Marlow; L’Enclume in Cumbria; or the canonical local gastropub. In Brixham: Rockfish Brixham at the harbour for canonical Devon fish-and-chips, the original Mitch Tonks venue; in Dartmouth (25 minutes east): The Seahorse for Mitch Tonks’s flagship seafood-and-grill.

1. *Dartmoor National Park* (Devon, England, UK). The 954 square kilometres of granite tors and bracken moorland rising west of the Devon coast, the highest open land in southern England, ringed by Bronze Age stone rows and Conan Doyle's hound
2. *Tintagel Castle* (Tintagel, Cornwall, England, UK). The thirteenth-century stronghold on a slate-cliff headland where Geoffrey of Monmouth placed Arthur's conception; the dark-age settlement beneath it traded with Byzantium, the modern footbridge a leap across the ravine

### 2. Star Wars Day

**Port:** Tozeur, Tunisia
**Date:** Tue May 4
**Flags:** FANDOM

May 4, the unofficial fan holiday that became official with Disney’s 2012 acquisition of Lucasfilm, named for the punning catchphrase ’May the Fourth be with you.’ The flagship celebration for the cinematic pilgrim is in the Tunisian Sahara, where George Lucas filmed the original 1976 Tatooine scenes for A New Hope and where most of the original exterior locations still stand 50 years later, accessible by 4x4 from the oasis city of Tozeur. The Tatooine pilgrimage rhythm: fly into Tozeur-Nefta International (TOE), drive 90 minutes to the Mos Espa film set on the edge of the Chott el Gharsa salt flats (the pod-racing town from The Phantom Menace, still preserved by the Tunisian government with the dome-and-archway adobe buildings open to walk through); afternoon to the Sidi Bouhlel canyon near Tozeur (the Star Wars Canyon, where the Tusken Raiders ambushed Luke and where R2-D2 escaped the Jawas); evening drive south through the Chott el Djerid salt lake to the Berber troglodyte village of Matmata, where Luke’s underground homestead was filmed inside the actual Hotel Sidi Driss, still operating as a working hotel where travelers can sleep in the same vaulted dining room where Aunt Beru served blue milk; May 4 itself climaxes at sunrise at the Lars Homestead exterior on the Chott el Djerid 30 km west of Nefta, restored in 2012 by a fan-funded preservation project.

**The Berth.** Hotel Dar HI in Nefta for the Patrick Michel-designed eco-luxury palm-grove pavilions; the Anantara Tozeur Resort; the Hotel Sahara Palace in Nefta; or the Hotel Sidi Driss in Matmata for the canonical fan pilgrimage stay in Luke Skywalker’s actual underground homestead. Tunis arrival: The Residence Tunis or the Four Seasons at Gammarth. Le Maquam Azur in Tozeur for the smaller boutique-budget; Movenpick Hotel Tunis at the airport for the arrival-night dependable.

**The Galley.** Tozeur and Nefta: Le Petit Prince for the modern Tunisian fine-dining; Restaurant Diar Cheraiet for the canonical Tozeurian brik à l’oeuf and lamb mechoui; Nour El Ain for the couscous au mouton. Matmata: dining at Hotel Sidi Driss on the actual Star Wars set. Tunis: Dar El Jeld; Le Golfe at the Residence. Restaurant Le Berger in Tozeur old medina for the canonical brik à l’oeuf and ojja merguez; Restaurant Chams El Ain in Nefta for the canonical date-stuffed lamb in the palm grove.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Carthage* (Tunis Governorate, Tunisia). The ruined Punic capital razed by Rome in 146 BCE and rebuilt as Roman Carthage three centuries later, the Antonine Baths above the bay still the largest outside Italy; UNESCO 1979
2. *Amphitheatre of El Jem* (El Jem, Mahdia Governorate, Tunisia). The third-century Roman amphitheatre rising 35 metres from the flat Tunisian plain, the third-largest in the empire and the best-preserved in North Africa; UNESCO 1979, capacity 35,000 in a town of 12,000 today

### 3. Cinco de Mayo

**Port:** Puebla, Mexico
**Date:** Wed May 5
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Annual May 5 reenactment at the Forts of Loreto and Guadalupe in Puebla, Mexico, the May 5, 1862 battle in which a vastly outnumbered Mexican army under General Ignacio Zaragoza defeated the invading French Imperial forces, briefly halting Napoleon III’s intervention. The battle is more significant in Mexico (where it’s called the Día de la Batalla de Puebla and observed primarily in Puebla itself) than in the United States, where Cinco de Mayo has evolved into a broader celebration of Mexican-American heritage. Puebla itself is a UNESCO World Heritage Site with the most baroque churches per square block in the Americas.

**The Berth.** Mexico City: Las Alcobas; Four Seasons; Casa Habita. Oaxaca: Quinta Real; Los Amantes. Yucatán: Chablé Yucatán; Hacienda Temozón. In Puebla itself, the festival city: Banyan Tree Puebla at the foot of Popocatépetl for the contemporary luxury 30 minutes from city center; La Purificadora by Ricardo Legorreta on the Paseo San Francisco for the canonical Puebla design-boutique in the converted 1884 water- purification building.

**The Galley.** Mexico City: Pujol; Quintonil; Sud 777; Contramar. Oaxaca: Casa Oaxaca; Origen; Las Quince Letras. Yucatán: Kuuk in Mérida; Hartwood in Tulum. In Puebla: El Mural de los Poblanos in the Centro Histórico for canonical Pueblan tasting (mole poblano, chiles en nogada in season, chalupas, cemitas); Casa Reyna for the canonical Pueblan family table since 1900.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Historic Centre of Puebla* (Puebla, Mexico). The grid-plan colonial city of 1531, the cathedral's twin bell towers, the talavera-tile facades on every other house; UNESCO 1987, the city where mole poblano and chiles en nogada were both invented
2. *Great Pyramid of Cholula* (Cholula, Puebla, Mexico). The largest pyramid by volume on Earth, four hundred metres a side and twenty storeys high, the conquistadors built a church on the summit not knowing the hill itself was a temple; the Aztec ascent tunnels open to walkers

### 4. Brighton Festival

**Port:** Multiple venues across Brighton & Hove, East Sussex
**Date:** Sat May 1 – Sun May 23, 23 days
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

The 61st annual edition; the largest curated multi-arts festival in England, the global capital of British creative culture each May, and one of the great living arts festivals in Europe, three weeks each May when the seaside city of Brighton & Hove (combined population ~280,000, on the East Sussex coast 50 miles south of London) becomes the cultural center of England, hosting 200+ events across theatre, music, dance, circus, visual art, film, literature, debate, outdoor programming, and family events at venues throughout the city, alongside the parallel Brighton Fringe, the third-largest fringe festival in the world after Edinburgh and Adelaide, with 1,000+ open-access events. The festival was conceived in 1964 by Ian Hunter (the Scottish-born arts impresario who had previously co-founded the Edinburgh International Festival’s parallel programming); the Brighton Festival Society was formed in 1965, and the inaugural festival was held in 1967, featuring the first ever exhibition of Concrete Poetry in the UK (the visual-poetic art form pioneered in São Paulo in the 1950s by Brazilian artists Augusto and Haroldo de Campos with Décio Pignatari).

**The Berth.** London: The Connaught, The Beaumont, The Zetter Townhouse, or The Hoxton. Country: Heckfield Place, The Newt in Somerset, or Soho Farmhouse. In Brighton itself: The Grand Brighton on King’s Road, the 1864 Victorian seafront grand-dame; Drakes of Brighton on Marine Parade for the design-boutique seafront with the canonical festival-week base.

**The Galley.** London: St. John, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers; L’Enclume in Cumbria; or any local gastropub Sunday roast. In Brighton: The Salt Room at the Hilton Brighton Metropole for canonical Brighton seafood; The Little Fish Market on Upper Market Street for the eight-seat seasonal tasting menu by Duncan Ray.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Royal Pavilion* (Brighton, East Sussex, England, UK). John Nash's Indo-Saracenic seaside palace built 1815 to 1823 for the Prince Regent, onion domes and minarets over a banqueting room hung with a thirty-foot dragon chandelier; the most exotic building in England
2. *Seven Sisters Cliffs* (East Sussex, England, UK). The seven chalk headlands marching from Cuckmere Haven to Beachy Head, the unbuilt counterpart to the Dover cliffs; the South Downs Way runs along the top, the cliff retreating sixty centimetres a year
