### 5. Athens Street Food Festival

**Port:** Palio Amaxostasio OSY, Gazi-Kerameikos, Athens
**Date:** Fri–Sun May 21–23
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE, ART

The 12th annual edition; Greece’s largest food festival and the founding event of the modern Greek street-food movement, the marquee Athenian moment in the Mediterranean spring food calendar, a three-weekend, nine-day festival that draws 100,000+ visitors per edition to the post-industrial OSY Tram Depot in the Gazi-Kerameikos neighborhood, the city’s hipster-creative quarter beneath the Acropolis. Founded in 2016 by a small team of Athenian food entrepreneurs as a single-weekend showcase of international street food in a city that, until then, had no equivalent festival format outside the traditional taverna canon, the inaugural edition’s success was so immediate and so culturally galvanizing that it sparked an entire movement: dozens of new street-food trucks, restaurants, and chef-driven pop-up concepts across Greece have launched in the festival’s wake, transforming Greek food culture in less than a decade. The festival celebrated its 10th anniversary in 2026 and has become the cornerstone of Greece’s food calendar between Greek Orthodox Easter (Sunday May 2) and the start of the Athens & Epidaurus Festival in early June.

**The Berth.** Hotel Grande Bretagne on Syntagma, Acropolis from the rooftop; the Electra Metropolis for the budget choice; or the Margi in Vouliagmeni for the seaside. The Dolli in Plaka for the design- boutique two minutes from the Acropolis with the rooftop pool; Coco-Mat Athens BC at Asomaton for the design-budget boutique 10 minutes’ walk from the festival venue at Gazi.

**The Galley.** Vezené for new Greek; Spondi in Pangrati for the Michelin two-star; To Mavro Provato in Pangrati for canonical mezedes; Brettos in Plaka for the after-dinner ouzo. Diporto in the Central Market basement since 1887 for the canonical Athenian taverna; Café Avissinia in the flea-market square for the canonical mezze with live rebetiko.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Acropolis of Athens* (Athens, Greece). The marble citadel rising 156 metres above Athens, the Parthenon raised between 447 and 432 BCE in the brief age of Pericles; UNESCO 1987, the metopes still showing the centaurs and lapiths in their broken line above the columns
2. *Temple of Olympian Zeus* (Athens, Greece). The colossal sanctuary begun in the sixth century BCE by Peisistratos and finally finished by Hadrian seven hundred years later; fifteen of the original 104 Corinthian columns still standing 17 metres high

### 9. Memphis in May World Championship BBQ

**Port:** Liberty Park, Midtown Memphis, Tennessee
**Date:** Wed–Sat May 12–15, 4 days
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The 51st annual edition; the ’Super Bowl of Swine’, the largest pork barbecue contest in the world, the most celebrated BBQ competition on Earth, the foundation of American competition barbecue, and the most important event in the international BBQ calendar each year. Founded in 1978 as the marquee event of the broader Memphis in May International Festival (founded 1977), an annual month-long civic celebration that honors a different country each year and historically encompassed four major events: the Beale Street Music Festival (the iconic three-day rock/blues/soul festival paused after 2024), the World Championship Barbecue Cooking Contest (the festival’s enduring centerpiece), the Great American River Run, and the Sunset Symphony. The BBQ contest was envisioned as the city’s answer to the national debate about American barbecue regional supremacy: at a time in the late 1970s when Texas, Kansas City, and the Carolinas each claimed their own BBQ traditions, the founding committee asked: in Memphis, the city that smokes whole hog with the patience of a religious ritual and dry-rubs its ribs into Tennessee perfection, why don’t we crown a true world champion? The first contest in 1978 drew approximately 26 teams competing for $4,500 in prize money in a small Memphis park.

**The Berth.** The Peabody for the duck-march at five; or The Central Station for the railway-revival option. The Guest House at Graceland for the festival-pilgrimage Elvis-themed boutique at the gates of Graceland; Hotel Indigo Memphis Downtown for the modern dependable on Union Avenue.

**The Galley.** Central BBQ on Central Avenue for the dry-rub ribs; The Arcade Restaurant on South Main for the Elvis booth and breakfast; Charlie Vergos’ Rendezvous for the peppery sauceless ribs. Cozy Corner on North Parkway for the canonical Memphis Cornish hen barbecue and the wet-rub ribs; Payne’s Bar-B-Q on Lamar Avenue for the canonical Memphis chopped-pork sandwich on a slaw-dressed white-bread bun.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Graceland* (Memphis, Tennessee, USA). Elvis Presley's 1939 Colonial Revival mansion on a hill in south Memphis, bought in 1957 for $102,500, the rooms kept exactly as he left them in August 1977; second only to the White House in annual visitors
2. *National Civil Rights Museum & Lorraine Motel* (Memphis, Tennessee, USA). The motel where Martin Luther King was shot on the balcony of Room 306 on April 4, 1968, now the centerpiece of the country's main civil-rights museum; the wreath on the railing replaced each year on the anniversary

### 11. Fiestas de San Isidro Labrador

**Port:** Madrid, Spain
**Date:** Civic festival anchored Sat May 15
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD, ART

Patron saint’s feast day with surrounding programming approximately Sat May 8 – Sun May 16 (9 days); plus the parallel Feria Taurina de San Isidro at Plaza de Toros Monumental de Las Ventas running Sat May 1 – Sun Jun 13, the most important civic festival of Madrid’s annual calendar, the centerpiece of the Madrileño year, the single greatest concentration of traditional Castilian-Madrid culture on Earth, and one of the great spring festivals of the Iberian Peninsula. A layered nine-day civic celebration anchored on the Saturday May 15 feast day of Madrid’s patron saint, running concurrently with the Feria Taurina, the most acclaimed bullfighting fair in the world (the ’World Championship of Bullfighting’), held over the surrounding 44 days at Las Ventas. The festival honors San Isidro Labrador (Saint Isidore the Laborer/Farmer, c. 1070–1130), Madrid’s medieval patron saint, born in the modest village that would become Madrid, husband of Santa María de la Cabeza (Saint Mary of the Head, also canonized), a poor agricultural laborer in the service of the Vargas family for whom (per the medieval hagiographic tradition recorded by Juan Diácono) he was credited with more than 100 miracles, most famously his ability to find water.

**The Berth.** The Westin Palace on Plaza de las Cortes; The Ritz; the Mandarin Oriental Ritz; or the small NH Collection on Atocha for the budget. Bless Hotel Madrid on Calle Velázquez for the design-set Salamanca district boutique; Four Seasons Hotel Madrid at Centro Canalejas for the modern luxury.

**The Galley.** DiverXO for the splurge; Casa Lucio on Cava Baja for canonical Madrileño and the eggs; Botín on Cuchilleros, the world’s oldest restaurant; Café Comercial in Bilbao after midnight. Sacha in Tetuán for the canonical Madrid bistronomic destination; Sala de Despiece in Chamberí for the canonical contemporary tapas counter, Javier Bonet’s open-kitchen Spanish.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Plaza Mayor & Royal Palace* (Madrid, Spain). The 1620 enclosed square at the centre of the Habsburg capital and the white limestone Palacio Real four streets west, 3,418 rooms making it the largest functioning royal palace in Europe; the kings live elsewhere now, the state ceremonies still here
2. *Plaza de Cibeles* (Madrid, Spain). The neoclassical roundabout at the heart of Madrid, the chariot of the goddess Cybele in marble at the centre, the white Palacio de Comunicaciones cathedral-of-a-post-office on one corner; the fountain Real Madrid still climbs to celebrate

### 12. Cannes Film Festival

**Port:** Palais des Festivals, Cannes, French Riviera
**Date:** Tue–Sat May 11–22, 12 days
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

The 80th milestone edition; the world’s most prestigious film festival, the cultural capital of international cinema for nearly eight decades, the most photographed red carpet on Earth, eleven days each May when the small French Riviera resort town of Cannes (population 75,000) becomes the absolute center of the world’s film industry, drawing 35,000+ film professionals and 4,500+ journalists from 80+ countries to the seafront Palais des Festivals et des Congrès at the heart of La Croisette. Founded by French Minister of National Education Jean Zay in 1938, at the suggestion of historian Philippe Erlanger and film journalist Robert Favre Le Bret, as a deliberate counterweight to the Mussolini-influenced Venice Film Festival of the late 1930s (where Goebbels’ chosen films had repeatedly won the top prize), the inaugural Festival was scheduled for September 1, 1939 with the U.S. opening film The Hunchback of Notre Dame premiered the night of August 31. On September 1, the morning of the festival’s first official day, German troops invaded Poland; on September 3 France and the United Kingdom declared war on Germany; the Cannes Festival was cancelled and the building requisitioned for war use, the festival not opening until 1946.

**The Berth.** Hotel Martinez on the Croisette; the Carlton; or the Five Seas for the smaller-luxury option. Hôtel Barrière Le Majestic Cannes on the Croisette, the canonical 1926 festival grand-dame at the central red-carpet; Hôtel Belle Plage Cannes for the boutique-budget option on the western seafront.

**The Galley.** La Palme d’Or at the Martinez for the splurge; Astoux et Brun for the bouillabaisse; Vesuvio for the late-night pizza on Rue Félix Faure. La Petite Maison de Nicole on Rue Lieutenant Allard for canonical Niçoise rosé-and-petits-farcis lunch; Da Bouttau in the Old Town for canonical Cannes seafood lunch since 1860, the oldest restaurant in the city.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Promenade de la Croisette* (Cannes, French Riviera, France). The two-kilometre seafront boulevard between Pointe de la Croisette and Palais des Festivals, palms and Belle Époque hotels along one side, white sand and the Mediterranean on the other; the red carpet runs here each May
2. *Île Sainte-Marguerite & Fort Royal* (Lérins Islands, French Riviera, France). The pine-shaded island fifteen minutes off Cannes by ferry, the Fort Royal where the Man in the Iron Mask was kept from 1687 to 1698, his cell still preserved with its iron-grilled view of the bay

### 14. Pražské Jaro

**Port:** Rudolfinum & Obecní dům, Prague
**Date:** Wed May 12 – Thu Jun 3, ~3 weeks
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

The 82nd annual edition; one of the world’s most respected classical music festivals, the most renowned classical music event in the Czech Republic, twenty-four days each spring when the Czech capital becomes a stage for the world’s greatest orchestras, conductors, soloists, and chamber ensembles, with concerts spread across the spectacular Rudolfinum concert hall on the bank of the Vltava River, the Art Nouveau Obecní dům (Municipal House) with its Smetana Hall, and dozens of additional historic venues throughout one of Europe’s most architecturally beautiful cities. The festival was founded in 1946 as the first major cultural event in post-war Czechoslovakia, under the patronage of Czechoslovak president Edvard Beneš (the wartime government-in-exile leader who returned to Prague after liberation), and was conceived as both a celebration of the country’s restored independence after Nazi occupation and a deliberate cultural statement of European reintegration. The festival opens every year with Bedřich Smetana’s symphonic poem Má Vlast (“My Homeland”) on the anniversary of the composer’s death.

**The Berth.** Augustine Rosewood on Letenská Street; Mandarin Oriental in Malá Strana; or the Aria Hotel for the music-themed budget. Hotel U Prince on Old Town Square for the heritage boutique with the rooftop view of the astronomical clock; The Mosaic House in Vodičkova for the design-set budget boutique.

**The Galley.** Field on Pařížská for the Michelin tasting; Lokál in Old Town for canonical Czech; U Modré Kachničky for game and old Bohemia; Hemingway Bar after midnight. La Degustation Bohême Bourgeoise in Haštalská for the Michelin-starred Czech tasting menu; Café Savoy in Smíchov for the canonical Prague café since 1893 with the Vienna-style Sunday breakfast.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Charles Bridge & Prague Castle* (Prague, Czechia). The 1357 Gothic bridge raised by Charles IV across the Vltava lined with 30 baroque saints, the castle on the far hill the largest ancient castle complex in the world; UNESCO 1992 with the whole of historic Prague
2. *Astronomical Clock & Old Town Square* (Prague, Czechia). The fifteenth-century mechanical clock on the south wall of the Old Town Hall, the Walk of the Apostles passing the open shutters every hour; the cobbled square below ringed by Gothic and baroque spires Kafka grew up among

### 17. Fátima Pilgrimage

**Port:** Sanctuary of Fátima, Cova da Iria, Portugal
**Date:** Wed–Thu May 12–13
**Flags:** CULTURE

Annual May pilgrimage commemorating the first apparition of the Virgin Mary to three shepherd children, Lúcia dos Santos, Francisco Marto, and Jacinta Marto, on May 13, 1917; one of the largest Marian pilgrimages on Earth, drawing 250,000–500,000 pilgrims to the small town two hours north of Lisbon. The May 12 evening Candlelight Procession from the Capelinha das Aparições is the central spectacle: a sea of white-clad pilgrims walking by candlelight, with the Pilgrim Statue of Our Lady of Fátima carried at the front; the May 13 morning Mass on the Sanctuary esplanade and the Procession of Farewell with the Pilgrim Virgin’s blessing close the pilgrimage. The October 12–13 anniversary pilgrimage commemorating the Miracle of the Sun draws comparable numbers; many pilgrims walk the final kilometres on their knees across the esplanade. Confirmed Catholic site since the 1930 Vatican investigation; Pope Francis canonized Francisco and Jacinta here in 2017.

**The Berth.** Lisbon: Bairro Alto Hotel; Memmo Alfama; Santa Clara 1728. Porto: The Yeatman; Vincci Porto. Algarve: Vila Vita Parc. In Fátima itself: Hotel Fátima Boutique on Rua Jacinta Marto for the canonical pilgrim-base; Hotel Domus Pacis Fátima, the religious-order-run pilgrim hotel directly opposite the Sanctuary. In Tomar 35 minutes south for the Templar-castle side trip: Hotel dos Templários for the heritage castle-view stay.

**The Galley.** Lisbon: Belcanto; Cervejaria Ramiro; Pastéis de Belém. Porto: The Yeatman dining room; Cantinho do Avillez; the Mercado do Bolhão. Algarve: regional grilled fish at any cataplana taberna. In Fátima: Tia Alice on Rua do Adro for the canonical rural Portuguese, the chanfana lamb stew, the bacalhau à Brás. In Tomar: Casa Matreno for the canonical tablecloth-and-wine.

**The Bearings.**

2. *Alcobaça Monastery* (Alcobaça, Portugal). The Cistercian church founded 1153 with the longest nave in Portugal, the tombs of Pedro and Inês de Castro carved face-to-face so they will rise together at the last judgement; UNESCO 1989

**The Galley.** Amsterdam: De Kas; De Compagnon; Mata Hari; Café de Klos. The Hague: Restaurant Calla’s; Catch by Simonis for the harbour. In Vorden: Bistro Pallandt van Keppel at Hotel Pallandt van Keppel for the canonical Achterhoek country dining; in Arnhem: Maaltijd & Co for the modern Dutch tasting menu.

2. *Het Loo Palace* (Apeldoorn, Gelderland, Netherlands). The Dutch baroque country palace begun 1684 for William III and Mary II, the formal axial gardens excavated from beneath an English landscape lawn and reinstated in the 1970s exactly as Daniel Marot drew them

### 20. Sanja Matsuri

**Port:** Asakusa, Tokyo
**Date:** Fri–Sun May 14–16
**Flags:** CULTURE

Tokyo’s wildest summer festival, held over the third weekend of May at Sensō-ji Temple in Asakusa, the largest Shinto matsuri in the city, drawing 1.8 million visitors across three days to celebrate the three founders of Sensō-ji (the Hinokuma brothers and Hajinomatsuchi who, according to legend, found a small statue of Kannon in the Sumida River in 628 CE). Officially known as Asakusa Jinja Reitaisai, the popular name Sanja Matsuri (’Three Shrine Festival’) refers to the three founding figures whose enshrined kami are the spiritual focus. 100+ portable shrines (mikoshi) are carried through the streets by 9,000 men and women in matching happi coats; the yakuza presence is famously visible (chest tattoos shown openly only this weekend).

**The Berth.** Park Hyatt Tokyo for the Lost-In-Translation view; The Aman Tokyo in Otemachi; or the Hoshinoya for Edo restraint. The Tokyo Edition Toranomon for the modern luxury by Ian Schrager; Trunk Hotel Yoyogi Park for the design-set boutique with the Yoyogi Park terraces.

**The Galley.** Sushi Saito for the omakase ritual (book three months ahead); Tsuta for the first Michelin-starred ramen; Birdland for yakitori; Den for new kaiseki. Ushinomiya in Asakusa for the canonical festival-week yakiniku across from the Sensō-ji approach; Daikokuya Tempura on Asakusa’s Edo Street since 1887 for the canonical tendon, fried prawn-and-vegetable rice bowl.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Sensō-ji Temple* (Asakusa, Tokyo, Japan). The oldest temple in Tokyo, founded 645 around a Kannon statue pulled from the Sumida by two fishermen; through the giant red Kaminarimon lantern, the Sanja shrine beside it dedicated to the same three
2. *Meiji Shrine* (Shibuya, Tokyo, Japan). The Shinto shrine of 1920 dedicated to Emperor Meiji and Empress Shoken, set in 70 hectares of forest planted from 100,000 trees donated by people across Japan; the largest torii in Tokyo at the south entrance

Largest music festival in Africa and one of the largest in the world, founded 2001 under the patronage of King Mohammed VI, over 2.5 million attendees across six stages: Bouregreg (Western pop, free entry), OLM Souissi (Arabic and African headliners), Salé (traditional Moroccan and Sufi), and three smaller venues. ### 24. BottleRock Napa Valley

**Port:** Napa Valley Expo, Napa, California
**Date:** Fri–Sun May 28–30
**Flags:** ART, FOOD, CULTURE

The 15th annual Memorial Day weekend edition; the most distinguished music-and-food festival in California, the spiritual launch of the American summer festival season, and the most successful fusion of music, wine, and culinary programming in the U.S. festival calendar, three days when the small city of Napa (population 79,000) becomes the convergence point of America’s biggest pop and rock acts, the country’s most accomplished chefs, and the entire Napa Valley wine industry, drawing 120,000+ attendees over three days to the 30-acre Napa Valley Expo fairgrounds in downtown Napa. Founded in 2013 by Napa entrepreneurs Bob Vogt, Gabe Meyers, and Jordan Stein as a deliberately wine-country-themed alternative to the Coachella/Bonnaroo dust-and-camping festival format. The founding premise: a music festival held within walking distance of restaurants and hotels, with wine and chef programming as foundational features rather than afterthoughts, in the most beautiful agricultural landscape in California. After serious financial difficulties in the inaugural 2013 edition, the festival was acquired by Latitude 38 Entertainment in 2014, which deepened the wine-and-food integration with the Napa Valley Vintners trade association.

**The Berth.** Auberge du Soleil in Rutherford on the hillside; Meadowood; Bardessono in Yountville; or Cottages of Napa Valley for the budget-classic. The Carneros Resort & Spa at the southern end of the Valley for the canonical Carneros cottage-style; Stanly Ranch, Auberge Resorts in the southernmost Napa for the modern luxury working-ranch retreat.

**The Galley.** The French Laundry (Thomas Keller), book three months ahead; Bouchon for the bistro; SingleThread in Healdsburg for the Sonoma equivalent; Oxbow Public Market in downtown Napa for the lunch graze. Press in St. Helena for the canonical Napa steakhouse and wine cellar with the 12,000+ bottle Napa Valley wine list; Charter Oak in St. Helena for the modern Californian by Chris Kostow.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Robert Mondavi Winery* (Oakville, Napa Valley, California, USA). The 1966 Cliff May mission-revival winery on Highway 29 that built modern American fine wine, Robert Mondavi's bell tower the gateway to Napa from the south; the To-Kalon vineyard behind it growing fruit since 1868
2. *Old Faithful Geyser of California* (Calistoga, Napa Valley, California, USA). The cold-water geyser at the head of the valley erupting every twenty to ninety minutes to eighteen metres, one of three Old Faithfuls in the world; the Calistoga mud baths a half-mile down the road

### 27. Cooper’s Hill Cheese-Rolling

**Port:** Cooper's Hill, Brockworth, Gloucestershire, UK
**Date:** Mon May 31
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

The annual Spring Bank Holiday Monday lunacy near Brockworth, Gloucestershire, in which dozens of competitors throw themselves down a 1:2 slope after a wheel of Double Gloucester cheese, first to the bottom (alive) wins the cheese. Unbroken tradition since at least 1826; the slope so steep that injuries are routine and ambulances are pre-positioned at the foot. Four men’s downhill races, the women’s downhill, and the children’s uphill. The crowd packs the slope; bring sturdy shoes and a flexible pain threshold.

**The Berth.** London anchored: The Connaught, The Beaumont, The Zetter Townhouse, or the Hoxton. Country: Heckfield Place, The Pig hotels, or Soho Farmhouse. In the Cotswolds: The Wild Rabbit at Kingham for the canonical Cotswolds modern British pub-with-rooms by Lady Bamford; The Bell at Sapperton for the canonical Gloucestershire village pub, the local Old Spot pork pie.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Gloucester Cathedral* (Gloucester, Gloucestershire, England, UK). The Norman abbey church begun 1089 and finished as Perpendicular Gothic in the fourteenth century, the fan-vaulted cloister the first of its kind in England; the Harry Potter Hogwarts corridors filmed in its quiet shadows
2. *Berkeley Castle* (Berkeley, Gloucestershire, England, UK). The pink-sandstone castle held by the Berkeley family without interruption since 1153, the only castle in England to make that claim; Edward II murdered here in September 1327 in a cell on the inner court

### 28. Cheung Chau Bun Festival

**Port:** Cheung Chau Island, Hong Kong
**Date:** 8th day of the 4th lunar month (mid-May)
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Cheung Chau (literally ’Long Island’) is a small dumbbell-shaped island in the southwest Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, 10 km offshore from Central, reached by a 35-minute ferry from Pier 5 of the Central Ferry Pier. Population 23,000, predominantly Cantonese fishing-village heritage. The Bun Festival is the island’s signature annual event, inscribed on China’s National Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2011 and unique to Cheung Chau. Its origin traces to an 18th-century plague that killed many islanders; survivors pledged to the Pak Tai (Northern Emperor) and the deity led them to drive out the evil spirits, after which they began the annual Bun Festival as a thanksgiving rite. Three iconic features make it unmistakable: (1) the Bun Towers, three 20-metre conical towers built from steel scaffolding and covered in 9,000 lucky pink-and-white sweet steamed buns, erected outside the Pak Tai Temple; the climactic event is the midnight Bun Scrambling Competition on the 8th day, where 12 competitors race to the top of the central tower to grab as many buns as possible, the highest-placed buns being the luckiest. (2) The Children’s Floating Parade, preschoolers dressed as historical or contemporary Chinese figures appear to ’float’ in mid-air via hidden steel frames, paraded through the streets the morning of the festival. (3) The three-day vegetarian observance, the entire island goes vegetarian for the festival’s three days; even McDonald’s on Cheung Chau serves only mushroom burgers and vegetarian dishes during the period.

**The Berth.** On Cheung Chau: Warwick Hotel Cheung Chau, the only proper hotel on the island and the sole option for the festival night. In central Hong Kong (35 minutes by ferry): The Peninsula Hong Kong in Tsim Sha Tsui for the canonical 1928 grand-dame; Mandarin Oriental Hong Kong in Central for the modern luxury.

**The Galley.** On Cheung Chau during the festival (all vegetarian): Ming Hing Bakery for the canonical Ping On (Peace) buns, the official festival bun, available all year. In central Hong Kong post-festival: Lung King Heen at the Four Seasons for the three-Michelin-star Cantonese; Yat Lok in Central for canonical roast goose.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Tian Tan Buddha* (Po Lin Monastery, Lantau Island, Hong Kong). The 34-metre bronze Buddha seated on his lotus throne at the top of 268 granite steps, completed 1993; the cable car from Tung Chung climbs four kilometres of ridge to reach him
2. *Cheung Po Tsai Cave* (Cheung Chau Island, Hong Kong). The narrow granite cleft on the southwest shore of Cheung Chau where the early-nineteenth-century pirate Cheung Po Tsai is said to have hidden his treasure; a fishing village still on the harbour, no cars on the island

### 29. Quyllur Rit’i

**Port:** Sinakara Valley, Vilcanota Range, Cusco, Peru
**Date:** Fri–Sun May 14–16 (Pentecost weekend)
**Flags:** CULTURE

The most spectacular Andean pilgrimage on Earth, observed over Pentecost weekend at the foot of Sinakara mountain, 4,750 metres above sea level in the Vilcanota mountain range, 100 km east of Cusco. Held in honor of El Señor de Q’oyllur Rit’i (the Lord of the Snow Star), the image of Christ said to have appeared to a Quechua shepherd boy named Mariano Mayta in 1780. The festival is, more fundamentally, the deepest surviving expression of Andean Catholicism’s syncretic fusion with pre-Hispanic Quechua spirituality, timed to coincide with the pre-Inca observance of the Pleiades constellation’s return to the night sky (Qollqa), which signaled the agricultural new year in the Inca calendar. UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage since 2011. Three days of religious processions: dancers from eight Quechua villages (the ’nations’ of Q’oyoriti) climb to the high altar in the alpine basin in matching ñawpaq qhari and ukuku costumes (the ukukus are the trickster bear-mountain spirit dancers); 90,000+ pilgrims walk the 8 km from Mahuayani village up the canyon to the basin altar. The most spiritually charged moment is the pre-dawn descent of the ukukus from the glacier above the basin, who carry blocks of glacial ice back down to be melted into holy water. Physically punishing: high altitude, freezing nights, no running water, no electricity in the basin camp. One of the most rewarding spiritual experiences in the Americas.

**The Berth.** In Cusco (the staging base): Belmond Hotel Monasterio in the converted 1592 Jesuit monastery on Plazoleta Nazarenas for the canonical Cusco grand-dame; Inkaterra La Casona for the Relais & Châteaux 16th-century mansion. At Mahuayani (the trailhead): camping at the festival ground only.

**The Galley.** In Cusco: Cicciolina on Triunfo Street for the canonical Cusco bohemian fine-dining; Chicha por Gastón Acurio on Plaza Regocijo for the canonical Andean modern by Peru’s most famous chef; Mil in the Sacred Valley at 3,680 metres for chef Virgilio Martínez’s altitude-laboratory tasting menu.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Machu Picchu* (Cusco Region, Peru). The fifteenth-century Inca citadel set at 2,430 metres on a ridge between Huayna Picchu and the Vilcanota, never found by the conquistadors, brought to the world by Hiram Bingham in 1911; UNESCO 1983
2. *Sacsayhuamán* (Cusco, Peru). The Inca fortress on the hill above Cusco, walls of 200-tonne andesite blocks fitted without mortar so tightly a knife will not pass between, the Spaniards quarrying the upper courses to build the colonial city below

### 30. Vivid Sydney

**Port:** Sydney CBD waterfront, NSW, Australia
**Date:** late May through mid-June, 23 nights
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

The largest festival of light, music, and ideas in the southern hemisphere, Sydney’s marquee winter event, founded 2009 by Tourism New South Wales as a deliberate civic experiment to fill the city’s tourism shoulder season between the autumn cruise calendar and the August school-holiday surge. Across 23 nights in late May through mid-June, the entire CBD waterfront becomes a free outdoor gallery: the iconic Vivid Light projection-mapping of the Sydney Opera House sails (the festival’s signature image, with a different international artist commission each year), the Customs House at Circular Quay, the Museum of Contemporary Art on the West Circular Quay, the Sydney Harbour Bridge pylons, and the Royal Botanic Garden running 18 km of curated light installations from interactive sculptures to laser-and-sound shows. Parallel programming includes Vivid Music (200+ acts across small Sydney venues, focused on emerging Australian and Asia-Pacific electronic acts), Vivid Ideas (a TED-style talks program at Carriageworks in Eveleigh), and Vivid Food (chef collaborations across waterfront restaurants). The festival draws 2.5 million attendees annually and has spawned imitators, Singapore’s i Light, Lyon’s Fête des Lumières co-development partnerships, and Melbourne’s White Night.

**The Berth.** Park Hyatt Sydney at Hickson Road for the Harbour-and-Opera-House views from every window, the festival’s visual epicenter; Capella Sydney in the converted Department of Education building on Loftus Street for the contemporary luxury walking distance to the Royal Botanic Garden light walk.

**The Galley.** Quay at Overseas Passenger Terminal for chef Peter Gilmore’s canonical Sydney harbour-side fine-dining with the Opera House at the table; Bennelong inside the Opera House itself for the city-icon dining beneath the sails by Peter Gilmore.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Royal Botanic Garden Sydney* (Sydney, New South Wales, Australia). The 1816 harbourside botanic garden on Farm Cove, the first farm of the colony and now the green crescent between the Opera House and Mrs Macquarie's Chair; the country's national herbarium founded here
2. *The Rocks Historic Precinct* (Sydney, New South Wales, Australia). The sandstone-and-shingle alleys at the western foot of the Harbour Bridge, the original 1788 settlement of the First Fleet, the oldest pub in Australia still pouring; the weekend market the city's loudest

### 1. Documenta 16

**Port:** Kassel, Germany
**Date:** June through September
**Flags:** ART

Held every five years in Kassel, Germany since 1955; the most important contemporary art exhibition in the world after the Venice Biennale, founded by Arnold Bode as a deliberate post-war reckoning with the Nazi era’s suppression of modernist art. Documenta 16 spans 100 days across multiple venues, the Fridericianum (among the earliest purpose-built public museums in Europe, 1779), the Documenta Halle, the Neue Galerie, and dozens of unconventional sites scattered across the city. Each edition is shaped by a different artistic director with near-total curatorial freedom, producing a show that functions as a five-year temperature check on contemporary art’s most urgent conversations. Three days minimum to walk the principal venues; ICE train from Frankfurt or Berlin.

**The Berth.** Berlin: Hotel Adlon Kempinski; Soho House Berlin; 25hours Bikini. Munich: Bayerischer Hof. Hamburg: The Fontenay. Frankfurt: Roomers. In Kassel itself: Schlosshotel Bad Wilhelmshöhe in the converted ducal hunting palace above the Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe (UNESCO site); Hotel Stadthotel Kassel for the modern boutique-budget walking distance to the Fridericianum.

**The Galley.** Berlin: Markthalle Neun; Mustafa’s Gemüse Kebap; Lode & Stijn. Munich: Tantris; Hofbräuhaus; Schneider Bräuhaus. Hamburg: Fischmarkt; Bullerei. Frankfurt: Adolf Wagner; Lafleur. In Kassel: Park Restaurant Schöne Aussicht at the Bergpark for canonical Hessen regional cooking with the view over the cascades; Voit Bohème on Wilhelmshöher Allee for the modern German bistronomy.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Bergpark Wilhelmshöhe* (Kassel, Hesse, Germany). The 240-hectare baroque-and-romantic hill park ascending to the giant Hercules monument, the water cascades flowing every Wednesday and Sunday afternoon between May and October; UNESCO 2013, the largest hillside park in Europe
2. *Brothers Grimm Museum & Schloss Wilhelmshöhe* (Kassel, Hesse, Germany). The white neoclassical palace at the foot of the Bergpark, the Grimm brothers' collected fairy tales archived inside; Rembrandt's Saskia van Uylenburgh and Rubens's Crowning of the Virtuous Hero both kept here

Cinc Sentits on Carrer d’Aribau for the Michelin-starred Catalan tasting menu; Bar Mut on Pau Claris for the canonical Barcelona neighborhood gastrobar.

1. *Casa Batlló & Casa Milà* (Passeig de Gràcia, Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain). Two of Gaudí's modernista apartment blocks on the city's grand promenade, one with a dragon-scale ceramic roof and balcony masks, the other an undulating limestone wave with chimney warriors on the roof; UNESCO 1984
2. *Gothic Quarter & Barcelona Cathedral* (Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain). The medieval core between the Ramblas and the Via Laietana, narrow stone alleys widening at the Plaça del Rei and the fourteenth-century cathedral whose 28-metre cloister keeps 13 geese, one for each year Saint Eulàlia lived before her martyrdom

### 4. Fes Festival of World Sacred Music

**Port:** Fes, Morocco
**Date:** Fri–Sat early-mid June, 9 days
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

Designated by the United Nations in 2001 as a major event contributing to the dialogue of civilizations; founded 1994. Sacred music traditions from across world religions performed in the courtyards of the Fes medina (UNESCO-listed since 1981), inside Bab Al Makina palace gates, and at the Batha Museum gardens. Sufi qawwali from Pakistan, Tibetan Buddhist throat singing, Coptic chant, Ashkenazi cantorial, Andalusian classical, all in one of the world’s great medieval cities.

**The Berth.** La Mamounia in Marrakech, the gardens, the bar, the riad rooms; or Royal Mansour for the riad-of-riads; or the smaller Riad El Fenn for the boutique. In Fes itself, the festival city: Riad Fes Relais & Châteaux in the Fes el-Bali medina for the converted- palace luxury; Hotel Sahrai on a hilltop above the medina for the modern luxury with views; Palais Faraj in Fes Jdid for the 19th-century palace boutique.

**The Galley.** Le Tobsil in Marrakech for the canonical pastilla; La Maison Arabe for the cooking school dinner; Café Clock in the medina for the camel burger. In Fes: La Maison Bleue in Bab Boujloud for the canonical Fessi fine-dining since 1990 in the converted family palace; Café Clock Fes for the camel burger and the cooking-school evenings; Restaurant Numero 7 for the chef’s table modern Moroccan-Mediterranean.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Fes el-Bali Medina* (Fes, Morocco). The walled ninth-century city of nine thousand alleys, the world's largest car-free urban area, the leather tanneries still using the indigo and saffron vats of the eleventh century; UNESCO 1981
2. *Volubilis* (Meknes Province, Morocco). The Roman provincial capital of Mauretania Tingitana, abandoned around 285 CE, the great floor mosaics still in their original triclinia under the Atlas light; UNESCO 1997, the storks nesting on the basilica

### 5. Gnaoua World Music Festival

**Port:** Essaouira, Morocco
**Date:** mid-June
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

Four-day Gnaoua World Music Festival in Essaouira, Morocco, held annually in late June on the Atlantic coast, founded 1998 to showcase the spiritual trance music of the Gnaoua people (descendants of West African enslaved people brought to Morocco) in fusion with jazz, blues, and global music. 500,000 attendees free across the medina’s open-air stages; the lila ceremonies (all-night Gnaoua spiritual rituals) run in private spaces for invited audiences. Essaouira itself is a UNESCO-listed 18th-century walled port, the Mogador of medieval traders.

**The Berth.** La Mamounia in Marrakech; or Royal Mansour for the riad-of-riads; or Riad El Fenn for the boutique. In Essaouira itself, the festival is here: Heure Bleue Palais Relais & Châteaux in the converted 19th-century riad on the medina ramparts; Riad Watier for the design-boutique in a 200-year-old riad five minutes from the harbour; Le Jardin des Douars outside the medina for the eco-luxury Atlantic-coast garden retreat.

**The Galley.** Le Tobsil in Marrakech; La Maison Arabe for the cooking school; Café Clock in the medina for the camel burger; Mechoui Alley for the lamb. In Essaouira: Umia on Rue de la Skala for the contemporary Mediterranean-Moroccan in the medina; La Table by Madada for the canonical Essaouira seafood tasting menu.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Essaouira Medina* (Essaouira, Morocco). The eighteenth-century Atlantic fortress-town designed by a French prisoner of the Alaouite sultan Sidi Mohammed, white houses with blue shutters behind the bronze cannons of the Skala; UNESCO 2001, the trade winds rising every afternoon
2. *Marrakech Medina* (Marrakech, Morocco). The eleventh-century Almoravid capital with the Koutoubia minaret rising 77 metres above the souks, the Jemaa el-Fnaa snake-charmers' square spread out beneath the High Atlas; UNESCO 1985

The showcase event that replaced E3, the gaming industry’s annual marquee announcement showcase, founded 2020 by Geoff Keighley, broadcast live globally and supported by satellite events at major studios across LA throughout the same week. ### 7. Hampton Blackbeard Festival

**Port:** Hampton, Virginia
**Date:** Fri–Sun June 4–6
**Flags:** PIRATE

The original Blackbeard festival, in its 23rd year, commemorating the November 1718 capture of Blackbeard’s severed head and the trial of his crew at the Hampton courthouse, three days of fully costumed pirate camps along the downtown Hampton waterfront, replica ship cannon battles in Hampton River, and the historic Blackbeard’s Crew Trial reenactment Saturday afternoon.

The largest living-history museum in the United States, the eighteenth-century Virginia colonial capital restored across 300 acres with 88 original buildings and forty trades practised in period dress; the Capitol where Henry first spoke of treason
2. *Mariners' Museum & USS Monitor Center* (Newport News, Virginia, USA). The largest maritime museum in the western hemisphere, the recovered turret of the USS Monitor that fought the Merrimack at Hampton Roads in March 1862 displayed in a glass conservation tank with the gun-port shutters still visible

### 8. Festas de Lisboa

**Port:** Lisbon, Portugal
**Date:** Sat–Sun Jun 12–13
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Feast day of Santo António de Lisboa; the climax of the city’s month-long Santos Populares celebration. Night of June 12: the historic Marchas Populares parade down Avenida da Liberdade, neighborhood marching groups in elaborate costumes choreographed for a full year, judged competitively, the Mouraria, Alfama, and Bairro Alto Marchas are the rivals. Across Alfama, Mouraria, Bica, and Madragoa every doorway and balcony is hung with paper streamers and colored lanterns; sardinhas assadas grilling on every corner with bifanas, caldo verde, and cold imperial Sagres beer; manjericos (basil pots) sold at every kiosk with poetic verses tucked among the leaves as gifts to lovers. The morning of June 13 brings the Casamentos de Santo António, the city-sponsored mass weddings of dozens of Lisbon couples in Sé Cathedral, the saint of love invoked. Arrive on Avenida da Liberdade by 7 p.m. on June 12 for the parade.

**The Berth.** Bairro Alto Hotel on Praça Luís de Camões; the Pestana Pousada de Lisboa; or the Lumiares for the budget. Memmo Alfama Hotel in the Alfama quarter for the rooftop- pool boutique with Tagus views over the Marchas Populares route; Hotel da Estrela in Lapa for the design-boutique walking distance to the Madragoa Santos Populares celebration.

**The Galley.** Belcanto by José Avillez for the splurge; Cervejaria Ramiro in Anjos for shellfish; Time Out Market for the canonical Lisbon round; A Cevicheria in Príncipe Real. Mini Bar by José Avillez at the São Luiz Theatre for the cocktail-tasting cousin of Belcanto; A Travessa in Madragoa for the canonical Belgian-Portuguese in the converted 17th- century convent.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Castelo de São Jorge* (Lisbon, Portugal). The Moorish hilltop castle whose stones see every century of Lisbon from the eighth to the present, taken by Afonso Henriques in 1147 and royal residence for three hundred years; the peacocks now keep the walls
2. *Sé de Lisboa* (Lisbon, Portugal). The Romanesque cathedral begun 1147 on the foundations of a mosque, twin bell towers like a fortress, the rose window the only piece of Gothic to survive the 1755 earthquake; the cloister excavations exposing a Roman street below

### 9. Cannabis Liberation Day

**Port:** Flevopark, Amsterdam, Netherlands
**Date:** Sun Jun 13 (second Sunday of June)
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

The 19th annual edition of Cannabis Bevrijdingsdag, the Dutch cannabis-culture festival held each second Sunday of June at Flevopark on Amsterdam’s eastern edge; the Netherlands’ canonical annual gathering of the cannabis community and the European counterweight to the American 4/20 tradition, set in the city that has anchored European cannabis culture for half a century. Founded in 2009 by the VOC (the League for the Lifting of the Cannabis Prohibition), the festival’s stated mission is full Dutch legalization, the famous Amsterdam coffee shops have been tolerated since 1976 under the gedoogbeleid (toleration policy) for the front-door retail sale of small quantities, while the back-door supply chain (cultivation and wholesale) has remained illegal, the long-running paradox the festival exists to protest. Free entry, ~50,000 attendees across the day, with music stages featuring Dutch and international reggae, dub, and electronic acts. Pair with the Hash Marihuana & Hemp Museum in Damrak (the world’s first cannabis museum, since 1985); Cannabis College in De Wallen; the historic coffee shops.

**The Berth.** The Dylan Amsterdam on Keizersgracht for the canonical canal-house luxury in a 1626 merchant residence; Hotel Pulitzer on Prinsengracht for the 25 connected 17th-century canal houses; Hotel De L’Europe since 1896; Conservatorium Hotel; The Hoxton Amsterdam on Herengracht. W Amsterdam at Spuistraat for the design-set rooftop pool; Sir Albert Amsterdam in De Pijp for the design-boutique near the Albert Cuyp Market.

**The Galley.** De Kas in Frankendael Park for the canonical greenhouse-to-table; De Silveren Spiegel since 1614 for the oldest restaurant in Amsterdam; Vermeer at NH Barbizon Palace; Rijks at the Rijksmuseum; Toscanini in the Jordaan; Café Loetje; Albert Cuyp Market; Tempo Doeloe for the canonical Indonesian rijsttafel. Choux on Plantage Doklaan for the modern vegetable-forward tasting; Lt Cornelis in Westerdoksdijk for the modern Dutch with the canonical Sunday brunch.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Rijksmuseum* (Amsterdam, Netherlands). Pierre Cuypers's 1885 Dutch Renaissance Revival temple of national art, the Night Watch hanging in its purpose-built Gallery of Honour, Vermeer's Milkmaid in a hush four rooms away; reopened 2013 after a decade of restoration
2. *Anne Frank House* (Amsterdam, Netherlands). The seventeenth-century canal-side warehouse on Prinsengracht 263 whose secret annex hid the Frank family from July 1942 to August 1944, the diary discovered on the floor; the swinging bookcase still set against the entry

### 12. Rouen Armada

**Port:** Rouen, Normandy, France
**Date:** Tue–Fri June 8–18

Held every 4–5 years; the largest gathering of tall ships in the world, hosted along the Seine river quays of Rouen, typically 40+ tall ships and naval vessels from across Europe and beyond moored end-to-end across the city’s waterfront, all open to public boarding (free entry). ### 13. CMA Fest

**Port:** Downtown Nashville, Tennessee
**Date:** Thu–Sun Jun 3–6, 4 days
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE, FOOD

The 56th annual edition of the festival born as Fan Fair in 1972; the longest-running country music festival in the world, the central event in the global country music calendar, central to the Nashville music economy, the most artist-fan-relationship-driven major music festival on Earth, four days each early June when downtown Nashville transforms into the global epicenter of country music. Hundreds of artists performing across multiple daytime stages across the city center, plus four nights of headlining concerts at the 69,143-seat Nissan Stadium (home of the NFL’s Tennessee Titans), drawing 90,000+ daily attendees from all 50 U.S. states and 39+ countries to the city that BBC, AP, and Rolling Stone have all called ’Music City.’ The festival’s distinctive ethos: artists donate their time to perform, they are not paid for festival appearances, so that ticket proceeds directly benefit music education through the CMA Foundation, with over $27 million invested in music education programs across the United States since the partnership began in 2006.

**The Berth.** The Hermitage Hotel since 1910, Tennessee’s grand dame; Bobby Hotel for the modern; The Joseph for the design-set. Thompson Nashville in the Gulch for the design-set boutique; The Hutton Hotel on West End Avenue for the music-themed boutique with the Analog at the Hutton listening room.

**The Galley.** Husk Nashville; Rolf and Daughters; Arnold’s Country Kitchen for meat-and-three; Hattie B’s for hot chicken; Pancake Pantry for breakfast. The Catbird Seat for the canonical Nashville tasting menu, chef’s-counter seating around the open kitchen; Carne Mare at the W Nashville for the modern Italian by Andrew Carmellini.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Grand Ole Opry House* (Nashville, Tennessee, USA). The 4,400-seat barn-roofed home of the world's longest-running radio broadcast since 1974, six feet of the old Ryman stage cut and inset into the Opry circle so every performer still stands on the same wood
2. *Ryman Auditorium* (Nashville, Tennessee, USA). The 1892 brick tabernacle that became the Mother Church of country music when the Opry moved in for thirty-one years from 1943, the pews still in place; the acoustics rated by Travel + Leisure the best in America

### 14. The Governors Ball Music Festival

**Port:** Flushing Meadows-Corona Park, Queens, NYC
**Date:** Fri–Sun Jun 4–6
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE, FOOD

The 17th annual edition; the trademark New York City music festival, the defining event of New York’s summer music calendar, the largest annual music gathering in the largest American city, three days when the historic 1,255-acre park that hosted both the 1939 and 1964 New York World’s Fairs becomes the convergence point of contemporary American and international pop, rock, hip-hop, electronic, indie, and global music programming, drawing 150,000+ attendees across the three days to the iconic Queens park where the Unisphere, the 12-story stainless-steel globe sculpture that is Queens’ most recognizable landmark, anchors the festival site directly between the Astronaut Court and the iconic Queens Museum. The festival was launched in 2011 by three young New York entrepreneurs Jordan Wolowitz, Tom Russell, and Yoni Reisman through Founders Entertainment. The founding premise: New York City, the world’s most consequential music city, the home of the American music industry, deserved a major outdoor music festival worthy of the metropolis.

The Greenwich Hotel in Tribeca for the design-set Robert De Niro boutique with the in-house Locanda Verde; The Beekman, A Thompson Hotel in the Financial District for the heritage Victorian rotunda.

2. *Empire State Building* (Manhattan, New York, USA). The 1931 Art Deco limestone shaft topped by a mooring mast that never moored a single airship, 102 storeys raised in 410 days during the Depression; the world's tallest building until 1970, the spire lit a different colour every night

### 15. Bonnaroo Music and Arts Festival

**Port:** Great Stage Park, Manchester, Tennessee
**Date:** Thu–Sun Jun 10–13
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

The 25th anniversary edition; the Glastonbury of the United States, the highest-tier destination camping music festival in North America, four days each mid-June when the rural Tennessee dairy-and-cattle farm 60 miles southeast of Nashville becomes a temporary city of 80,000+ attendees camped across the 700-acre Great Stage Park farm, with 150+ musical performances across multiple stages running essentially 24 hours a day from Wednesday-evening campground openings through Sunday-night closing sets, plus comedy, cinema, sustainability workshops, art installations, and the iconic communal camping and music festival ethos that has defined the American festival movement of the 21st century. The festival’s name Bonnaroo is Creole-Cajun French slang for ’a really good time,’ derived from the Louisiana French expression bon à rouler or the Cajun-Creole bonne à rou, a deliberate gesture toward the Louisiana-French roots of the American Deep South and the festival’s spiritual claim to inherit the post-Woodstock American jam-band tradition through a Crescent City lens.

**The Berth.** Most attendees camp on-site at Great Stage Park, the festival’s official 700-acre tent-and-RV city. Off-site: The Hermitage in Nashville, The Joseph, Bobby Hotel, or the historic Manchester Inn 5 miles from the festival gates. Soho House Nashville in the Gulch for the design-boutique private- members hotel; Holston House Nashville for the heritage 1928 boutique on Hayes Street.

**The Galley.** Festival-week: 50+ on-site food vendors specializing in Southern barbecue and street food. Off the grounds: Sonny’s BBQ in Manchester. On the Nashville drive: Husk Nashville; Rolf and Daughters; Arnold’s Country Kitchen; Hattie B’s Hot Chicken; Pancake Pantry. The Hampton Social Nashville in the Gulch for the canonical Friday afterglow oyster bar; Skull’s Rainbow Room in Printers Alley for the canonical 1948 Nashville supper club.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Lookout Mountain & Ruby Falls* (Chattanooga, Tennessee, USA). The Cumberland Plateau ridge where Union forces drove the Confederates off in November 1863, the Ruby Falls cavern 340 metres below the summit holding a 44-metre underground waterfall discovered by Leo Lambert in 1928
2. *Great Smoky Mountains National Park* (Tennessee & North Carolina, USA). The 522,000-acre Appalachian range straddling the Tennessee-North Carolina line, the most-visited national park in the country, named for the haze rising off the densest broadleaf forest east of the Mississippi; UNESCO 1983

### 19. Festa de São João do Porto

**Port:** Porto, Portugal
**Date:** Wed–Thu Jun 23–24
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Night of Saint John the Baptist’s eve into his feast day; one of Europe’s largest and least-known street festivals, celebrated in Porto for over 600 years. 200,000+ revelers fill Ribeira, the Cais de Gaia, and the Avenida dos Aliados across the night of June 23. The signature ritual: people tap each other on the head with soft plastic hammers (originally leeks, the medieval pagan fertility symbol) and wave garlic flowers in greeting. Manjericos (basil pots) with poetic verses change hands as love tokens. At midnight on June 24, the spectacular fireworks display launches from both banks of the Douro and from the Dom Luís I bridge, watched from every hillside, rooftop, and rabelo boat on the river.

**The Berth.** Lisbon: Bairro Alto Hotel; Memmo Alfama; Santa Clara 1728. Porto: The Yeatman; Vincci Porto. Algarve: Vila Vita Parc. In Porto for the festival night: Maison Albar Le Monumental Palace on Avenida dos Aliados for the Art-Déco grand-dame on the parade route; Torel Avantgarde on Rua da Restauração for the design-boutique with Douro views over the midnight fireworks.

**The Galley.** Grilled sardinhas, caldo verde, bifanas, broa de milho cornbread; drink Super Bock (never Sagres in Porto). Earlier evening, June 22 brings the Rusgas neighborhood parades; the main free concert at Avenida dos Aliados begins around 1 a.m. Antiqvvm in Massarelos for the canonical Porto Michelin-starred panoramic; Tabique for the canonical Porto modern small-plates with the natural-wine cellar.

**The Bearings.**

### 26. Isle of Wight Festival

**Port:** Seaclose Park, Newport, Isle of Wight

The 26th modern annual edition (counting from the 2002 revival); the first major music festival of the UK summer calendar, the spiritual prologue to the British festival summer, and one of among the most historically-consequential music festivals on Earth, four days each June when Seaclose Park on the bank of the River Medina in Newport on the Isle of Wight (the diamond-shaped 147-square-mile island in the English Channel, separated from the Hampshire mainland by the Solent strait, accessible only by ferry from Southampton, Portsmouth, or Lymington) becomes a temporary 55,000-capacity festival ground hosting major rock, pop, and indie programming across multiple stages. Isle of Wight Festival has the deepest historical pedigree of any music festival on this calendar, with origins tracing to the countercultural 1968–1970 original festivals that helped define the rock-festival format itself. The original Isle of Wight Festivals were founded by the Foulk brothers, Ron Foulk, Ray Foulk, and their younger brother Bill Foulk, operating through their company Fiery Creations Limited.

### 30. Finnish Midsummer

**Port:** Seurasaari, Helsinki, Finland
**Date:** Fri–Sun Jun 25–27 (Midsummer Day Sat Jun 26)
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Juhannus, the Finnish Midsummer celebration, the country’s most important secular holiday and the defining Finnish cultural event of the year; the Saturday between June 20 and June 26 (Midsummer Day falls on Saturday, June 26). The festival predates Christianity, the pre-Christian Finns honored Ukko, the thunder-god, at the solstice, and was Christianized in the 12th–13th centuries as Saint John the Baptist’s day (Johanneksen päivä). On the holiday weekend, the Finnish flag flies for 24 unbroken hours (the only date this is mandated), the cities empty as nearly the entire population retreats to their summer cottage (mökki) on a lake, and the four pillars of Juhannus take their ritual place: the kokko bonfire at sunset (though sunset is only nominal at this latitude, the sun barely dips below the horizon), the sauna at length (Finnish sauna culture inscribed on UNESCO’s ICH List in 2020), the swim in cold lake water, and the long Karelian table of new potatoes, dill, smoked salmon, herring, lihapullat (meatballs), strawberries, and Koskenkorva schnapps. The flagship public celebration is at the Seurasaari Open-Air Museum on a forested island in central Helsinki.

**The Berth.** Hotel Kämp on Pohjoisesplanadi for the canonical Helsinki grand-hotel since 1887; Lilla Roberts in Punavuori for the design-boutique with the WWII bunker bar; Hotel St. George for the modern- luxury Yayoi Kusama installation; Hotel Haven on Unioninkatu. Lake District: Hotelli Punkaharju on the Punkaharju esker; or Lehmonkärki on Lake Päijänne. Hotel Maria Helsinki for the modern luxury boutique on Maria Street; Hotel U14 at Korkeavuorenkatu for the design-boutique in the converted Civil Police building.

**The Galley.** Olo on Pohjoisesplanadi for the Michelin-starred modern-Nordic; Demo on Uudenmaankatu for the longest-running Michelin-starred kitchen since 2007; Restaurant Savoy on Eteläesplanadi for the Alvar Aalto interior; Salutorget on Senate Square; Kuurna in Kruununhaka; Ravintola Sea Horse since 1934; the Old Market Hall; Karl Fazer Café since 1891. Spis on Yrjönkatu for the modern Nordic small-plates; Ravintola Olo Bistro for the canonical Finnish New Nordic tasting.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Suomenlinna Fortress* (Helsinki, Finland). The sea fortress raised by the Swedes between 1748 and 1788 on six islands at the mouth of the Helsinki harbour, the largest naval fortress of its kind in the world; UNESCO 1991, the ferry runs every twenty minutes
2. *Helsinki Cathedral & Senate Square* (Helsinki, Finland). Carl Ludvig Engel's neoclassical white-Lutheran cathedral of 1852 rising over the granite Senate Square, modelled on a Russian Greek Cross plan with a green copper dome and four corner cupolas; the city's compass needle

### 31. Inti Raymi

**Port:** Three ceremonial sites across Cusco, Peru
**Date:** Thu June 24 (winter solstice, S. Hemisphere)
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

Qorikancha (Templo del Sol) at 9:00 a.m., Plaza de Armas (former Haukaypata) at 11:00 a.m., and Sacsayhuamán Esplanade at Chukipampa at 1:30 p.m., Thursday June 24, the winter solstice in the Southern Hemisphere; the 84th annual modern reenactment edition; the second-largest festival in South America after Rio Carnival, the most important and most-attended celebration of the year in Cusco, the most ancient continuously practiced Earth-and-Sun celebration tradition still performed anywhere on Earth. A ceremonial tour-de-force in which 800+ artists perform a deeply researched theatrical reenactment of the most sacred ritual of the Inca empire in Quechua across three of the original ceremonial sites in the city that was the capital of the largest empire in pre-Columbian American history. The original Inti Raymi was created by the Inca emperor Pachacutec in the year 1430 (the same emperor who built Machu Picchu and rebuilt Cusco into its imperial form) as the celebration of the Inca New Year, the winter-solstice moment when the sun, having reached its farthest point from the Earth in the Southern Hemisphere, reverses course and the days begin to lengthen again.

**The Berth.** Belmond Palacio Nazarenas behind the cathedral; the JW Marriott built into a 16th-century convent. Palacio del Inka, a Luxury Collection Hotel, in the 16th-century building five minutes from Plaza de Armas; Casa San Blas Boutique in San Blas for the heritage Cusco budget boutique.

**The Galley.** Cicciolina above Calle Triunfo; MAP Café inside the Pre-Columbian Museum; Chicha by Gastón Acurio in San Blas. Limo in Cusco for the canonical Cusco Andean-Asian fusion by Coque Ossio; Pacha Papa in San Blas for the canonical Cusco coca leaf tea and pachamanca traditional dining.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Qorikancha* (Cusco, Peru). The Inca Temple of the Sun whose curved Inca foundations the Spanish built the convent of Santo Domingo on top of in 1534, the gold-plated walls torn down for Atahualpa's ransom; the curved Inca seam still visible beneath the church
2. *Ollantaytambo* (Sacred Valley, Cusco Region, Peru). The Inca royal estate and the only place the Spanish were defeated in pitched battle, Manco Inca holding the high fortress against Pizarro's brother in 1537; the village below still laid out on the Inca grid, the highest doorways the cobbles of the original streets

### 32. Festival de Parintins

**Port:** Parintins, Tupinambarana Island, Amazonas, Brazil
**Date:** Fri–Sun Jun 25–27
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

The last weekend of June; the second-largest festival in Brazil after Rio Carnival, recognized as Cultural Heritage of Brazil. Held in the 35,000-seat purpose-built Bumbódromo arena on a small Amazon River island four hours by boat from Manaus, the fierce competition between two folkloric oxen, Boi Garantido (red, founded 1913) and Boi Caprichoso (blue, founded 1913), each fielding 4,000+ costumed performers across three nights to dramatize the legend of Bumba Meu Boi (the resurrected ox). The arena is divided in half by team color, and the audience for each side falls completely silent during the rival’s performance, the only event of its kind in the Americas. The town of 100,000 doubles in population for the weekend; visitors sleep in hammocks aboard the boats they arrived in. Coca-Cola sells half-red, half-blue cans during the festival, the only place in the world Coca-Cola is also blue. Eat tucumã, tambaqui from the river, açaí na tigela.

**The Berth.** São Paulo: Tivoli Mofarrej or Hotel Unique; Rio: Belmond Copacabana Palace or Fasano Ipanema; Salvador: Fasano Salvador or Pestana Convento do Carmo. Manaus area for the river-base: Anavilhanas Jungle Lodge in the Anavilhanas Archipelago for the canonical Amazon luxury lodge upriver from Manaus; Juma Amazon Lodge in the Mamori-Arara reserve for the canonical floating lodge in the flooded forest.

**The Galley.** São Paulo: D.O.M. (Alex Atala); Mocotó for the canonical Northeastern; Tordesilhas for the regional. Rio: Lasai, Aprazível. Salvador: Casa di Vina, Paraíso Tropical for the moqueca. In Manaus: Caxiri for the canonical Amazonian regional cooking by chef Felipe Schaedler; Banzeiro for the canonical Amazonian fine-dining with the canonical tambaqui and jambu.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Teatro Amazonas* (Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil). The pink-and-cream rubber-boom opera house raised in the deep Amazon in 1896, the dome of 36,000 French ceramic tiles painted in the colours of the Brazilian flag, the chandeliers of Murano glass, the curtain hand-painted in Paris by Crispim do Amaral
2. *Meeting of the Waters / Encontro das Águas* (Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil). The six-kilometre confluence where the black Rio Negro meets the muddy Solimões to make the Amazon, the two rivers running side by side without mixing because of differences in temperature and speed and density

### 33. Game of Thrones Studio Tour

**Port:** Linen Mill Studios, Banbridge, Northern Ireland
**Date:** Sat late June
**Flags:** FANDOM, GAME

Annual special-event series; held at the actual filming location where 30% of HBO’s Game of Thrones was shot across all eight seasons (2011–2019), the world’s only official Game of Thrones Studio Tour, opened February 2022 in the original Linen Mill Studios. The standard Studio Tour runs year-round through preserved authentic sets: Winterfell’s Great Hall (preserved exactly as filmed, the long table where the Stark family ate intact), Castle Black’s courtyard, the throne room of Dragonstone, the Iron Throne itself, the High Sept of Baelor, plus Jon Snow’s Long Claw and Sansa’s wedding dress on display. The Evening with Cast events are special after-hours dinners with original cast members rotating through the next two editions, Ian McElhinney (Ser Barristan Selmy), Ian Beattie (Ser Meryn Trant), Dominic Carter (Janos Slynt), and others, Q&A panels, cast-led set tours, themed banquet, photo opportunities. June marks the 16-year anniversary of GoT’s April 17, 2011 series premiere. 30 minutes from Belfast; pair with the Northern Ireland filming locations (the Dark Hedges as the King’s Road, Castle Ward as Winterfell exteriors, Ballintoy Harbour as Pyke).

**The Berth.** Belfast: The Merchant Hotel in the converted 1860s bank; or Bullitt Hotel for the boutique. Causeway Coast: Galgorm Resort & Spa. Lough Erne Resort in Enniskillen for the modern five- star Causeway-edge luxury; Bishop’s Gate Hotel in Derry-Londonderry for the heritage 1899 boutique near the city walls.

**The Galley.** Belfast: OX restaurant; The Muddler’s Club; Made in Belfast; Yard Bird for the rotisserie chicken; St George’s Market on Saturday. EIPIC in Belfast by chef Alex Greene for the Michelin-starred contemporary Northern Irish; The Mourne Seafood Bar on Bank Street for the canonical Belfast Mourne-coast seafood.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Giant's Causeway* (County Antrim, Northern Ireland, UK). The 40,000 hexagonal basalt columns left by a 60-million-year-old lava flow stepping into the North Atlantic, the legend giving Finn McCool credit for building it to walk to Scotland; UNESCO 1986, Northern Ireland's only UNESCO site
2. *Dark Hedges* (Stranocum, County Antrim, Northern Ireland, UK). The eighteenth-century avenue of beech trees planted by the Stuart family to impress visitors to Gracehill House, the boughs intertwined across the lane; filmed as the Kingsroad in the second-season opening of Game of Thrones

### 34. The Vikings Locko Park Festival

**Port:** Locko Park, Derbyshire, UK
**Date:** Sat–Sun June 26–27
**Flags:** VIKING

The mega-scale once-every-5-years gathering of The Vikings (the UK Viking re-enactment society, founded 1971), typically 1,500+ Vikings encamped on the 18th-century Locko Park estate, with the largest Viking-Age battle reenactment in Britain (700-strong shieldwalls), period archery, longship demonstrations, and the iconic three-day Saxon-Viking war game across the parkland.

In Derbyshire near the festival: Cavendish Hotel Baslow on the Chatsworth estate for the canonical Peak District country house; Hassop Hall Hotel near Bakewell for the heritage 16th- century manor option.

**The Galley.** London: St. John, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers in Marlow; L’Enclume in Cumbria; or the canonical local gastropub. In the Peak District: Fischer’s Baslow Hall for the canonical Peak District Michelin-recommended; The Old Hall Hotel in Buxton for the canonical Buxton small-luxury restaurant since the 17th century.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Chatsworth House* (Derbyshire, England, UK). The seat of the Cavendish dukes of Devonshire on the Derwent since 1549, the seventeenth-century baroque palace rebuilt by Capability Brown's hand on the landscape; the painted hall, the cascade water feature, the largest private collection in England
2. *Derwent Valley Mills* (Derbyshire, England, UK). The chain of eighteenth-century textile mills along the Derwent including Richard Arkwright's 1771 Cromford Mill, the cradle of the modern factory system; UNESCO 2001, the model for industrial towns across the world

### 35. Frederikssund Viking Festival

**Port:** Frederikssund, Denmark
**Date:** Sat–Sun last weekend of June through first weekend of July
**Flags:** VIKING

Denmark’s longest-running Viking festival, founded 1952, 75 years of Viking-themed open-air theater, with 200+ amateur actors performing a full-scale Viking-saga play in the natural amphitheater on the Roskilde Fjord; intermission camp life and traditional Danish Viking-era food. The amateur tradition is itself the cultural heritage event, distinct from the more reenactment-heavy festivals at Trelleborg and Foteviken.

**The Berth.** Copenhagen: Hotel d’Angleterre on Kongens Nytorv; Hotel Sanders in the historic block; or Nimb at Tivoli for the festival proximity. Closer to the festival ground in Roskilde (30 minutes from Frederikssund): Hotel Prindsen for the heritage 1695 grand- dame; Comwell Sport Roskilde for the modern dependable.

**The Galley.** Geranium for the three-Michelin-star; Restaurant Barr on the harbour; Apollo Bar at Charlottenborg for the natural-wine bistro; smørrebrød at Schønnemann for the canonical lunch. Snekken Café & Restaurant at the Roskilde Viking Ship Museum for the canonical Viking-themed harbor dining; 108 by Kristian Baumann (formerly of Noma) for the canonical Copenhagen casual New Nordic.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Frederiksborg Castle* (Hillerød, Denmark). Christian IV's Dutch Renaissance castle of 1610 on three small islands in the Hillerød lakes, the largest Renaissance castle in Scandinavia, the Knights' Hall, chapel, and Great Hall holding the National Museum of History since 1882
2. *Trelleborg Viking Ring Fortress* (Slagelse, Zealand, Denmark). The geometrically perfect ring fortress raised by Harald Bluetooth around 980 CE on a low promontory between two streams, the inner ring of sixteen long-houses arranged in four groups of four; UNESCO 2023 with three sister fortresses

### 36. Karmøy Viking Festival

**Port:** Avaldsnes, Karmøy, Norway
**Date:** Wed–Sun last week of June
**Flags:** VIKING

Festival on the actual seat of Norwegian kings Harald Fairhair and Olaf Tryggvason, Avaldsnes was the royal estate of Harald, the first king of a unified Norway, and is the historical heart of Viking-Age Norway. Held in the museum-village Nordvegen Historiesenter and at the Saint Olav’s Church (founded 1250 on Harald’s royal seat); 800+ Viking reenactors from across Northern Europe, longship sailings on the Karmsund strait.

**The Berth.** Oslo: The Thief on Tjuvholmen; Grand Hotel on Karl Johans gate; or Amerikalinjen in the converted shipping-line headquarters. Bergen: Opus XVI in the heritage building near Bryggen. Hotel Continental Oslo for the canonical 1900 Oslo grand-dame opposite the National Theatre; In Haugesund near Karmøy: Scandic Maritim Hotel on the Karmsund strait for the festival-base lodging.

**The Galley.** In Oslo: Maaemo by Esben Holmboe Bang for the three-Michelin-star modern Norwegian; Mathallen Oslo food hall in Vulkan for the canonical Norwegian food-hall casual. In Haugesund near Karmøy: Lothes Mat & Vinhus for the canonical Haugesund seafood since 1907, the daily catch from the Karmsund strait, the open-fire-grilled lamb from the Karmøy hill pastures.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Bryggen* (Bergen, Norway). The Hanseatic wharf on the eastern shore of the Vågen, narrow gable-fronted timber merchants' houses leaning into one another, the German Hanse running the stockfish trade out of these alleys for four centuries from 1360; UNESCO 1979
2. *Preikestolen / Pulpit Rock* (Strand, Rogaland, Norway). The 604-metre granite cliff jutting flat above the Lysefjord, the top a 25-metre square slab with no railing and a sheer drop on three sides; an hour and forty minutes by foot from the parking, the trail beginning where the road ends

### 37. Le Mans 24 Hours

**Port:** Circuit de la Sarthe, Le Mans, France
**Date:** Sat–Sun third weekend of June
**Flags:** CULTURE

The 24 Heures du Mans is the most respected endurance motor race in the world, run annually since 1923 on the 13.626-kilometre Circuit de la Sarthe, a hybrid permanent track and public roads circuit south of the medieval city of Le Mans in the Pays de la Loire region of western France. Two cars at a time around the clock for twenty-four hours, the longest sustained motorsport event on Earth, the founding leg of the unofficial Triple Crown of Motorsport (alongside the Monaco Grand Prix and the Indianapolis 500), and the cultural home of long-distance prototype racing since the Bentley Boys, Porsche, Ferrari, Ford GT, and Audi Sport tradition. The 95th edition runs the third weekend of June, 250,000+ attendees camped in the woods around the Mulsanne Straight and the Porsche Curves for the full 24 hours, the 14th-century half-timbered medieval city of Le Mans (the UNESCO-adjacent Cité Plantagenêt walled old town) packed for the surrounding week of pre-race events: the scrutineering parade through Place de la République, the driver’s parade through the city, and the autograph session at the cathedral plaza. The race start is at 4 p.m. on Saturday; the chequered flag at 4 p.m. on Sunday is the most photographed moment in motorsport.

**The Berth.** In Le Mans: Domaine de Chatenay in the Pays-de-Loire countryside outside Le Mans for the heritage 18th-century château hotel; Hôtel Chantecler Le Mans in central Le Mans for the heritage dependable in the Cité Plantagenêt walking distance to the cathedral. In Saumur (90 minutes south, the Loire wine option): Château de Verrières for the heritage Loire château stay.

**The Galley.** In Le Mans: L’Auberge des 7 Plats in the Cité Plantagenêt for the canonical Sarthois country cooking, the rillettes du Mans, the poulet du Mans en cocotte; La Réale for the modern French in the medieval old town. In Saumur: Le Gambetta for the Michelin-starred contemporary Loire by chef Mickaël Pihours.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Cathédrale Saint-Julien du Mans* (Le Mans, France). The cathedral of Romanesque and Gothic worked into one nave between 1060 and 1430, the Plantagenet apse a wonder of flying buttresses; the tomb of Berengaria of Navarre, the only English queen never to set foot in England, kept in the south chapel
2. *Châteaux of the Loire Valley* (Loire Valley, France). Three hundred kilometres of river lined with the royal and noble châteaux of the French Renaissance, Chambord and Chenonceau and Amboise and Blois the most photographed; UNESCO 2000, the only major French wine region without a great red

### 38. Sant Joan de Ciutadella

**Port:** Ciutadella, Menorca, Balearic Islands, Spain
**Date:** Wed–Thu Jun 23–24
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

The most spectacular festival on the Balearic Islands and one of the most distinctive traditional festivals in the western Mediterranean, observed June 23–24 in the medieval walled town of Ciutadella on the western tip of Menorca, the smaller, quieter, and architecturally more impressive of the two main Balearic Islands. The festival’s origins trace back to at least 1301 when King Jaime II of Aragon recognized the Sant Joan festival in Ciutadella as a chartered civic event; the festival’s modern form crystallized in the 14th century under the Cofraria de Sant Joan dels Cavallers (the Brotherhood of Saint John of the Knights), and has been observed continuously every June 23–24 across seven centuries except for the Spanish Civil War years (1936–1939). Three signature elements make Sant Joan unforgettable: (1) the caixers (riders) on stunning Cavall Menorquí horses, the local Andalusian-cross breed, parade in elaborate 17th-century dress through the narrow medieval streets of Ciutadella; the horses are trained to rear up on their hind legs on command and ’dance’ through the crowd while the riders remain mounted sidestyle. (2) The pomada cocktail (Menorcan gin from the Xoriguer distillery in Mahón with cloudy lemonade and mint) flows through every plaza. (3) The closing-night Jocs des Pla games where caixers compete in three traditional cavalry games. Book accommodation a year ahead.

**The Berth.** In Ciutadella: Hotel Tres Sants in the converted heritage palace in the historic center walking distance to the parade route; Sant Joan de Binissaida in the countryside outside Ciutadella for the heritage finca conversion. In Mahón (45 minutes east): Cristine Bedfor Guest House in the converted 19th-century mansion.

**The Galley.** In Ciutadella: Café Balear on Marina del Port for the canonical Ciutadella seafood at the harbour; Es Tast de na Sílvia for the canonical modern Menorquí by chef Sílvia Anglada, the lobster caldereta (Menorca’s signature dish). In Mahón: Ses Forquilles for the canonical Mahón tapas- and-natural-wine bar.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Talayotic Menorca* (Menorca, Balearic Islands, Spain). The Bronze Age and Iron Age megalithic culture that left towers, T-shaped taula sanctuaries, and naveta tombs scattered across the small island between 1600 and 123 BCE; UNESCO 2023, the densest prehistoric landscape per square kilometre in Europe
2. *Naveta des Tudons* (Ciutadella, Menorca, Spain). The Bronze Age communal burial chamber shaped like an upturned boat, raised between 1200 and 800 BCE in carefully cut limestone, hundreds of disarticulated skeletons once stacked inside; the oldest standing building in Spain

### 1. Anime Expo

**Port:** Los Angeles Convention Center
**Date:** Thu–Sun July 1–4
**Flags:** GAME

Largest anime convention in North America, founded 1992, 350,000+ attendees over four days, the AX Dance and AX Concert headlining J-pop and J-rock acts, voice-actor guests from across all current dubs, the AMV Contest, the Anime Expo Cosplay Competition, the Exhibit Hall and Artist Alley filling the entire LA Convention Center, plus the iconic 4 a.m. queue for Hall A panels.

**The Berth.** Hotel Bel-Air for the Old Hollywood; the Sunset Tower; the Ace Downtown. The Beverly Hills Hotel on Sunset for the canonical 1912 Pink Palace grand-dame; The Maybourne Beverly Hills for the modern Mayfair-luxury option.

1. *Bradbury Building* (Los Angeles, California, USA). George Wyman's 1893 office building on Broadway, the wrought-iron stair, cage elevators, and pink Italian marble of its five-storey skylit atrium filmed in Blade Runner and a hundred other pictures; the oldest commercial building in central LA
2. *Olvera Street* (Los Angeles, California, USA). The 1781 Spanish pueblo lane preserved as a Mexican market street since 1930, the Avila Adobe of 1818 the oldest house in the city; the National Park of El Pueblo de Los Angeles still anchors downtown LA at her colonial origin

### 2. Battle of the Somme Commemoration

**Port:** Thiepval Memorial, Picardy, France
**Date:** Thu Jul 1
**Flags:** CULTURE

Anniversary of the worst single day in British military history, July 1, 1916, 19,240 men killed in twelve hours. Annual ceremony at the Thiepval Memorial with 72,000 names of the missing carved into Lutyens’s arch, Last Post by buglers of the Royal Marines, the National Anthems of the UK and France; satellite ceremonies at Beaumont-Hamel and Lochnagar Crater the same day.

**The Berth.** Paris: Hôtel de Crillon, Le Meurice, Lutetia. Provence: La Bastide de Gordes; Hotel Crillon le Brave. Burgundy: Le Cep in Beaune; Loire: Domaine des Hauts de Loire. Closer to the battlefield in Picardy: Hôtel Carlton Lille on Rue de Paris for the heritage 1910 Belle-Époque grand-dame 90 minutes north; Château de Belignies for the heritage 18th-century château hotel 45 minutes from the Memorial.

**The Galley.** Paris: Le Comptoir du Relais; Septime; L’Arpège; Frenchie. Provence: La Mirande in Avignon; Baumanière. Burgundy: Lameloise in Chagny; Loire: Le Choiseul in Amboise. In Lille: L’Huîtrière on Rue des Chats Bossus for the canonical Lille seafood (closed but the spirit lives at the relocated brand); La Laiterie in Lambersart for canonical Flemish-French Michelin-starred by chef Benoît Bernard.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Thiepval Memorial* (Thiepval, Picardy, France). Lutyens's red-brick triumphal arch of 1932 above the Somme valley, the 72,337 names of the British and South African missing of 1916 carved across sixteen interlocking piers; the largest British war memorial anywhere
2. *Vimy Ridge Canadian National Memorial* (Pas-de-Calais, France). Walter Allward's twin-pylon limestone memorial on the ridge taken by all four Canadian divisions on April 9, 1917, the only joint Canadian assault of the war; the 100-hectare ground given by France to Canada in perpetuity
