### 40. Festa Major de Gràcia

**Port:** Gràcia neighborhood, Barcelona, Spain
**Date:** Sun–Sat Aug 15–21
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

The most spectacular neighborhood festival in Barcelona and one of the most photographed urban-decoration festivals in the world, observed annually August 15–21 in the Gràcia neighborhood, the bohemian village within the city in northern Barcelona (the area of Gaudí’s Park Güell and the Casa Vicens, the first house Gaudí ever designed). The festival traces to the 19th-century neighborhood pride of Gràcia (an independent town until annexed by Barcelona in 1897); residents began the festival as a deliberate civic celebration of their distinct village identity against the growing Catalan capital. The signature event is the Carrer Guarnits competition: each of Gràcia’s narrow streets is transformed by its residents into an elaborate themed installation built entirely from recycled materials (plastic bottles, cardboard, paper, fabric scraps, vintage objects), each street competing for the year’s award. The 22 participating streets choose themes weeks in advance and devote months to building; when complete, the streets become underwater seascapes, jungle canopies, medieval villages, intergalactic spacescapes, all hand-built and overhanging the cobblestones. Walking through the decorated streets at twilight when the lights come on is one of the most magical experiences in any European city. Free, 24/7 access. The festival also includes the giant human-tower competitions (Castellers de la Vila de Gràcia), 24-hour street concerts on the plazas, the iconic correfoc (fire-running parade) on closing night, and the final-night fireworks.

**The Berth.** In or near Gràcia: Hotel Casa Fuster on Passeig de Gràcia at the foot of the Gràcia neighborhood for the canonical 1908 modernist palace luxury (the heritage flagship); Hotel ME Barcelona by Foster + Partners on Provença for the modern design-luxury walking distance to Gràcia; Hotel Praktik Garden in Gràcia for the design-set boutique-budget directly in the festival neighborhood.

**The Galley.** In Gràcia: Bar La Plata on Carrer del Torrent de l’Olla for the canonical Gràcia tapas joint (anchovies, tomato bread, beer in glass mugs, that’s the entire menu); Berbena on Carrer de Minerva for the canonical Gràcia natural-wine bistronomic; La Pubilla on Plaça de la Llibertat for the canonical Catalan family-cooking restaurant with the Sunday menu del dia.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Sagrada Família* (Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain). The basilica Gaudí worked on for the last 43 years of his life and was buried in the crypt of, six of the planned eighteen towers still to rise; the nave a forest of branching stone trees lit by stained glass calibrated to the hour of the day
2. *Hospital de Sant Pau* (Barcelona, Catalonia, Spain). Lluís Domènech i Montaner's modernista hospital complex of 1902, twenty-seven pavilions decorated in painted tile, mosaic, and stained glass, the world's largest Art Nouveau site; UNESCO 1997 with the Palau de la Música

### 41. Sturgis Motorcycle Rally

**Port:** Sturgis, South Dakota
**Date:** Fri–Sun Aug 6–15
**Flags:** CULTURE

The largest motorcycle rally in the world and the most pivotal single-event gathering in the American motorcycle calendar, observed annually over ten days in early August in the Black Hills city of Sturgis, South Dakota (population 7,000 year-round; rally attendance: 500,000–700,000 motorcyclists). Founded in 1938 by the Jackpine Gypsies Motorcycle Club as a small Indian Motorcycle dealer-sponsored stunt show. The 86th edition. For ten days each August, the Black Hills region becomes the international capital of American motorcycle culture: the historic Main Street of Sturgis is closed to all but motorcycle traffic, the Buffalo Chip amphitheater hosts major headliner concerts (recent acts include ZZ Top, Lynyrd Skynyrd, Slash, and Kid Rock), and the Full Throttle Saloon (the world’s largest biker bar) operates at maximum capacity. The signature ride pattern: arrive Saturday night, anchor in Sturgis Monday–Thursday, day-rides each day through the Black Hills loop to Mount Rushmore (40 minutes south), Crazy Horse Memorial, Custer State Park (the Needles Highway and Wildlife Loop), Devil’s Tower (90 minutes west into Wyoming), and the Spearfish Canyon scenic byway.

**The Berth.** In Sturgis: Lodge at Deadwood Hotel in nearby Deadwood (10 minutes north) for the canonical Black Hills heritage with the 1876 frontier history; Sturgis Buffalo Chip Campground for the canonical rally camping experience with the festival concerts on-site; Best Western Plus Sturgis Inn for the dependable rally-base in central Sturgis. In Rapid City (45 minutes south): The Rushmore Hotel for the modern dependable; Hotel Alex Johnson since 1928 for the heritage Black Hills option.

**The Galley.** In Sturgis: The Knuckle Saloon on Main Street for the canonical rally-week biker bar with the dueling-piano stage; Loud American Roadhouse on Main Street for the canonical rally-week steakhouse. In Deadwood: Mavericks Steakhouse & Cocktails for the modern Black Hills steakhouse; Saloon No. 10 for the canonical historic Deadwood saloon where Wild Bill Hickok was shot in 1876. In Rapid City: Murphy’s Pub & Grill on Main Street for the canonical Black Hills pub-grub; Tally’s Silver Spoon for the canonical breakfast.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Mount Rushmore* (Keystone, South Dakota, USA). The 18-metre granite portraits of Washington, Jefferson, Roosevelt, and Lincoln carved into the southeast face of Mount Rushmore between 1927 and 1941, Gutzon Borglum the sculptor, the chamber behind Lincoln's head sealed in 1998 with the founding documents
2. *Crazy Horse Memorial* (Crazy Horse, South Dakota, USA). The Lakota memorial begun 1948 by sculptor Korczak Ziolkowski at the request of Henry Standing Bear, the head of Crazy Horse 27 metres high, the horse beneath still to be cut; never accepting federal money, the sculpture eight decades along

### 42. World Bog Snorkelling Championships

**Port:** Llanwrtyd Wells, Powys, Wales
**Date:** Mon Aug 30 (Bank Holiday)
**Flags:** CULTURE

The most absurd sporting event on the British Isles’ calendar and one of perhaps the most unique annual festivals in the world, observed annually on the August Bank Holiday Monday in the small Welsh village of Llanwrtyd Wells (population 850, in the Cambrian Mountains of Powys, mid-Wales). Founded in 1976 by Welsh publican Gordon Green of the Neuadd Arms Hotel as a deliberately weird tourist-attraction stunt to draw visitors to what was then the smallest town in Britain. The competition: contestants in flippers and a snorkel must swim 110 meters down a peat-bog trench cut into the moorland behind the village, then back, without traditional swimming strokes, only flipper power, through the icy, peat-stained water without raising their heads above the surface to breathe. The fastest time wins. The course is genuinely unpleasant: zero visibility, water temperature 8–12°C, the bog water is acidic (pH 4–5) and tastes of decomposed sphagnum moss, and the trench is barely wider than a contestant’s body. 200+ competitors from around the world compete each year; the world record is 1 minute 18 seconds. The festival has spawned an entire calendar of Llanwrtyd Wells absurd sporting events: the mid-July Real Ale Wobble, the August Bank Holiday Bog Snorkelling, the September Man vs. Horse Marathon (humans race horses across the mountains), and the November Bog Triathlon. The entire weekend is a celebration of contrarian English-Welsh humour.

**The Berth.** In Llanwrtyd Wells: The Neuadd Arms Hotel since 1750 for the canonical festival headquarters pub-with-rooms (the festival founder’s pub, where you collect your wristband and where the post- race trophy ceremony is held); The Carlton Riverside for the canonical small-village B&B with the Irfon River view. In nearby Builth Wells (15 minutes north): The Lion Hotel for the canonical Welsh market-town heritage.

**The Galley.** In Llanwrtyd Wells: the Neuadd Arms pub kitchen for canonical Welsh lamb stew and Welsh rarebit; Drovers Rest in central Llanwrtyd Wells for the canonical Welsh family-cooking. In the wider mid-Wales region: The Felin Fach Griffin in Brecon (45 minutes south) for the canonical Welsh gastropub with the canonical Sunday roast.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Brecon Beacons National Park* (Powys, Wales, UK). The 1,344-square-kilometre upland of Old Red Sandstone in mid-Wales, Pen y Fan at 886 metres the highest peak south of Snowdonia, the SAS selection march goes over it; an International Dark Sky Reserve since 2013
2. *Centre for Alternative Technology* (Machynlleth, Powys, Wales, UK). The off-grid sustainability community built into a disused slate quarry above the Dyfi valley since 1973, the water-balanced cliff railway carrying visitors up to the visitor centre; one of the longest-running ecological experiments in Britain

### 43. Janmashtami

**Port:** Mathura, Vrindavan & Dwarka, India
**Date:** Mon Aug 30
**Flags:** CULTURE

Hinduism’s most spectacular birthday celebration and one of the major annual festivals in the Krishna Janmabhumi pilgrim circuit, observed annually on the 8th day (Ashtami) of the dark fortnight of Bhadrapada (August 30). Janmashtami marks the birth of Lord Krishna, the 8th avatar of Vishnu, born at midnight in the Mathura prison cell of his uncle Kamsa in approximately 3228 BCE according to Hindu chronology. Three sacred sites anchor the festival’s pilgrim geography: (1) Mathura (the birthplace, 145 km south of Delhi), specifically the Krishna Janmabhoomi temple complex built directly over the prison cell; (2) Vrindavan (10 km north of Mathura, where Krishna grew up among the cowherd Gopis); and (3) Dwarka in Gujarat, the kingdom Krishna ruled as an adult. Signature events: the midnight Mahabhishekha at the Janmabhoomi temple at the exact moment of Krishna’s birth, where priests bathe the central murti in milk, yogurt, honey, ghee, and gangajal water; the day-long Dahi Handi where teams of young men form 9-tier human towers to break suspended pots of yogurt-and-butter; and the night-long Raslila dramatic performances of Krishna and Radha’s dance with the Gopis. Pair the pilgrimage with the Taj Mahal in nearby Agra (45 minutes from Mathura).

**The Berth.** In Mathura: Brijwasi Royal Hotel near the Krishna Janmabhoomi for the canonical pilgrim-base 5 minutes from the festival temple; ITC Mughal in nearby Agra (45 minutes) for the modern luxury Mughal-themed grand-dame near the Taj Mahal. In Vrindavan: Nidhivan Sarovar Portico for the modern festival-base near the major Krishna temples; ISKCON Krishna-Balaram Guest House for the canonical Krishna-devotee pilgrim experience.

**The Galley.** In Mathura/Vrindavan: Brijwasi Mishthan Bhandar on Goverdhan Chowk in Mathura for the canonical Brij-mandali sweets (the milk-based barfi, the lassi, the canonical Mathura peda since 1937); Govinda’s Vegetarian Restaurant at ISKCON Vrindavan for the canonical sattvic Krishna-consciousness vegetarian buffet; Lassiwala at Vidyapith Crossing for the canonical pilgrimage-route lassi. In Agra: Esphahan at the Oberoi Amarvilas for the canonical Mughlai fine-dining with the Taj Mahal view.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Taj Mahal* (Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India). Shah Jahan's white-marble mausoleum for Mumtaz Mahal, twenty thousand workers over twenty years, the inlaid pietra dura still tight after 370 monsoons; UNESCO 1983, the dome a different colour at every hour
2. *Krishna Janmabhoomi Temple* (Mathura, Uttar Pradesh, India). The temple complex built and rebuilt across centuries on the prison cell where Krishna is said to have been born to Devaki and Vasudeva, the Mathura sandstone walls scarred and repaired since Aurangzeb's seventeenth-century demolition

### 44. Onam Festival

**Port:** Kerala, India
**Date:** Sun Aug 29 – Tue Sept 7 (climax Sept 7)
**Flags:** CULTURE, FOOD

Kerala’s most important festival and the most spectacular harvest festival in southern India, observed annually over ten days during the Malayalam month of Chingam, with the climactic Thiruvonam day falling on September 7. The festival’s origin traces to the mythological return of the demon-king Mahabali, a benevolent Asura king of ancient Kerala banished to the underworld by Vishnu’s Vamana avatar but granted permission to visit his kingdom annually; Onam marks Mahabali’s annual return. Three signature elements: (1) the Pookalam, the spectacular flower-carpet installations laid out daily on the front courtyards of every Malayali home, each day adding a new concentric ring of flowers (jasmine, marigold, hibiscus, chrysanthemum) and 10 layers complete by Thiruvonam; (2) the Snake Boat Races (Vallam Kali), specifically the Nehru Trophy Boat Race held annually on Punnamada Lake near Alappuzha on the second Saturday of August (August 14), where 100+ rowers in white-and-red mundus paddle 100-foot chundan vallam snake boats in a 1,400-meter sprint to Vanchipattu boat songs; (3) the Onam Sadhya, the quintessential 26-course Malayalam vegetarian feast served on a banana leaf, observed simultaneously across Kerala on Thiruvonam. Pair the festival with the Kerala backwaters and Fort Kochi.

**The Berth.** In Kochi (the Kerala festival base): Brunton Boatyard in Fort Kochi for the canonical heritage Edwardian dockyard-conversion luxury; The Malabar House in Fort Kochi for the canonical Relais & Châteaux boutique in the converted Portuguese colonial mansion; Taj Malabar Resort & Spa on Willingdon Island for the modern luxury overlooking the harbor. In Alappuzha (for the Snake Boat Race): Marari Beach Resort for the canonical Kerala backwaters luxury; Spice Coast Cruises for the canonical houseboat (kettuvallam) experience.

**The Galley.** In Fort Kochi: Old Harbour Hotel restaurant for the canonical Kerala fine-dining with the harbor view; Kashi Art Café for the canonical Kochi café and the Sunday breakfast; Hotel Saravana Bhavan in Ernakulam for the canonical South Indian thali. Festival-day: every restaurant and home in Kerala will be serving the canonical Onam Sadhya banana-leaf feast, eat at any traditional venue or accept the canonical home-invitation from any Malayalam acquaintance.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Kerala Backwaters* (Alappuzha & Kollam, Kerala, India). The 900 km of interconnected lagoons, canals, and rivers running parallel to the Arabian Sea coast of Kerala, the wooden kettuvallam houseboats still poled between the rice paddies and coconut groves; the Punnamada lake the route of the Nehru Trophy snake-boat race
2. *Fort Kochi* (Kochi, Kerala, India). The Portuguese-Dutch-British colonial port at the mouth of the Vembanad estuary, the Chinese fishing nets still being raised and lowered along Vasco da Gama Square, the 1503 Saint Francis Church the oldest European church in India

### 1. Oxonmoot

**Port:** St Anne's College, Woodstock Road, Oxford UK
**Date:** Thu–Sun first weekend of September
**Flags:** FANDOM

The 54th annual gathering of the Tolkien Society, founded 1974, held at St Anne’s College since 2021, the largest annual Tolkien convention in the world with 500+ delegates from across the globe in Oxford and online via Zoom. The four-day program: academic papers on Tolkien’s legendarium delivered Friday through Sunday mornings, the Saturday-evening Masquerade in full Middle-earth costume, the Saturday Poetry Reading where delegates recite Tolkien’s poems and his translation of Beowulf, the on-site Art Show, and entertainments spanning songs, sketches, and dance. The closing Enyalië ceremony Sunday afternoon (’Remembrance’ in Tolkien’s Sindarin), wreath-laying at Tolkien’s grave in Wolvercote Cemetery, where he is buried alongside his wife Edith with their tomb inscribed ’Beren and Lúthien’, the Chairman’s address, a selected reading from Tolkien, and the recital of Namárië in Quenya, has been the moving conclusion since the very first Oxonmoot of September 1974.

**The Berth.** The Old Parsonage on Banbury Road for the boutique; The Randolph (now Graduate Oxford) on Beaumont Street; or the Macdonald Eastgate near Magdalen Bridge for the proximity. The Old Bank Hotel on High Street for the canonical Oxford boutique opposite All Souls College; Burlington House in Summertown for the heritage Victorian B&B walking distance to St Anne’s.

**The Galley.** Gee’s on Banbury for the conservatory dining-room; The Eagle and Child (the Bird and Baby) for the Inkling pilgrimage pint; Brown’s on Woodstock for the Oxford brasserie; Magdalen Arms in Iffley for the gastropub Sunday roast. Oxford Kitchen in Summertown for the canonical Oxford Michelin-recommended modern British; The Anchor on Hayfield Road in Walton Manor for the canonical Oxford neighbourhood gastropub.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Bodleian Library & Radcliffe Camera* (Oxford, England, UK). The university library founded 1602 around Duke Humphrey's older reading room, the circular Radcliffe Camera of 1748 the third-oldest library in England still in daily use; every book printed in Britain comes here by law
2. *Christ Church College & Cathedral* (Oxford, England, UK). Cardinal Wolsey's college of 1525 completed by Henry VIII after the cardinal's fall, the only college in the world whose chapel is also a cathedral; Lewis Carroll wrote Alice for the dean's daughter Alice Liddell in the rooms looking onto the meadow

---

### 2. Dragon Con

**Port:** Atlanta, Georgia
**Date:** Fri–Mon Labor Day weekend Sept 3–6
**Flags:** GAME, FANDOM

Cosplay capital of the United States, founded 1987, 80,000+ attendees across five host hotels in downtown Atlanta connected by skybridges, the Saturday Dragon Con Parade through downtown drawing 100,000+ spectators, 4,000+ hours of programming across 30+ tracks (Star Wars, Star Trek, Doctor Who, Marvel, anime, gaming, horror, science, robotics, every fandom has its own track), and the legendary all-night party scene that runs until the Marriott bar closes at dawn.

**The Berth.** The St. Regis Atlanta in Buckhead; Hotel Clermont in the historic Poncey-Highland; or Bellyard West Midtown for the design-modern. The Whitley, A Luxury Collection Hotel in Buckhead for the canonical modern luxury; Atlanta Marriott Marquis in downtown for the canonical Dragon Con host-hotel option (one of the five interconnected festival venues).

**The Galley.** Bacchanalia for the canonical Atlanta tasting menu; Mary Mac’s Tea Room since 1945 for the Southern; Staplehouse for the contemporary American; Busy Bee Cafe for the soul-food canon. Atlas at the St. Regis Atlanta by chef Christopher Grossman for the canonical Atlanta modern American with the iconic French Impressionist collection on the walls; Hot Dog Pete’s for the canonical Atlanta downtown chili-dog late-night.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Martin Luther King Jr. National Historical Park* (Atlanta, Georgia, USA). The Sweet Auburn district preserved around King's birth home on Auburn Avenue, Ebenezer Baptist Church where he preached, the reflecting pool and white marble tomb beside Coretta Scott King in the King Center
2. *Stone Mountain* (DeKalb County, Georgia, USA). The largest exposed granite monadnock in the world rising 251 metres east of Atlanta, the controversial Confederate bas-relief of Lee, Jackson, and Davis on the north face still the largest in the world; the summit walked since pre-Columbian times

### 3. Festival-Mediaval

**Port:** Selb, Bavaria, Germany
**Date:** Fri–Sun first weekend of September
**Flags:** CASTLE

One of Europe’s largest medieval music and culture festivals, in its 22nd year, three days of medieval, neofolk, and pagan music on multiple stages (Faun, Corvus Corax, In Extremo all play here regularly), period market with 200+ vendors, full medieval encampment, and the iconic Saturday-night fire-and-juggling show. Held in the historic porcelain town of Selb on the Czech border.

**The Berth.** Berlin: Hotel Adlon Kempinski; Soho House Berlin; 25hours Bikini. Munich: Bayerischer Hof. Hamburg: The Fontenay. Frankfurt: Roomers. In Bavaria near Selb: Schloss Thiergarten in Bayreuth (45 minutes south) for the heritage 18th-century baroque hunting-lodge boutique; Hotel Sonne in Bayreuth for the canonical Wagner- festival dependable. In Hof (15 minutes from Selb): Central-Hotel on Kulmbacher Strasse for the canonical Franconian dependable.

**The Galley.** Berlin: Markthalle Neun; Mustafa’s Gemüse Kebap; Lode & Stijn. Munich: Tantris; Hofbräuhaus; Schneider Bräuhaus. Hamburg: Fischmarkt; Bullerei. Frankfurt: Adolf Wagner; Lafleur. In Bayreuth: Eule Brewery Restaurant for the canonical Franconian destination (the Wagner family’s restaurant of choice for a century); Oskar Restaurant for the canonical Franconian fine-dining near the Markgräfliches Opernhaus.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Wartburg Castle* (Eisenach, Thuringia, Germany). The eleventh-century hilltop castle where Luther translated the New Testament into German in eleven weeks of 1521 hiding from the Emperor, the inkwell-on-the-wall of legend; UNESCO 1999, Wagner set Tannhäuser in its great hall
2. *Bayreuth Margravial Opera House* (Bayreuth, Bavaria, Germany). Giuseppe and Carlo Galli Bibiena's 1748 rococo court opera house built for Margravine Wilhelmine of Brandenburg-Bayreuth, the largest baroque opera theatre in Europe to survive intact with its original stage machinery; UNESCO 2012

### 4. Naples Pizza Village

**Port:** Lungomare Caracciolo, Naples
**Date:** early September
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

A five-day pizza festival on Naples’ Lungomare seafront in mid-September, drawing 700,000+ visitors, the world’s largest event dedicated to a single dish, organized by the Associazione Pizzaiuoli Napoletani since 2012. Fifty pizzaioli at long communal stands turn out classic Margherita, Marinara, and an evolving slate of regional invention pizzas across five days; the Trofeo Caputo World Pizza Championship runs the final weekend. Pair with the Saturday-morning Sant’Elmo Castle climb for the panoramic view, then the evening passeggiata back along Via Caracciolo.

**The Berth.** The Grand Hotel Vesuvio on the Lungomare; or the Romeo Hotel in the porto for the modernist option. Excelsior Vittoria in Sorrento (45 minutes south) for the canonical Bay-of-Naples Belle-Époque grand-dame on the Sorrentine cliffs; The Britannique on Corso Vittorio Emanuele for the heritage 1869 boutique with the canonical Naples bay- view.

**The Galley.** L’Antica Pizzeria da Michele for the Margherita; Sorbillo for the second pizza; Trattoria Nennella in the Spanish Quarters for canonical Napoletano. Pepe in Grani by Franco Pepe in Caiazzo (1 hour north) for the canonical Campania pizza pilgrimage destination (book months ahead); Concettina ai Tre Santi by Ciro Oliva in the Sanità district for the canonical Naples modern pizza.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Pompeii* (Pompeii, Campania, Italy). The Roman city buried by Vesuvius on August 24, 79 CE under metres of pumice and ash, kept whole by the sealing, the bread still in the ovens; UNESCO 1997 with Herculaneum, only two-thirds of the city excavated still
2. *Mount Vesuvius* (Naples, Campania, Italy). The 1,281-metre stratovolcano above the Bay of Naples, the only active volcano on the European mainland, last erupted March 1944 with the Allies camped at her feet; the climb to the smoking crater rim a one-hour switchback from the parking

### 5. Antietam Reenactment

**Port:** Sharpsburg, Maryland
**Date:** weekend nearest Sep 17
**Flags:** CULTURE

Annual mid-September reenactment at Antietam National Battlefield in Sharpsburg, Maryland, the September 17, 1862 battle that became the bloodiest single day in American history, with 22,717 casualties (killed, wounded, missing) in 12 hours. The tactical Confederate withdrawal afterward gave Lincoln the moral victory he needed to issue the Emancipation Proclamation five days later. 1,500+ reenactors representing both armies refight key engagements at the Cornfield, the Sunken Road (Bloody Lane), and Burnside Bridge. The National Park Service runs the customary interpretive program; the Antietam National Cemetery on the bluff above the battlefield holds 4,776 Union dead.

**The Berth.** Stay in Frederick, MD (30 minutes east): Hotel Frederick; or in Hagerstown: Plaza Hotel and Suites. Antietam Inn & Hartle House Bed and Breakfast in Sharpsburg itself for the canonical festival-base in the village; Bavarian Inn in Shepherdstown, West Virginia (15 minutes east) for the canonical heritage Potomac-side dining-with-rooms.

**The Galley.** Frederick: Volt (Bryan Voltaggio); Family Meal for the modern American; Brewer’s Alley for the canonical brewpub. Press in Frederick by chef Bryan Voltaggio for the canonical Frederick modern American sister to Volt; The Press Room in Shepherdstown for the canonical Civil-War-country modern American.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Antietam National Battlefield* (Sharpsburg, Maryland, USA). The 12-square-mile farmland where 22,717 men were killed, wounded, or missing in 12 hours of September 17, 1862, the bloodiest single day in American history; the tactical Confederate withdrawal afterward gave Lincoln the moral footing for the Emancipation Proclamation
2. *Harpers Ferry* (Harpers Ferry, West Virginia, USA). The Potomac-and-Shenandoah river-junction town where John Brown raided the federal armory in October 1859 and lit the fuse on the Civil War, captured and recaptured eight times during the war; the engine house Brown was cornered in still on Camp Hill

---

### 6. Battle of Vienna Commemoration

**Port:** Kahlenberg, Vienna, Austria
**Date:** Sat–Sun Sept 11–12
**Flags:** CASTLE, CULTURE

The anniversary of the 1683 battle in which Polish king Jan III Sobieski’s winged hussars descended from the Kahlenberg heights and broke the Ottoman siege of Vienna, the largest cavalry charge in history (18,000 horse), the high-water mark of Ottoman expansion in Europe. Annual mass at the Kahlenberg Church with Polish military attaché, hussar reenactor units in full feathered armor, viewing platforms over the Vienna battlefield.

**The Berth.** Hotel Sacher on Philharmonikerstraße, the cake address; the Hotel Imperial; or the Park Hyatt at Am Hof. Rosewood Vienna on Petersplatz for the modern luxury in the converted 19th-century Böhler insurance building; The Guesthouse Vienna on Führichgasse for the canonical Vienna design-boutique behind the Albertina.

**The Galley.** Steirereck in the Stadtpark for the Austrian canon; Plachutta for Tafelspitz; any Beisl in Spittelberg for the Wiener Schnitzel and Grüner. Konstantin Filippou on Dominikanerbastei for the canonical Vienna two-Michelin-star modern Austrian-Greek tasting; Heuriger Wieninger am Nussberg in the Vienna vineyards for the canonical Wachau-wine-and-Heuriger picnic.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Schönbrunn Palace* (Vienna, Austria). The Habsburg summer palace of 1,441 rooms built by Maria Theresa from 1740 on the green hill west of Vienna, the Gloriette folly crowning the formal gardens; UNESCO 1996, Mozart played for the empress here at age six
2. *Stephansdom / St Stephen's Cathedral* (Vienna, Austria). The Romanesque-into-Gothic cathedral at the centre of Vienna, the diamond-patterned tile roof and the 137-metre South Tower the city's compass needle; Mozart was married here in 1782 and given a third-class funeral in the rain in December 1791

### 7. Shaky Knees Music Festival

**Port:** Piedmont Park, Midtown Atlanta
**Date:** Fri–Sun Sept 17–19
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

The 15th annual edition; the most acclaimed indie-rock festival in the American South, the spiritual headquarters of indie and alternative music in the Southeast, three days when the Olmsted-designed historic central park of Atlanta becomes the convergence point of the indie-rock canon, drawing 40,000+ attendees per day to the rolling 200-acre piedmont park in Midtown Atlanta. Founded in 2013 by Atlanta entrepreneur and music industry veteran Tim Sweetwood as a deliberate counterweight to the EDM-dominated festival circuit of the early 2010s. Sweetwood told Consequence of Sound at launch that he envisioned Shaky Knees as ’a festival focused purely on music,’ explicitly the indie rock and alternative side, and that he wanted to keep it intentionally smaller than Bonnaroo or Coachella to preserve the experience quality. The first edition in mid-May 2013 was held over two days at Historic Fourth Ward Park and the Masquerade Music Park in eastside Atlanta with 9,000 attendees per day and headliners The Lumineers, Jim James, and Band of Horses; both days sold out, and the festival’s identity was set immediately.

**The Berth.** The St. Regis Atlanta in Buckhead; Hotel Clermont in the historic Poncey-Highland; or Bellyard West Midtown for the design-modern. The Hotel Clermont in Poncey-Highland (already listed); add Hotel Indigo Atlanta Midtown on Peachtree Street for the modern dependable walking distance to Piedmont Park; The Georgian Terrace Hotel on Peachtree opposite the Fox Theatre for the canonical heritage 1911 Atlanta grand-dame.

**The Galley.** Bacchanalia for the canonical Atlanta tasting menu; Mary Mac’s Tea Room since 1945 for the Southern; Staplehouse for the contemporary American; Busy Bee Cafe for the soul-food canon. Aria in Buckhead by chef Gerry Klaskala for the canonical Atlanta heritage modern American; Empire State South by chef Hugh Acheson on Crescent Avenue for the canonical Atlanta modern Southern by the legend.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Atlanta History Center & Swan House* (Atlanta, Georgia, USA). The 33-acre Buckhead museum holding the 1928 Edward Vason Jones-designed Swan House, the largest collection of Civil War artefacts in the South, and the Cyclorama of the 1864 Battle of Atlanta moved here from Grant Park in 2019
2. *World of Coca-Cola* (Atlanta, Georgia, USA). The museum of the soft drink invented by Atlanta pharmacist John Pemberton in 1886, the working bottling line, the tasting room with 60 flavours from Coca-Cola products across the world; the vault of the secret formula at the centre

### 8. Battle of Stamford Bridge Reenactment

**Port:** East Riding of Yorkshire, UK
**Date:** weekend nearest Sept 25
**Flags:** VIKING

Annual mid-September reenactment near Stamford Bridge, East Riding of Yorkshire, the September 25, 1066 battle in which Harold Godwinson’s Anglo-Saxons crushed the Norwegian invasion under Harald Hardrada and Harold’s brother Tostig, killing both. The exhausted English then marched south to meet William the Conqueror at Hastings three weeks later. The local reenactment society stages the battle on the original ground; living-history Viking and Saxon camps; the iconic Berserker bridge defense by a single Norwegian.

**The Berth.** London anchored: The Connaught, The Beaumont, The Zetter Townhouse, or the Hoxton. Country: Heckfield Place, The Pig hotels, or Soho Farmhouse. In York (15 minutes from Stamford Bridge): The Grand, York on Station Rise for the canonical heritage Edwardian 1906 railway grand-dame; Grays Court on Chapter House Street for the canonical York boutique inside the medieval city walls; Middlethorpe Hall & Spa in Bishopthorpe for the canonical Yorkshire country-house Relais & Châteaux 5 km south of York.

**The Galley.** London: St. John, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers in Marlow; L’Enclume in Cumbria; or the canonical local gastropub. In York: Skosh on Micklegate for the canonical York modern British small-plates; The Star Inn the City on Lendal Bridge for the canonical Yorkshire Andrew Pern restaurant on the Ouse; Bettys Café Tea Rooms on St Helen’s Square since 1936 for the canonical Yorkshire afternoon tea.

**The Bearings.**

1. *York Minster* (York, North Yorkshire, England, UK). Two and a half centuries of building between 1220 and 1472, the great central tower above the longest medieval nave in northern England, the chapter house an octagonal sunburst of glass; the Roman principia foundations still in the undercroft
2. *Castle Howard* (York, North Yorkshire, England, UK). Vanbrugh's first house, begun 1699 for the third Earl of Carlisle in the rolling Howardian Hills, the great hall topped by a painted dome; Evelyn Waugh's Brideshead on screen, still the home of the Howards

### 10. Feast of San Gennaro

**Port:** Little Italy, New York City
**Date:** 11 days, mid-September
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

An 11-day Italian-American festival in Manhattan’s Little Italy, held mid-September around the Cathedral of the Most Precious Blood on Mulberry Street, celebrating the patron saint of Naples since 1926; the largest religious festival in New York. Six blocks of food stalls, sausage and peppers, zeppole, arancini, calzones, cannoli, flanking the Saturday-night candlelit procession when San Gennaro’s bust is paraded through the streets. The annual Cannoli Eating Contest runs Saturday afternoon. The neighborhood gives way more to Chinatown each year, but for these eleven days Mulberry Street remains unmistakably Naples.

**The Berth.** In NYC for the festival walking distance to Little Italy: The Bowery Hotel on the Bowery for the canonical Lower East Side / Little Italy design-luxury walking distance to Mulberry Street; The Mercer in SoHo for the canonical NYC design-set boutique-luxury two blocks from Little Italy; The Greenwich Hotel in Tribeca for the heritage Robert De Niro boutique; The Crosby Street Hotel in SoHo for the canonical Firmdale Hotels design-luxury.

2. *Empire State Building* (Manhattan, New York, USA). The 1931 Art Deco limestone shaft topped by a mooring mast that never moored a single airship, 102 storeys raised in 410 days during the Depression; the world's tallest building until 1970, the spire lit a different colour every night

The birthday of both Bilbo and Frodo Baggins, established as official by the American Tolkien Society in 1978, readings from The Hobbit and LOTR at libraries, bookshops, universities, and Tolkien Society chapter meetings worldwide; second breakfast and elevenses parties in many homes; the Tolkien Society’s online Hobbit Day program runs through the week.

2. *The Eagle and Child* (St Giles', Oxford, England, UK). The 17th-century pub on St Giles' where Tolkien and Lewis and the Inklings met Tuesday mornings from 1933 to 1962 in the Rabbit Room, where Lord of the Rings was read aloud chapter by chapter to a small, sceptical, beloved audience

### 14. Oktoberfest

**Port:** Theresienwiese, Munich, Germany
**Date:** Sat Sept 18 – Sun Oct 3
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The world’s largest folk festival and beer festival, founded 1810 to celebrate the wedding of Crown Prince Ludwig, 6 million+ visitors over 16 days, 14 large tents and 21 smaller ones operated by the six Munich breweries (Augustiner, Hacker-Pschorr, Hofbräu, Löwenbräu, Paulaner, Spaten); 7.7 million one-liter Maß krugs of Wiesnbier are served, with Hendl roast chicken, Schweinshaxe pork knuckle, and pretzels on every table. Reservations for tent tables open early in the year and book up immediately; standing-room space at most tents available without reservation but arrive by 9 a.m. on weekends.

**The Berth.** Bayerischer Hof on Promenadeplatz; or the Mandarin Oriental on Neuturmstraße. The Charles Hotel on Sophienstrasse for the canonical Rocco Forte modern luxury opposite the Old Botanical Garden; Hotel Torbräu on Tal since 1490 for the canonical Munich oldest hotel heritage (the canonical Bavarian dependable).

**The Bearings.**

1. *Neuschwanstein Castle* (Hohenschwangau, Bavaria, Germany). Ludwig II's white-limestone fairy-tale castle on a Bavarian alpine spur, begun 1869 and unfinished at his mysterious death in 1886; the model for Disney's Sleeping Beauty Castle, six million visitors annually

### 19. Galway International Oyster & Seafood

**Port:** Spanish Arch, Galway City, Ireland
**Date:** Fri–Sun Sept 24–26
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The 74th annual edition; the world’s longest-running oyster festival and the most internationally recognized Irish food festival, described by The Sunday Times as ’one of the 12 greatest shows on earth’ and listed in the AA Travel Guide as one of Europe’s Seven Best Festivals. Founded September 1954 by Brian Collins, manager of the Great Southern Hotel (now the Hotel Meyrick on Eyre Square), to extend Galway’s tourist season into a quieter month. By 1968 the Irish Oyster Opening Championship had been formalized; by 1977, Ireland’s Willie Moran set the world record by opening 30 oysters in 1 minute 31 seconds, a record that still stands. The festival moved into Galway City proper in 1984 as part of the city’s Quincentenary celebrations and has been anchored at the Spanish Arch (the medieval defensive arch on the Long Walk where the city’s stone walls meet the Corrib River) ever since.

**The Berth.** The Hotel Meyrick (the festival’s original 1954 host, on Eyre Square, recently restored); Glenlo Abbey Hotel (the converted 18th-century estate 5 km west, with the Pullman dining cars from the actual Orient Express on the property). The G Hotel Galway by Philip Treacy on Wellpark for the canonical Galway design-luxury on Lough Atalia; The House Hotel in the Latin Quarter for the design-boutique walking distance to the Spanish Arch festival site.

**The Galley.** Aniar for the Michelin-starred New Irish (JP McMahon); Loam for the seasonal contemporary; Ard Bia at Nimmos for Saturday brunch; Sheridans Cheesemongers. Kai Café & Restaurant in the West End by chef Jess Murphy for the canonical Galway casual fine-dining; McDonagh’s Seafood House on Quay Street since 1902 for the canonical Galway fish-and-chips and the half-dozen Galway Bay oysters (the canonical festival-day spot).

**The Bearings.**

1. *Cliffs of Moher* (County Clare, Ireland). The 14-kilometre sheer slate-and-shale wall above the Atlantic, 214 metres at their highest at O'Brien's Tower, six million seabirds nesting in the cliff fissures during summer; the most visited natural site in Ireland
2. *Connemara National Park* (Letterfrack, County Galway, Ireland). The 2,000 hectares of bog, heath, and the Twelve Bens granite peaks, the boggy fields a tangled mosaic of stone walls and white-thorn hedgerow, Connemara ponies still wild on the slopes; Ireland's wildest western landscape

Florilege in Aoyama (already mentioned in July V32 Fuji Rock); add Sezanne at Four Seasons Tokyo by chef Daniel Calvert for the canonical Tokyo two-Michelin-star modern French; Ginza Onodera for the canonical Ginza omakase.

2. *Mount Nokogiri* (Chiba, Japan). The 329-metre Saw Tooth Mountain rising from Tokyo Bay south of Yokohama, the Nihon-ji temple carved into the stone since 725, the 31-metre Daibutsu carved 1783 the largest pre-modern stone Buddha in Japan; the Hell View overlook from the cliff edge

### 21. World Gourmet Festival Bangkok

**Port:** Anantara Siam Bangkok Hotel, Thailand
**Date:** Mon–Sun Sep 13–19
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The 27th annual edition; one of Asia’s premier gastronomic events, the foundation of Bangkok’s identity as Southeast Asia’s leading culinary destination, the longest-running luxury-hotel-anchored gourmet festival in the Asia-Pacific region, and one of arguably the most significant annual gatherings of Michelin-starred chefs anywhere on Earth, six days each autumn when the storied Anantara Siam Bangkok Hotel transforms into a global culinary stage, with Michelin-starred chefs from the world’s most acclaimed kitchens flying into Thailand to collaborate, cook side-by-side, and present once-a-year tasting menus that cannot be experienced anywhere else. The 2025 edition (the 25th annual silver-anniversary milestone) brought together sixteen Michelin-starred restaurants plus award-winning venues honored in the World’s 50 Best and Asia’s 50 Best lists, establishing the festival as the most concentrated single-week assembly of global culinary talent in Asia.

**The Berth.** The Mandarin Oriental on the Chao Phraya, the 1876 author’s wing where Conrad and Maugham stayed; the Capella Bangkok for the modern. Anantara Siam Bangkok on Rajadamri Road, the festival’s host venue itself for the canonical festival-immersive stay; The Siam in Dusit on the Chao Phraya for the canonical Bangkok Asian Art-Déco luxury.

**The Galley.** Gaggan Anand for the splurge; Jay Fai’s Michelin street stall in Phra Nakhon (the goggles, the crab omelette); Thip Samai for the canonical pad Thai near Khao San. Sorn by chef Yodkwan U- pumpruk for the canonical Bangkok Michelin-starred southern Thai (already noted on July’s Phi Ta Khon); Nahm at COMO Metropolitan by chef Pim Techamuanvivit for the canonical Bangkok modern Thai with the iconic Asia’s 50 Best lineage.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Grand Palace & Wat Phra Kaew* (Bangkok, Thailand). The royal palace complex built 1782 by Rama I, the Wat Phra Kaew chapel housing the small Emerald Buddha of green jasper carved in the fourteenth century; the most sacred Buddhist image in Thailand, the king dresses it for each season
2. *Ayutthaya Historical Park* (Ayutthaya, Thailand). The 700-year-old Siamese capital sacked by Burma in 1767 and left ruined, the brick temple stupas of Wat Mahathat with the buddha-head wrapped in fig roots, the line of Wat Phra Si Sanphet's three white chedis; UNESCO 1991

### 22. Terra Madre

**Port:** Turin, Italy
**Date:** biennial, next edition late September 2028
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

Slow Food’s biennial flagship gathering in Turin (Lingotto and Parco Dora) every even-numbered September; founded by Carlo Petrini in 1996 as the answer to industrial agriculture, the event now draws 350,000 visitors and 5,000 small producers from 150 countries, the Ark of Taste in living form. Five days of regional tastings, Indigenous food forums, fishermen’s pavilions, the Slow Cheese hall, the Slow Wine catalogue tastings, and the Theaters of Taste with rotating chef demonstrations. The single most concentrated traditional-food event on the planet; Turin tram lines run the festival shuttle.

**The Berth.** Rome: Hotel de Russie; Hassler. Florence: Hotel Savoy; J.K. Place. Milan: Bulgari Milano. Venice: Aman Venice; Cipriani. In Turin, the festival is here, the spiritual capital of Slow Food: Turin Palace Hotel on Via Sacchi for the canonical 1872 heritage grand-dame near Porta Nuova station; NH Collection Torino Piazza Carlina on Piazza Carlo Emanuele II for the design-set boutique in the converted 18th-century building (Nietzsche stayed here in 1888); Casa Cavour in the converted 18th-century Cavour family palazzo for the heritage boutique near Piazza Carlo Felice.

**The Galley.** Rome: Roscioli; Felice a Testaccio; Da Cesare al Casaletto. Florence: Enoteca Pinchiorri; Sostanza; All’Antico Vinaio. Milan: Trussardi alla Scala; Trattoria Milanese. Venice: Alle Testiere; Antiche Carampane. In Turin: Del Cambio on Piazza Carignano since 1757 for the canonical Turin heritage grand-restaurant (Cavour and Verdi’s table); Combal.Zero by chef Davide Scabin in Rivoli (15 minutes west) for the canonical Piemonte avant-garde modern Italian Michelin- starred; Eataly Torino Lingotto at the Slow Food/Eataly flagship for the canonical Slow-Food- philosophy market-and-dining.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Residences of the Royal House of Savoy* (Turin, Piedmont, Italy). The eleven royal palaces and country estates built by the Savoy across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the Royal Palace of Turin at the centre and Stupinigi and Venaria Reale among the others; UNESCO 1997
2. *Mole Antonelliana* (Turin, Piedmont, Italy). The 167-metre brick spire-on-a-dome originally built as a synagogue from 1863, finished as a city monument 1889, now the National Museum of Cinema; the elevator rises through the centre of the open dome to an observatory below the spire

### 23. Bumbershoot

**Port:** Seattle Center, Seattle, Washington
**Date:** Fri–Sun Labor Day weekend Sept 3–5
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

The largest urban arts and music festival in the Pacific Northwest, observed annually over Labor Day weekend at Seattle Center, the 74-acre former World’s Fair grounds. Founded in 1971, the name “Bumbershoot” is British slang for umbrella, a deliberately ironic nod to Seattle’s reputation for rain at the end of the dry summer. The festival operates across all the Seattle Center venues simultaneously: the iconic 605-foot Space Needle as the festival skyline marker; the Climate Pledge Arena (formerly KeyArena) hosting the main music stage; the Pacific Science Center as the immersive arts space; McCaw Hall as the theatrical and dance programming venue; the Museum of Pop Culture (the Frank Gehry-designed building) as the festival’s spiritual heart with its permanent music exhibits; the International Fountain plaza as the open-air mainstage. The lineup curates indie rock, hip-hop, electronic, and folk from across the Pacific Northwest (Seattle’s grunge alumni continue to make surprise appearances) and the broader American alternative-music scene. The arts programming includes comedy, theatre, dance, visual art installations, and the iconic Flatstock poster show featuring 200+ rock-poster artists.

**The Berth.** In Seattle: The Edgewater Hotel on Pier 67 for the canonical 1962 Seattle World’s Fair grand- dame on the Elliott Bay waterfront (where The Beatles stayed in 1964); Hotel Theodore on Pine Street for the design-set boutique heritage; The Inn at the Market in Pike Place for the canonical Seattle market-side boutique with views of Elliott Bay; Pan Pacific Hotel Seattle on the Westin block for the modern festival-base dependable.

**The Galley.** In Seattle: Canlis since 1950 in Queen Anne for the canonical Seattle fine-dining institution overlooking Lake Union (the canonical Sunday family-style supper); The Walrus and the Carpenter in Ballard by chef Renee Erickson for the canonical Seattle oyster bar with the canonical Hama Hama oysters; Pike Place Market for the canonical Seattle morning ritual (Pike Place Chowder, Beecher’s Cheese, Ellenos Greek Yogurt); JuneBaby in Ravenna by chef Edouardo Jordan for the canonical Seattle Southern cooking.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Pike Place Market* (Seattle, Washington, USA). The 1907 farmer's-and-fishmonger's market hanging off the bluff above Elliott Bay, the original neon clock still keeping time over Pike Place; the salmon still thrown from ice to scale
2. *Chihuly Garden and Glass* (Seattle, Washington, USA). The 2012 permanent installation of Dale Chihuly's blown-glass sculpture at the foot of the Space Needle, the glasshouse of suspended yellow-red Persians and the outdoor garden where glass and plants are interwoven; the Sealife Tower the colossus of the collection

### 24. Braemar Highland Gathering

**Port:** Princess Royal & Duke of Fife Memorial Park, Braemar,
**Date:** Sat first Saturday of September
**Flags:** CULTURE

Scotland’s most famous Highland Games and the most pivotal annual cultural event in the Royal Deeside calendar, observed each first Saturday of September on the Princess Royal & Duke of Fife Memorial Park in the Aberdeenshire village of Braemar (population 460, in the eastern Cairngorms 90 km west of Aberdeen). The 207th annual gathering. The Royal connection is the festival’s anchor: King Charles III maintains the patronage tradition established by Queen Victoria in 1848, when the royal family began attending as part of their annual summer residence at nearby Balmoral Castle (where Victoria built the modern Scottish royal retreat in 1856 and where the present royal family still spends August–September). Signature events: the Heavy Events (Tossing the Caber, the 5.94-meter, 79.5-kg log thrown end-over-end; the Hammer Throw; the 56-pound Weight Throw; Putting the Stone); the Pipe Bands competition with 50+ bands from Scotland and the Commonwealth in massed-pipe formations; the Highland Dancing (Sword Dance, Highland Fling, Seann Triubhas); and the Hill Race up the 859-meter Morrone summit and back. The Royal Family typically attends in person; the King, Queen, and senior royals process onto the field in tartan kilts before the games commence. 16,000 attendees fill the grandstands.

**The Berth.** In Braemar: The Fife Arms Hotel in central Braemar, a contemporary Hauser & Wirth-owned design-luxury hotel in the converted 1856 Victorian coaching inn (the most consequential rural hotel renovation in Scotland in the 21st century, with original Lucian Freud and Pablo Picasso artworks in the rooms); Braemar Lodge Hotel on Glenshee Road for the canonical traditional Victorian sporting-hotel; Callater Lodge B&B for the canonical Braemar B&B option.

**The Galley.** In Braemar: The Clunie Dining Room at The Fife Arms for the canonical Braemar fine-dining (the canonical Scottish seasonal tasting with the Royal Deeside game and salmon); Flying Stag at The Fife Arms for the casual gastropub option; The Bothy at The Fife Arms for the canonical pub lunch. In the wider Royal Deeside: The Boat Inn at Aboyne (30 minutes east) for the canonical Aberdeenshire gastropub.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Cairngorms National Park* (Highland & Aberdeenshire, Scotland, UK). The 4,528 km² national park of the eastern Highland plateau, five of the six highest peaks in Scotland, the largest native forest in Britain at Mar Lodge and Glen Tanar, the country's last reindeer herd in the Cairngorm corrie
2. *Balmoral Castle* (Royal Deeside, Aberdeenshire, Scotland, UK). The Scottish baronial castle built by Prince Albert from 1853 for Queen Victoria, the royal family's private Highland estate every August and September since; Victoria died here in 1901, the granite walls and the conical-roofed tower still as Albert drew them

### 25. Toronto International Film Festival

**Port:** Downtown Toronto, Ontario, Canada
**Date:** Thu–Sun Sept 9–19
**Flags:** ART, CULTURE

North America’s most important film festival and one of the three Big-A international film festivals on Earth (alongside Cannes and Venice), observed annually over eleven days in early-to-mid September across downtown Toronto. Founded in 1976 by Bill Marshall, Henk van der Kolk, and Dusty Cohl as the “Festival of Festivals” (originally a curated selection of the year’s best films from other festivals); renamed Toronto International Film Festival in 1994. The 52nd annual edition. TIFF is widely considered the most influential awards-season film festival in North America (Oscar campaigns are launched here; the People’s Choice Award has predicted 11 of the last 15 Best Picture Oscar winners). The festival operates across multiple downtown venues simultaneously: the TIFF Bell Lightbox on King Street West (the festival’s purpose-built year-round headquarters, opened 2010, with five cinemas and the archetypal opening-night Roy Thomson Hall premiere); the Princess of Wales Theatre, the Royal Alexandra Theatre, the Royal Ontario Museum’s Eaton Auditorium, the Scotiabank Theatre Toronto, and the iconic outdoor Festival Street pedestrianization of King Street West for the festival’s first weekend. 250+ films screen across the eleven days including 100+ world premieres; 480,000+ attendees from across the global film industry.

**The Berth.** In Toronto: Four Seasons Hotel Toronto on Yorkville Avenue for the canonical TIFF-celebrity- residence luxury (the actual hotel where the major TIFF talent stays); The Hazelton Hotel in Yorkville for the canonical TIFF design-luxury; The Ritz-Carlton Toronto on Wellington Street West for the canonical modern downtown luxury opposite the Roy Thomson Hall; The Drake Hotel on Queen Street West for the design-set boutique-arts hotel.

**The Galley.** In Toronto: Alo on Spadina by chef Patrick Kriss for the canonical Toronto Michelin-starred contemporary; Edulis for the canonical Toronto modern Mediterranean tasting; Buca on King for the canonical Toronto modern Italian (chef Rob Gentile’s flagship); Lee Restaurant by chef Susur Lee for the canonical Toronto modern Asian fusion; The Drake Café for the canonical TIFF- week informal lunch; Schmaltz Appetizing on Roncesvalles for the canonical Toronto Jewish- deli morning ritual.

**The Bearings.**

1. *CN Tower* (Toronto, Ontario, Canada). Toronto's communications spire of post-tensioned reinforced concrete completed 1976, the glass floor of the main observation deck set 342 metres above Front Street; the elevators climb at six metres per second
2. *Niagara Falls* (Niagara Falls, Ontario, Canada). The 51-metre Horseshoe Falls on the Canadian side and the 50-metre American Falls opposite, the most powerful waterfall in North America by volume, the Maid of the Mist still climbing into the spray since 1846; an hour and a half south of Toronto

### 26. Reno Air Races

**Port:** Reno-Stead Airport, Nevada
**Date:** Wed–Sun third week of September, 5 days
**Flags:** CULTURE

The largest closed-circuit air race in the world and the most important annual aviation event in the western United States, observed annually over five days in the third week of September at Reno-Stead Airport, 14 miles north of Reno, Nevada. The 60th annual edition (founded 1964). The races feature six classes of aircraft competing on a 6.97-mile pylon-marked oval course at altitudes of 50–100 feet above the desert floor: (1) Unlimited (the signature class, modified WWII fighter-bomber aircraft including P-51 Mustangs, F8F Bearcats, and Hawker Sea Furies, with top speeds approaching 500 mph); (2) Jet (modified L-39 Albatros trainer jets); (3) Sport (kit-built composite aircraft); (4) T-6 (vintage WWII trainers); (5) Formula One (small experimental class); (6) Biplane. The races run heats throughout each day with the championship finals on Sunday afternoon. Between heats, the iconic Air Force Thunderbirds and Navy Blue Angels demonstration teams perform aerobatic displays; vintage warbird formations make appearance flyovers; and the Reno High Roller Tour brings actual WWII-veteran fighter pilots to fly heritage demonstration laps. 200,000+ attendees across the festival week. Note: confirm the current host airport, as the festival has indicated possible relocation in recent years.

**The Berth.** In Reno: Atlantis Casino Resort Spa on South Virginia Street for the canonical Reno casino- resort luxury; The Whitney Peak Hotel on Virginia Street for the design-boutique non-gaming luxury; Peppermill Reno on South Virginia Street for the canonical Reno mega-casino. Many attendees camp on the airfield grounds during the races.

**The Galley.** In Reno: Old Granite Street Eatery on West Granite Street for the canonical Reno modern American with the canonical wood-fire programming; Liberty Food & Wine Exchange on Granite Street for the canonical Reno wine-bar; The Twisted Fork on Mae Anne Avenue for the canonical Reno late-night breakfast (24-hour aviation-themed pub-grub). In Carson City (35 minutes south): The Union on Curry Street for the canonical Carson modern American.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Lake Tahoe* (Nevada-California border, USA). The cobalt-blue alpine lake at 1,897 metres in the Sierra Nevada, the second-deepest in the United States at 501 metres, the clearest Western water above 30 metres; Mark Twain called it the fairest picture the whole earth affords
2. *Donner Memorial State Park* (Truckee, California, USA). The pass where 87 westbound pioneers were caught by November snow in 1846, 39 of them surviving to spring; the Pioneer Monument stands the height of the snow that winter, 6.7 metres, and the museum holds what was left when the rest were dug out

### 27. Folsom Street Fair

**Port:** Folsom Street, SoMa, San Francisco
**Date:** Sun last Sunday of September (Sep 26)
**Flags:** CULTURE, ART

The largest leather-and-kink themed street fair in the world and one of the defining annual events in the global queer calendar, observed each last Sunday of September on Folsom Street in San Francisco’s South of Market (SoMa) district. Founded in 1984 by neighborhood gay community organizers Michael Valerio, Kathleen Connell, and the Folsom Street Events nonprofit as a deliberately queer-leather neighborhood pride event in response to the early AIDS crisis that was devastating SoMa’s leather bars. The 44th annual edition. The fair occupies thirteen city blocks (Folsom Street between 8th and 13th Streets, plus the cross streets); 400,000+ attendees from around the world; entry is by suggested donation ($10–20) with proceeds going to local AIDS, LGBTQ+, and HIV charities (over $7 million distributed to community organizations across the fair’s history). The fair’s programming spans the leather and kink communities, demonstration stages, the Mr. Folsom and Ms. Folsom contests, the world’s largest gathering of leather title-holders, and the iconic on-street vendor village. The fair is unapologetically adult-themed (full nudity is permitted under California law); the festival’s policy is ’look but don’t photograph without consent.’ The pre-fair weekend includes the defining Mr. SF Leather Contest at the SF Eagle (398 12th Street); the post-fair Magnitude dance party closes the weekend. Pair the visit with the GLBT Historical Society Museum in the Castro.

**The Berth.** In SoMa for the festival-route walking distance: Hotel Zelos on Market Street for the modern design-luxury at Powell Street BART; The Pickwick Hotel on Mission Street for the canonical 1928 heritage boutique; The Inn San Francisco on South Van Ness for the canonical Castro/SoMa-adjacent Victorian B&B (the canonical queer-owned and -operated heritage stay since 1976). In the wider city: The Fairmont San Francisco on Nob Hill; The Battery in the Financial District.

**The Galley.** In SoMa near Folsom Street: Zuni Café on Market Street for the canonical SF roast chicken since 1979; Saison on 4th Street for the canonical SF three-Michelin-star modern American; Wayfare Tavern on Sacramento by chef Tyler Florence for the canonical SF heritage tavern. Castro- adjacent: Frances on 17th Street by chef Melissa Perello for the canonical SF Michelin-starred modern Californian.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Golden Gate Bridge* (San Francisco, California, USA). The international-orange suspension span across the strait the Spanish called Boca del Puerto de San Francisco, opened May 1937 in the depths of the Depression; the 1.7 km of main cable made of 27,572 individual wire strands
2. *Mission Dolores* (San Francisco, California, USA). Mission San Francisco de Asís of 1776, the oldest intact building in San Francisco and the sixth Spanish mission of Alta California, the adobe-walled chapel surviving every earthquake including 1906; Alfred Hitchcock filmed the Vertigo cemetery scenes in the graveyard

The world’s largest hot-air balloon event, founded 1972, 600+ balloons taking off in coordinated mass ascensions at dawn each morning across 78 acres of the Balloon Fiesta Park, plus the iconic Special Shape Rodeo (200+ shaped balloons including Darth Vader, panda bears, and an enormous wedge of cheese), and the spectacular Balloon Glow evening events with 200+ balloons illuminated stationary on the field at dusk.

2. *Chaco Culture National Historical Park* (Nageezi, New Mexico, USA). The 850-1150 CE Ancestral Puebloan ceremonial centre on the high desert mesa of northwest New Mexico, fourteen great houses of dressed sandstone aligned to lunar and solar standstills; UNESCO 1987

The largest Renaissance festival in the Southeast, in its 33rd year, eight weekends across a 22-acre fully built Tudor village 25 minutes north of Charlotte, full lists jousting on a championship tournament field, daily pirate shows, 16 stages, the popular Highland Fling weekend in mid-October, 250+ artisan shops, and the iconic Royal Feast (separate ticket).

### 6. Great American Beer Festival

**Port:** Levitt Pavilion, Denver, Colorado
**Date:** Thu–Sat Oct 7–9
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

The 46th edition; America’s premier beer festival and cultural phenomenon, the most renowned craft-beer competition on Earth, the spiritual Olympics of American brewing. Founded in 1982 by Charlie Papazian, the legendary nuclear engineer turned homebrewing evangelist who in 1978 had founded the American Homebrewers Association and in 1984 published The Complete Joy of Homebrewing (still the best-selling homebrewing book of all time, 1+ million copies), as a small adjunct to the AHA’s fourth annual conference at the Harvest House Hotel in Boulder, Colorado in June 1982. The first festival featured 24 participating breweries, 47 beers, and 800 attendees. From those modest beginnings, GABF has grown across nearly five decades into the world’s largest ticketed beer festival, the most-followed craft-beer competition, and the cultural high point of the American beer year. The festival moved from Boulder to Denver in 1984; outgrew the original Currigan Hall venue and moved to the iconic Colorado Convention Center in 2000 (where it ran for 25 years, anchoring downtown Denver’s autumn calendar); and in 2026, despite community pushback, relocated outdoors to Denver’s Levitt Pavilion at Ruby Hill Park for the open-air era, where it remains.

**The Berth.** Denver: The Brown Palace since 1892; The Crawford Hotel in Union Station; Halcyon Cherry Creek. Aspen: The Little Nell; Hotel Jerome. The Ramble Hotel in RiNo (River North) for the canonical Denver craft-beer-district design-boutique; Hotel Teatro opposite the Denver Center for the heritage Tramway Building Belle-Époque luxury.

**The Galley.** Denver: Frasca for the Michelin Italian; Fruition Restaurant; Linger. Aspen: Element 47 at The Little Nell; Matsuhisa Aspen. Mercantile Dining & Provision at Union Station by chef Alex Seidel for the canonical Denver modern American; Beckon by chef Duncan Holmes for the canonical Denver chef’s-counter tasting menu in RiNo.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Red Rocks Amphitheatre* (Morrison, Colorado, USA). The natural sandstone amphitheatre held between two 90-metre red-rock fins, opened as a venue in 1941; the Beatles played here, U2 filmed here, the acoustics still unrepeated
2. *Garden of the Gods* (Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA). The 1,367-acre red-sandstone fins and balanced rocks at the foot of Pikes Peak, named in 1859 by a surveyor who thought it a place fit for the gods to assemble; National Natural Landmark since 1971, admission free since deeded to the city in 1909

Belgium’s largest pop-culture and sci-fi convention, held twice yearly (April and October) at Flanders Expo in Ghent, three days, 40,000+ attendees, one of the major Benelux events on the comic-con circuit. 2. *Gravensteen Castle* (Ghent, East Flanders, Belgium). The Castle of the Counts built 1180 on a Roman fort by Philip of Alsace, modelled on the castles he saw on the Second Crusade; the only intact medieval moated castle in Flanders, the gun port view of central Ghent still spectacular

### 8. Alba International White Truffle Fair

**Port:** Alba, Piedmont, Italy
**Date:** Sat–Sun weekends October through early December
**Flags:** FOOD

The world’s most prestigious white truffle event, founded 1929, held in the medieval Piedmontese town of Alba, the storied home of the white truffle (Tuber magnatum pico, the most expensive food on Earth by weight). The World Truffle Auction in early November sets the year’s record price; the Saturday-Sunday market at the Cortile della Maddalena offers truffles directly from the trifolau hunters; pair with white-truffle dinners at every restaurant in town and Barolo wines from the surrounding Langhe hills.

**The Berth.** Rome: Hotel de Russie; Hassler. Florence: Hotel Savoy; J.K. Place. Milan: Bulgari Milano. Venice: Aman Venice; Cipriani. In Piedmont, the festival’s home, the Langhe wine country: Casa di Langa, a Relais & Châteaux resort in the converted Cerretta Estate above Alba for the modern Langhe wine-country luxury; Villa La Madonna in Monastero Bormida (45 minutes east) for the heritage 17th-century manor on the wine-country hills; Palazzo Finati in Alba’s historic center for the canonical 19th-century heritage boutique walking distance to the truffle market.

**The Galley.** Rome: Roscioli; Felice a Testaccio; Da Cesare al Casaletto. Florence: Enoteca Pinchiorri; Sostanza; All’Antico Vinaio. Milan: Trussardi alla Scala; Trattoria Milanese. Venice: Alle Testiere; Antiche Carampane. In the Langhe: Piazza Duomo in Alba by chef Enrico Crippa for the canonical three-Michelin-star Piedmonte modern (the canonical garden-to-table tasting); Da Cesare in Albaretto della Torre by chef Cesare Giaccone for the canonical Langhe trifolau-table truffle destination (book months ahead); La Ciau del Tornavento in Treiso for the canonical Barolo-and-tartufi cellar dining; Osteria Le Tre Lanterne on Via dei Fabbri for the canonical Alba truffle-season trattoria.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Langhe-Roero & Monferrato Vineyards* (Piedmont, Italy). The hilltop villages and vineyards of southern Piedmont where Barolo and Barbaresco have been made since the eleventh century, the white truffles of Alba grown in the same calcareous marl; UNESCO 2014, the most-photographed wine landscape in Italy
2. *Residences of the Royal House of Savoy* (Turin & Piedmont, Italy). The eleven royal palaces and country estates built by the Savoy across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the Royal Palace of Turin at the centre and Stupinigi and Venaria Reale among the others; UNESCO 1997

### 9. Feria Nacional del Mole

**Port:** San Pedro Atocpan, Milpa Alta, Mexico City
**Date:** throughout October
**Flags:** FOOD, CULTURE

An eight-day mole festival in San Pedro Atocpan, Milpa Alta borough on the southern edge of Mexico City, held mid-October since 1977; San Pedro produces 90% of the mole consumed in Mexico City and the festival is the year’s reckoning of which paste-makers got it right. Eighty-plus moles compete, from the seven canonical Oaxacan moles (negro, rojo, amarillo, verde, chichilo, manchamantel, coloradito) to local Atocpan inventions and one-off experimental pastes. Eat mole over turkey at Mercado de Mole stalls; buy paste in plastic bags by the kilo to take home; watch the Sunday molcajete-grinding contest on the central stage.

**The Berth.** Mexico City: Las Alcobas; Four Seasons; Casa Habita. Oaxaca: Quinta Real; Los Amantes. Yucatán: Chablé Yucatán; Hacienda Temozón. Hotel Carlota on Río Amazonas in Cuauhtémoc for the canonical CDMX design-boutique; Casa Polanco in the converted 1940s mansion for the modern luxury near Bosque de Chapultepec.

**The Galley.** Mexico City: Pujol; Quintonil; Sud 777; Contramar. Oaxaca: Casa Oaxaca; Origen; Las Quince Letras. Yucatán: Kuuk in Mérida; Hartwood in Tulum. Rosetta in Roma Norte by chef Elena Reygadas for the canonical CDMX modern Italian-Mexican; Maximo Bistrot by chef Eduardo García for the canonical Mexico City modern Mexican farm-to- table.

**The Bearings.**

The Aztec twin-shrine pyramid at the heart of Tenochtitlán uncovered 1978 beneath the Zócalo, the shrines of Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc rebuilt in seven concentric stages between 1325 and 1521; the museum holds the eight-tonne carved Coyolxauhqui stone unearthed by accident in 1978
2. *Teotihuacán* (State of Mexico, Mexico). The city built around the first century CE with the third-largest pyramid in the world by volume, abandoned by 750 and a ruin already when the Aztecs named it the place where the gods were born; UNESCO 1987

### 13. Battle of Hastings Reenactment

**Port:** Battle Abbey, East Sussex, UK
**Date:** Sat–Sun Oct 16–17
**Flags:** VIKING, CASTLE

The annual mid-October reenactment at Battle Abbey, East Sussex, the October 14, 1066 battle in which William of Normandy defeated Harold II’s Anglo-Saxon army, killing the king and establishing Norman rule over England. English Heritage stages the essential reenactment on the actual battlefield (the abbey was founded by William on the spot where Harold fell), with 1,000 reenactors representing the Norman cavalry and the Saxon shield wall. The high altar of the abbey was placed exactly where Harold died; the foundations remain visible.

**The Berth.** London anchored: The Connaught, The Beaumont, The Zetter Townhouse, or the Hoxton. Country: Heckfield Place, The Pig hotels, or Soho Farmhouse. In East Sussex near the battlefield: The Powder Mills Hotel in Battle itself for the canonical festival- base Georgian country house at the abbey gates; Newick Park Hotel in Newick for the heritage 18th-century country house 45 minutes west; The George in Rye for the canonical Sussex coaching-inn heritage 30 minutes east.

**The Galley.** London: St. John, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers in Marlow; L’Enclume in Cumbria; or the canonical local gastropub. In East Sussex: The Mirabelle at the Grand Hotel Eastbourne for the canonical Sussex coastal heritage fine- dining; Webbe’s at the Fish Café in Rye by chef Paul Webbe for the canonical Sussex seafood (already noted on July V21 Hastings Pirate).

**The Bearings.**

1. *Battle Abbey* (Battle, East Sussex, England, UK). The Norman abbey William the Conqueror founded on the spot where Harold fell on October 14, 1066, the high altar placed exactly on the king's death-place; the abbey ruined at the Dissolution but the gatehouse, dorter, and foundation lines still walked
2. *Pevensey Castle* (Pevensey, East Sussex, England, UK). The Roman Saxon Shore fort of Anderitum where William the Conqueror landed September 28, 1066, the Norman castle raised inside the Roman walls in the years after, twice held in siege but never taken; the moat now a green field

The anniversary of the 1813 battle that broke Napoleon’s German empire; Europe’s largest Napoleonic-era reenactment alongside Waterloo, with ~6,000 period-uniformed reenactors from across Europe (French, Prussian, Russian, Austrian, Saxon line), encampments around the Völkerschlachtdenkmal monument at the original battlefield.

### 15. Trafalgar Day

**Port:** Portsmouth Historic Dockyard, UK & Royal Navy worldwide
**Date:** Thu Oct 21
**Flags:** PIRATE, CULTURE

The annual October 21 commemoration of the 1805 Battle of Trafalgar, the Royal Navy’s decisive victory under Nelson over the French and Spanish fleets, ending Napoleon’s invasion threat to Britain. HMS Victory, Nelson’s flagship, remains in dry dock at Portsmouth Historic Dockyard and is the standard Trafalgar Day site, with a wreath-laying at the Quarterdeck plaque marking where Nelson fell. The Royal Navy holds a parade and 21-gun salute; the Trafalgar Square fountain is illuminated in his honor; the Royal Maritime Museum at Greenwich runs parallel programming. Pair with the National Maritime Museum at Greenwich and HMS Belfast on the Thames.

**The Berth.** Choose your home capital, the festival is observed simultaneously across continents. The most photogenic public observances are typically in the capital city or principal cultural centre. In Portsmouth for the canonical HMS Victory observance: The Queens Hotel Portsmouth on Clarence Parade for the canonical 1861 Victorian heritage on Southsea Common; Holiday Inn Express Portsmouth-North for the modern festival-base dependable. In London for the Trafalgar Square observance: The Trafalgar St James at the corner of Trafalgar Square for the canonical festival-day location.

**The Galley.** Whatever the local diaspora cooks for the day, the dish defines the place. Look for community kitchens, temples, family-style restaurants, and street food specifically associated with the festival. In Portsmouth: Restaurant 27 on South Parade by chef Kevin Bingham for the canonical Portsmouth Michelin-Bib Gourmand modern British; Old Customs House at Vernon Buildings for the canonical Portsmouth Historic Dockyard waterfront dining. In London: Rules on Maiden Lane since 1798 for the canonical British game and traditional cooking destination near Trafalgar.

**The Bearings.**

1. *HMS Victory* (Portsmouth Historic Dockyard, England, UK). Nelson's 104-gun first-rate flagship at Trafalgar, still commissioned as the flagship of the First Sea Lord, in dry dock at Portsmouth since 1922; the brass plaque on the quarterdeck where Nelson fell still set in the deck planks above the cockpit
2. *Mary Rose Museum* (Portsmouth Historic Dockyard, England, UK). The 1545 Tudor warship that capsized in the Solent in front of Henry VIII, recovered from the seabed in 1982 and displayed beside HMS Victory in a purpose-built museum; some 19,000 personal possessions of her crew of around 415 on display

### 16. Yorktown Day

**Port:** Yorktown Battlefield, Virginia
**Date:** Tue Oct 19
**Flags:** CULTURE

The annual October 19 commemoration at Yorktown Battlefield, Virginia, the October 19, 1781 surrender of Cornwallis to Washington that effectively ended the American Revolutionary War. The Yorktown Day Association organizes the traditional ceremony: a parade through Yorktown’s historic district, a wreath-laying at the French Cemetery (honoring Rochambeau’s army), the Patriotic Exercises at the Victory Monument, and the dramatic afternoon “Surrender Field” reenactment of the British grounding of arms. The Park Service runs the Yorktown Battlefield Visitor Center year-round.

**The Berth.** Richmond: The Jefferson Hotel since 1895; Quirk Hotel for the design-set. Williamsburg: Williamsburg Inn. Charlottesville: Keswick Hall; The Clifton. The Williamsburg Lodge, an Autograph Collection hotel near Colonial Williamsburg for the canonical Colonial-themed festival-base 15 minutes from Yorktown; The Westin Reston Heights outside DC (2.5 hours north) for the canonical festival-week extension.

**The Galley.** Richmond: L’Opossum for canonical modern Southern; Heritage in The Fan. Williamsburg: The Trellis; The Cheese Shop. Charlottesville: The Local; Tavola for Italian. Le Yaca in Kingsmill (10 minutes from Yorktown) for the canonical Williamsburg-area French; The Carrot Tree Kitchens in Yorktown itself for the canonical local Colonial-era American.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Yorktown Battlefield* (Yorktown, Virginia, USA). The York River siege of September and October 1781 where Cornwallis surrendered 8,000 men to Washington and Rochambeau, effectively ending the Revolutionary War; the redoubts, the surrender field, and the Moore House where the terms were signed all preserved
2. *Jamestown Settlement* (Jamestown, Virginia, USA). The 1607 first permanent English settlement in the Americas, the original 1607 James Fort palisade and church now excavated and exposed; the living-history Jamestown Settlement Museum nearby with the three full-scale replica ships moored on the river

### 17. Tbilisoba

**Port:** Tbilisi, Georgia

Tbilisi’s annual two-day city celebration in early October, Georgian capital’s autumn harvest festival in the historic Old Town, featuring the city’s wine harvest (rtveli), street fairs, traditional polyphonic singing, sword dancing (khorumi), and the legendary Tbilisi food culture in concentrated form. Khachapuri (every regional variant: Adjarian boat, Imeretian round, Megrelian double-cheese), khinkali (the soup-dumpling), mtsvadi (Georgian shashlik), and chacha (the local grappa) flow freely along Rustaveli Avenue and through the Old Town’s cobbled lanes.

The autumnal Viking Álfablót, the historic blood-sacrifice to the elves performed across pre-Christian Scandinavia at the autumn equinox, mentioned in the Eddic poem Austrfararvísur. 1. *Lucca City Walls* (Lucca, Tuscany, Italy). The Renaissance-built 4.2-kilometre encircling wall of red brick and earth, finished 1645 and never tested by siege, now a tree-lined promenade above the medieval town; the only fully intact Renaissance city wall in Italy
2. *Piazza dei Miracoli* (Pisa, Tuscany, Italy). The grass-and-marble square holding the Cathedral, Baptistery, Camposanto, and the Leaning Tower, the four masterpieces of Pisan Romanesque between 1063 and 1372; UNESCO 1987, 14 kilometres from Lucca

### 21. MCM Comic Con London Autumn

**Port:** ExCeL London
**Date:** Fri–Sun late October
**Flags:** GAME

London’s major comic-con, held twice yearly (May and October) at ExCeL London in the Docklands, three days, 130,000+ attendees, the UK’s largest pop-culture event. Heavy anime, manga, and tabletop gaming representation alongside Hollywood celebrity guests; the ExCeL’s massive halls accommodate the queues. The autumn edition typically draws stronger anime publishers (Crunchyroll). Take the DLR to Prince Regent station for the venue; stay at Crowne Plaza London Docklands or in central London for the cultural day-trips between con days.

1. *Tower Bridge* (London, England, UK). Horace Jones's Victorian Gothic bascule bridge of 1894 with its twin towers and high-level walkway, the bascules still raised about 800 times a year; the glass floor of the walkway added 2014 for those willing to look 42 metres down at the traffic
2. *St Paul's Cathedral* (London, England, UK). Christopher Wren's English baroque cathedral begun 1675 and finished 1710, replacing the medieval church burned in the Great Fire; the 108-metre lead-and-stone dome the second-tallest in the world when built, the Whispering Gallery in its drum

### 22. Diwali

**Port:** Throughout India and the Indian diaspora
**Date:** Fri Oct 29
**Flags:** CULTURE

The new-moon night of Kartik month; Hinduism’s most-celebrated festival, the five-day festival of lights commemorating Lord Rama’s return to Ayodhya, houses, businesses, and temples decorated with millions of clay-oil diya lamps and electric lights; rangoli geometric patterns chalked at every threshold; firework displays in every city; family reunion dinners with sweets (laddus, jalebis, gulab jamun) and gift exchanges. The Ganges-side ghats of Varanasi, the Golden Temple in Amritsar, and the streets of Mumbai are the spectacles.

**The Berth.** City-dependent: Mumbai (Taj Mahal Palace), Delhi (The Oberoi), Jaipur (Rambagh Palace), Udaipur (Lake Palace), Goa (Taj Exotica). Pilgrimage routes: regional Taj or ITC properties anchor most. In Varanasi for the Ganges-ghats Diwali pilgrimage: Brijrama Palace on Darbhanga Ghat for the canonical heritage 18th-century palace; Taj Ganges Varanasi for the canonical modern Diwali-night Ganges-ghats luxury.

**The Galley.** Regional canonical: Mumbai’s Bombay Canteen; Delhi’s Indian Accent; Goa’s Vinayak; Jaipur’s Suvarna Mahal; Kolkata’s 6 Ballygunge Place. Eat the regional thali wherever you land. In Mumbai: Trishna in Kala Ghoda for the canonical Mumbai modern Mangalorean seafood; Bademiya behind the Taj Mahal Palace for the canonical Mumbai late-night kebab destination.

**The Bearings.**

1. *Golden Temple* (Amritsar, Punjab, India). The Harmandir Sahib at the heart of the Sikh faith, the gold-leafed sanctum sitting in the centre of the Pool of Nectar at the heart of Amritsar; the langar kitchen here feeds 100,000 free meals a day to all comers, the largest community kitchen on Earth
2. *Ayodhya & the Ram Mandir* (Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, India). The Sarayu-river city named in the Ramayana as the birthplace of Rama, the new Ram Mandir consecrated January 2024 on the site of the demolished sixteenth-century Babri mosque, a pilgrimage destination of unprecedented size since
