# Book the Second. Pilgrimages of Humanity

*Twenty-nine themed trails, ten stops each. Each pilgrimage is named for the spirit of the journey.*

---

## Pilgrimage I. All That Is Gold

Year-round destinations for Lord of the Rings fans visiting the UK. Best paired with the Tolkien Weekend at Sarehole (late May), Oxonmoot in Oxford (Sept 2-5), or Hobbit Day (Sept 22). Birmingham + Oxford make a perfect 3-4 day Tolkien trip.

> Not all those who wander are lost.
> *J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings*

### Stop 1. Sarehole Mill

**Waypoint:** Birmingham (Hall Green)

Where the Shire was born. The eighteenth-century working watermill in Hall Green on the southern edge of Birmingham stood beside the fields where a young J.R.R. Tolkien lived from 1896 to 1900 (ages 4-8), the formative years he later called "the longest-seeming and most formative part of my life." The mill itself appears thinly veiled in the Old Mill at Hobbiton in The Lord of the Rings; the surrounding Sarehole Brook and Moseley Bog became the Old Forest and the Withywindle. Working watermill, free entry, with Tolkien interpretive panels. The Tolkien Society's annual Tolkien Weekend here in late May, pageantry, readings, and costume, is the event this stop is timed for. Pair with Moseley Bog (six-minute walk) and The Plough and Harrow on Hagley Road, where Tolkien spent his last night in England before WWI.

**The Berth.** The Edgbaston for the boutique cocktail-bar hotel; Hotel du Vin in the converted Victorian eye hospital; or the Grand Hotel on Colmore Row for the heritage.

**The Galley.** Adam's for the Michelin star in the Jewellery Quarter; Carters of Moseley for the modern British; Pushkar in Brindleyplace for the canonical Birmingham balti; Otto's Wood-Fired Pizza for the Brummie casual.

> If more of us valued food and cheer and song above hoarded gold, it would be a merrier world.
> *J.R.R. Tolkien, The Hobbit*

### Stop 2. Moseley Bog

**Waypoint:** Birmingham

Where the Old Forest grew. The wild fragment of ancient woodland five minutes' walk from Sarehole Mill is the place Tolkien named as the literal inspiration for the Old Forest of The Lord of the Rings. Forty acres of bog, oak, and birch on the edge of Birmingham, peaty, atmospheric, threaded with paths over wooden boards through the wettest sections; a Local Nature Reserve since 1980. In summer the canopy closes; in winter the bare limbs and dark water are precisely the Old Forest of Frodo's escape from the Shire. Pair with Sarehole Mill (six-minute walk) and the small Tolkien Garden at Sarehole.

**The Berth.** The Edgbaston for the boutique cocktail-bar hotel; Hotel du Vin in the converted Victorian eye hospital; or the Grand Hotel on Colmore Row for the heritage.

**The Galley.** Adam's for the Michelin star in the Jewellery Quarter; Carters of Moseley for the modern British; Pushkar in Brindleyplace for the canonical Birmingham balti; Otto's Wood-Fired Pizza for the Brummie casual.

> The wide world is all about you: you can fence yourselves in, but you cannot forever fence it out.
> *J.R.R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring*

### Stop 3. Perrott's Folly & Edgbaston Waterworks Tower

**Waypoint:** Birmingham

Where the Two Towers stand. Two red-brick Victorian towers half a mile apart in Edgbaston, visible from the windows of young Tolkien's home on Stirling Road. Perrott's Folly (1758), seven storeys of inexplicable Gothic eccentricity built by John Perrott for reasons no historian has fully reconstructed, and the Edgbaston Waterworks Tower (1870), an Italianate brick chimney for the pumping station, became, in Tolkien's imagination, Minas Morgul and Minas Tirith, the dark tower of the East and the white tower of the West. Stand on Waterworks Road at dusk and the geometry is obvious. The Folly is occasionally open for tours (check the Friends of Perrott's Folly schedule); the Waterworks Tower remains in active use and is viewed only from the street. Pair with the short walk south to Edgbaston Reservoir, the model for the lake at Helm's Deep in many readers' minds.

**The Berth.** The Edgbaston for the boutique cocktail-bar hotel; Hotel du Vin in the converted Victorian eye hospital; or the Grand Hotel on Colmore Row for the heritage.

**The Galley.** Adam's for the Michelin star in the Jewellery Quarter; Carters of Moseley for the modern British; Pushkar in Brindleyplace for the canonical Birmingham balti; Otto's Wood-Fired Pizza for the Brummie casual.

> From the ashes a fire shall be woken, a light from the shadows shall spring.
> *J.R.R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring*

### Stop 4. The Birmingham Oratory

**Waypoint:** Edgbaston, Birmingham

Where the orphan found a guardian, and a faith. When Tolkien's widowed mother Mabel died in 1904, worn down by poverty and diabetes when John Ronald was twelve, she left her two boys to Father Francis Morgan, a kindly half-Welsh, half-Spanish priest of the Birmingham Oratory, the great church founded by John Henry Newman. Father Francis became the boys' guardian, feeding and educating them, paying Tolkien's way to Oxford, standing as the father he had already lost. The Catholic faith his mother had suffered for, and which he kept all his life, became the bedrock of his imagination, the light behind the eucatastrophe, the sudden joyous turn he believed every true story echoed. The Oratory still stands, an Italianate basilica of marble and gold, Newman's own rooms preserved within. Sit in the hush where a grieving boy found a second father, and consider how loss, faith, and kindness fed the deepest roots of Middle-earth.

**The Berth.** Birmingham: the Edgbaston for the boutique cocktail-bar hotel; Hotel du Vin in the converted Victorian eye hospital; or the Grand Hotel on Colmore Row for heritage grandeur near the centre.

**The Galley.** Birmingham: Adam's for the Michelin star; Carters of Moseley for modern British; Pushkar in Brindleyplace for the canonical Birmingham balti; the curry houses of the Balti Triangle, a city institution.

> I do not expect history to be anything but a long defeat, though it contains some samples of final victory.
> *J.R.R. Tolkien, in a letter*

### Stop 5. Bodleian Library Tolkien Archive

**Waypoint:** Oxford

Where the maps of Middle-earth are kept. The Bodleian holds Tolkien's personal papers, manuscripts, drawings, and the original maps of Middle-earth, deposited by his estate beginning in 1979. The Weston Library (the modern wing of the Bodleian, opened 2015) hosts rotating Tolkien exhibitions every few years drawing from the archive. Permanent reading-room access requires a Bodleian Reader Card and a stated research purpose; for visitors, the Weston's Treasures Gallery typically displays a small rotating Tolkien selection. Pair with the Ashmolean (10 minutes' walk) and the Bodleian's Divinity School and Duke Humphrey's reading room, Hogwarts on screen, but actually older.

**The Berth.** The Old Parsonage on Banbury Road for the boutique; The Randolph (now Graduate Oxford) on Beaumont Street; or the Macdonald Eastgate near Magdalen Bridge for the proximity.

**The Galley.** Gee's on Banbury for the conservatory dining-room; The Eagle and Child (the Bird and Baby) for the Inkling pilgrimage pint; Brown's on Woodstock for the Oxford brasserie; Magdalen Arms in Iffley for the gastropub Sunday roast.

> Still round the corner there may wait a new road or a secret gate.
> *J.R.R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring*

### Stop 6. Exeter College & Merton College

**Waypoint:** Oxford

Where the don made his home. Tolkien matriculated at Exeter College, Oxford in 1911 and read Classics, then English Language and Literature; he later returned as Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon at Pembroke (1925-45), then Merton Professor of English Language and Literature at Merton (1945-59), where his rooms in Merton Street remain. Exeter Chapel holds his memorial bust; Merton's Mob Quad is the oldest medieval quadrangle in Oxford. The Eagle and Child pub on St Giles' (the Bird and Baby) was the Inklings' Tuesday-morning haunt for nearly thirty years until 1962; the Thursday-evening readings of Lord of the Rings happened across town in Lewis's Magdalen rooms.

**The Berth.** The Old Parsonage on Banbury Road for the boutique; The Randolph (now Graduate Oxford) on Beaumont Street; or the Macdonald Eastgate near Magdalen Bridge for the proximity.

**The Galley.** Gee's on Banbury for the conservatory dining-room; The Eagle and Child (the Bird and Baby) for the Inkling pilgrimage pint; Brown's on Woodstock for the Oxford brasserie; Magdalen Arms in Iffley for the gastropub Sunday roast.

> The Road goes ever on and on, down from the door where it began.
> *J.R.R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring*

### Stop 7. 20 Northmoor Road

**Waypoint:** Oxford

Where The Hobbit was written. Tolkien's North Oxford home from 1930 to 1947 is the house where he wrote The Hobbit (published 1937) and most of The Lord of the Rings. A two-storey Edwardian semi-detached in red brick; a blue plaque marks the address. The house remains a private residence, view from the street only, but the garden is partially visible through the side gate, and the nearby Wolvercote Cemetery a short walk north holds his and Edith's joint grave under the names of Beren and Lúthien.

**The Berth.** The Old Parsonage on Banbury Road for the boutique; The Randolph (now Graduate Oxford) on Beaumont Street; or the Macdonald Eastgate near Magdalen Bridge for the proximity.

**The Galley.** Gee's on Banbury for the conservatory dining-room; The Eagle and Child (the Bird and Baby) for the Inkling pilgrimage pint; Brown's on Woodstock for the Oxford brasserie; Magdalen Arms in Iffley for the gastropub Sunday roast.

> It's a dangerous business, going out your front door. You step onto the Road, and there's no knowing where you might be swept off to.
> *J.R.R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring*

### Stop 8. The Eagle and Child

**Waypoint:** 49 St Giles', Oxford

Where The Lord of the Rings was first read aloud. For over thirty years, in a snug back room they called the Rabbit Room, Tolkien and C.S. Lewis and their circle of friends, the Inklings, met on Tuesday mornings over pints at this seventeenth-century pub, affectionately the Bird and Baby, to talk and argue and read aloud. The formal readings of works-in-progress, including the chapters of The Lord of the Rings as Tolkien wrote them and the Narnia and space-trilogy drafts from Lewis, happened separately on Thursday evenings in Lewis's Magdalen rooms across town; but the pub friendship that made them possible lived here. The pub sign shows an eagle bearing off a child, an apt emblem for an author whose heroes are so often snatched from doom by great eagles. The Eagle and Child has been closed for restoration in recent years, its reopening long promised; across the wide street, the Lamb and Flag, another Inklings haunt, carries the torch. Raise a pint where Middle-earth was first spoken into the air, and toast the friendship that made it.

**The Berth.** Oxford: the Old Parsonage on Banbury Road for the boutique; the Randolph (now Graduate Oxford) on Beaumont Street for the grand; or a college-quarter room within walking distance of St Giles'.

**The Galley.** Oxford: the Eagle and Child or the Lamb and Flag for the Inklings pint and a proper pie; Gee's on Banbury for the conservatory; Brown's on Woodstock for the brasserie; the Turf Tavern, hidden down its alley, for the historic ale.

> It is the strangest place in the world to find one of the rarest things on earth: a circle of friends who love one another truly.
> *after the spirit of the Inklings*

### Stop 9. The Oxford Botanic Garden

**Waypoint:** Rose Lane, Oxford

Where his favourite tree stood, and the Ents were born. The oldest botanic garden in Britain, founded in 1621 beside the Cherwell across from Magdalen College, was one of Tolkien's quiet refuges, and here grew the tree he loved above all others: an immense, twisted black pine, Pinus nigra, its great limbs flung skyward like a many-armed giant about to stride away. He was famously photographed leaning against it near the end of his life, and it is impossible to stand beneath it, as it was, and not see the Ents, the shepherds of the trees who walk and speak in The Lord of the Rings. The old pine grew unsafe and had to be felled in 2014, to the grief of readers worldwide; in 2021 a sapling grown from its line was replanted near the spot, and pilgrims leave little cairns of pinecones at its foot. Walk the walled garden where Tolkien sat in the green silence, find the young tree carrying on the old one's life, and feel how deeply he loved growing things.

**The Berth.** Oxford: the Old Bank Hotel on the High, steps from the garden; the Old Parsonage; or the Macdonald Eastgate by Magdalen Bridge for the proximity to the Botanic Garden and the river.

**The Galley.** Oxford: punt-side picnics on the Cherwell in summer; the Magdalen Arms in Iffley for the gastropub Sunday roast; Gee's; afternoon tea in the old city; the covered market's stalls for a walking lunch.

> It is not the strong who survive, nor the wise, but the small hands that do the work while the eyes of the great are elsewhere.
> *after J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings*

### Stop 10. Tolkien's Grave

**Waypoint:** Wolvercote Cemetery, Oxford

Where Beren and Lúthien lie. Wolvercote Cemetery, two miles north of Oxford city centre, holds the joint grave of John Ronald Reuel Tolkien (d. September 2, 1973) and his wife Edith Mary Tolkien (d. November 29, 1971), under a single grey granite headstone inscribed with the Beren and Lúthien names from the Silmarillion. Wolvercote is a working public cemetery on Banbury Road; the Tolkien grave is in section J, marked on the cemetery map at the gate. Devotees bring stones, leaves, and the occasional pipe-weed.

**The Berth.** The Old Parsonage on Banbury Road for the boutique; The Randolph (now Graduate Oxford) on Beaumont Street; or the Macdonald Eastgate near Magdalen Bridge for the proximity.

**The Galley.** Gee's on Banbury for the conservatory dining-room; The Eagle and Child (the Bird and Baby) for the Inkling pilgrimage pint; Brown's on Woodstock for the Oxford brasserie; Magdalen Arms in Iffley for the gastropub Sunday roast.

> I at last with weary feet will turn towards the lighted inn, my evening-rest and sleep to meet.
> *J.R.R. Tolkien, The Lord of the Rings*

---

## Pilgrimage II. Where the Bulls Run

Year-round destinations for the literary traveler in Pamplona, with two essential extensions into Madrid and one into the Pyrenees. Best paired with San Fermín itself (July 6-14), the seven days Hemingway returned to nine times, made world-famous in The Sun Also Rises in 1926, and which have drawn writers, drinkers, and the genuinely brave ever since. Three days in Pamplona, a day north for the fishing chapter, a night or two south for Madrid.

> There is no friend as loyal as a book.
> *Ernest Hemingway*

### Stop 1. Café Iruña

**Waypoint:** Plaza del Castillo, Pamplona

Where Jake Barnes drank through the fiesta. Hemingway's writing café from his first San Fermín in 1923, the same belle-époque interior of marble columns and gilt mirrors where Jake Barnes and Brett Ashley drink through The Sun Also Rises. Inside, in El Rincón de Hemingway, a bronze of the man leans on the bar. Order a coffee, then a wine, then a vermut. Watch the plaza fill as the morning runs end.

**The Berth.** Gran Hotel La Perla on Plaza del Castillo (Hemingway's room is preserved); Hotel Maisonnave in the old town; or Hotel Tres Reyes near the Citadel.

**The Galley.** Bar Gaucho on Calle Espoz y Mina for pintxos; Casa Otano for chuletón de buey; Café Iruña on the Plaza for the daily Hemingway-table reservation.

> I did not care what it was all about. All I wanted to know was how to live in it.
> *Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises*

### Stop 2. Hotel La Perla

**Waypoint:** Plaza del Castillo, Pamplona

Where Hemingway stayed during multiple San Fermín visits. The Hemingway Suite has been preserved with original furnishings and the same view over the plaza, he watched the bulls go past from his window. Even if you can't book it (and during San Fermín you cannot), the lobby is a small museum.

**The Berth.** Gran Hotel La Perla on Plaza del Castillo (Hemingway's room is preserved); Hotel Maisonnave in the old town; or Hotel Tres Reyes near the Citadel.

**The Galley.** Bar Gaucho on Calle Espoz y Mina for pintxos; Casa Otano for chuletón de buey; Café Iruña on the Plaza for the daily Hemingway-table reservation.

> The journey itself is my home.
> *Matsuo Bashō*

### Stop 3. Calle Estafeta

**Waypoint:** Pamplona

Where the bulls run at dawn. The narrow uphill street the bulls run, lined with the bars and balconies that have served runners since before Hemingway showed up. During San Fermín these bars open at four in the morning. The other 358 days it's an ordinary, beautiful old-town street where you can stand on the corner and read chapter 15 against the actual cobblestones.

**The Berth.** Gran Hotel La Perla on Plaza del Castillo (Hemingway's room is preserved); Hotel Maisonnave in the old town; or Hotel Tres Reyes near the Citadel.

**The Galley.** Bar Gaucho on Calle Espoz y Mina for pintxos; Casa Otano for chuletón de buey; Café Iruña on the Plaza for the daily Hemingway-table reservation.

> Nobody ever lives their life all the way up except bullfighters.
> *Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises*

### Stop 4. Plaza de Toros & Monumento a Hemingway

**Waypoint:** Pamplona

Where the run ends and the bronze man stands. The bullring at the end of the run, where the encierro deposits its survivors. The bronze of Hemingway outside the gate was placed by the city of Pamplona in 1968, seven years after his death, and bears his own description of the man as a writer who 'loved Pamplona deeply.' During San Fermín, the corridas here are the cultural event. The rest of the year, you can walk in and stand alone in the empty arena.

**The Berth.** Gran Hotel La Perla on Plaza del Castillo (Hemingway's room is preserved); Hotel Maisonnave in the old town; or Hotel Tres Reyes near the Citadel.

**The Galley.** Bar Gaucho on Calle Espoz y Mina for pintxos; Casa Otano for chuletón de buey; Café Iruña on the Plaza for the daily Hemingway-table reservation.

> Bullfighting is the only art in which the artist is in danger of death.
> *Ernest Hemingway, Death in the Afternoon*

### Stop 5. Restaurante Casa Otano

**Waypoint:** Calle San Nicolás, Pamplona

Where Navarra comes to the table. The living temple of Navarrese cooking, since 1959. Cordero al chilindrón, alcachofas con jamón, pimientos del piquillo, the local Garnacha. Hemingway's preferred restaurant, Casa Marceliano, in the old market, is long gone; Otano is the closest contemporary equivalent in spirit and in cooking. Reserve.

**The Berth.** Gran Hotel La Perla on Plaza del Castillo (Hemingway's room is preserved); Hotel Maisonnave in the old town; or Hotel Tres Reyes near the Citadel.

**The Galley.** Bar Gaucho on Calle Espoz y Mina for pintxos; Casa Otano for chuletón de buey; Café Iruña on the Plaza for the daily Hemingway-table reservation.

> This wine is too good for toast-drinking, my dear. You don't want to mix emotions up with a wine like that.
> *Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises*

### Stop 6. Hostal Burguete

**Waypoint:** Roncesvalles, 30 miles north of Pamplona

Where the piano still bears his signature. The Pyrenean village where Jake Barnes and Bill Gorton go trout fishing in chapters 11 and 12 of The Sun Also Rises. The Hostal Burguete still has the upright piano Hemingway played and signed in July 1923, the inscription is on the keyboard. The Irati river still has trout. The perfect day trip from Pamplona, especially if San Fermín has worn you down.

**The Berth.** Gran Hotel La Perla on Plaza del Castillo (Hemingway's room is preserved); Hotel Maisonnave in the old town; or Hotel Tres Reyes near the Citadel.

**The Galley.** Bar Gaucho on Calle Espoz y Mina for pintxos; Casa Otano for chuletón de buey; Café Iruña on the Plaza for the daily Hemingway-table reservation.

> You can't get away from yourself by moving from one place to another.
> *Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises*

### Stop 7. The Irati River

**Waypoint:** the Navarrese Pyrenees, near Burguete

Where Jake and Bill went fishing. In the middle of The Sun Also Rises, a novel of drink and desire and the bullfight, Hemingway set its quietest and most beloved chapter: Jake Barnes and Bill Gorton leave the noise of Pamplona for a few clean days of trout fishing on the Irati River, walking up through the beechwoods above Burguete to a cold green stream and fishing it in the morning light, eating their lunch and drinking wine cooled in the river. It is the still heart of the book, the brief grace before the fiesta's reckoning, and it is pure Hemingway: the prose stripped to the bone, the happiness located entirely in doing a simple thing well in a beautiful place. The Irati still rushes down out of the Navarrese-Basque Pyrenees through one of the largest beech forests in Europe, its upper reaches as lovely and lonely as he found them. Walk up the river with a rod or without one, find a pool under the beeches, cool a bottle in the current, and understand what Hemingway came to these mountains to feel.

**The Berth.** The Navarrese Pyrenees: the Hostal Burguete itself for the literary night; the rural guesthouses of the Irati valley and the Aezkoa; or Roncesvalles at the pass for the pilgrim's hostel where the Camino begins.

**The Galley.** Navarrese mountain cooking: trout in the style of Navarra, wrapped around cured ham; the lamb and game of the high valleys; Idiazabal sheep cheese; a bottle of Navarra red cooled, as Bill and Jake liked it, in the cold river.

> I was a little ashamed, and regretted that I was such a rotten Catholic, but realized there was nothing I could do about it.
> *Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises*

### Stop 8. Sobrino de Botín

**Waypoint:** Calle de los Cuchilleros, Madrid

Where the novel ends, over roast suckling pig. The oldest restaurant in continuous operation anywhere on Earth, founded 1725. The cochinillo asado here is what Jake Barnes orders in the closing chapter of The Sun Also Rises: 'We had roast young suckling pig and drank Rioja Alta.' Still on the menu. Still cooked in the original wood-fired oven, which by tradition a young Goya waited tables beside before he could afford pigments. Two-and-a-half hours south of Pamplona by AVE.

**The Berth.** The Westin Palace on Plaza de las Cortes; The Ritz; or the small NH Collection Madrid Plaza de la Reina for mid-range proximity to the centre.

**The Galley.** Casa Lucio on Cava Baja for canonical Madrileño and the eggs; Sobrino de Botín, the world's oldest restaurant; Mercado de San Miguel for the late-evening graze; StreetXO at El Corte Inglés for Dabiz Muñoz on a budget.

> Oh, Jake, we could have had such a damned good time together. Yes. Isn't it pretty to think so?
> *Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises*

### Stop 9. Cervecería Alemana

**Waypoint:** Plaza de Santa Ana, Madrid

Where he drank while writing his war novel. Hemingway's Madrid bar of choice, opened 1904, a few hundred meters from the Hotel Suecia where he stayed during the Spanish Civil War while reporting for NANA and drafting For Whom the Bell Tolls. A caña, a tortilla española, conversation with whoever's at the next table. The walls are unchanged. Good final stop on the trail.

**The Berth.** The Westin Palace on Plaza de las Cortes; The Ritz; or the small NH Collection Madrid Plaza de la Reina for mid-range proximity to the centre.

**The Galley.** Casa Lucio on Cava Baja for canonical Madrileño and the eggs; Sobrino de Botín, the world's oldest restaurant; Mercado de San Miguel for the late-evening graze; StreetXO at El Corte Inglés for Dabiz Muñoz on a budget.

> It is awfully easy to be hard-boiled about everything in the daytime, but at night it is another thing.
> *Ernest Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises*

### Stop 10. Ronda

**Waypoint:** Andalusia, southern Spain

Where the bullfight was born, and Hemingway lost his heart. On a high plateau split by a vertiginous gorge in the white-village country of Andalusia stands Ronda, the town Hemingway loved above all others in Spain and called the place to go for a honeymoon or a romance. Its Plaza de Toros, built in 1785, is the oldest and one of the most beautiful bullrings in Spain and the cradle of modern bullfighting on foot, where the Romero dynasty laid down the rules of the corrida. Here fought Cayetano Ordonez, whom Hemingway made the matador Pedro Romero in The Sun Also Rises, and decades later Hemingway returned to watch Cayetano's son Antonio, his close friend, in the dueling summer he chronicled in The Dangerous Summer. The terrible cliff in For Whom the Bell Tolls, where villagers are flung into the gorge, was drawn from Ronda. Stand at the lip of the Tajo gorge where the Puente Nuevo leaps the chasm, and feel the deep, dark Spain that Hemingway spent his life trying to understand.

**The Berth.** Ronda: the Parador on the very edge of the gorge; the historic Hotel Reina Victoria where Rilke stayed; the boutique hotels of the old Moorish town across the Puente Nuevo.

**The Galley.** Andalusian: rabo de toro (oxtail stew), the local specialty; Iberian ham and the mountain charcuterie of the Serrania; the wines of the Ronda hills, a rising region; gazpacho and salmorejo; a long lunch with a view down the Tajo.

> That is where you should go if you ever go to Spain on a honeymoon or if you ever bolt with anyone.
> *Ernest Hemingway on Ronda, Death in the Afternoon*

---

## Pilgrimage III. At the Crossroads

Year-round destinations along the road the blues traveled, from the cotton country of the Mississippi Delta where it was born, north through Memphis to Chicago where it went electric and fathered rock and roll, and down at last to New Orleans where all American music seems to pool. The blues came out of the hardest life in America, sharecroppers and prison farms and Saturday-night juke joints, and became the root from which nearly everything else grew. Best paired with Clarksdale's Juke Joint Festival in April and the New Orleans Jazz & Heritage Festival at the southern end. Drive it slowly, with detours down the gravel roads, Memphis barbecue at the start, hot tamales and fried catfish through the Delta, red beans and rice at the finish. Stop at every historical marker. Follow the sound of a guitar through a screen door. The road is the pilgrimage, and the blues is the prayer.

> The blues had a baby, and they named it rock and roll.
> *Muddy Waters*

### Stop 1. Dockery Farms

**Waypoint:** Highway 8, near Cleveland, MS

Where the Delta blues was born. On this cotton plantation between Cleveland and Ruleville, Charley Patton, the rough, roaring father of the Delta blues, lived and played, and here Howlin' Wolf, Son House, Robert Johnson, and Pops Staples all worked or passed through to hear him. More than any other single place, this is where the music began, in the field hollers and the Saturday-night frolics of a working plantation around 1900. The old commissary and gas pumps and the cotton gin still stand by the railroad track, and the place is free, open, and almost always empty. Stand on the weathered porch in the great silence of the Delta, the cotton running flat to the horizon, and understand that the most influential music of the twentieth century rose from this dirt. B.B. King himself named Dockery the likeliest birthplace of it all. Listen to the quiet, and hear what the music was answering.

**The Berth.** Stay in Clarksdale, the Delta's blues capital, half an hour north: the Shack Up Inn, restored sharecropper shacks on a former plantation; or the Riverside Hotel, in business since 1944.

**The Galley.** Delta soul food and tamales: Abe's Bar-B-Q in Clarksdale, since 1924; Hicks and Larry's for the Delta hot tamale, the region's strange and delicious specialty; gas-station tamales at any Highway 61 stop.

> The blues are the roots, and everything else is the fruits.
> *Willie Dixon*

### Stop 2. The Crossroads

**Waypoint:** Highways 61 & 49, Clarksdale, MS

Where the legend was made. At the intersection of Highway 61, the Blues Highway, and Highway 49, the road to Parchman prison farm, a tall sculpture of three blue guitars marks the spot where, the story goes, the young Robert Johnson met the devil at midnight and traded his soul for the gift of the guitar. He had been, by Son House's account, a hopeless player; he vanished for a season and came back so good that no natural explanation would do. The truth is that he practiced in obscurity and studied his elders, but the legend is the truer kind of myth, the price the blues exacts from those who play it for real. The corner today is a busy intersection with a chrome guitar and a motel, half marketing and half holy ground, but standing here at dusk while an eighteen-wheeler thunders past is genuinely strange. Drop to one knee at the crossroads as the pilgrims do, then walk to Ground Zero for the music.

**The Berth.** Clarksdale: the Shack Up Inn for the sharecropper-shack experience; the Riverside Hotel, where Bessie Smith died in 1937; the boutique Travelers Hotel downtown for the modern option.

**The Galley.** Abe's Bar-B-Q, right at the Crossroads since 1924; Ground Zero Blues Club, co-owned by Morgan Freeman, for music and burgers; Hicks Hot Tamales; the Delta Blues Museum's neighborhood for lunch.

> I went down to the crossroad, fell down on my knees.
> *Robert Johnson, "Cross Road Blues"*

### Stop 3. Cat Head Delta Blues & Folk Art

**Waypoint:** Clarksdale, MS

Where you find out where the music is tonight. Roger Stolle's record store and folk-art gallery is the unofficial visitor's center for the entire Delta, and the single best place to find out where the music is actually happening tonight. Books, vinyl, hand-painted posters, outsider art, and Roger himself, who knows every musician still playing within two hundred miles and will tell you whether to head for Red's, the last true juke joint in town, or Ground Zero. He founded the Juke Joint Festival each April, the best week of the year to come, when the whole town fills with music on every porch and corner. This is no museum piece: the Delta blues is still a living, breathing, Saturday-night thing, and Cat Head is its switchboard. Walk in, ask who's playing, and follow the answer into the dark.

**The Berth.** Clarksdale: the Shack Up Inn; the Riverside Hotel; the Travelers Hotel. In April for the Juke Joint Festival, book months ahead; the whole Delta fills up.

**The Galley.** Red's juke joint for the music; Abe's Bar-B-Q; Hicks Hot Tamales; Larry's Hot Tamales; Yazoo Pass for coffee and breakfast before a day on the back roads.

> Ain't but one kind of blues, and that consists of a male and female that's in love.
> *Son House*

### Stop 4. Robert Johnson's Grave

**Waypoint:** Little Zion Church, Money Road, Greenwood, MS

Where the King of the Delta Blues may rest. Three sites in Mississippi claim the grave of Robert Johnson, who recorded just twenty-nine songs before he was poisoned at a juke joint near Greenwood in 1938, dead at twenty-seven, and grew after death into the most influential bluesman who ever lived. This one, beneath a pecan tree behind the little white Zion Missionary Baptist Church on Money Road, is the site most scholars now favor, on the strength of a deathbed account given in the 1990s. Pilgrims leave whiskey bottles, guitar picks, and coins on the headstone, and the other two graves, in Quito and Morgan City, draw their own faithful. The drive out Money Road runs past the store where Emmett Till was accused, dark country in every sense. Stand under the pecan tree in the Delta hush, pour a little whiskey in the grass, and pay your respects to the man who sold his soul, or just practiced harder than anyone alive.

**The Berth.** Greenwood: the Alluvian, a surprisingly luxurious boutique hotel downtown (with a cooking school and spa); or continue to base in Clarksdale up Highway 49.

**The Galley.** Greenwood: Lusco's, a Delta institution since 1933 with its private curtained booths; Giardina's at the Alluvian; the Crystal Grill for the pies; fried catfish anywhere you can find it.

> I got to keep movin', blues fallin' down like hail; there's a hellhound on my trail.
> *Robert Johnson, "Hellhound on My Trail"*

### Stop 5. The B.B. King Museum

**Waypoint:** Indianola, MS

Where the Delta's most beloved son came home. Built around the brick cotton gin where Riley B. King worked as a teenager driving tractors, the B.B. King Museum and Delta Interpretive Center is the most thorough single-stop blues museum anywhere, telling the whole story of the Delta through the life of the man who carried it to the world. Here are his actual archive, the Lucille guitars, the dazzling stage suits, the tour bus, and the long arc of a sharecropper's son who played more than fifteen thousand shows and made the blues beloved on every continent. He chose to be buried here on the museum grounds, home at last in the town where he began. Indianola still holds its homecoming each year. See the gin where he labored, then the stage he conquered, and feel the whole distance of the blues in one building.

**The Berth.** Indianola and the central Delta: base in Greenwood at the Alluvian, or in Cleveland at the Cotton House, a stylish modern hotel near the Grammy Museum Mississippi.

**The Galley.** Indianola: the Crown for catfish and the famous catfish-and-spinach; Delta tamales; Cleveland's restaurants near Delta State; soul food, fried chicken, and sweet tea across the central Delta.

> The blues was bleeding the same blood as me.
> *B.B. King*

### Stop 6. Beale Street

**Waypoint:** Memphis, Tennessee

Where the Delta blues found its first city. Up Highway 61 from the Delta, Beale Street in Memphis was the place the country bluesmen came to be heard, the main stem of Black American music and commerce in the early twentieth century. Here W.C. Handy, the self-styled Father of the Blues, published "Memphis Blues" and "St. Louis Blues" and first set the music down on paper for the world; here the clubs and pawnshops and theaters made stars of Delta unknowns. Beale today is a neon entertainment strip, more tourist than holy, but the bones are real: Handy's statue stands in the park named for him, his shotgun house is preserved nearby, and on a good night the music still pours from a dozen doors at once. Walk Beale after dark, find the band that sounds least rehearsed and most alive, and stand where the Delta first plugged into the city.

**The Berth.** Memphis: the Peabody for the lobby ducks and the rooftop; the Madison Hotel downtown; or Big Cypress Lodge inside the Bass Pro pyramid for sheer local character.

**The Galley.** Memphis barbecue: Charles Vergos' Rendezvous for the dry-rub ribs; Cozy Corner for bologna sandwiches and Cornish hens; Gus's for the world-famous fried chicken; the Arcade on South Main for breakfast.

> The blues come from nothingness, from want, from desire.
> *W.C. Handy, the Father of the Blues*

### Stop 7. Sun Records

**Waypoint:** 706 Union Avenue, Memphis

Where rock and roll was born. In a storefront studio on Union Avenue, Sam Phillips first recorded the raw electric blues of Howlin' Wolf, Ike Turner, and B.B. King, and then, in July 1954, captured a teenage Elvis Presley fusing that Black music with white country into something the world had never heard. Jerry Lee Lewis, Johnny Cash, Roy Orbison, and Carl Perkins followed. What happened in this single small room, the meeting of the Delta blues with the hillbilly tradition, changed popular music forever. The original acoustic tile, the floor, and the very microphone Elvis sang into are all still here. By day it is a museum; by night it still operates as a working studio. Stand on the X that marks where the King stood, and feel how thin the wall was between the field holler and the global stage.

**The Berth.** Memphis: the Peabody downtown; the Madison Hotel; the Central Station Hotel in the old train depot for the railroad-and-music atmosphere.

**The Galley.** Memphis soul and barbecue: the Rendezvous; Cozy Corner; Gus's fried chicken; the Four Way in Soulsville for classic soul food near Stax.

> The blues, it got people, Black and white, to think about life, how difficult, yet also how good it can be.
> *Sam Phillips, founder of Sun Records*

### Stop 8. Stax & Soulsville

**Waypoint:** 926 E. McLemore Ave., Memphis

Where the blues turned to soul. A few miles south of Beale, in a converted movie theater, Stax Records cut some of the deepest soul music ever made: Otis Redding, Isaac Hayes, Booker T. & the M.G.s, Sam & Dave, the Bar-Kays. What set Stax apart was the house band itself, Black and white musicians playing together as equals in still-segregated Memphis, years before the rest of the country caught up, and you can hear that hard-won unity in the groove. The original building was torn down in 1989; the Stax Museum of American Soul Music is a faithful rebuilding on the same hallowed lot, the gospel storefront and Hayes's gold Cadillac and all. This is where the Delta's blues, carried to the city and electrified, bloomed into the soul that would conquer the world. Stand in the rebuilt studio and feel the music lift from grief into joy.

**The Berth.** Memphis: the Peabody; the Madison; or a room in the South Main arts district, walkable to the Civil Rights Museum at the Lorraine Motel, an essential and shattering stop.

**The Galley.** Soulsville and South Memphis: the Four Way for classic soul food; Cozy Corner and Payne's for barbecue; the Rendezvous downtown; fried catfish and greens with sweet tea.

> Walking the dog, just a-walking the dog; if you don't know how, I'll show you how to walk the dog.
> *Rufus Thomas, Stax Records*

### Stop 9. Chess Records, Chicago

**Waypoint:** 2120 S. Michigan Ave., Chicago

Where the Delta blues went electric and fathered rock and roll. When McKinley Morganfield, soon to be Muddy Waters, boarded a bus at the Clarksdale Greyhound station for Chicago in 1943, he carried the Delta blues north to the city, plugged it into an amplifier, and turned it loud. At Chess Records, in the building at 2120 South Michigan that the Rolling Stones would later make into a song, Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, Willie Dixon, Little Walter, and Bo Diddley forged the electric Chicago blues, the immediate parent of rock and roll. The Stones took their name from a Muddy Waters song; Chuck Berry cut his epochal sides here. The building survives as Willie Dixon's Blues Heaven Foundation, preserved and open for tours. Stand in the studio where the amplified Delta became the music of the whole modern world, and trace the straight line from a sharecropper's porch to every stage on Earth.

**The Berth.** Chicago: the Chicago Athletic Association on Michigan Avenue; the Blackstone nearby; or any South Loop hotel within reach of the old Chess studio and the blues clubs.

**The Galley.** Chicago: Buddy Guy's Legends club for blues and Louisiana cooking; deep-dish pizza; the South Side soul-food tradition; a hot dog and a blues set to close the night.

> When you ain't got no money, you've got the blues.
> *Muddy Waters*

### Stop 10. Preservation Hall

**Waypoint:** 726 St. Peter Street, New Orleans

Where all the music pools at last. The blues road ends in New Orleans, the city where every current of American music seems to gather and mingle. At Preservation Hall, traditional New Orleans jazz, the blues' first cousin, has played on without pause for over sixty years: bench seating, no air conditioning, no drinks, no microphones, nothing on the walls but hand-lettered signs and a portrait of the band's elders. The line forms an hour before each set, and it is worth every minute. Afterward, walk five minutes to Frenchmen Street, where the living scene plays until four in the morning. From a Delta porch to a French Quarter hall, the music has run its whole course. The pilgrimage doesn't end so much as dissolve into the city, into a second line, into the warm night. Surrender to it.

**The Berth.** New Orleans: the Pontchartrain on St. Charles; the Hotel Monteleone in the French Quarter for the Carousel Bar; the Roosevelt for old grandeur; the Ace for the music-minded.

**The Galley.** New Orleans: Commander's Palace in the Garden District; Antoine's, since 1840; Café du Monde for beignets; Cochon for whole-hog; Galatoire's for the Friday-afternoon ritual.

> The blues? It's the mother of American music. That's what it is, the source.
> *B.B. King*

---

## Pilgrimage IV. You Only Live Twice

Year-round destinations across London and Jamaica for the spy-fiction faithful, with two essential English country detours. Best timed to slot into any London-anchored event already on the calendar, the BBC Proms (mid-July through early September), Notting Hill Carnival (Aug 29-30), MCM Comic Con London (late May or late October), or Destination Star Trek UK (early November) all bring you to the right country, and Bond's London is what you do on the off-days. Three days for the London-Kent-Wiltshire loop, plus a separate Caribbean leg for Goldeneye. This is two trips, not one.

> The world is not enough.
> *the Bond family motto, Ian Fleming*

### Stop 1. Dukes Bar

**Waypoint:** Dukes Hotel, St James's Place, London

Where the martini was perfected. The bar where Fleming drank martinis throughout the 1950s, and where Alessandro Palazzi has been mixing them, gin, frozen, garnished with a piece of Amalfi lemon peel cut at the table, for over twenty years. Two-drink limit per customer, by house policy, because the martinis are designed to be enjoyed slowly. Wood-paneled, no windows, no music, no sign on the street. The single most defensible "where the line came from" claim in cocktail history. Start of the trail. Begin sober.

**The Berth.** The Connaught in Mayfair; The Beaumont in Marylebone; The Zetter Townhouse in Clerkenwell for the mid-budget; or The Hoxton Shoreditch for the design-set option.

**The Galley.** St. JOHN in Smithfield for the canonical English; Sketch in Mayfair; Padella in Borough for the Friday-night queue; Quo Vadis in Soho for the late lunch; Brick Lane on Sunday morning for the bagel.

> Never say no to adventures. Always say yes, otherwise you'll lead a very dull life.
> *Ian Fleming*

### Stop 2. St James's Street

**Waypoint:** Boodle's, London

Where Fleming's clubland became Bond's. The street that runs from Piccadilly down to St James's Palace, lined with the gentlemen's clubs Fleming haunted his entire adult life. Boodle's, at No. 28, was Fleming's club; he based the fictional Blades, where M and Bond play bridge against Hugo Drax in Moonraker, directly on it. Members only. But you can walk the street, eat dinner at Wiltons (45 Jermyn Street, just around the corner; Fleming ate there often), and absorb the atmosphere of the world Bond was meant to belong to. Nearby on Whitehall stands the Old War Office, the Edwardian palace where Britain's wars were run for a century and where Fleming, as personal assistant to the Director of Naval Intelligence in WWII, knew the corridors professionally; that wartime experience became the operational realism of the Bond novels. The building is now a Raffles hotel with a themed Spy Bar. Worth a martini and a long look around.

**The Berth.** The Connaught in Mayfair; The Beaumont in Marylebone; The Zetter Townhouse in Clerkenwell for the mid-budget; or The Hoxton Shoreditch for the design-set option.

**The Galley.** St. JOHN in Smithfield for the canonical English; Sketch in Mayfair; Padella in Borough for the Friday-night queue; Quo Vadis in Soho for the late lunch; Brick Lane on Sunday morning for the bagel.

> Once is happenstance. Twice is coincidence. Three times is enemy action.
> *Ian Fleming, Goldfinger*

### Stop 3. SIS Building

**Waypoint:** Vauxhall Cross, London

Where the real MI6 keeps its secrets. The actual headquarters of the actual Secret Intelligence Service, the real M's actual office. Used as the cinematic MI6 since GoldenEye in 1995, partially destroyed onscreen multiple times since. Visible across the Thames from the Embankment near Lambeth Bridge. Don't try to walk in. Photograph from the river and move on.

**The Berth.** The Connaught in Mayfair; The Beaumont in Marylebone; The Zetter Townhouse in Clerkenwell for the mid-budget; or The Hoxton Shoreditch for the design-set option.

**The Galley.** St. JOHN in Smithfield for the canonical English; Sketch in Mayfair; Padella in Borough for the Friday-night queue; Quo Vadis in Soho for the late lunch; Brick Lane on Sunday morning for the bagel.

> Surround yourself with human beings, my dear James. They are easier to fight for than principles.
> *Ian Fleming, Casino Royale*

### Stop 4. 16 Victoria Square

**Waypoint:** Belgravia, London

Where Fleming and Ann lived from 1953 onward, the London house he edited the Bond manuscripts in between his annual two-month writing trips to Goldeneye. Private home, blue English Heritage plaque marks it. Quiet residential square in Belgravia. Walk past, then continue south through Eaton Square toward St James's Park, retracing what would have been Fleming's commute to his clubs.

**The Berth.** The Connaught in Mayfair; The Beaumont in Marylebone; The Zetter Townhouse in Clerkenwell for the mid-budget; or The Hoxton Shoreditch for the design-set option.

**The Galley.** St. JOHN in Smithfield for the canonical English; Sketch in Mayfair; Padella in Borough for the Friday-night queue; Quo Vadis in Soho for the late lunch; Brick Lane on Sunday morning for the bagel.

> There is only one recipe for a best seller: you have to get the reader to turn over the page.
> *Ian Fleming*

### Stop 5. Pinewood Studios & the 007 Stage

**Waypoint:** Iver Heath, Buckinghamshire

Where Bond is built. Since Dr. No in 1962, nearly every James Bond film has been made at Pinewood Studios, the great film factory in the Buckinghamshire countryside west of London, and in 1976, for The Spy Who Loved Me, the producers built the largest sound stage in the world to hold a set containing three nuclear submarines: the 007 Stage, since rebuilt twice after fires and still the beating heart of Bond production. Here Ken Adam designed the impossible volcano lair and the gleaming villain headquarters that defined the look of the films; here the gadgets were dreamed and the sets struck and rebuilt across sixty years. Pinewood is a working studio, not a museum, so access is limited to occasional tours and special events; check ahead. But to stand at the gates of the place where the most enduring fantasy in cinema is hammered together out of plywood and genius is its own pilgrimage. This is the workshop behind the dream.

**The Berth.** Buckinghamshire and west London: the country-house hotels around the Chilterns; Stoke Park (itself a Bond location in Goldfinger and Tomorrow Never Dies), minutes away; or base in London and drive out.

**The Galley.** The Chilterns: the gastropubs of the Buckinghamshire villages; the Crown at Burchetts Green for a Michelin meal; Stoke Park's dining for the Bond connection; a pint in a beamed country pub on the way back to town.

> A martini. Shaken, not stirred.
> *James Bond*

### Stop 6. Royal St George's Golf Club

**Waypoint:** Sandwich, Kent

Where Bond beat Goldfinger on the links. Fleming was a member here, and the "Royal St Mark's" course in Goldfinger, site of the most famous golf match in English fiction, where Bond beats Auric Goldfinger by switching balls on the 17th, is a thinly disguised version of it. Two-hour drive from London or train to Sandwich. The pub afterward at The Bell Hotel in Sandwich is correct. Reserve the round well in advance; the club hosts the Open Championship periodically.

**The Berth.** The Salutation in Sandwich (the Lutyens-designed manor with garden); or in nearby Canterbury (15 minutes west): The Falstaff in Canterbury; ABode Canterbury.

**The Galley.** Canterbury: The Goods Shed for the Kentish food market; Hide & Fox for the modern; The Pound for the pub-with-rooms.

> I am a poet in deeds, not often in words.
> *Ian Fleming, Goldfinger*

### Stop 7. Glencoe

**Waypoint:** the Scottish Highlands

Where Bond goes home. So impressed was Ian Fleming by Sean Connery's performance that he wrote a Scottish heritage into the later novels, revealing in You Only Live Twice that Bond's father came from Glencoe and that the boy had been sent to Fettes College in Edinburgh. Half a century later, Skyfall made that backstory unforgettable: it is here, on the A82 beneath the brooding peaks of Buachaille Etive Mor, that Bond's silver Aston Martin DB5 carries a wounded M north through the most spectacular landscape in Britain to the lonely family estate where the story turns. The house, Skyfall Lodge, was a set built and burned on the moor; but the glen is gloriously real, a deep glaciated valley of mist and scree and sudden sun, hauntingly beautiful and shadowed by the 1692 massacre that gave it its sorrowful fame. Drive the A82 through the glen in changing weather, pull over where the peaks rise sheer, and feel why the filmmakers brought the world's coldest spy home to thaw.

**The Berth.** The Highlands: the Kingshouse Hotel on Rannoch Moor at the head of the glen; the Glencoe boutique inns; or grand Highland sporting hotels within reach for the full Bond-in-Scotland sweep.

**The Galley.** Highland: venison, langoustine, and Scottish beef; a dram of Highland single malt by a peat fire; the Clachaig Inn, a climbers' institution in the glen; fresh seafood from the west-coast lochs.

> We're going back in time. To where it all started.
> *James Bond, Skyfall*

### Stop 8. Piz Gloria, the Schilthorn

**Waypoint:** above Murren, Bernese Oberland, Switzerland

Where the villain's lair spins above the Alps. High above the Lauterbrunnen valley in the Swiss Bernese Oberland, on the 2,970-metre summit of the Schilthorn, spins a revolving restaurant called Piz Gloria, and it was here, in 1969, that On Her Majesty's Secret Service filmed the mountaintop clinic where Blofeld hatched his plot, the only Bond film to star George Lazenby and, for many, the most emotionally devastating of all. The production helped finish the half-built restaurant in exchange for using it, and the Schilthorn has embraced its 007 fame ever since, with a Bond World exhibition, a Q-branch interactive, and the restaurant still slowly turning to show all 360 degrees of the Eiger, Monch, and Jungfrau. The journey up by a series of cable cars from Murren is itself a spectacle. Ride the cables to the top, take a table as the whole white wall of the high Alps wheels past the glass, and order, of course, a martini.

**The Berth.** Bernese Oberland: stay car-free in clifftop Murren or in Wengen across the valley; the grand hotels of Interlaken below; or a chalet in Lauterbrunnen among the waterfalls for the alpine idyll.

**The Galley.** Swiss alpine: fondue and raclette; rosti and air-dried Alpine beef; the revolving Piz Gloria restaurant itself for the full Bond lunch; Swiss chocolate and a kirsch to finish, with the Eiger turning past the window.

> This never happened to the other fellow.
> *James Bond, On Her Majesty's Secret Service*

### Stop 9. St James the Great Church

**Waypoint:** Sevenhampton, Wiltshire

Where Fleming is buried, alongside Ann (who died in 1981) and their son Caspar (who died in 1975). Country churchyard in a small Wiltshire village; modest stone obelisk. Almost always empty. The pilgrim equivalent of Tolkien's Wolvercote, the quiet stop, the one that returns the writer to scale. Two-and-a-half hours west of London by car.

**The Berth.** Wiltshire: a coaching inn or country-house hotel near Marlborough; the village pubs-with-rooms around Swindon and the Vale of the White Horse; or a Cotswolds-edge manor a short drive north.

**The Galley.** Wiltshire and the Cotswolds: a proper ploughman's and a pint of local ale in a beamed village pub; country-house dining near Marlborough; West Country cheeses, game in season, and a Sunday roast in the green English quiet Fleming came home to.

> You only live twice: once when you are born, and once when you look death in the face.
> *Ian Fleming, You Only Live Twice*

### Stop 10. Goldeneye

**Waypoint:** Oracabessa, Jamaica

Where every Bond novel was written. The house Fleming bought in 1946 and where he wrote all fourteen Bond novels and short story collections during his annual two-month winter visits between 1952 and 1964. Now part of Chris Blackwell's resort, Blackwell, the Island Records founder who produced Bob Marley, bought the property from Fleming's estate, but the original Fleming villa is preserved with his writing desk, his bed, and the slatted window facing the Caribbean. A short drive away: Laughing Waters Beach, where Honey Ryder rises out of the water in Dr. No (1962). The pilgrimage's southern terminus, and the place where the entire enterprise actually happened.

**The Berth.** Goldeneye in Oracabessa (Ian Fleming's actual estate, where every Bond was written); or Round Hill in Montego Bay; or Strawberry Hill in the Blue Mountains.

**The Galley.** Goldeneye's Bizot Bar; Pikni at Goldeneye for the contemporary; Scotchies in Montego Bay for the canonical jerk; Boston Bay Beach in Portland for the original jerk pits.

> I shall not waste my days in trying to prolong them. I shall use my time.
> *Ian Fleming, You Only Live Twice*

---

## Pilgrimage V. Every Day a Journey

Year-round destinations across northern Honshu tracing the journey Matsuo Bashō walked with his disciple Kawai Sora in 1689, recorded in Oku no Hosomichi, the Narrow Road to the Deep North, one of the most influential travel books ever written. Best done in autumn (mid-October through early November) for the kōyō, Tohoku's spectacular fall colors, which is when Bashō himself reached the journey's end at Ōgaki. The spring version, after the late-April cherry blossom front reaches northern Japan, retraces his actual departure. Pairs with Tokyo Game Show (late September) at the start if you go in autumn, or with hanami (late March through April) for the spring version. Two weeks for the full route by rail and rented car; one week if you skip the western leg from Kanazawa to Ōgaki.

> Days and months are travelers of eternity. So are the years that pass by.
> *Matsuo Bashō, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, 1689*

### Stop 1. Senju Ōhashi & Bashō Memorial Museum

**Waypoint:** Adachi / Kōtō Wards, Tokyo

Where the journey began. On the morning of May 16, 1689, Bashō and Sora left their friends at the Senju Ōhashi bridge over the Sumida River and started walking north. A small statue and stone marker stand at the bridge departure point near Senju-Ōhashi station. The Bashō Kinenkan (Memorial Museum) in Kōtō Ward, beside the site of his hut, holds his manuscripts, his straw sandals, and his actual travel inkstone. Stand on the bridge at dawn. Look north. Then start.

**The Berth.** Aman Tokyo in Otemachi for the panoramic onsen; the Park Hyatt Shinjuku of Lost in Translation; the Hoshinoya Tokyo for the modern ryokan in Marunouchi.

**The Galley.** Sukiyabashi Jiro (booking three months ahead); Den (Zaiyu Hasegawa); Narisawa; Tsukiji and Toyosu for the dawn-market sushi; tonkatsu at Maisen in Aoyama; ramen at Afuri.

> Spring is passing — the birds cry, and the fishes' eyes are full of tears.
> *Matsuo Bashō, at Senju, The Narrow Road to the Deep North*

### Stop 2. Nikkō Tōshōgū

**Waypoint:** Tochigi Prefecture

Where the shrine blazed with gold leaf. Bashō's first major stop, a hundred kilometers north of Edo, where he visited the elaborate mausoleum of Tokugawa Ieyasu and wrote: ara tōto / aoba wakaba no / hi no hikari, "How awesome / The green leaves, young leaves / In the sunlight." The shrine complex is now UNESCO World Heritage, a riot of gold leaf, dragons, and the famous "see no evil, hear no evil, speak no evil" carving. Sleep in nearby Yumoto Onsen, where Bashō also stopped.

**The Berth.** Stay in Nikkō: Nikkō Kanaya Hotel since 1873 (Japan's oldest Western-style hotel); or Hoshino Resorts KAI Nikkō on Lake Chūzenji.

**The Galley.** Yuba (tofu skin) is the Nikkō specialty, Hippari Dako for the canonical; Meiji-no-Yakata for heritage Western-Japanese; Gyoshintei for kaiseki in the temple grounds.

> A flash of lightning — into the gloom goes the heron's cry.
> *Matsuo Bashō*

### Stop 3. The Shirakawa Barrier

**Waypoint:** Fukushima Prefecture

Where the journey truly began. For the classical poets of Japan, the Barrier of Shirakawa was the gate to Oku, the wild deep north, the threshold beyond which a traveler passed out of the known world. Bashō had dreamed of it before he ever set out: it was longing to cross this barrier, he wrote, that the spirits of the road had used to lure him from his hut. When at last he reached it, he found the old checkpoint long abandoned, a quiet place of grass and trees on a forgotten frontier, and felt that only now had his journey to the deep north truly begun. Generations of poets before him had marked the crossing with verses, and Bashō, moved and unable to better them, recorded instead his companion Sora's simple poem of adorning oneself with white blossoms to cross in style. Little remains today but a shrine and a grove in the gentle Fukushima hills, marked and quiet. Stand at the old barrier where the deep north begins, and feel the threshold every pilgrim must cross.

**The Berth.** Fukushima: the hot-spring inns of Nasu and the Shirakawa hills; ryokan with their tatami rooms and cedar baths; or base in the castle town of Shirakawa itself for the quiet country pace.

**The Galley.** Fukushima country cooking: the celebrated Kitakata ramen of the region; soba from the northern hills; sake from Fukushima's prize-winning breweries, among Japan's finest; grilled river fish and mountain vegetables.

> Adorned with sprays of white unohana blossom, we crossed the barrier in our finest array.
> *Kawai Sora, at Shirakawa, recorded by Bashō*

### Stop 4. Matsushima Bay

**Waypoint:** Miyagi Prefecture

Where beauty struck the poet silent. One of Japan's "Three Great Views" (Nihon Sankei), a bay scattered with 260 pine-covered islands. Bashō was so overwhelmed that, by his own account, he could not compose a haiku. (The famous "Matsushima ya / aa Matsushima ya / Matsushima ya" attributed to him is almost certainly apocryphal, the silence was the response.) Take the morning ferry through the islands.

**The Berth.** Stay in Matsushima Bay: Matsushima Ichinobo overlooking the bay; or in Sendai: Westin Sendai; Sendai Kokusai Hotel.

**The Galley.** Matsushima: oysters at any of the kaki-goya (oyster huts) along the bay; Donjiki Chayaten for canonical zaru soba. Sendai: gyūtan (beef tongue) at Rikyū or Tasuke.

> The sea darkens; the voices of the wild ducks are faintly white.
> *Matsuo Bashō*

### Stop 5. Hiraizumi: Chūson-ji & Mōtsū-ji

**Waypoint:** Iwate Prefecture

Where Bashō wrote the most famous haiku of the entire journey, standing on the ruined site of the 12th-century Fujiwara capital: natsukusa ya / tsuwamono domo ga / yume no ato, "Summer grass / All that remains / Of warriors' dreams." Chnson-ji's Konjikidn, the gold-leaf hall built in 1124, still stands. UNESCO World Heritage. The kuhi, haiku stones, along the temple path mark Bashō's exact stopping points.

**The Berth.** Stay in Hiraizumi: Hotel Musashibo; or in Morioka (30 minutes north): Hotel Metropolitan Morioka.

**The Galley.** Hiraizumi: temple-grounds shojin ryori vegetarian; Morioka: wanko soba (the bottomless soba challenge) at Azumaya; Pyongyang Cold Noodles at Pyonpyon Sha.

> A cicada shell; it sang itself utterly away.
> *Matsuo Bashō*

### Stop 6. Yamadera

**Waypoint:** Yamagata Prefecture

Where the cicadas sank into the rocks. 1,015 stone steps up a forested mountainside to the cliff temple. Bashō climbed it on July 13, 1689, exact date documented, and wrote: shizukasa ya / iwa ni shimiiru / semi no koe, "Such stillness / The cries of the cicadas / Sink into the rocks." Climb in late afternoon. Hear the cicadas at the top in summer, or the silence in autumn. The most concentrated single moment on the trail.

**The Berth.** Stay in Yamagata City: Yamagata Grand Hotel; or in Tendō (15 minutes north for the onsen): Tendo Hotel.

**The Galley.** Yamagata: imoni (the autumn taro-and-pork stew); shōnai dashi at any traditional ryōtei; Yamagata-beef sukiyaki at Sagoreya. Sakata: kokon noodles.

> Crossing long fields, frozen in its saddle, my shadow creeps by.
> *Matsuo Bashō*

### Stop 7. Mogami River & Sakata

**Waypoint:** Yamagata Prefecture

Where he rode the river's summer rains. Bashō shot the Mogami River by boat and wrote: samidare wo / atsumete hayashi / mogamigawa, "Gathering up / All the rains of summer / The swift Mogami." He arrived at the Sea of Japan at Sakata, where the local poet Fugyoku hosted him for nine days. Sakata's Sankyo Sōko (12 preserved Edo-era rice warehouses) and the Sakata Sengyo Ichiba seafood market are still operating. The kaisendon at the market is the meal.

**The Berth.** Stay in Yamagata City: Yamagata Grand Hotel; or in Tendō (15 minutes north for the onsen): Tendo Hotel.

**The Galley.** Yamagata: imoni (the autumn taro-and-pork stew); shōnai dashi at any traditional ryōtei; Yamagata-beef sukiyaki at Sagoreya. Sakata: kokon noodles.

> Coolness of the melons flecked with mud in the morning dew.
> *Matsuo Bashō*

### Stop 8. The Dewa Sanzan

**Waypoint:** Yamagata Prefecture

Where the journey reached its sacred summit. The Three Mountains of Dewa, Haguro, Gassan, and Yudono, have been for over a thousand years the holiest center of Shugendō, the Japanese mountain asceticism that seeks rebirth through pilgrimage over sacred peaks. Climbing them in turn is to pass symbolically through death and rebirth: Haguro for the present world, Gassan for the world of the dead, Yudono for the world to come. Bashō climbed all three in the summer of 1689 and counted it the spiritual summit of his journey, composing at each a haiku of quiet awe; bound by the pilgrim's vow of secrecy, he could write of the holiest, Yudono, only that his sleeve was wet with tears. The thousand-year cedar avenue and five-story pagoda of Mount Haguro, the white-clad yamabushi still treading the old paths, make this among the most profound sacred landscapes in Japan. Climb the two thousand four hundred and forty-six stone steps of Haguro through the ancient cedars, and feel the deepest meaning of the road.

**The Berth.** Yamagata: the pilgrim lodgings (shukubo) at the foot of Mount Haguro, where you sleep and eat as the yamabushi do; the hot-spring inns of the Shonai plain; or the temple lodgings on the mountain itself.

**The Galley.** The pilgrim's table: shojin ryori, the elegant vegetarian temple cuisine of the yamabushi, mountain vegetables and wild plants prepared with great care; Shonai rice, among Japan's best; local sake; mountain mushrooms in autumn.

> Of Mount Yudono I cannot speak — yet see how wet my sleeve.
> *Matsuo Bashō, at the Dewa Sanzan*

### Stop 9. Kanazawa

**Waypoint:** Ishikawa Prefecture

Where he lingered longest among friends. Bashō's longest single stop on the journey, nine days hosted by local poets in the castle town of the Maeda clan. The Higashi Chaya geisha district and the Naga-machi samurai quarter still preserve the Edo-era streets he walked. nmichn Market, in continuous operation since 1721, is the equal of Tsukiji at a fraction of the size. Two nights minimum. The seafood is the reason, Kanazawa is one of Japan's quiet food capitals.

**The Berth.** Stay in Kanazawa: Hyatt Centric Kanazawa near the station; Nikkō Kanazawa for the heritage; or KAI Kaga in nearby Yamashiro Onsen for the ryokan.

**The Galley.** Kanazawa: Tsubajin for canonical Kaga kaiseki; Tagosaku for sushi; Omicho Market food stands for kaisendon; Higashiyama district's tea houses for kintsuba and matcha.

> First winter rain — even the monkey seems to want a raincoat.
> *Matsuo Bashō*

### Stop 10. Ōgaki

**Waypoint:** Gifu Prefecture: Journey's End

Where Bashō ended the journey in late October 1689, met by old friends at the river. The Oku no Hosomichi Musubi no Chi Memorial Hall marks the spot, a small museum on a quiet riverbank that almost no foreign visitors find. Modest, often empty. The pilgrimage closes the way it opened: a man standing at a river thinking about distance.

**The Berth.** Stay in Takayama: Hida Hotel Plaza or Honjin Hiranoya Kachoan; or in Ōgaki: Comfort Hotel Ōgaki.

**The Galley.** Takayama: Hida-gyū (Hida beef) at Maruaki; canonical Takayama miso soup; mitarashi dango on the morning-market street. Ōgaki: traditional ryokan kaiseki.

> Dividing like a clam from its shell, I depart for Futami — autumn is passing.
> *Matsuo Bashō, the closing verse of The Narrow Road to the Deep North*

## Pilgrimage VI. The Road That Made the Man

Year-round destinations across South America tracing the 8,000-kilometer journey Ernesto "Che" Guevara and Alberto Granado made by motorcycle in 1952, later recorded in The Motorcycle Diaries, the formative trip that turned a young Argentine medical student into a continental revolutionary. The route runs from Buenos Aires across the Andes to Chile, north through the Atacama and into Peru, ending in the Amazon. Best done in the southern-hemisphere spring or autumn (Oct-Nov or Mar-Apr) to avoid Patagonian winter and Amazonian rains. Three weeks for the full Buenos Aires-to-Lima arc by overland buses, hire car, and one Andean flight; ten days for an abbreviated Patagonia-and-Atacama leg.

> Hasta la victoria, siempre — until victory, always.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara*

### Stop 1. Buenos Aires

**Waypoint:** Buenos Aires, Argentina

Where the road began. The Argentine capital from which Ernesto Guevara and Alberto Granado pushed La Poderosa, the wheezing 500cc Norton, out the front gate of Granado's family home in January 1952. Walk the Plaza de Mayo where the Madres still march, the Recoleta cemetery for Eva Perón's tomb, and the Hospital de Clínicas where Guevara was finishing his medical degree the year he left. Pair with the bookish San Telmo lanes south of the plaza for the city Guevara never quite finished reading.

**The Berth.** Buenos Aires anchors: Faena, Alvear Palace, Palacio Duhau, or Casa Lucía.

**The Galley.** Don Julio in Palermo for canonical parrilla; El Preferido for bodegón; Tegui for contemporary; Café Tortoni on Avenida de Mayo.

> This is not a story of heroic feats; it is a glimpse of two lives running parallel for a time.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries*

### Stop 2. Casa Natal de Ernesto Guevara

**Waypoint:** Rosario, Argentina

Where Ernesto Guevara was born on June 14, 1928, Calle Entre Ríos 480, central Rosario. The apartment building is private but a plaque marks it. A few blocks away in Plaza Cooperación stands the Monumento al Che, a four-meter bronze placed in 2008, Argentina's most direct civic acknowledgment of him. Rosario itself is worth the day: the Paraná river, the football culture (Messi was born here too), the Italian-Argentine cooking. A logical first stop before flying south.

**The Berth.** Buenos Aires: Faena, Alvear Palace, Palacio Duhau, or Casa Lucía. Mendoza: Cavas Wine Lodge or The Vines Resort & Spa for the wine country.

**The Galley.** Buenos Aires: Don Julio in Palermo for the canonical parrilla; El Preferido for the bodegón; Tegui for contemporary. Mendoza: 1884 Restaurante Francis Mallmann at Bodega Escorihuela.

> Our true vocation was to move for eternity along the roads and seas of the world.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries*

### Stop 3. Museo Casa del Che Guevara

**Waypoint:** Alta Gracia, Córdoba Province, Argentina

Where Ernesto spent most of his childhood, the family moved to Alta Gracia in 1932 because of his asthma, and he stayed until he was 14. The house ("Villa Nydia") is now a museum with the original family furniture, his school notebooks, his medical textbooks, and the chess set he played as a teenager. Modest, well-curated, an hour outside Córdoba city. The asthma is the part most pilgrims forget, he had it badly his entire life, including the entire time on the motorcycle. Worth knowing before the rest.

**The Berth.** Buenos Aires: Faena, Alvear Palace, Palacio Duhau, or Casa Lucía. Mendoza: Cavas Wine Lodge or The Vines Resort & Spa for the wine country.

**The Galley.** Buenos Aires: Don Julio in Palermo for the canonical parrilla; El Preferido for the bodegón; Tegui for contemporary. Mendoza: 1884 Restaurante Francis Mallmann at Bodega Escorihuela.

> Let the world change you, and you can change the world.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries*

### Stop 4. Cruce Andino: Bariloche to Petrohué

**Waypoint:** Argentina / Chile

Where they crossed the Andes by boat. The lake-crossing route over the Andes that Ernesto and Alberto took in February 1952, boats across Lake Nahuel Huapi, then Lake Frías, then Lake Todos los Santos, with bus or hike between them. Same boats more or less, same lakes, same view. The route is now operated as a tourist crossing (Cruce Andino) but the geography hasn't changed since the Pleistocene. A full day. End in Puerto Varas, Chile, with German-Chilean kuchen and a sunset over Volcán Osorno.

**The Berth.** Santiago: The Singular Santiago in Lastarria; W Santiago in Las Condes; or Lastarria Boutique Hotel for the heritage. Atacama: Tierra Atacama or Awasi Atacama.

**The Galley.** Santiago: Boragó for the canonical New Chilean; La Calma de Rufino for the seasonal in Lastarria; Bocanáriz for the wine bar with regional small plates.

> What do we leave behind when we cross each frontier? Each moment seems split in two.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries*

### Stop 5. Valparaíso

**Waypoint:** Chile

Where Ernesto and Alberto spent several days in March 1952, observing the port, the working-class hillsides, the contrast with bourgeois Santiago. Che's Valparaíso diary entries are some of the most politically attentive of the entire trip. The cerros (hill neighborhoods), the funiculars built in the 1880s, the murals layered over each other for fifty years. La Sebastiana, Pablo Neruda's house, post-Che but spiritually adjacent, is here too. Eat chorrillana at any port-area bar; pisco sours mean something different in Chile than in Peru.

**The Berth.** Santiago: The Singular Santiago in Lastarria; W Santiago in Las Condes; or Lastarria Boutique Hotel for the heritage. Atacama: Tierra Atacama or Awasi Atacama.

**The Galley.** Santiago: Boragó for the canonical New Chilean; La Calma de Rufino for the seasonal in Lastarria; Bocanáriz for the wine bar with regional small plates.

> When the great guiding spirit cleaves humanity into two antagonistic halves, I will be with the people.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries*

### Stop 6. Chuquicamata Copper Mine

**Waypoint:** near Calama, Atacama Desert, Chile

Where his politics began to crystallize. The largest open-pit copper mine in the world, then and now. Here Ernesto and Alberto met an unemployed communist couple sleeping in the desert, and Che's politics first took shape. He wrote: "The couple, frozen by the desert night, was for me a living representation of the proletariat anywhere in the world." Public tours of the mine still run from Calama daily. The scale is overwhelming, pits a kilometer deep. The town of Chuquicamata itself was abandoned in 2007 due to mine expansion; you can walk through the empty streets where the miners lived.

**The Berth.** Santiago: The Singular Santiago in Lastarria; W Santiago in Las Condes; or Lastarria Boutique Hotel for the heritage. Atacama: Tierra Atacama or Awasi Atacama.

**The Galley.** Santiago: Boragó for the canonical New Chilean; La Calma de Rufino for the seasonal in Lastarria; Bocanáriz for the wine bar with regional small plates.

> We are one single mestizo race from Mexico to the Magellan Straits.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries*

### Stop 7. Cusco

**Waypoint:** Peru

Where Che had his sustained encounter with indigenous Latin America, the colonial Plaza de Armas, the Inca-cyclopean walls in the side streets, the Sacsayhuamán fortress above the city, the markets at San Pedro. He stayed for nearly a month and wrote the journey's most reflective entries. Cusco is now heavily touristed, but the Cusco Che saw is still in the side streets, the chicherías where the women still ferment chicha morada in their courtyards, the cuy and lomo saltado at family restaurants in San Blas. Pair with Inti Raymi (June 24) if your timing allows.

**The Berth.** Belmond Hotel Monasterio in the converted 1592 monastery; Inkaterra La Casona on Plaza Nazarenas; JW Marriott on Calle Ruinas for the colonial chic.

**The Galley.** Cicciolina above Plaza de Armas; MAP Café in the Pre-Columbian Art Museum; Pachapapa in San Blas for the cuy and pachamanca; Chocolate Museum on Calle Garcilaso for the workshop.

> The division of America into unstable and illusory nations is a complete fiction.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries*

### Stop 8. Machu Picchu

**Waypoint:** Peru

Where Alberto's photograph of Ernesto standing in front of the ruins (April 1952) became one of the iconic images of the trip. Che wrote that Machu Picchu was "a definite source of inspiration." The site needs no introduction. What needs introduction is Aguas Calientes at the base, eat at the local market, not the tourist restaurants, and consider the second-day climb up Huayna Picchu for the view down onto the ruins from a different angle than the postcards.

**The Berth.** Lima: Belmond Miraflores Park or Hotel B in Barranco. Cusco: Belmond Hotel Monasterio. Sacred Valley: Inkaterra Hacienda Urubamba.

**The Galley.** Lima: Central (Virgilio Martínez) for the altitude-by-altitude tasting; Maido (Mitsuharu Tsumura) for Nikkei; La Mar for ceviche; Astrid y Gastón for the Acurio classic.

> Wandering around our America has changed me more than I thought. I am not the same me I was.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries*

### Stop 9. Lima & Dr. Hugo Pesce

**Waypoint:** Peru

Where the mentor pointed the way. Coming down at last from the Andes to the Peruvian coast, the two travelers reached Lima, and there Ernesto sought out Dr. Hugo Pesce, the country's leading leprologist and a committed Marxist, who took the ragged young Argentine in, fed and housed him, talked politics with him deep into the night, and arranged the journey on to the leper colony at San Pablo. Pesce's influence ran deeper than medicine: here was a brilliant doctor who had chosen to serve the poorest and to think hard about why they were poor, and the example lodged in Guevara for life. A decade later, a world-famous revolutionary, Che sent Pesce a copy of his first book inscribed with thanks. Lima itself, the old viceregal capital, spreads its Baroque churches and balconied mansions above the gray Pacific, and has become in our own time one of the great food cities of the world. Walk the colonial center and the cliffs of Barranco, and stand where a teacher set a restless young man on his road.

**The Berth.** Lima: the storied Country Club Lima Hotel in leafy San Isidro; the boutique hotels of bohemian Barranco above the sea; or a colonial guesthouse in the historic center near the Plaza Mayor.

**The Galley.** Peruvian, a world cuisine: ceviche fresh from the Pacific; lomo saltado and ají de gallina; anticuchos from a street grill; the great tasting menus of Lima's celebrated restaurants; a pisco sour to begin.

> I now know, by an almost fatalistic conformity with the facts, that my destiny is to travel.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries*

### Stop 10. San Pablo Leper Colony

**Waypoint:** Peruvian Amazon (via Iquitos)

Where Che and Alberto worked for three weeks in June 1952, living and treating leprosy patients, swimming across the Amazon to the colony itself for the first time on Che's 24th birthday. The moral heart of the entire journey, where the medical-student-turned-revolutionary first articulated what he later called "the unity of the Latin American people" expressed in shared suffering. The colony still operates as a small community on the Amazon, two days by boat from Iquitos. Almost no tourists reach it. The journey itself is the point. The pilgrimage doesn't end so much as drift downriver.

**The Berth.** Casa Morey on the Iquitos waterfront; or DoubleTree by Hilton across from the Plaza de Armas; or the upriver Treehouse Lodge for the jungle stay.

**The Galley.** Al Frío y al Fuego (the floating restaurant on the Itaya); ChezMaggy for paiche and palmito; Belén Market food row at dawn for juane and tacacho.

> The future belongs to the people.
> *Ernesto 'Che' Guevara*

---

## Pilgrimage VII. Winter Is Coming

Year-round destinations for the Song of Ice and Fire and Game of Thrones faithful, beginning at GRR Martin's actual home in Santa Fe and tracking the show's principal European and North African filming locations across Croatia, Northern Ireland, Iceland, Spain, Catalonia, and Morocco. Best timed to slot into MagicCon Bonn (mid-June, which reliably draws GoT cast regulars), the Gnaoua World Music Festival in Essaouira (also mid-June, on the Astapor stop), or Lucca Comics & Games in October. Ten to fourteen days for the European-Moroccan ring, plus a separate American leg for Santa Fe, two trips, not one.

> Words are wind.
> *George R.R. Martin, A Song of Ice and Fire*

### Stop 1. Jean Cocteau Cinema & Beastly Books

**Waypoint:** Santa Fe, NM

Where the world was written. George R.R. Martin's restored Art Deco arthouse cinema and adjoining bookstore in Santa Fe, New Mexico, the closest thing to a Westeros visitor center on this side of the Atlantic. Martin bought the abandoned 1930s theater in 2013, restored its single auditorium, and turned the lobby into a rotating display of props, costumes, and signed memorabilia from Game of Thrones, House of the Dragon, and his earlier work. Beastly Books next door stocks signed first editions and rare ASOIAF translations. The cinema screens a mix of arthouse, classic, and genre programming year-round; check for occasional Martin-hosted events and Wild Cards readings. The starting point of the trail because this is where the world was written.

**The Berth.** La Fonda on the Plaza, the heritage hotel since 1922; Inn of the Five Graces in the Barrio de Analco; or the Bishop's Lodge in Tesuque just north of town.

**The Galley.** Geronimo on Canyon Road for the contemporary Southwestern; The Shed since 1953 for the canonical New Mexican; Café Pasqual's on Don Gaspar for breakfast; Tomasita's for Saturday lunch.

> A reader lives a thousand lives before he dies; the man who never reads lives only one.
> *George R.R. Martin, A Dance with Dragons*

### Stop 2. GRR Martin's actual home base since 1979

**Waypoint:** and the only stop on this trail he himself walks

Regularly. The Jean Cocteau, which he bought and restored in 2013, screens cult films and hosts signing events with him and visiting writers; Beastly Books next door is his small independent bookstore, full of his recommendations and the occasional signed first edition.
