Meow Wolf's House of Eternal Return, the immersive art experience he was an early backer of, is fifteen minutes away. The Sky Railway, his vintage steam train running into the high desert, is forty. Hot green chile at the Shed in the plaza, posole at La Choza, breakfast tamales at the farmers' market on Saturdays. Three days minimum. Watch his blog for event announcements before booking.

**The Berth.** Stay in Santa Fe: La Fonda on the Plaza since 1922; Inn of the Five Graces in the Barrio de Analco; or Bishop's Lodge in Tesuque just north of town.

**The Galley.** Geronimo on Canyon Road for contemporary Southwestern; The Shed since 1953 for canonical New Mexican; Café Pasqual's on Don Gaspar for breakfast; Tomasita's for Saturday lunch.

> I have lived a thousand lives and loved a thousand loves. I've walked on distant worlds and seen the end of time — because I read.
> *George R.R. Martin*

### Stop 3. Dubrovnik

**Waypoint:** Croatia (King's Landing)

Where King's Landing reigned for eight seasons. The walled Adriatic port that became the principal King's Landing across all eight seasons. Walk the entire 1.2 miles of city walls, the seaward stretches were used for nearly every Red Keep exterior; the Jesuit Stairs (Uz Jezuite) are the actual Walk of Shame steps where Cersei was forced down to the crowd. Across the harbor, Lokrum Island stood in for Qarth (the monastery now houses an Iron Throne replica); Trsteno Arboretum, half an hour up the coast, was the Red Keep's gardens; the abandoned quarry at Duban was Blackwater Bay. Buža Bar on the cliff outside the walls for sundown. Two days, three is better, and avoid July and August unless cruise-ship crowds are part of the pilgrimage you signed up for.

**The Berth.** Dubrovnik: Hotel Excelsior on Frana Supila; Villa Dubrovnik on the cliffs; or the Pucić Palace in the Old Town. Split: Cornaro Hotel or Villa Diana.

**The Galley.** Dubrovnik: 360° Restaurant on the city walls; Proto for the canonical seafood; Konoba Dubrava for the rural-Dalmatian peka. Split: Bokeria for the modern Dalmatian; Konoba Matejuška for the canonical fish.

> Why is it always the innocents who suffer most, when you high lords play your game of thrones?
> *George R.R. Martin, A Clash of Kings*

### Stop 4. Malta & Gozo

**Waypoint:** the Maltese Islands (the original King's Landing)

Where King's Landing was born. Before the production moved to Dubrovnik, the whole sun-baked capital of the Seven Kingdoms was filmed here, on the golden-limestone islands of Malta, in the first season. The ancient walled city of Mdina, one of the best-preserved medieval towns in Europe, was King's Landing itself: through its great gate Catelyn Stark rode into the capital, and just inside it Ned and Catelyn said their last farewell; in Mesquita Square, Jaime Lannister's men cut down Ned's guards. Fort Ricasoli stood in for the Red Keep, the gardens of a Rabat priory for its grounds. And across the channel on the little island of Gozo, in the wild cove of Dwejra, Daenerys married Khal Drogo beneath the great stone Azure Window, which the sea pulled down in a storm in 2017, though the dramatic cove remains. The Knights of St. John built these honey-colored walls, and they look like Westeros because Westeros borrowed their light. Walk through the gate of Mdina at golden hour, and stand in the first King's Landing of all.

**The Berth.** Malta: a palazzo hotel within the silent walls of Mdina itself, magical after the day crowds leave; the boutique hotels of Valletta, the Knights' Baroque capital; or a seaside room toward the Three Cities.

**The Galley.** Maltese: rabbit stew (fenkata), the national dish; pastizzi and ftira; the fresh fish and the Mediterranean produce; Gozitan cheeses and wine; a long lunch in a Mdina courtyard restaurant behind the old walls.

> When you play the game of thrones, you win or you die.
> *Cersei Lannister, in King's Landing*

### Stop 5. Castle Ward & the Northern Ireland Loop

**Waypoint:** Belfast

Where Winterfell stood and the show was made. Belfast was the show's actual production headquarters for a decade. Linen Mill Studios in Banbridge has been converted into the official Game of Thrones Studio Tour since 2022, original sets, costumes, the Iron Throne itself. From Belfast, a two-day driving loop hits Castle Ward (the Winterfell exterior, with archery in the actual courtyard), the Dark Hedges (the King's Road), Cushendun Caves (where Melisandre gave birth to the shadow), Ballintoy Harbour (the Iron Islands' Lordsport), and Tollymore Forest (where the Stark children find the direwolf pups in the pilot). St George's Market in Belfast on Saturday mornings; dinner at the Mourne Seafood Bar.

**The Berth.** Belfast: The Merchant Hotel in the converted 1860s bank; or Bullitt Hotel for the boutique. Causeway Coast: Galgorm Resort & Spa.

**The Galley.** Belfast: OX restaurant; The Muddler's Club; Made in Belfast; Yard Bird for the rotisserie chicken; St George's Market on Saturday.

> The north remembers.
> *George R.R. Martin, A Dance with Dragons*

### Stop 6. Lake Mývatn & Vatnajökull

**Waypoint:** Iceland (Beyond the Wall)

Where the lands beyond the Wall begin. The Land of Always Winter from the show, and the closest thing in the present world to Westeros north of the Wall. Drive Route 1 east from Reykjavík; spend two nights in the Mývatn area, where Grjótagjá, the geothermal cave Jon and Ygritte share, and the Hverir mud pots stood in for the wildling lands. Continue to Vatnajökull, Europe's largest glacier, where the Wall and the wight battle were filmed on the glacier tongues. Þingvellir National Park, an hour from Reykjavík, was the path to the Eyrie. Skyr, lamb soup, Arctic char, hákarl if you must. Best in late February or March, while the snow is still real and the Northern Lights are still out, or in summer when the daylight never ends and the highlands are open.

**The Berth.** Reykjavík: The Reykjavik Edition on Austurbakki; Tower Suites at Hotel Reykjavík Saga; or Hotel Borg on Austurvöllur for the heritage. North/East: Hotel Húsafell or Sigló Hótel in Siglufjörður.

**The Galley.** Reykjavík: Dill for the Michelin-starred New Nordic; Matur og Drykkur in the harbour for canonical Icelandic; Bæjarins Beztu Pylsur for the lamb hot dog. Around the Ring Road: hotel restaurants and roadside lamb soup.

> A cold wind was blowing from the north, and it made the trees rustle like living things.
> *George R.R. Martin, A Game of Thrones*

### Stop 7. Real Alcázar de Sevilla & Plaza de Toros de Osuna

**Waypoint:** Andalusia

Where Dorne held court and Drogon descended. Two stops, an hour apart, that anchor the Mediterranean leg. The Real Alcázar, a Mudéjar palace continuously inhabited by Spanish royalty since the 14th century, was the Water Gardens of Dorne, where Doran Martell holds court in season 5. Skip the queue with a timed-entry ticket and go in the morning before the heat. Then drive 90 minutes east to Osuna, a quiet white-walled town in the Andalusian campo, and stand in the bullring, the Plaza de Toros de Osuna was Daznak's Pit, where Drogon arrives to rescue Daenerys. The town is otherwise utterly off-circuit; you'll have it to yourself. Pair with Semana Santa in Sevilla (Mar 21-28) or Feria de Abril.

**The Berth.** Seville: Hotel Alfonso XIII; Hospes Las Casas del Rey de Baeza. Granada: Parador de Granada inside the Alhambra. Córdoba: Hospes Palacio del Bailío.

**The Galley.** Seville: Cañabota for the modern Andalusian; Casa Morales for canonical tapas; Tradevo. Granada: Restaurante Faralá in the Albaicín. Córdoba: Bodegas Campos.

> Valar morghulis — all men must die.
> *George R.R. Martin, A Song of Ice and Fire*

### Stop 8. San Juan de Gaztelugatxe

**Waypoint:** the Basque coast, Spain (Dragonstone)

Where Daenerys climbed to Dragonstone. On the wild Biscay coast of the Basque Country, a tiny island crowned with a 10th-century hermitage is joined to the mainland by a serpentine stone bridge and a stairway of two hundred and forty-one steps that zigzags up the rock above the crashing Cantabrian Sea. This is San Juan de Gaztelugatxe, and from Season 7 it became the causeway of Dragonstone, the ancestral seat of House Targaryen, up which Daenerys climbs on her long-awaited return to claim her birthright in Westeros. It had been a place of pilgrimage for a thousand years before the dragons came: pilgrims still climb the steps and ring the hermitage bell three times for luck. The setting is genuinely sublime, one of the most dramatic coastlines in Europe, and the climb is a real one. Ring the bell at the top, look out over the Bay of Biscay where Daenerys's dragons wheeled, and feel the pull of the ancestral home that every exile dreams of.

**The Berth.** The Basque coast: stay in nearby Bakio or Bermeo among the fishing harbors and surf beaches; or base in cosmopolitan Bilbao, half an hour away, for the Guggenheim and the great Basque city.

**The Galley.** Basque: the pintxos bars of Bilbao and the coast, the finest small-plate eating in the world; grilled turbot and the catch of the Cantabrian; txakoli, the crisp local white poured from on high; a seaside cider house near Gaztelugatxe.

> I was born to rule the Seven Kingdoms, and I will.
> *Daenerys Targaryen*

### Stop 9. Girona

**Waypoint:** Catalonia (Braavos and Hidden King's Landing)

Where Arya ran the streets of Braavos. A walled medieval Catalonian town an hour north of Barcelona that doubled for both Braavos and a stand-in King's Landing in season 6. The 86 stone steps of the Cathedral of Saint Mary appear repeatedly in the Sept of Baelor scenes; the narrow Carrer del Bisbe Josep Cartañà is Arya's Braavos chase scene where she's stabbed by the Waif; the Banys Àrabs (12th-century Arab Baths) were the House of Black and White interior. Walk it all in a morning. The old Jewish Quarter is one of the best-preserved in Europe; eat at El Celler de Can Roca if you booked a year ahead, or at Bar Boira in Plaça de la Independència if you didn't. Easily added to a Barcelona trip or a Costa Brava swing.

**The Berth.** Barcelona: Hotel Casa Fuster; El Palace; Cotton House Hotel. Girona: Hotel Llegendes de Girona Catedral.

**The Galley.** Barcelona: Disfrutar; Tickets; Bar Cañete; Quimet i Quimet. Girona: El Celler de Can Roca (Roca brothers' three-Michelin-star); Massana for the canonical.

> A girl has no name.
> *Arya Stark, in Braavos*

### Stop 10. Essaouira

**Waypoint:** Morocco (Astapor)

Where Daenerys freed the Unsullied. The fortified Atlantic port whose ramparts and skala, the cannon-lined sea wall, became Astapor, where Daenerys freed the Unsullied. Walk the ramparts at sunset, then descend into the medina (UNESCO-listed). Pairs perfectly with the Gnaoua World Music Festival in mid-June; otherwise come for the Atlantic wind, grilled sardines straight off the boats at the port, and tagines you'll think about for years. Three-hour drive west from Marrakech. The natural endpoint of the trail, the southern edge of Slaver's Bay, the last filming location before the show invented its own geography in the final seasons, the place where the pilgrimage runs out of map.

**The Berth.** La Mamounia in Marrakech, the gardens, the bar, the riad rooms; or Royal Mansour for the riad-of-riads; or the smaller Riad El Fenn for the boutique.

**The Galley.** Le Tobsil in Marrakech for the canonical pastilla; La Maison Arabe for the cooking school dinner; Café Clock in the medina for the camel burger; Mechoui Alley behind the souks for the lamb.

> I will take what is mine with fire and blood.
> *Daenerys Targaryen, at Astapor*

---

## Pilgrimage VIII. The Way of the Stars

Year-round destinations along the Camino Francés, the 800-kilometer Way of Saint James from the French Pyrenees across northern Spain to the apostle's tomb in Santiago de Compostela, the most-walked pilgrimage in the Western world. Walked since at least the 9th century by Catholic pilgrims venerating the relics of Saint James; walked today by every kind of seeker, the devout, the skeptical, the recently divorced, the recently retired, the recently graduated, Korean tour groups, German cyclists, French families. The full Francés takes 30-35 days on foot; the last 100 kilometers from Sarria qualifies you for the Compostela certificate at the Pilgrim's Office. Pamplona, covered separately in this calendar via San Fermín, sits on day three of the route. Best begun in late April or May (cool, green, before the summer crowds) or in September (clear, cool, harvest season). The credencial, the pilgrim's passport stamped at every albergue, is the souvenir. The walk itself is the practice. Buen camino.

> Buen camino — good way.
> *the traditional Camino de Santiago greeting*

### Stop 1. Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port

**Waypoint:** French Basque Country

Where the pilgrim road begins. The traditional starting point on the French side of the Pyrenees. The Pilgrim Office on Rue de la Citadelle issues the credencial, the pilgrim's passport, stamped at every albergue between here and Santiago, and offers the canonical warning that the first day over the mountains is the hardest of the entire walk. Eat well before you start: a proper Basque dinner at Hôtel-Restaurant des Pyrénées or any small place in the medieval old town (axoa, gâteau basque, a glass of Irouléguy). Buy walking poles if you don't have them. The morning departure climbs 1,200 vertical meters before noon.

**The Berth.** Biarritz: Hôtel du Palais on the seafront; Hôtel des Basses Pyrénées Bayonne in central Bayonne; or Brindos Lac & Châteaux on the lake.

**The Galley.** Le Chistera or Bar du Marché in Bayonne; Bistrot Berria in Bayonne; in Biarritz: Le Bistrot Saint Charles; in Saint-Jean-de-Luz: Le Kaiku.

> Ultreïa et suseïa — onward and upward.
> *the pilgrim's cry, Codex Calixtinus*

### Stop 2. Roncesvalles

**Waypoint:** Navarre

Where Roland fell and the first night falls. The first night in Spain after the Pyrenees crossing. The Royal Collegiate Church of Santa María, where Charlemagne's nephew Roland died in 778, in the battle commemorated three centuries later by the Song of Roland, holds a daily Pilgrim's Mass at 8 p.m. with a multilingual blessing for arriving pilgrims. The albergue, run by Dutch volunteers, sleeps two hundred in stacked bunks; lights-out at 10 p.m., silence enforced. The simplicity of the dinner, the pilgrim's menu of soup, fish, wine, bread, fruit, all for pocket change, sets the tone for the next month. Pamplona is two days down the trail.

**The Berth.** Pamplona: Gran Hotel La Perla on Plaza del Castillo; Hotel Maisonnave; or Hotel Tres Reyes. Roncesvalles: Casa Sabina for the pilgrim's stop.

**The Galley.** Pamplona: Bar Gaucho on Calle Espoz y Mina; Casa Otano for chuletón; Café Iruña on the Plaza for Hemingway. Roncesvalles: pilgrim menu at Casa Sabina.

> The pilgrim road is a thing of penance, and a thing of joy.
> *the Veneranda Dies sermon, Codex Calixtinus*

### Stop 3. Logroño & La Rioja

**Waypoint:** wine country

Where the road becomes a feast. One week in, the Camino crosses the Ebro on the Puente de Piedra into Logroño, and within an hour of dropping your pack you discover Calle Laurel, the pintxo street, and realize the Camino is also a feast. Three-euro tapas, two-euro Rioja crianza, the same circulating crowd of pilgrims and locals all night. Vineyards line the trail for the next several days. The Cathedral of Santa María de la Redonda has its Twin Towers rising over the old town; the wine is the point here. Sleep at the municipal albergue for the full pilgrim experience or at a small pensión if your knees need a private room.

**The Berth.** Marqués de Riscal (the Frank Gehry-designed in Elciego); NH Logroño Herencia Rioja in the centre; or Hotel Calle Mayor for the boutique.

**The Galley.** Logroño: Asador Egües for canonical asado; Tondeluna for the modern; the Calle del Laurel pintxo crawl (Bar Soriano, Blanco y Negro, Bar Tio Agus).

> People always arrive at the right moment at the place where someone awaits them.
> *Paulo Coelho, The Pilgrimage*

### Stop 4. Burgos Cathedral

**Waypoint:** Castilla y León

Where the pilgrim rests at the halfway mark. Two weeks in, halfway-ish: Burgos Cathedral, completed in 1567, UNESCO-listed, the burial place of El Cid, is one of the masterpieces of European High Gothic. Enter through the Puerta del Sarmental on the south facade. Climb to the upper galleries to see the Papamoscas, the 16th-century mechanical figure that opens its mouth and 'eats flies' on every hour strike. Eat morcilla de Burgos (rice-and-blood sausage), milk-fed lamb, and the local Ribera del Duero. Most pilgrims take their first rest day here, wash everything, sleep eleven hours, remember why they started. The Mesetas, the high dry plains, begin tomorrow.

**The Berth.** Burgos: Landa Hotel Burgos. León: Parador de León in the converted San Marcos monastery. Salamanca: Hotel Don Gregorio.

**The Galley.** Burgos: Cobo Vintage for the Michelin-starred castellano. León: Cocinandos for the modern; Bodega Regia for canonical castellano. Salamanca: Víctor Gutiérrez for the modern.

> A ship is safest in port, but that is not what ships were built for.
> *Paulo Coelho, The Pilgrimage*

### Stop 5. The Meseta

**Waypoint:** the high plateau, Castilla y León

Where the journey turns inward. Beyond Burgos the Camino climbs onto the Meseta, the vast high tableland of central Spain, and for some two hundred kilometers the trail runs dead straight across a treeless ocean of wheat under an enormous sky, village to distant village, with nothing to distract the walker from the rhythm of their own feet and the company of their own mind. Many pilgrims dread the Meseta and some skip it by bus; those who walk it often find it the truest part of the whole Camino, the stretch where the body goes quiet and something deeper begins to speak, the spiritual heart of the road. At Castrojeriz a ruined castle crowns the hill, and just beyond, the steep climb to the Alto de Mostelares opens the plateau to the horizon in every direction. Walk the Meseta slowly, do not skip it, let the long flat miles and the huge silence do their patient work, and learn what the pilgrims mean when they say the Camino changes you.

**The Berth.** The Meseta: the simple pilgrim albergues of Hontanas, Castrojeriz, and Boadilla del Camino, some in restored medieval hospices; small rural inns; the austere comfort of a clean bunk after a long day's walk.

**The Galley.** Castilian plateau cooking: the hearty cocido and lentil stews; roast lamb and suckling pig in the larger towns; Castilian bread and Manchego-style cheese; the robust reds of the Ribera del Duero, just to the south; the pilgrim's menu del día.

> The Meseta is where the Camino stops being a walk and becomes a pilgrimage.
> *the wisdom of the Camino*

### Stop 6. León & the Cathedral of Light

**Waypoint:** Castilla y León

Where the light pours through medieval glass. Three weeks in, the Cathedral of León, the Pulchra Leonina, completed in 1302, holds 1,800 square meters of medieval stained glass, the most of any cathedral in the French Gothic style and one of the great surviving medieval glass programs in Europe. The 13th-century glass was disassembled and reset in the 19th century and now glows in any weather. Visit twice if you can, once at noon, once near sunset. Sleep at the Hostal San Marcos (a 16th-century pilgrim hospital, now a parador on the Bernesga river) if your knees and your wallet permit. The Barrio Húmedo is the tapas neighborhood; cecina, morcilla, and a bottle of Bierzo somewhere along Calle de Cervantes.

**The Berth.** Burgos: Landa Hotel Burgos. León: Parador de León in the converted San Marcos monastery. Salamanca: Hotel Don Gregorio.

**The Galley.** Burgos: Cobo Vintage for the Michelin-starred castellano. León: Cocinandos for the modern; Bodega Regia for canonical castellano. Salamanca: Víctor Gutiérrez for the modern.

> When you travel, you experience, in a very practical way, the act of rebirth.
> *Paulo Coelho, The Pilgrimage*

### Stop 7. The Cruz de Ferro

**Waypoint:** Monte Irago, León

Where the pilgrim lays down the burden. At the highest point of the Camino Francés, fifteen hundred meters up on the lonely Monte Irago beyond Astorga, a simple iron cross stands atop a tall weathered pole, and at its foot has risen, over a thousand years, an immense mound of stones. The tradition is old and the practice is simple: each pilgrim carries a stone, brought from home or gathered along the way, and lays it here, and with it lays down whatever weight they have chosen it to carry, a grief, a sin, a prayer, the name of someone loved or lost. Many stones bear written words; some pilgrims kneel; some simply add their pebble to the cairn and walk on. It is the most quietly powerful moment on the whole road. Come early, before the tour groups, take from your pack the stone you have carried all these miles, set it down at the foot of the iron cross, and walk on toward Santiago lighter.

**The Berth.** The mountains of León: the albergues of Rabanal del Camino and Foncebadón, the once-abandoned village now revived for pilgrims; or stay below in handsome Astorga, with its Gaudí palace and its cathedral.

**The Galley.** Maragato country: the cocido maragato, the great regional feast eaten famously in reverse, meats first and soup last; Astorga's celebrated chocolate and its mantecadas; hearty mountain stews; a warming meal before the high crossing.

> Lord, may this stone I lay at the foot of the cross be a sign of my pilgrimage to Santiago.
> *the traditional prayer at the Cruz de Ferro*

### Stop 8. O Cebreiro

**Waypoint:** Galicia

Where the Camino climbs into Galicia. Around day twenty-five, the Camino enters Galicia by climbing 600 vertical meters in a single morning into a fog-wrapped stone-circle village of pre-Christian palloza huts, several of which now serve as bars. The 9th-century Igrexa de Santa María Real, one of the oldest standing pilgrim churches on the entire route, holds a relic from a 1300 Eucharistic miracle. Mist sweeps the village most mornings; you can stand in cloud at the wayside cross at dawn. Caldo gallego, pulpo a feira, fresh queixo do Cebreiro on hot crusty bread, a small glass of orujo for the chill. The light, the weather, and the language change here. The last 150 kilometers feel different from everything that came before.

**The Berth.** Santiago de Compostela: Parador Hostal dos Reis Católicos (the 1499 royal pilgrim hospice). A Coruña: Hotel Riazor on Riazor Beach.

**The Galley.** Santiago: Casa Marcelo for the Michelin one-star modern Galician; A Tafona; O Curro da Parra for canonical Galician. A Coruña: Salitre for the seafood; Pablo Gallego.

> We must never stop dreaming. Dreams provide nourishment for the soul, just as a meal does for the body.
> *Paulo Coelho, The Pilgrimage*

### Stop 9. Santiago de Compostela

**Waypoint:** Galicia

Where every road finally arrives. The Cathedral of Santiago, built over the apostle's tomb on the site of the 9th-century discovery, is the architectural and emotional climax of the journey. The Pilgrim's Mass is at noon (and again at 7:30 p.m.); when offerings on a given day are large enough, the Botafumeiro, the 1.6-meter brass censer hung from the transept ceiling, swung by eight tiraboleiros pulling on a thick rope, flies in roaring arcs across the church at the climax of the mass. Hug the saint's statue behind the high altar. Then walk to the Oficina del Peregrino on Rúa Carretas to present your stamped credencial and receive the Compostela (in Latin, with your name in the genitive). Eat pulpo at any pulpería, scallops anywhere, the local Albariño, and queimada, the flaming Galician spirit-and-raisin punch, somewhere late.

**The Berth.** Santiago de Compostela: Parador Hostal dos Reis Católicos (the 1499 royal pilgrim hospice). A Coruña: Hotel Riazor on Riazor Beach.

**The Galley.** Santiago: Casa Marcelo for the Michelin one-star modern Galician; A Tafona; O Curro da Parra for canonical Galician. A Coruña: Salitre for the seafood; Pablo Gallego.

> The extraordinary is always found in the ordinary and simple ways of everyday people.
> *Paulo Coelho, The Pilgrimage*

### Stop 10. Cape Finisterre

**Waypoint:** A Costa da Morte

Where the pilgrim walks to the end of the world. The optional 90-kilometer extension along Galicia's 'Coast of Death' to the so-called End of the World, what medieval pilgrims believed was the literal western edge of the inhabited earth. Three days on foot from Santiago through Galician forest and small fishing villages. The lighthouse at Cabo Fisterra is the geographic terminus. Tradition: at sunset on the cliff below the lighthouse, you burn a single item of your walking clothes (something the wind cannot easily carry, pilgrims have started Galician forest fires), and you watch the Atlantic until the sun finishes. Percebes, gooseneck barnacles, the great Galician seafood, at any harbor restaurant, a cold bottle of Albariño from the Rías Baixas just south. For those who walk the extension, the pilgrimage doesn't end in Santiago. It ends here.

**The Berth.** Stay in Santiago de Compostela (90 minutes east): Parador Hostal dos Reis Católicos; A Quinta da Auga; Hotel Costa Vella. Or in Finisterre: Hotel Mariquito.

**The Galley.** Finisterre: Restaurante O Centolo on the harbour for the canonical pulpo and percebes; Tira do Cordel for cliff-top dining; in Santiago: Casa Marcelo; Mercado de Abastos.

> At Finisterre the sun dies into the ocean, and there the world of rebirth begins.
> *the Camino de Finisterre tradition*

---

## Pilgrimage IX. The Path to the Far Shore

Year-round destinations along the geography of the Buddha's life and the spread of his teaching across Asia, built on the four places the Buddha himself named on the night of his death as the places a devout follower should visit, where he was born (Lumbini), where he awakened (Bodh Gaya), where he first taught (Sarnath), and where he passed into final nirvana (Kushinagar), expanded outward to the great living centers of the tradition: the relic-cities of Sri Lanka, the gold of Burma, the stone mandala of Java, the snow ranges of the Himalaya, and the rock gardens of Japan. The Indian core forms the classic Buddhist Circuit across Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and southern Nepal; best traveled October through March, out of the heat, often in the white clothing of the lay pilgrim. The wider sites are separate journeys across Buddhist Asia. Best paired with Vesak (the full moon of May, the Buddha's birth, awakening, and passing all observed on one day across the Theravada world) or with the Tibetan Mönlam prayer festivals at Bodh Gaya each winter. The Circuit is roughly ten days; the whole of Buddhist Asia is a life's work. Walk slowly. The path is the teaching.

> All conditioned things are impermanent. Work out your salvation with diligence.
> *the Buddha's last words, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*

### Stop 1. Lumbini

**Waypoint:** Rupandehi District, Nepal

Where he was born. In a garden at Lumbini, in the Nepali Terai near the Indian border, Queen Māyādevī gave birth to Siddhārtha Gautama around 563 BCE, holding the branch of a sal tree, the future Buddha. The exact spot is marked by a stone now sheltered inside the Māyādevī Temple, and beside it stands a sandstone pillar erected by the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in 249 BCE, its inscription recording that the emperor himself came here in person to worship at the birthplace, the single oldest documentary confirmation of any event in the Buddha's life. The sacred garden holds the ancient Puskarini pond where Māyādevī is said to have bathed before the birth, and a Bodhi tree hung with prayer flags. Around the core, the nations of the Buddhist world have each built a monastery in their own architecture, Thai, Burmese, German, Chinese, Tibetan, a quiet modern parliament of the dharma. UNESCO World Heritage. Begin here, at the beginning.

**The Berth.** Lumbini: Hotel Kasai or the Buddha Maya Garden Hotel for the comfortable; or the meditation-focused guesthouses run by the international monasteries themselves.

**The Galley.** Nepali-Indian Terai cooking: dal bhat, sel roti, simple thali; the vegetarian canteens at the larger monasteries; lassi and chiya (spiced milk tea) anywhere.

> Health is the greatest gift, contentment the greatest wealth, faithfulness the best relationship.
> *the Dhammapada*

### Stop 2. Bodh Gaya & the Mahabodhi Temple

**Waypoint:** Bihar, India

Where he awakened. The single most important place in the Buddhist world: the spot beneath a peepal tree on the bank of the Phalgu River where Siddhārtha, after six years of wandering and ascetic extremity, sat down in meditation, vowed not to rise until he understood the cause of suffering, and at dawn became the Buddha, the Awakened One. The Bodhi Tree standing there now is a direct descendant of the original (grown from a cutting taken to Sri Lanka by Ashoka's daughter and carried back centuries later after the Indian original was destroyed). The Mahabodhi Temple beside it, a 55-meter brick spire whose core dates to the Gupta period around 500 CE, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and the active heart of global Buddhism. Every winter the Tibetan schools hold their great Mönlam prayer festivals here, and tens of thousands of pilgrims in maroon and white circumambulate the temple day and night. Sit under the tree at dawn. This is where it happened.

**The Berth.** Bodh Gaya: the Oaks Bodhgaya; Hotel Bodhgaya Regency; or, for the full experience, a room at one of the national monasteries (Thai, Bhutanese, Tibetan).

**The Galley.** Bihari and Tibetan vegetarian: thukpa and momos in the Tibetan quarter; the monastery canteens; Be Happy Café and the traveler cafés near the temple gate.

> We are what we think. All that we are arises with our thoughts. With our thoughts we make the world.
> *the Dhammapada, opening verse*

### Stop 3. Sarnath

**Waypoint:** near Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh, India

Where he first taught. In the Deer Park at Sarnath, a few miles north of Varanasi, the newly awakened Buddha found the five ascetics who had once been his companions and gave them his first teaching, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the Setting in Motion of the Wheel of the Dharma: the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path. This is the moment Buddhism began as a teaching rather than a private realization. The great Dhamekh Stupa, a 43-meter cylinder of brick and stone first raised by Ashoka and enlarged around 500 CE, marks the spot; nearby stood the Ashokan pillar whose four-lion capital is now the national emblem of India (the original is in the Sarnath Museum, and the Wheel of Dharma from its base is the chakra on the Indian flag). Each evening pilgrims gather to chant the first sermon in the air where it was first spoken. Combine with a dawn boat on the Ganges at Varanasi, an hour away, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth.

**The Berth.** Varanasi: the Taj Nadesar Palace; BrijRama Palace on the ghats; or Suryauday Haveli for the riverside heritage.

**The Galley.** Banarasi vegetarian: kachori-sabzi and jalebi for breakfast; the thali at Kashi Chat Bhandar; Banarasi paan to finish; the Deer Park canteen at Sarnath itself.

> Just as the great ocean has one taste, the taste of salt, so this teaching has one taste, the taste of liberation.
> *the Buddha, Udāna*

### Stop 4. Kushinagar

**Waypoint:** Uttar Pradesh, India

Where he passed into final nirvana. At Kushinagar, an old man of eighty, the Buddha lay down on his right side between two sal trees, gave his disciples their last instruction, and died, entering the parinirvana, the final passing beyond rebirth. The Mahaparinirvana Temple holds a superb 1,500-year-old reclining Buddha in red sandstone, six meters long, the face composed in the moment of letting go; pilgrims drape it in fresh saffron and gold cloth daily. Behind it rises the Nirvana Stupa over the spot of the death, and a kilometer east the Ramabhar Stupa marks the cremation site, where pilgrims circumambulate and sometimes weep. Of the four great places this is the quietest and the most affecting, the end of a human life that changed the history of the mind. The Buddha's final words are carved here and recited everywhere: appamādena sampādetha, strive on with diligence.

**The Berth.** Kushinagar: the Lotus Nikko Hotel (Japanese-built); Hotel Royal Residency; or the guesthouses at the Burmese and Tibetan monasteries.

**The Galley.** Simple Uttar Pradesh vegetarian thali; the monastery canteens (the Burmese serves a fine mohinga on festival days); chai at any roadside stall.

> All compounded things are subject to decay. Strive on with diligence.
> *the Buddha's final words, recited daily at Kushinagar*

### Stop 5. Kandy & the Temple of the Tooth

**Waypoint:** Sri Lanka

Where the Buddha's tooth is enshrined. In the hill city of Kandy, the last royal capital of Sri Lanka, the Sri Dalada Maligawa, the Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic, houses what tradition holds to be a tooth of the Buddha, brought to the island in the 4th century CE hidden in a princess's hair. The relic has been the palladium of Sinhalese kingship for sixteen centuries, whoever held the Tooth held the right to rule, and it is still treated as a living presence: drummers and offerings three times daily, the inner chamber opened only briefly. Each summer (the full moon of July or August) the Esala Perahera carries a replica casket through Kandy on a caparisoned elephant, by torchlight, with whip-crackers, dancers, and a hundred elephants, one of the great religious processions on Earth, already on this calendar. Combine with the ancient relic-cities of the Cultural Triangle, Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, and the cave temples of Dambulla, where 2,000 years of devotion are painted across the rock.

**The Berth.** Kandy: the colonial Queen's Hotel by the lake; Kings Pavilion; or the boutique Santani wellness resort in the hills. Cultural Triangle: Ulagalla; Heritance Kandalama (the Geoffrey Bawa landmark).

**The Galley.** Sri Lankan rice and curry: hoppers and string hoppers, kottu, pol sambol; the Kandy Muslim Hotel for the local; tea at any hill-country estate above the city.

> Hatred is never appeased by hatred in this world. By love alone is hatred appeased. This is an eternal law.
> *the Dhammapada*

### Stop 6. Adam's Peak

**Waypoint:** central highlands, Sri Lanka

Where pilgrims climb through the dark to a sacred footprint. The conical 2,243-meter peak in the Sri Lankan highlands holds at its summit a footprint-shaped depression in the rock that Buddhists revere as the print of the Buddha's left foot, left on his legendary visit to the island, the mountain Sinhalese call Sri Pada, 'the sacred foot.' It is one of the few sites on Earth held holy by four faiths at once, the same print being the footprint of Shiva to Hindus, of Adam to Muslims, of St. Thomas to some Christians. Pilgrims climb through the night, by the light of the lamps strung the length of the trail and the chant of the devout, some five thousand steps to the summit, timing the ascent to reach the top before dawn. At sunrise the mountain casts a perfect triangular shadow across the cloud and the western plains, the ira sevaya, the 'sun service,' and the bells ring. The season runs from the December full moon to the May full moon, when the weather permits the climb.

**The Berth.** Base at Dalhousie (Nallathanniya) for the popular route: Slightly Chilled Lounge & Bar; Punsisi Rest; or the Green House. Or stay in the tea country at Ceylon Tea Trails for the grand.

**The Galley.** Hot kotthu and dal at the trailhead stalls before the climb; sweet tea at the rest huts on the way up; a proper Sri Lankan breakfast back at the base after sunrise.

> Better than a thousand hollow words is one word that brings peace.
> *the Dhammapada*

### Stop 7. Shwedagon Pagoda

**Waypoint:** Yangon, Myanmar

Where Burma's golden heart rises. The Shwedagon Pagoda rises 99 meters above Yangon on Singuttara Hill, a bell-shaped stupa sheathed in hundreds of gold plates and crowned with a finial set with thousands of diamonds and rubies, the whole edifice plated in real gold and re-gilded by the donations of the faithful. Tradition holds it enshrines relics of four Buddhas, including eight hairs of Gautama himself, which would make it older than any other surviving Buddhist monument; archaeology dates the present structure across many centuries of rebuilding and gilding. Around the central stupa runs a marble terrace crowded with shrines, prayer pavilions, and planetary posts where Burmese Buddhists pour water over the image that corresponds to the day of the week on which they were born. Walk the terrace clockwise at dusk, barefoot on the cool marble, as the gold catches the last light and the whole hill begins to glow. Check current travel advisories for Myanmar carefully before any visit.

**The Berth.** Yangon: the colonial Strand Hotel (since 1901); the Belmond Governor's Residence in a teak mansion; or the Savoy Hotel for the boutique.

**The Galley.** Burmese: mohinga (the catfish-noodle national breakfast) at any morning stall; tea- leaf salad (lahpet thoke); Feel Myanmar Food for the canonical; Rangoon Tea House.

> Be a lamp unto yourselves; be a refuge unto yourselves, seeking no other refuge.
> *the Buddha, Mahāparinibbāna Sutta*

### Stop 8. Borobudur

**Waypoint:** Central Java, Indonesia

Where the path to enlightenment is built in stone. Constructed around 800 CE under the Shailendra dynasty and then lost for centuries under volcanic ash and jungle until its 19th-century rediscovery, Borobudur is the largest Buddhist monument on Earth: a single colossal stepped pyramid of two million blocks of grey andesite, laid out as a three-dimensional mandala of the Buddhist cosmos. The pilgrim ascends through three levels, the world of desire at the base (its carved panels of earthly life), the world of form on the square terraces (1,460 relief panels narrating the Buddha's lives and the path), and the formless world at the summit, three circular terraces holding 72 bell-shaped perforated stupas, each with a seated Buddha inside, around one great central stupa. To climb it is to walk the path to enlightenment as architecture. Arrive before dawn, when the mist lies in the valley and the volcanoes of Merapi and Merbabu stand on the horizon. UNESCO World Heritage. Pair with the great Hindu temple of Prambanan nearby.

**The Berth.** Yogyakarta / Borobudur: Amanjiwo (the Aman resort facing the monument); Plataran Borobudur; or the boutique Phoenix Hotel in Yogyakarta city.

**The Galley.** Javanese: gudeg (the jackfruit stew of Yogyakarta); nasi goreng and sate; the royal cuisine at Bale Raos near the Kraton; kopi joss (charcoal coffee) at a Yogya street stall.

> You yourselves must strive; the Buddhas only point the way.
> *the Dhammapada*

### Stop 9. Lhasa, the Jokhang & the Potala

**Waypoint:** Tibet

Where the pilgrims prostrate on the roof of the world. In Lhasa, at 3,650 meters, two monuments hold the spiritual and temporal history of Tibetan Buddhism. The Jokhang Temple, founded in the 7th century, is the holiest temple in Tibet, built to house the Jowo Shakyamuni, an image of the Buddha said to have been blessed in his lifetime; pilgrims prostrate full-length around the Barkhor circuit that rings it, sliding forward body-length by body-length, some having traveled across the plateau this way for months. The Potala Palace, the thirteen-story winter palace of the Dalai Lamas rising on its red hill, is one of the wonders of the world, though its central figure has lived in exile since 1959, a fact every honest pilgrim carries up the steps with them. Altitude is real here; acclimatize for days before arriving, and note that travel to Tibet requires permits arranged in advance through the Chinese authorities. Spin a prayer wheel. Walk the kora clockwise with the pilgrims. The air is thin and the devotion is total.

**The Berth.** Lhasa: the St. Regis Lhasa Resort; the Shangri-La Lhasa; or the boutique House of Shambhala in the old Tibetan quarter near the Barkhor.

**The Galley.** Tibetan: tsampa (roasted barley), thukpa, momos, yak butter tea (an acquired and necessary taste at altitude); the rooftop cafés around the Barkhor for the view.

> If you want others to be happy, practice compassion. If you want to be happy, practice compassion.
> *the 14th Dalai Lama*

### Stop 10. Kyoto: Ryōan-ji & the Zen Temples

**Waypoint:** Japan

Where the teaching became silence and stone. The Buddhism that traveled north from India through China arrived in Japan as Zen, and nowhere is its spirit more concentrated than in the temple gardens of Kyoto. At Ryōan-ji, fifteen rocks sit in a rectangle of raked white gravel, walled, bare, and arranged so that from no single vantage can all fifteen be seen at once, the most famous dry-landscape (karesansui) garden in the world, a teaching with no words and no explanation that the temple itself declines to give. Up the eastern hills, Kiyomizu-dera's great wooden stage juts over the maple valley, and the Golden Pavilion of Kinkaku-ji floats on its pond nearby. Sit on the veranda at Ryōan-ji for as long as it takes. The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths in the Deer Park; here, two and a half thousand years and four thousand miles later, fifteen stones in gravel teach the same thing in another language entirely. The pilgrimage ends in silence.

**The Berth.** Kyoto: the ryokan Tawaraya (since the early 1700s) or Hiiragiya for the canonical; the Ritz-Carlton Kyoto on the Kamogawa; or a temple-lodging (shukubo) for the dawn meditation.

**The Galley.** Kyoto: shōjin ryōri (the Zen temple vegetarian cuisine) at Shigetsu in Arashiyama; kaiseki at Kikunoi; yudofu (hot tofu) near Nanzen-ji; matcha and wagashi anywhere.

> Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā — gone, gone, gone beyond, gone altogether beyond. O what an awakening!
> *the Heart Sutra, closing mantra*

---

## Pilgrimage X. Where the Earth Still Speaks

Year-round destinations along the great natural cathedrals of the Earth, the places that humble the human scale entirely and have drawn pilgrims of a different kind, the naturalist, the climber, the wanderer, the seeker of awe. Unlike the trails of saints and soldiers, this pilgrimage has no single founder and no relics; its scripture is written in granite, deep time, migration, and light. Anchored to the temples of American wilderness that John Muir and Henry David Thoreau made holy (Yosemite, Walden), to the living laboratory where Darwin read the history of life itself (the Galápagos), to the great theaters of wild animal life (the Serengeti, the Great Barrier Reef, the Amazon), to the highest and oldest things on Earth (the Himalaya, the giant sequoias), and to the two polar wonders at the ends of the world (the aurora, Antarctica). Best traveled by season, each stop has its own window, noted below. No festival anchors this trail; the festival is the planet itself, on the move. The longest pilgrimage in this book by distance, and the only one whose cathedral was never built by human hands.

> In every walk with nature one receives far more than he seeks.
> *John Muir*

### Stop 1. Yosemite & the Range of Light

**Waypoint:** Sierra Nevada, California

Where American wilderness became sacred. The glacier-carved granite valley of Yosemite, walls of pale stone rising three thousand feet from the meadow floor, El Capitan and Half Dome and the high country beyond, is the place where John Muir spent ten years 'wandering and wondering' and came to call the whole Sierra Nevada not the Snowy Range but the Range of Light. His campaign to protect it helped invent the national park idea, and the three nights he camped here with Theodore Roosevelt in 1903 set the conservation movement in motion. Muir first climbed Cathedral Peak in 1869 and wrote that no holier temple had ever been consecrated by the heart of man. Stand in the meadow at dawn when the first light catches the top of El Capitan, or walk the high country of Tuolumne Meadows in late summer. Best May through October (the high country opens only after the snow clears); the waterfalls run hardest in May and June. Reserve far ahead; the valley is loved nearly to death.

**The Berth.** In the park: the grand 1927 Ahwahnee Hotel under the granite walls; or Yosemite Valley Lodge near the falls. Gateway: Rush Creek Lodge near the Big Oak Flat entrance; Tenaya Lodge near the south gate.

**The Galley.** The Ahwahnee Dining Room under its 34-foot ceiling; the classic Mountain Room at the Lodge; provisions and a meadow picnic; the Jackson family's pie at the Wawona.

> Climb the mountains and get their good tidings. Nature's peace will flow into you as sunshine flows into trees.
> *John Muir, Our National Parks, 1901*

### Stop 2. Walden Pond

**Waypoint:** Concord, Massachusetts

Where one man went to the woods on purpose. On the Fourth of July, 1845, Henry David Thoreau moved into a one-room cabin he had built on the north shore of Walden Pond, on land owned by his friend Ralph Waldo Emerson, and lived there two years, two months, and two days, 'to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life.' The book he made of it, Walden (1854), is the founding text of American nature writing and of the idea that simplicity and solitude in nature are a spiritual discipline. The pond itself, a clear glacial kettle pond one hundred and two feet deep, is now a state reservation; the cabin site is marked by stone posts and a cairn that visitors have added to for a century and a half, and a faithful replica stands near the parking lot. Walk the mile-and-a-half loop around the water, swim in summer, and read a page on the small beach. Concord is also Emerson, the Alcotts, and Hawthorne, the whole American Transcendental moment in one small town. Year-round; loveliest in October.

**The Berth.** Concord: the Colonial Inn on Monument Square (since 1716); the boutique North Bridge Inn. Or stay in nearby Cambridge or Boston, forty minutes by car or rail.

**The Galley.** The Colonial Inn for the New England canonical; 80 Thoreau in Concord for the modern; Helen's for the diner breakfast; Verrill Farm for the farm-stand picnic.

> I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life.
> *Henry David Thoreau, Walden*

### Stop 3. The Galápagos Islands

**Waypoint:** Ecuador, on the Equator

Where the history of life was read for the first time. The young naturalist Charles Darwin reached this volcanic archipelago aboard HMS Beagle on September 15, 1835, and spent five weeks ashore; he called it 'a little world within itself.' The tameness of the animals, the giant tortoises, the marine iguanas, the mockingbirds and finches that differed subtly from island to island, lodged in his mind, and within two years of returning to England he had begun to assemble the theory of evolution by natural selection that he published in 1859. Six hundred miles off the coast of Ecuador and astride the Equator, the islands remain one of the least-spoiled wild places on Earth: blue-footed boobies, sea lions on the docks, penguins on the equator, tortoises a century and a half old. Most pilgrims travel by small live-aboard ship among the islands with a licensed naturalist guide. The wildlife shows year-round; December to May is warmer and calmer, June to November cooler with the richest sea life. The Charles Darwin Research Station on Santa Cruz is the place to begin.

**The Berth.** Aboard: a small expedition vessel (the Aqua Mare, the Origin, or a comparable licensed yacht). On land: Pikaia Lodge or Finch Bay on Santa Cruz.

**The Galley.** Ecuadorian-Pacific seafood: ceviche, encocado, fresh-caught wahoo and grouper; the ship's galley; the small marisquerías of Puerto Ayora on Santa Cruz.

> The natural history of this archipelago is very remarkable: it seems to be a little world within itself.
> *Charles Darwin, The Voyage of the Beagle*

### Stop 4. The Serengeti & the Great Migration

**Waypoint:** Tanzania

Where the great migration turns its endless wheel. Across the short-grass plains of the Serengeti, whose name comes from the Maasai siringet, 'the place where the land runs on forever,' some two million wildebeest, zebra, and gazelle move in a vast clockwise circuit through the year, following the rains and the grass, the largest overland migration of mammals anywhere on the planet. Predators move with them, the lion prides, the cheetahs on the termite mounds, the crocodiles waiting at the river crossings. The spectacle has no single home; it is a wheel that turns through the Serengeti and the neighboring Maasai Mara across the year, and the famous Mara and Grumeti river crossings, where the herds plunge through the water and the crocodiles take their share, fall roughly July through October. The calving on the southern plains, half a million wildebeest born in a few weeks, comes in January and February. There is no off-season; there is only where the wheel has turned to. Combine with the Ngorongoro Crater.

**The Berth.** The classic tented camps that move with the herds: Singita, &Beyond, Nomad, or Asilia. For the crater: the Ngorongoro Crater Lodge on the rim.

**The Galley.** Camp dining under canvas and stars; Tanzanian and pan-African cooking at the luxury camps; nyama choma (grilled meat) and ugali in Arusha at the start or end.

> The question is, are we happy to suppose that our grandchildren may never be able to see an elephant except in a picture?
> *David Attenborough*

### Stop 5. The Giant Sequoias

**Waypoint:** Sequoia & Kings Canyon, California

Where the largest living things on Earth still stand. In the groves of the western Sierra Nevada grow the giant sequoias, Sequoiadendron giganteum, the most massive trees in the world: the General Sherman Tree in Sequoia National Park, by volume the largest single-stem living thing on the planet, stands 275 feet tall, is over 36 feet across at the base, and is estimated to be more than two thousand years old, a living thing that was already ancient when Rome fell. The sequoias depend on fire to release their seeds and clear the ground for their seedlings, and they have outlasted ice ages, droughts, and empires by simply standing still and growing. Walk the Congress Trail through the Giant Forest in the low gold light of late afternoon and stand at the foot of the Sherman; the silence of a sequoia grove is unlike any other quiet. Year-round, though the high road may close in winter snow; loveliest in autumn or after fresh snow on the red bark.

**The Berth.** In the park: Wuksachi Lodge in the Giant Forest area. Gateway: Three Rivers has small inns and cabins (the Gateway Restaurant and Lodge on the river).

**The Galley.** The Peaks Restaurant at Wuksachi; the riverside Gateway in Three Rivers; trail- provisions and a grove picnic; the cafés and the citrus stands of Three Rivers.

> The clearest way into the Universe is through a forest wilderness.
> *John Muir, John of the Mountains*

### Stop 6. The Great Barrier Reef

**Waypoint:** Queensland, Australia

Where the largest living structure breathes underwater. Off the coast of Queensland stretches the Great Barrier Reef, 1,400 miles of coral built by tiny living polyps over some twenty thousand years, home to 1,500 species of fish, 400 kinds of coral, six of the world's seven sea turtle species, and an abundance that has no equal in the sea. To slip beneath the surface here is to enter the densest concentration of life and color on the planet, parrotfish, reef sharks, rays, turtles, the slow drift of the coral gardens. It is also a pilgrimage of urgency: warming and acidifying seas have bleached vast stretches of the reef in recent years, and to dive it now is to witness both the wonder and the wound, a reason to come while the coral still blazes. The southern and central reef off the Whitsundays and Cairns is the usual gateway. Best June through October, the dry season, for the clearest water. Snorkel or dive with a reef-certified, low-impact operator; touch nothing.

**The Berth.** On the islands: Lizard Island or Hayman Island for the luxury reef-edge; qualia on Hamilton Island. Mainland: Cairns and Port Douglas (the boutique Reef House).

**The Galley.** Queensland seafood: barramundi, mud crab, Moreton Bay bugs; the beachfront restaurants of Port Douglas; tropical fruit and a cold beer after the day's diving.

> We won't have a society if we destroy the environment.
> *Margaret Mead*

### Stop 7. The Amazon Rainforest

**Waypoint:** Brazil, Peru & Ecuador

Where a tenth of all life on Earth lives. The Amazon basin holds the largest rainforest on the planet, 2.7 million square miles across nine countries, drained by a river that carries one-fifth of all the fresh water that flows on the surface of the world. It is the single richest reservoir of life anywhere: perhaps ten percent of all known species live here, more kinds of fish in the river than in the entire Atlantic, a square mile of forest holding more tree species than all of North America. To travel it, by riverboat up the Rio Negro from Manaus, or from a jungle lodge in the Peruvian or Ecuadorian headwaters, is to feel the sheer density of life pressing in from every side: the dawn howler-monkey chorus, pink river dolphins, macaws at a clay lick, the green going on without end. It is the other urgent pilgrimage of this trail; the forest is being cleared at a terrible rate, and to stand inside it is to understand exactly what is at stake. Best in the dry season (roughly June to November), when the trails are walkable and the wildlife concentrates along the shrinking water.

**The Berth.** Peru: the Inkaterra Reserva Amazónica or a Tambopata research lodge. Brazil: the Anavilhanas Lodge on the Rio Negro. Ecuador: Napo Wildlife Center.

**The Galley.** Amazonian river cooking: tambaqui and pirarucu fish, heart of palm, açaí, farofa; the lodge kitchens; the riverside markets of Manaus or Iquitos at either end.

> The environment is where we all meet; where all have a mutual interest; it is the one thing all of us share.
> *Lady Bird Johnson*

### Stop 8. The Himalaya & Sagarmatha

**Waypoint:** Nepal

Where the highest mountains on Earth rise. The Himalaya, the youngest and tallest mountain range in the world, still rising as the Indian plate drives under Asia, holds all fourteen of the planet's peaks above eight thousand meters, crowned by Everest, 29,032 feet, which the Nepalis call Sagarmatha, 'forehead of the sky,' and the Tibetans Chomolungma, 'goddess mother of the world.' One need not climb it, the great pilgrimage here is the trek through the Khumbu to Everest Base Camp, or the gentler walk to the monastery at Tengboche at 12,700 feet, where the Buddhist monastery sits against a wall of ice and the prayer flags snap in the wind off the highest mountains on Earth. The Sherpa people, Tibetan Buddhists who have lived in the high valleys for five centuries, are the soul of the range as much as the peaks are. Walk slowly; the altitude demands it, and the slowness is the point. Best in the pre-monsoon spring (March to May) or the clear post- monsoon autumn (late September to November).

**The Berth.** Trekking lodges and teahouses along the Khumbu route; the comfortable Yeti Mountain Home lodges; in Kathmandu at either end: Dwarika's Hotel, a living museum of Newari craft.

**The Galley.** Sherpa and Nepali mountain food: dal bhat (endless and restorative), thukpa, tsampa, yak cheese, sweet milk tea; Dwarika's in Kathmandu for the Newari feast.

> It is not the mountain we conquer, but ourselves.
> *Sir Edmund Hillary*

### Stop 9. The Northern Lights

**Waypoint:** the Arctic, above 66° North

Where the sky itself catches fire. When charged particles from the sun strike the upper atmosphere and spiral down the lines of the Earth's magnetic field, they set the high air aglow in curtains of green and red and violet, the aurora borealis, the northern lights, a thing humans have watched and made myth of for as long as there have been humans in the North. To see it well you must go far north, into the auroral oval that rings the magnetic pole, and wait, in the cold, under a clear dark sky, away from all city light. The great viewing grounds are Norwegian Lapland (Tromsø), Swedish Lapland (Abisko, statistically the clearest sky in the North), Finnish Lapland, Iceland, and the Yukon. There is no guarantee, the aurora comes when it comes, and the waiting in the silence and the dark is part of the pilgrimage. Best from late September to late March, in the long Arctic night, ideally near a solar maximum. Dress as if your life depends on it, and look up.

**The Berth.** Norway: the Lyngen North or a Tromsø design hotel. Sweden: the original Icehotel in Jukkasjärvi, or the Abisko mountain lodge. Finland: the glass igloos of Kakslauttanen for watching the sky from bed.

**The Galley.** Arctic and Sámi cooking: reindeer, Arctic char, cloudberries, the New Nordic table; warming bowls and aquavit by the fire after a night out under the lights.

> The aurora borealis shakes over the vault of heaven its veil of glittering silver, changing now to yellow, now to green, now to red.
> *Fridtjof Nansen, Farthest North*

### Stop 10. Antarctica

**Waypoint:** the bottom of the world

Where the last true wilderness ends the world. Antarctica is the highest, driest, coldest, windiest, and emptiest continent, a landmass larger than Europe buried under ice up to three miles thick that holds seventy percent of the fresh water on Earth, governed by no nation and dedicated by treaty to peace and science. To reach it most pilgrims sail south across the Drake Passage from the tip of South America to the Antarctic Peninsula, two days of the roughest sea on Earth, and emerge into a silence and a scale that nothing prepares you for: tabular icebergs the size of cities, glaciers calving into a mirror sea, penguin colonies a hundred thousand strong, whales surfacing beside the small boat, light that does not behave the way light does anywhere else. It is the closest a traveler can come to seeing the planet as it was before us. Best November to March, the austral summer, when the sea ice opens enough for ships to pass. There is nowhere farther to go. The pilgrimage ends at the bottom of the world, in the silence, where the cathedral was never anything but ice and light.

**The Berth.** Aboard a small expedition ship (Quark, Lindblad/National Geographic, Ponant, or Aurora Expeditions). Fly-cruise options cross the Drake by air from Punta Arenas.

**The Galley.** The expedition ship's table; hot soup and chocolate after the Zodiac landings; a last steak and Malbec in Ushuaia, the southernmost city, at either end.

> We shall not cease from exploration, and the end of all our exploring will be to arrive where we started and know the place for the first time.
> *T. S. Eliot, Four Quartets*

---

## Pilgrimage XI. Toward the House of God

Year-round destinations along the geography of Islam, the faith and the civilization. This trail has two parts, and the distinction is essential. The first is the Hajj and the Umrah themselves, the pilgrimage to Mecca that is the fifth pillar of Islam and an obligation once in a lifetime for every Muslim with the means, performed at the Kaaba, on the plain of Arafat, and across the holy sites of the Hijaz. Mecca and the heart of Medina are open to Muslims only, by the law of Saudi Arabia and the tradition of fourteen centuries, and so those stops here are written for the Muslim pilgrim who will walk them and as a window for every reader who will not. The second part is the wider pilgrimage across the great surviving monuments of Islamic civilization, Jerusalem, Córdoba, Istanbul, Cairo, Samarkand, Konya, which are open to all and which carry the art, science, and devotion of one of the world's great cultures. The Hajj falls in Dhul-Hijjah on the lunar calendar and so moves through the seasons; Umrah may be made year-round. Best paired with Ramadan for the wider sites, when the Muslim world is at its most luminous after dark.

> Labbayka Allāhumma labbayk — Here I am, O God, here I am.
> *the Talbiyah, the pilgrim's call, recited on the road to Mecca*

### Stop 1. The Kaaba & the Masjid al-Haram

**Waypoint:** Mecca, Saudi Arabia (Muslims only)

Where a quarter of humanity turns to pray. In the courtyard of the Masjid al-Haram, the Great Mosque of Mecca, stands the Kaaba, a cube of grey stone draped in the black, gold-embroidered kiswah, the house that Muslims believe Abraham and his son Ishmael raised for the worship of the one God, and the qibla toward which the faithful turn in prayer five times a day. The pilgrim enters in ihram, two seamless white cloths that erase every mark of wealth and rank, and performs the tawaf, circling the Kaaba seven times counterclockwise in a slow human tide; then the sa'i, walking seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwah in memory of Hagar's search for water for her son, and drinks from the well of Zamzam that tradition says sprang up to save them. To stand in that courtyard among two million people from every nation, all in the same white cloth circling the same ancient stone, is the visible image of what the faith means by submission. Entry to Mecca is restricted to Muslims.

**The Berth.** Mecca (for pilgrims): the towers of the Abraj Al Bait overlooking the Haram for the proximity; the many pilgrim hotels of the Ajyad district; most pilgrims travel with an organized Hajj or Umrah group that arranges lodging.

**The Galley.** Meccan and pan-Islamic pilgrim fare: Zamzam water; dates and Arabic coffee (qahwa); rice-and-lamb kabsa and mandi; the food of a hundred nations sold around the Haram, the whole ummah eating together.

> And proclaim to mankind the Hajj. They will come to you on foot and on every lean camel, from every distant mountain pass.
> *the Qur'an, Surah Al-Hajj 22:27*

### Stop 2. Arafat, Mina & Muzdalifah

**Waypoint:** the plains east of Mecca (Muslims only)

Where the pilgrim stands before God. Beyond the rites at the Kaaba, the Hajj proper unfolds across three places in the desert east of Mecca over several days of the month of Dhul-Hijjah. At Mina, the vast tent city, the pilgrims gather; on the ninth day they move to the plain of Arafat and stand from noon to sunset in the wuquf, the standing before God, on and around the Jabal al-Rahmah, the Mount of Mercy, where the Prophet Muhammad delivered his Farewell Sermon, the single rite without which the Hajj is not valid. After sunset they travel to Muzdalifah and sleep under the open sky, gathering pebbles. Then back to Mina for the stoning of the Jamarat, three pillars marking where Abraham rejected the devil's temptation, and the sacrifice of Eid al-Adha, the festival shared by the whole Muslim world. The standing at Arafat is a foretaste of the Day of Judgment: every pilgrim in white, every distinction erased, the whole of humanity before God. These sites lie within the restricted pilgrimage zone.

**The Berth.** Mina (for pilgrims): the fixed tent encampments assigned by Hajj group, air- conditioned in the modern era; the standing at Arafat and the night at Muzdalifah are spent largely in the open, as the rite requires.

**The Galley.** Simple provisioned meals within the Hajj logistics; the sacrificial meat of Eid al-Adha shared and distributed to the poor; water and dates through the long days of standing and prayer in the heat.

> There is no day on which God frees more servants from the Fire than the Day of Arafat.
> *the Prophet Muhammad, Hadith (Sahih Muslim)*

### Stop 3. The Prophet's Mosque

**Waypoint:** Medina, Saudi Arabia (central area, Muslims only)

Where the Prophet is buried. In Medina, the city that took in the Prophet Muhammad when Mecca cast him out, the Hijra of 622 that begins the Muslim calendar, stands the Masjid an-Nabawi, the Prophet's Mosque, which he himself helped to build and beneath whose green dome he is buried alongside the first two caliphs. Within it lies the Rawdah, the space between the Prophet's tomb and his pulpit that he called 'a garden from the gardens of Paradise,' where pilgrims press to pray. Visiting Medina is not a required part of the Hajj, but few pilgrims who have come so far do not make the journey. Beyond the mosque lie the Quba Mosque, the first mosque built in Islam, and the slope of Mount Uhud, where the early Muslim community fought one of its defining battles. The mosque and the tomb at the center of Medina are open to Muslims only; the wider city, in part, is more accessible. Pray in the Rawdah if you can reach it.

**The Berth.** Medina (for pilgrims): the hotels ringing the Masjid an-Nabawi for the dawn-prayer proximity; the Dar Al Taqwa and the Anwar Al Madinah Mövenpick among the closest; most arrive with the same group that organized the Mecca rites.

**The Galley.** Medinan dates, the finest in the world (the ajwa above all, the Prophet's own favorite); Hijazi cooking; the communal iftar meals laid out on the mosque carpets in Ramadan, stranger feeding stranger the length of the hall.

> Whoever visits me after my death is as if he had visited me in my life.
> *the Prophet Muhammad, Hadith*

### Stop 4. The Dome of the Rock & Al-Aqsa

**Waypoint:** Jerusalem

Where the Night Journey reached its height, and the one great sanctuary open to the traveler. On the Haram al-Sharif, the Noble Sanctuary, in the Old City of Jerusalem stands the Dome of the Rock, completed in 691, its golden dome over the rock from which Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad ascended through the heavens on the Night Journey, the Isra and Mi'raj, and one of the oldest and most beautiful works of Islamic architecture on Earth. Beside it stands the Al-Aqsa Mosque, the 'farthest mosque' named in the Qur'an, the original qibla toward which the first Muslims prayed before the direction turned to Mecca. The whole platform is sacred ground to three faiths and the most contested holy site in the world; access depends on the security and political situation, and non-Muslims are admitted only at restricted hours and not into the mosques. Stand in the Old City where Islam, Judaism, and Christianity press against one another within a few hundred meters, and feel the weight.

**The Berth.** Jerusalem: the American Colony Hotel in a 19th-century pasha's palace; the King David for the grand; or a guesthouse in the Old City's Muslim or Christian Quarter for the immersion.

**The Galley.** Jerusalem mixed-grill (meorav) and hummus at the Old City institutions; knafeh, the cheese-and-syrup pastry, at its best near Damascus Gate; za'atar manakish from a bakery at dawn; mint tea anywhere in the souq.

> Glory to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque.
> *the Qur'an, Surah Al-Isra 17:1*

### Stop 5. The Great Mosque of Córdoba

**Waypoint:** Andalusia, Spain

Where Islam built its western masterpiece. In Córdoba, capital of Al-Andalus when it was the most cultured city in Europe, stands the Mezquita, the Great Mosque begun in 785, its prayer hall a forest of 856 columns carrying red-and-white double horseshoe arches that seem to recede without end, one of the most beautiful interiors ever built by human hands. For three centuries Córdoba under the Umayyads was a place where Muslim, Jewish, and Christian scholars translated the Greeks, advanced medicine and mathematics, and lit a lamp of learning while much of Europe sat in the dark. After the Reconquista a cathedral was raised in the mosque's center, and the building stands today as both, a Catholic cathedral inside an Islamic mosque, the layered history visible in every stone. Walk the columned hall toward the mihrab with its golden Byzantine mosaics. Pair with the Alhambra in Granada, the Moorish palace-fortress that is the other great survival of Al-Andalus.

**The Berth.** Córdoba: the Balcón de Córdoba in a restored mansion near the Mezquita; the Hospes Palacio del Bailío. Granada: the Parador de Granada inside the Alhambra grounds; the boutique Casa Morisca.

**The Galley.** Córdoba: salmorejo (the thick chilled tomato cream) and rabo de toro at Bodegas Campos; Andalusian tapas in the Judería. Granada: free tapas with every drink, the last city in Spain to keep the custom.

> The world is divided into men who have wit and no religion and men who have religion and no wit.
> *Averroës (Ibn Rushd) of Córdoba*

### Stop 6. The Mosques of Istanbul

**Waypoint:** Turkey

Where two empires meet under one dome. Istanbul, the city astride Europe and Asia that was Byzantine Constantinople before it became the Ottoman capital, holds the supreme architecture of the Islamic east. The Hagia Sophia, raised by Justinian in 537 as the greatest church in Christendom, became a mosque at the Ottoman conquest of 1453, then a museum, and is a mosque again, its vast dome a thousand years ahead of its time. Across the square the Sultanahmet, the Blue Mosque, answers it with six minarets and a cascade of domes lined in twenty thousand Iznik tiles. Up the hill, the Süleymaniye, the masterpiece of the great architect Sinan, holds the city's finest proportions and the tombs of Süleyman the Magnificent and his beloved Roxelana. Spend the call to prayer on a rooftop at dusk as the muezzins answer one another across the skyline and the gulls turn over the Golden Horn. Pair with the Topkapı Palace and the Grand Bazaar below.

**The Berth.** Istanbul: the Four Seasons Sultanahmet in a former prison steps from the Blue Mosque; the Çırağan Palace Kempinski on the Bosphorus for the grand; a boutique hotel in Sultanahmet for the call-to-prayer dawn.

**The Galley.** Istanbul: kebab and meze at a Sultanahmet ocakbaşı; fresh fish under the Galata Bridge; börek and simit from the street; Turkish coffee and baklava at a historic çay bahçesi; a long Ottoman-palace dinner at Asitane.

> Beauty and the love of beauty are the marks of a believing heart.
> *attributed to Mimar Sinan, the Ottoman master architect*

### Stop 7. Islamic Cairo

**Waypoint:** Egypt

Where a thousand minarets crowd the sky. Cairo holds the densest concentration of medieval Islamic architecture anywhere on Earth, a UNESCO World Heritage quarter of mosques, madrasas, fountains, and gates layered across a thousand years. Al-Azhar, founded in 970, is among the oldest universities in the world and still the foremost seat of Sunni learning. The Mosque of Ibn Tulun, from 879, is the oldest in the city in its original form, its spiral minaret and vast austere courtyard a thing of perfect calm. The Sultan Hassan mosque-madrasa is a mountain of stone; the Citadel of Saladin crowns the skyline with the alabaster Mosque of Muhammad Ali. Walk the medieval spine of al-Mu'izz Street at night when the monuments are lit; lose an afternoon in the Khan el-Khalili bazaar over mint tea and shisha. Pair, of course, with the Pyramids at Giza on the city's edge, older than Islam by three thousand years and visible from the minarets.

**The Berth.** Cairo: the Marriott Mena House under the Pyramids; the historic Windsor Hotel downtown (a former royal bathhouse); the new St. Regis on the Nile corniche.

**The Galley.** Cairo: koshary (the lentil-rice-pasta national dish) at Abou Tarek; grilled pigeon and molokhia; ful and ta'amiya for breakfast; Om Ali for dessert; mint tea and shisha in the Khan el-Khalili at El Fishawy, open since 1773.

> He who does not thank people does not thank God.
> *the Prophet Muhammad, Hadith*

### Stop 8. Samarkand & the Registan

**Waypoint:** Uzbekistan, the Silk Road

Where the Silk Road blazes turquoise. Samarkand, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth and the jewel of the Silk Road, holds in the Registan the most magnificent public square of the Islamic world: three madrasas facing one another across an open plaza, their towering portals and ribbed domes sheathed in turquoise and cobalt tile, raised under Timur and his astronomer-king grandson Ulugh Beg in the 14th and 15th centuries. Nearby, the Gur-e-Amir holds Timur's tomb under a fluted azure dome, and the Shah-i-Zinda is an avenue of tiled mausoleums of heart-stopping color. Ulugh Beg's observatory, where he charted the stars with an accuracy unmatched for two centuries, sits on the city's edge, a reminder that this was a capital of science as well as faith. The blue of Samarkand, against the brown plain and the hard blue sky, is one of the things a traveler should see once before they die.

**The Berth.** Samarkand: the Hotel Registan Plaza for the comfortable; boutique courtyard guesthouses in the old town near the Registan; the modern Silk Road Samarkand resort complex.

**The Galley.** Uzbek: plov (the saffron rice-and-lamb pilaf, cooked by the cauldron); samsa baked in a tandoor; lepyoshka bread stamped and blistered; shashlik; green tea and dried apricots and the famous Samarkand non.

> Only the stars know how far my power and glory reached.
> *attributed to Timur (Tamerlane), Samarkand*

### Stop 9. Konya & the Tomb of Rumi

**Waypoint:** Anatolia, Turkey

Where the poet of love is buried. In Konya, on the Anatolian plateau, lies the tomb of Jalāl ad-Dīn Rūmī, the 13th-century mystic whose poetry of divine love is, eight hundred years on, among the most widely read in the world. The Mevlâna Museum, under its fluted green tower, was the lodge of the Mevlevi order Rumi inspired, the 'whirling dervishes' whose turning dance, the sema, is a moving meditation in which the dancer spins with one palm raised to heaven and one turned to earth, a conduit between them. Rumi called death his wedding night, the union at last with the divine beloved; pilgrims of every faith and none come to his tomb, drawn by verse that speaks past every border. Time a visit to the Şeb-i Arus festival in December, the anniversary of his death, when the sema is performed in his honor. Sit in the quiet of the tomb chamber among the green-turbaned sarcophagi and the scent of rosewater, and listen.

**The Berth.** Konya: the boutique Hich Hotel in a restored old-town house near the Mevlâna; the Bayır Diamond for the modern comfort; simple pilgrim guesthouses around the shrine.

**The Galley.** Konya: etli ekmek (the long thin Konya flatbread with meat); fırın kebabı, the slow-oven lamb; höşmerim and saffron pilaf; a sober, conservative city where the pleasures are of the table and the spirit, not the glass.

> Come, come, whoever you are. Wanderer, worshipper, lover of leaving, it doesn't matter. Ours is not a caravan of despair.
> *Jalāl ad-Dīn Rūmī*

### Stop 10. The Great Mosque of Kairouan

**Waypoint:** Tunisia

Where Islam first took root in the West. Kairouan, founded in 670, was the first Muslim city in North Africa and the base from which Islam spread across the Maghreb and into Spain; tradition counts it the fourth holiest city in Islam, and seven pilgrimages here were once held to equal one to Mecca. Its Great Mosque, the Mosque of Uqba, is one of the oldest and most important in the Muslim world, the prototype from which the mosques of the western Islamic lands descend: a vast walled courtyard, a forest of columns salvaged from Roman and Byzantine ruins, and a square minaret, the oldest standing minaret on Earth, that set the form for every minaret of the Maghreb and Al-Andalus, including Córdoba. The old walled medina around it, with its whitewashed houses and its makroudh (date pastry) shops, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. End the pilgrimage here, at the western root of the faith, where the trail that began at the Kaaba completes its arc across the whole world the call to prayer reaches.

**The Berth.** Kairouan: the Hotel La Kasbah inside a restored fortress; simple medina guesthouses for the immersion. Or base in Tunis (two hours north) and day-trip: the Dar El Jeld Hotel in a historic mansion.

**The Galley.** Tunisian: couscous (the Friday dish, at its finest here); brik à l'oeuf, the crisp egg pastry; harissa with everything; Kairouan's famous makroudh, the semolina- and-date sweet; mint tea with pine nuts.

> Say: Are those who know equal to those who do not know?
> *the Qur'an, Surah Az-Zumar 39:9*

---

## Pilgrimage XII. Where the Rivers Are Holy

Year-round destinations along the sacred geography of Hinduism, the oldest living pilgrimage tradition on Earth, where the act of travel to a holy place, the tirtha-yatra, the crossing to a 'ford' between this world and the divine, is older than scripture itself. Anchored to the canonical frameworks the faith has used for millennia: the Sapta Puri, the seven cities that grant moksha, liberation from the cycle of rebirth; the Char Dham, the four abodes at the cardinal points of India; the holy rivers and the Kumbh Mela that gathers on their banks; and the great temple cities of the Dravidian south. Most temple complexes welcome all respectful visitors, though a few inner sanctums are reserved for Hindus; dress modestly, remove your shoes, and move with the crowd. The pilgrim seasons follow the festivals and the Himalayan thaw. Best paired with Diwali (the festival of lights, autumn), Maha Shivaratri (the great night of Shiva, late winter), or the Kumbh itself, the largest gathering of human beings that has ever assembled anywhere on Earth.

> Lead me from the unreal to the real, from darkness to light, from death to immortality.
> *the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, the Pavamana mantra*

### Stop 1. Varanasi

**Waypoint:** Uttar Pradesh, on the Ganges

Where Hindus come to die and be freed. Varanasi, also Kashi, 'the City of Light,' and Banaras, is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth and the holiest place in the Hindu world, the city of Shiva, where it is believed that to die is to attain moksha and break the cycle of rebirth forever. Along the western bank, eighty-odd stone ghats descend to the Ganges; at dawn the pilgrims wade in to bathe in the sacred river while the sun rises over the far bank, and at the Dashashwamedh Ghat each evening the Ganga Aarti is performed with fire and conch and bell. At the Manikarnika Ghat the cremation fires never go out, have not gone out in centuries, and the dead are carried down through the lanes to be burned at the river's edge and returned to it. The Kashi Vishwanath Temple, one of the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva, stands at the heart of the old city. Take a boat at first light. Watch the city wake to the river. Nowhere on Earth holds life and death so close together, so calmly.

**The Berth.** Varanasi: the BrijRama Palace on Darbhanga Ghat (a restored riverside palace); the Taj Ganges; or a simple guesthouse in the old lanes for the immersion in the heart of the city.

**The Galley.** Banarasi vegetarian: kachori-sabzi and jalebi at dawn; the chaat at Kashi Chat Bhandar; the famous Banarasi paan to finish; thandai, the spiced milk drink, along the ghats; pure vegetarian throughout the holy city.

> In the city of Shiva, even death is a blessing.
> *the tradition of Kashi*

### Stop 2. The Triveni Sangam & the Kumbh Mela

**Waypoint:** Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh

Where the largest gathering of humanity bathes. At Prayagraj, called Tirtharaj, the 'king of pilgrimage places,' three rivers meet: the green Yamuna, the brown Ganga, and the invisible, mythical Saraswati, said to flow underground to join them, the Triveni Sangam, the most sacred confluence in Hinduism.
