Tradition holds that during the churning of the cosmic ocean, drops of amrit, the nectar of immortality, fell at four places, and the Kumbh Mela rotates among them, Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain, and Nashik, on a twelve-year cycle set by the planets. When the Kumbh comes to Prayagraj it draws the single greatest assembly of human beings ever gathered anywhere: the Maha Kumbh of 2025 recorded hundreds of millions of pilgrims over six weeks, the naked ash-smeared naga sadhus leading the processions to the water at the most auspicious hour. To bathe at the Sangam is believed to wash away sin and liberate one's ancestors. Take a boat to the exact confluence and watch the two visible rivers run side by side, brown and green, before they merge.

**The Berth.** Prayagraj: the boutique tented camps erected for the Kumbh and Magh Mela seasons (the most atmospheric way to stay); the Kanha Shyam hotel in town for the year-round comfort.

**The Galley.** Prayagraji and Awadhi vegetarian: puri-sabzi and samosa; the local sweets; kachori along the ghat lanes; the simple satvik food of the pilgrim camps, eaten cross-legged on the riverbank.

> At the confluence of the rivers, the sins of a lifetime dissolve.
> *the tradition of the Kumbh*

### Stop 3. Haridwar & Rishikesh

**Waypoint:** Uttarakhand, where the Ganges leaves the mountains

Where the Ganges meets the plains. At Haridwar, 'the gateway to God,' the Ganges emerges from the Himalaya onto the plains of northern India, one of the Sapta Puri and one of the four Kumbh Mela cities. Each evening at the Har Ki Pauri ghat the Ganga Aarti sends hundreds of leaf-boats of flame floating down the river in the dark, a sight that draws pilgrims from across the subcontinent. A few miles upstream lies Rishikesh, the 'yoga capital of the world,' where the river runs clear and green between forested hills, where the great ashrams sit along the banks (the Beatles famously came to the Maharishi's ashram in 1968), and where the suspension bridges of Lakshman Jhula and Ram Jhula carry sadhus, cows, and seekers across the holy water. This is the place to learn to sit, to breathe, to begin. Go in the cool months; rise for the dawn aarti; let the river, just down from the snows, run cold over your hands.

**The Berth.** Rishikesh: Ananda in the Himalayas (the grand wellness retreat in a maharaja's palace); the riverside Aloha on the Ganges; or an ashram stay (Parmarth Niketan) for the authentic discipline.

**The Galley.** Strictly vegetarian and alcohol-free in both holy towns: the satvik thali; chotiwala in Rishikesh; fresh fruit and lassi; German Bakery cafes along the Rishikesh banks for the traveler's respite; the ashram's own simple meals.

> The Ganga, Shiva's own river, fallen from heaven and caught in his hair.
> *the Puranas*

### Stop 4. Kedarnath & the Himalayan Char Dham

**Waypoint:** Garhwal Himalaya, Uttarakhand

Where the gods dwell in the high snows. In the high Garhwal Himalaya lie the Chota Char Dham, the four Himalayan shrines that are among the most arduous and revered pilgrimages in Hinduism: Yamunotri and Gangotri, the sources of the Yamuna and Ganga; Kedarnath, one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, where a stone temple to Shiva stands at 3,580 meters below a great peak, reached by a steep fourteen-kilometer trek (or by pony, palki, or now helicopter); and Badrinath, sacred to Vishnu, one of the original Char Dham of all India. These shrines open only from roughly late April to November, closing under the winter snows when the deity is symbolically carried down to the valley. In 2013 a catastrophic flood devastated Kedarnath, sparing the temple itself, which the faithful read as the god's own protection. To stand at Kedarnath in the thin cold air, the snow peaks close above and the valley falling away below, is to understand why the mountains themselves are held to be gods.

**The Berth.** The shrine towns offer simple pilgrim lodging (GMVN rest houses; basic guesthouses at Kedarnath, Badrinath, Gangotri). Base lower down at Ananda in the Himalayas, or the comfortable hotels of Joshimath and Guptkashi.

**The Galley.** Simple Garhwali pilgrim fare: hot dal and rice, aloo-puri, the warming kadha and chai at the trail huts; the prasad of the temples; little is sold high up, so the hot food at altitude is its own reward.

> The Himalaya is the abode of the gods; in a hundred ages you could not tell of its glories.
> *the Skanda Purana*

### Stop 5. Tirupati

**Waypoint:** Andhra Pradesh

Where a hundred thousand pilgrims come each day. On the seven hills of Tirumala in Andhra Pradesh stands the Venkateswara Temple, sacred to a form of Vishnu, the richest and most visited place of worship anywhere in the world, drawing as many as a hundred thousand pilgrims on an ordinary day and far more on festival days. Pilgrims climb the hill (many on foot, some prostrating the whole way), wait hours in the serpentine queues of the darshan, and offer their hair, the ritual tonsure that sends hundreds of tons of human hair to the temple each year, a gesture of surrendering vanity and ego to the god. The deity is adorned in gold and jewels; the laddu prasadam handed out at Tirupati is so prized it carries a geographical trademark. To witness the sheer scale of devotion here, the human tide moving through the temple day and night without pause, is to grasp the living force of Hinduism as a religion of more than a billion souls.

**The Berth.** Tirupati: the temple trust (TTD) operates extensive pilgrim accommodation on the hill at Tirumala; in Tirupati town below, the Marasa Sarovar Premiere and the Taj-managed properties for the comfortable stay.

**The Galley.** The famous Tirupati laddu, the trademarked temple prasadam; pure-vegetarian South Indian: dosa, idli, vada, sambar; the free annadanam meals served to pilgrims by the temple; filter coffee in the town below.

> Abandon all varieties of dharma and surrender unto Me alone; I shall deliver you from all sins. Do not fear.
> *the Bhagavad Gita 18.66*

### Stop 6. Madurai & the Meenakshi Temple

**Waypoint:** Tamil Nadu

Where the goddess marries her god each night. In Madurai, one of the oldest cities in India, rises the Meenakshi Amman Temple, the supreme example of South Indian temple architecture, a vast walled complex sacred to the goddess Meenakshi (a form of Parvati) and her consort Sundareshwarar (Shiva). Its fourteen gopurams, the towering pyramidal gate-towers, the tallest nearly fifty meters, are encrusted from base to summit with thousands of brightly painted carved figures of gods, demons, and beasts, a riot of color visible across the city. Inside lie the Hall of a Thousand Pillars, the golden lotus tank, and the inner sanctums (the innermost reserved for Hindus). Each night the image of Sundareshwarar is carried in procession to Meenakshi's chamber in a tender nightly rite of the divine marriage. Come for the evening ceremony, walk the pillared halls by lamplight, and look up at the gopurams at dusk as the colors deepen.

**The Berth.** Madurai: the Heritage Madurai (a former club designed by a noted architect); the Gateway Hotel Pasumalai on a hill above the city; or a simple hotel near the temple for the dawn and dusk ceremonies.

**The Galley.** Madurai is a great food city: the jigarthanda (a cold almond-and-milk drink); kari dosa and the famous non-vegetarian Madurai cooking; the banana-leaf vegetarian meals; filter coffee and South Indian breakfast everywhere.

> The goddess and her city are one; to enter Madurai is to enter her.
> *the Tamil tradition*

### Stop 7. Rameswaram

**Waypoint:** Tamil Nadu, the southern point of the Char Dham

Where Rama crossed to Lanka. On a slender island off the southeastern tip of India, reached by the soaring Pamban bridge over a turquoise sea, Rameswaram is the southern abode of the all-India Char Dham and one of the holiest sites of Shiva, where, the Ramayana tells, the god-prince Rama worshipped Shiva before crossing the sea to Lanka to rescue Sita, and where the chain of shoals running toward Sri Lanka is still called Rama's Bridge. The Ramanathaswamy Temple holds the longest temple corridor in the world, a thousand-plus carved pillars running in seemingly endless perspective, and twenty-two sacred wells (tirthas) within its walls, at each of which pilgrims are doused with a bucket of holy water in turn, walking the circuit soaking wet and joyful. Pilgrims come to unite the north and south of the sacred land, bringing Ganges water from Varanasi to offer here at the very opposite end of India. Walk the great corridor at dawn.

**The Berth.** Rameswaram: the Hyatt Place for the modern comfort; the Daiwik Hotels near the temple built for pilgrims; simpler lodges by the shore for the immersion in the island's quiet.

**The Galley.** Pure-vegetarian temple-town fare: South Indian thali on banana leaf; idli, dosa, pongal; fresh coconut water from the shore; the simple satvik meals of a holy island at the end of the land.

> Having worshipped Shiva, Rama crossed the sea.
> *the Ramayana*

### Stop 8. Puri & the Jagannath Temple

**Waypoint:** Odisha, the eastern Char Dham

Where the Lord of the Universe rides out. On the Bay of Bengal coast of Odisha, Puri is the eastern abode of the Char Dham, home to the great Jagannath Temple, sacred to Jagannath, 'Lord of the Universe,' a form of Vishnu worshipped here in a strange and beloved wooden image with great round eyes, carved anew every dozen years or so. Each summer the temple stages the Rath Yatra, the chariot festival, in which the deities are placed in three colossal wooden chariots, the largest over thirteen meters tall, and hauled through the streets by thousands of devotees on ropes, the festival that gave the English language the word 'juggernaut.' To pull the rope, or even to touch it, is held to be deeply blessed. The temple's inner precinct is reserved for Hindus, but the Rath Yatra spills into the public streets where all may witness it. The kitchen here is said to be the largest in the world, feeding tens of thousands daily with the mahaprasad offered to the god.

**The Berth.** Puri: the heritage Mayfair Heritage by the sea; the Chanakya BNR (a colonial railway hotel); or a simple sea-facing guesthouse on the long beach.

**The Galley.** The Jagannath mahaprasad, cooked in earthen pots and sold at the Ananda Bazaar beside the temple, the largest temple kitchen on Earth; Odia vegetarian; fresh seafood on the beach outside the holy precinct; chhena poda, the burnt-cheese sweet.

> He is the Lord of the Universe, and He rides out to meet His people.
> *the tradition of Jagannath*

### Stop 9. Dwarka & Somnath

**Waypoint:** Gujarat, the western Char Dham

Where Krishna's kingdom sank beneath the sea. On the far western tip of Gujarat, where the land runs out into the Arabian Sea, lies Dwarka, the western abode of the Char Dham and one of the Sapta Puri, revered as the kingdom of Krishna, the city he is said to have built and ruled, and which tradition holds the sea reclaimed after his death (marine archaeologists have indeed found submerged structures offshore). The Dwarkadhish Temple, its tall flag changing five times a day, rises above the confluence of the Gomti river and the sea. Down the coast stands Somnath, the first of the twelve Jyotirlingas, the temple of Shiva that was sacked and rebuilt again and again across a thousand years of invasion and stands today restored, facing the open ocean with nothing between it and Antarctica. Stand at Somnath at sunset where the temple meets the sea, and feel the deep endurance of a faith that has been broken and has rebuilt itself, over and over, for longer than almost any other on Earth.

**The Berth.** Dwarka: the Hotel Dwarka Residency and pilgrim hotels near the temple. Somnath: the Lords Inn and the Leela-managed comfort near the shore; or the Gujarat tourism lodges along the Saurashtra coast.

**The Galley.** Gujarati vegetarian thali, the great unlimited feast (dhokla, thepla, undhiyu, the sweet-and-savory balance); fresh from the temple-town kitchens; chaas (buttermilk) and jalebi-fafda; pure-vegetarian throughout this devout coast.

> Whenever righteousness declines, I manifest Myself, age after age.
> *Krishna, the Bhagavad Gita*

### Stop 10. Badrinath

**Waypoint:** Garhwal Himalaya, the northern Char Dham

The northern abode, where the trail returns to the mountains. High in the Garhwal Himalaya, at 3,300 meters on the bank of the Alaknanda river beneath the snow pyramid of Nilkanth, stands Badrinath, the northern abode of the original all-India Char Dham and one of the holiest shrines of Vishnu. The brightly painted temple, set against the bare high peaks, marks the place where, the tradition says, Vishnu meditated for an age while the goddess Lakshmi sheltered him as a badari (jujube) tree. Before the temple bubbles the Tapt Kund, a hot spring in which pilgrims bathe in the freezing mountain air before darshan. Beyond the village the road ends at Mana, the last settlement before the Tibetan frontier. To complete the Char Dham, north and south, east and west, the snows and the sea, is to have drawn a sacred circle around the whole of India, and to end it here, where the mountains touch the sky, is to end the pilgrimage at the roof of the holy land.

**The Berth.** Badrinath: simple pilgrim guesthouses and GMVN rest houses in the temple village; the comfortable hotels of Joshimath two hours below; the shrine is open only late April to November, closed under the winter snows.

**The Galley.** Hot satvik pilgrim food at altitude: dal, rice, rajma, aloo; the prasad of the temple; chai and warming kadha against the cold; the simple, sustaining meals of the high Himalayan shrines.

> From the unreal lead me to the real; this is the prayer at the journey's end.
> *the Upaniṣads*

---

## Pilgrimage XIII. By the Waters of Memory

Year-round destinations along the sacred geography of the Jewish people, whose pilgrimage tradition is the oldest of the three Abrahamic faiths. The Torah commands the aliyah la-regel, the 'ascent on foot,' three times a year on the Shalosh Regalim, the pilgrimage festivals of Pesach, Shavuot, and Sukkot, when all Israel was to go up to the Temple in Jerusalem. The Temple has lain in ruins since the Romans destroyed it in 70 CE, and the national pilgrimage ended with it, but the longing never did: 'next year in Jerusalem' has closed the Passover seder and the Yom Kippur fast for two thousand years of exile. This trail follows that longing, from the surviving Western Wall of the Temple, through the patriarchal and prophetic sites of the Land of Israel, to the mystical cities of the Galilee, and out to the great memory-places of the Diaspora where Jewish life flourished, was nearly extinguished, and endures. Most sites welcome respectful visitors; dress modestly, cover the head at holy places, observe the Sabbath rhythms. Best paired with the festivals themselves, when the Wall fills as it has not since the Temple stood.

> If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its cunning.
> *Psalm 137*

### Stop 1. The Western Wall & the Temple Mount

**Waypoint:** Jerusalem

Where Jews have prayed for two thousand years. The Western Wall, the Kotel, is the last surviving remnant of the retaining wall that Herod built around the Second Temple, the great limestone courses standing where the Temple itself once rose on the Mount above, the single most sacred site in Judaism. Jews have long come to its stones to pray, to weep (the old name was the Wailing Wall), and to press written prayers into its cracks; the plaza fills to overflowing on the festivals and at the priestly blessing of Passover and Sukkot. Above stands the Temple Mount, Har HaBayit, the site of both Temples and the place where Abraham bound Isaac, now occupied by the Dome of the Rock and Al-Aqsa and sacred to two faiths at once; Jewish religious law and the political reality both restrict Jewish prayer on the Mount itself. Approach the Wall and place your hand on the cool stone worn smooth by twenty centuries of hands.

**The Berth.** Jerusalem: the King David Hotel, the grande dame above the Old City; the Waldorf Astoria in a restored 1920s landmark; the boutique Mamilla overlooking the Jaffa Gate; or a guesthouse in the Jewish Quarter for the Sabbath within the walls.

**The Galley.** Jerusalem: hummus at Lina in the Old City; the Machane Yehuda market stalls; Mahneyuda and Machneyuda for the modern Israeli; challah and rugelach from Marzipan bakery on Friday; everything closes for Shabbat, so plan around it.

> Our feet are standing within thy gates, O Jerusalem.
> *Psalm 122*

### Stop 2. The City of David & the Old City

**Waypoint:** Jerusalem

Where the story begins. Below the Old City walls, on the narrow ridge south of the Temple Mount, lies the City of David, the original Jerusalem that King David captured and made his capital three thousand years ago, now one of the most active archaeological sites on Earth, where you can walk Hezekiah's Tunnel, hewn through solid rock in the 8th century BCE to carry the Gihon spring's water inside the walls before an Assyrian siege, the water still flowing knee-deep through the dark. Above, the Old City's Jewish Quarter, rebuilt after 1967, holds the restored Hurva Synagogue and the Cardo, the colonnaded Roman main street excavated beneath the modern lanes. The whole compressed square kilometer holds layer upon layer, Canaanite, Israelite, Babylonian, Roman, Byzantine, Crusader, Ottoman, the most fought-over ground in human history. Walk the ramparts at dusk; descend into the tunnels by day. History here is not in a museum. You are standing on it, and under it, and inside it.

**The Berth.** Jerusalem: the King David Hotel; the Waldorf Astoria; the boutique Mamilla by the Jaffa Gate; or the Sephardic House and other guesthouses inside the Old City for the fullest immersion in the Jewish Quarter.

**The Galley.** Jerusalem: the Old City hummus institutions; Machane Yehuda by day and night; Eucalyptus for biblical-ingredient cooking near the Old City wall; kanafeh and baklava in the Muslim Quarter; the Friday market crush before Shabbat.

> Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion.
> *Psalm 48*

### Stop 3. Hebron & the Cave of the Patriarchs

**Waypoint:** the West Bank

Where the patriarchs are buried. At Hebron stands the Cave of the Patriarchs, the Me'arat HaMachpelah, the burial place that the Book of Genesis records Abraham buying for four hundred shekels of silver as a tomb for Sarah, and where tradition holds the three patriarchs and matriarchs lie: Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah. The massive enclosure over the cave was built by Herod the Great, the same king who raised the Temple, and its stonework is the only Herodian building that still stands intact and in use anywhere. The site is holy to Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike, and is now divided between a synagogue and a mosque under heavy security; the political situation in Hebron is tense and should be checked carefully before any visit. To stand at the tomb of Abraham, the shared father of all three Abrahamic faiths, is to stand at the genealogical root of half the religious world.

**The Berth.** Most visit Hebron as a guided day trip from Jerusalem (an hour south) given the security situation. Base in Jerusalem (the King David, the Mamilla) or, for the biblical landscape, the Gush Etzion guesthouses on the way south.

**The Galley.** Hebron is famed for its grapes, glass, and pottery; simple Palestinian fare, hummus and falafel and fresh bread, in the city; most pilgrims carry provisions and return to Jerusalem to dine, around the day trip.

> And the field, and the cave that is therein, were made sure unto Abraham for a possession of a burying place.
> *Genesis 23*

### Stop 4. Safed

**Waypoint:** Upper Galilee

Where the Kabbalah came to flower. High in the hills of the Upper Galilee, Safed is the highest city in Israel and one of its four holy cities, and the place where, in the 16th century, the great mystics gathered to create the flowering of the Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition. Here Rabbi Isaac Luria, the Ari, taught his cosmology of the shattering and repair of the world, tikkun olam; here Rabbi Joseph Karo compiled the Shulchan Aruch, the code of Jewish law still followed today; here the hymn Lecha Dodi, sung in synagogues across the world to welcome the Sabbath bride, was written. The old city is a warren of cobbled lanes, ancient blue-painted synagogues (the Ari and the Abuhav among them), and the artists' quarter that has drawn painters and seekers for generations. The mountain air is clear and the light is famous. Come for Shabbat, when the whole town turns inward and the candles are lit and the streets fall silent.

**The Berth.** Safed: the boutique Artist Quarter guesthouses (Ruth Rimonim in a historic building); Villa Galilee for the view; the many tzimmer (B&B) rooms of the old city, especially atmospheric over Shabbat.

**The Galley.** Galilean and dairy: Safed's famous semi-hard Tzfat cheese; shakshuka and labneh; the bakeries of the old quarter; fresh Galilee produce; the meals begin and end with the Sabbath, planned around the candle-lighting.

> Come, my beloved, to meet the bride; let us welcome the Sabbath.
> *Lecha Dodi, written in Safed*

### Stop 5. Mount Meron & Tiberias

**Waypoint:** Galilee

Where the sages are buried. The Galilee holds the tombs of the great rabbis of the Mishnah and the Talmud, and two sites above all draw the pilgrim. On Mount Meron lies the tomb of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, the 2nd-century sage to whom tradition attributes the Zohar, the foundational text of the Kabbalah; on Lag BaOmer each spring, hundreds of thousands ascend the mountain for the hillula, a night of bonfires, song, and dancing that is among the largest gatherings in Israel. Down on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, the holy city of Tiberias holds the tombs of Maimonides (the Rambam, the greatest of medieval Jewish philosophers), Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai, who saved Judaism itself by founding the academy at Yavne after the Temple fell. To visit the graves of the tzaddikim, the righteous, and to pray there, is one of the oldest and most enduring Jewish devotions. Light a candle. Leave a stone, the visitor's mark, on the tomb.

**The Berth.** Tiberias: the Scots Hotel on the Galilee shore (a restored 19th-century hospice); the Setai Sea of Galilee for the grand; kibbutz guesthouses around the lake (Ginosar) for the landscape of the Galilee.

**The Galley.** Galilee: the St. Peter's fish (tilapia) fresh from the lake; Decks restaurant on the Tiberias shore; Galilean mezze; the produce and wine of the Golan and Upper Galilee; fish grilled by the water at sunset.

> Who is wise? One who learns from every person.
> *Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers*

### Stop 6. Masada

**Waypoint:** the Judean Desert, by the Dead Sea

Where the last stand was made. On a high isolated plateau above the Dead Sea, ringed by sheer cliffs, stand the ruins of Masada, Herod's mountain fortress-palace, where, after the fall of Jerusalem in 70 CE, a community of Jewish rebels held out against the Roman Tenth Legion in a siege that ended, the historian Josephus tells, when the defenders chose death over slavery and took their own lives rather than be captured, nearly a thousand of them, on the night before the wall was breached. Whether one reads it as tragedy, as heroism, or as both, Masada became a symbol of Jewish resistance and endurance; for years Israeli soldiers were sworn in here with the vow 'Masada shall not fall again.' Climb the Snake Path before dawn (or take the cable car) to stand on the summit as the sun rises over the Dead Sea and the mountains of Moab beyond, the light coming up over the lowest place on Earth. Combine with a float in the Dead Sea and the oasis of Ein Gedi nearby.

**The Berth.** Dead Sea: the spa hotels of Ein Bokek (the Herods, the Isrotel) on the shore; the Ein Gedi kibbutz guesthouse in its botanical garden; or base in Jerusalem and make the dawn ascent as a day trip.

**The Galley.** Dead Sea resort dining and the kibbutz dining halls; date honey from the desert plantations; the famous Ein Gedi dates and produce; carry water for the climb, and salt nothing, the Dead Sea does that for you.

> Masada shall not fall again.
> *Yitzhak Lamdan, and the oath of the Israeli soldier*

### Stop 7. Yad Vashem

**Waypoint:** Jerusalem

Where the six million are remembered. On the Mount of Remembrance in Jerusalem stands Yad Vashem, the World Holocaust Remembrance Center, the memorial to the six million Jews murdered by Nazi Germany and its collaborators between 1933 and 1945. The name comes from Isaiah, 'a memorial and a name' (yad vashem) for those who would otherwise have none. The Hall of Names holds the testimony pages of millions of victims under a great cone of photographed faces reflected in dark water below; the Children's Memorial remembers the million and a half murdered children in a single candle's flame multiplied endlessly by mirrors into a galaxy of points of light, each a child, while the names are read aloud without end. The Avenue of the Righteous Among the Nations honors the non-Jews who risked everything to save Jewish lives. No pilgrimage through Jewish history can omit this. Go, bear witness, and carry it out with you. This is the weight the whole trail must hold.

**The Berth.** Jerusalem: the King David; the Waldorf Astoria; the Mamilla; the Yad Vashem campus is on the western edge of the city near Mount Herzl, an easy approach from anywhere in Jerusalem.

**The Galley.** This is not a stop to pair with a meal. Eat simply, before or after, in the city; the experience asks for quiet and an empty afternoon around it, not a restaurant recommendation.

> Remember what Amalek did to you. Do not forget.
> *Deuteronomy 25*

### Stop 8. The Jewish Quarter of Prague

**Waypoint:** Bohemia, Czech Republic

Where Ashkenazi Europe still stands. In Prague's Josefov, the old Jewish quarter, stands the densest surviving ensemble of Jewish heritage in Europe. The Old-New Synagogue, completed around 1270, is the oldest active synagogue in Europe, and in its attic, legend says, lies the Golem, the clay man the great Rabbi Judah Loew, the Maharal, is said to have made to protect the community. The Old Jewish Cemetery is a haunting field where, with no room to expand, the dead were buried twelve layers deep over centuries, twelve thousand crooked headstones leaning together under the trees. The quarter survived the Holocaust by a grim irony, the Nazis preserved it as a planned 'museum of an extinct race,' so its synagogues now hold the largest collection of Judaica in Europe, including the children's drawings from the Terezín camp. The Pinkas Synagogue walls are inscribed by hand with the names of 77,297 Bohemian and Moravian Jews murdered in the Shoah. Walk the quarter slowly.

**The Berth.** Prague: the Four Seasons on the river by the Charles Bridge; the boutique Hotel Josef in the Jewish Quarter itself; the Augustine in a former monastery in the Lesser Town across the river.

**The Galley.** Prague: the kosher restaurants of Josefov (King Solomon, Dinitz); Czech-Jewish classics; the cafés of the old town; svíčková and dumplings for the Bohemian; Pilsner where it was born, for those who keep no kosher.

> The whole world is a very narrow bridge; the main thing is not to fear at all.
> *Rabbi Nachman of Breslov*

### Stop 9. Toledo & the Synagogues of Sepharad

**Waypoint:** Castile, Spain

Where the golden age of Sepharad flourished. Before the expulsion of 1492, Spain, Sepharad in Hebrew, held one of the greatest Jewish civilizations in history, a golden age of poetry, philosophy, science, and commerce, often alongside Muslim and Christian neighbors in the convivencia. In Toledo, two medieval synagogues survive: the Synagogue of Santa María la Blanca, built around 1180 with white horseshoe arches that look more like a mosque than a church or synagogue, the convivencia in stone; and the Synagogue of El Tránsito, with its exquisite carved-plaster Hebrew inscriptions, now the Sephardic Museum. Córdoba holds another, and the statue of its son Maimonides, the philosopher who fled the Almohad persecution. The Jews were expelled from Spain in 1492, the same year Columbus sailed, and did not legally return for centuries, but the Ladino songs, the recipes, and the keys to the lost houses were carried across the Mediterranean and kept for five hundred years. Walk the old Judería; the silence holds the memory.

**The Berth.** Toledo: the Parador de Toledo across the gorge with the famous El Greco view; the boutique Hotel Casa del Capitel in the old town. Or base in Madrid (the Ritz, the Urso) and day-trip to Toledo, thirty minutes by fast train.

**The Galley.** Toledo: Castilian roast lamb and partridge; marzipan, the city's famous sweet, of Sephardic-Moorish origin; the adafina and Sephardic dishes that survive in Spanish cooking; Manchego and a Toledo wine on the gorge terrace.

> The earth is the Lord's, and the fullness thereof.
> *Psalm 24, set to music by the poets of Sepharad*

### Stop 10. The Venice Ghetto

**Waypoint:** Venice, Italy

Where the word itself was born. On a small island in the Cannaregio district of Venice, in 1516, the Venetian Republic confined its Jews to a walled enclave on the site of an old foundry, the geto, and gave the world, along with the confinement, the word ghetto. The gates were locked at night and the community pressed upward for room, building Venice's first 'skyscrapers,' tenements of six and seven low-ceilinged stories around the campo. Yet within those walls a rich life flourished: five magnificent synagogues, the scuole of the German, Italian, Spanish, Levantine, and Ashkenazi communities, hidden behind plain facades and rising to gilded, beautiful interiors, three of them still in use. The ghetto produced scholars, printers, and poets across three centuries until Napoleon tore down the gates in 1797. End the pilgrimage here, in the place that named confinement and outlived it, where the synagogues still stand and the community, small but unbroken, still gathers, after the longest exile in history, still here.

**The Berth.** Venice: the Boscolo and boutique hotels of Cannaregio near the Ghetto; the grand Gritti Palace and Danieli on the Grand Canal; a quiet guesthouse in Cannaregio for the least touristed, most lived-in corner of the city.

**The Galley.** The Venetian-Jewish kitchen, one of Italy's great cuisines: sarde in saor, carciofi, the kosher Gam Gam by the Ghetto canal; bacaro cicchetti crawls in Cannaregio; fritole and the sweets the ghetto bakers gave to all Venice.

> Next year in Jerusalem.
> *the closing words of the Passover seder, for two thousand years*

---

## Pilgrimage XIV. For God and the Kingdom of Heaven

Year-round destinations along the long, contested arc of the Crusades, the holy wars launched from Europe between 1095 and 1291 to seize and hold the city of Jerusalem, sacred at once to three faiths. The Crusaders called their own expeditions a pilgrimage, an iter, an armed march to the Sepulchre of Christ, and this trail follows their road, from the field in France where it was preached to the walls of the city where it ended in defeat. It is a journey through some of the mightiest castles ever built, the holiest shrines in Christendom and Islam, and some of the cruelest events in medieval history, the massacre of Jerusalem in 1099, the sack of Christian Constantinople by Christian armies in 1204, the chivalry of Saladin who shamed his enemies by his mercy. This is history with no clean heroes, and the trail honors all who suffered and fought, Frank and Byzantine, Muslim and Jew and Eastern Christian alike. Travel it as a penitent might, not in triumph but in reckoning. Best in spring and autumn. Deus vult, they cried, God wills it; and God alone, in the end, will judge.

> They make a desert and call it peace.
> *Tacitus, on the cost of conquest*

### Stop 1. Clermont

**Waypoint:** Auvergne, central France

Where the holy war was preached. On 27 November 1095, in a field outside the city of Clermont in the Auvergne, Pope Urban II preached the sermon that launched the Crusades. He called on the knights of Europe, forever feuding and shedding Christian blood, to turn their swords eastward instead, to aid the Christians of the East and free Jerusalem from Muslim rule, and he promised remission of sins to all who went. The crowd, it is said, took up the cry 'Deus vult!', God wills it, and it became the war-shout of the whole enterprise. Whatever its tangle of motives, faith and greed, piety and plunder, land-hunger and genuine devotion, the speech at Clermont set in motion two centuries of war that would reshape Europe and the Near East and poison Christian-Muslim relations for a thousand years. Today Clermont- Ferrand is a handsome black-lava city beneath the volcanoes of the Auvergne, its cathedral built of dark volcanic stone. Stand where a pope's words sent a hundred thousand marching east, and consider how easily faith becomes a sword.

**The Berth.** Clermont-Ferrand: the city-center hotels near the black cathedral; or base in the volcanic country of the Puys, the regional park of extinct volcanoes that rings the city, for the spectacular landscape.

**The Galley.** Auvergnat: the great mountain cheeses (Cantal, Saint-Nectaire, bleu d'Auvergne); truffade and aligot, the potato-and-cheese dishes; Puy green lentils; charcuterie and a robust red from the volcanic slopes.

> God wills it.
> *the cry at Clermont, 1095*

### Stop 2. Constantinople

**Waypoint:** Istanbul, Turkey

Where the Crusaders turned on their own. The armies of the First Crusade gathered in 1096 at Constantinople, the gleaming capital of the Byzantine Empire, the greatest Christian city on Earth, whose emperor Alexius Comnenus had asked the West only for mercenaries and received instead a vast, unruly host. The relationship between Latin Crusader and Greek Christian was poisoned from the start by mutual suspicion, and it ended in one of history's great betrayals: in 1204, the Fourth Crusade, diverted by Venetian debt and dynastic intrigue, turned its swords not on any Muslim foe but on Constantinople itself, sacking the Christian city for three days, looting Hagia Sophia, and shattering the Byzantine Empire from which it never recovered. Stand in Hagia Sophia, for a thousand years the largest church in the world, now a mosque again, and grasp that the Crusades' deepest victims included the very Christians they set out to save.

**The Berth.** Istanbul: the grand Pera Palace of Orient Express fame; the boutique hotels of Sultanahmet by Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque; or a Bosphorus-view room looking across to Asia.

**The Galley.** Turkish: the meze and the grill (kebab, köfte); fresh fish on the Bosphorus; the sweets (baklava, lokum); Turkish coffee and çay; a rooftop dinner with the minarets and domes of the old city spread below.

> The Latins spared neither age nor sex; the city ran with Christian blood.
> *Niketas Choniates, Byzantine eyewitness, 1204*

### Stop 3. Antioch

**Waypoint:** Antakya, southern Turkey

Where the First Crusade nearly died, and was saved by a vision. The great fortress-city of Antioch, the gateway to Syria, held the First Crusade for eight grueling months in 1097 and 1098, the Crusaders starving outside its walls through a bitter winter until treachery let them in, and then, almost at once, besieged in their turn by a Muslim relief army, trapped and despairing within the city they had just taken. Then a poor pilgrim claimed a vision had revealed the Holy Lance, the spear that pierced Christ's side, buried beneath a church floor; whether miracle or fraud, the find so fired the starving army that they sallied out and routed a force many times their size. Antioch was the hinge of the whole Crusade and became the first great Crusader principality. The ancient city, modern Antakya, has been devastated again and again by the earthquakes of this fault-riven land, most recently and terribly in 2023. Stand in this old, much-suffering city where Christianity itself was first named, and where faith and desperation once worked a kind of miracle.

**The Berth.** Antakya: the city is rebuilding after the 2023 earthquake; check current conditions before travel. The Hatay region's restored old mansions and the boutique hotels of the area, where they have reopened, offer the base.

**The Galley.** Hatay cuisine, among Turkey's finest and most distinctive: künefe (the cheese-and- pastry dessert) born here; the rich meze; muhammara; the blend of Turkish, Arab, and Mediterranean flavors of this ancient crossroads city.

> The Lord has fought for us this day.
> *the chronicle of the First Crusade at Antioch*

### Stop 4. Jerusalem & the Holy Sepulchre

**Waypoint:** Jerusalem

Where the slaughter and the prayer met at dusk. On 15 July 1099, after a five-week siege, the First Crusade stormed the walls of Jerusalem and took the city, the goal of four years of suffering. What followed was a massacre: the Crusaders put much of the Muslim and Jewish population to the sword, and chroniclers on their own side wrote, with grim satisfaction, of riding in blood to the knees. At the journey's end the surviving Crusaders, weeping, laid down their arms and walked barefoot to pray at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, built over the site of Christ's crucifixion and tomb, the holiest place in Christendom and the destination of every Crusader's vow. The contrast, slaughter at dawn and prayer at dusk, is the Crusades in miniature. The Sepulchre still stands, shared uneasily by six Christian denominations under a status quo so fragile that a Muslim family has held the only key for centuries to keep the peace. Enter the dim, incense-heavy church, descend to the tomb, and hold in mind both the devotion and the blood that brought men here.

**The Berth.** Jerusalem: the historic American Colony Hotel; the King David; the boutique hotels and pilgrim hospices of the Old City, where the Hospitallers once ran the greatest hospital in the world, in the Muristan beside the Sepulchre.

**The Galley.** Jerusalem: hummus and the Old City's food; the markets of the four quarters; the shared and contested cuisines of the city; a quiet meal in the Christian Quarter near the church; everything closes for the sabbaths of three faiths in turn.

> They walked barefoot and weeping to the Sepulchre, the same hands that had wrought the slaughter.
> *after the chroniclers of 1099*

### Stop 5. The Horns of Hattin

**Waypoint:** Galilee, Israel

Where the Crusader kingdom was lost in a single day. On 4 July 1187, between two volcanic hills above the Sea of Galilee called the Horns of Hattin, the great Muslim sultan Saladin destroyed the army of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem. He had lured the Franks across a waterless plain in the July heat, set the dry grass alight around them, and let thirst and smoke do half his work; by evening the Crusader army was annihilated and the king of Jerusalem and the relic of the True Cross were in his hands. With the army gone, the kingdom lay open, and within months Saladin had taken Jerusalem itself, this time without massacre, sparing the inhabitants and allowing Christians to depart, a magnanimity that astonished and shamed a Europe that remembered 1099. Hattin broke the Crusader states and called forth the Third Crusade and Richard the Lionheart. The twin hills still rise above the Galilee, and the battlefield is open country. Climb the Horns, look out over the shimmering plain, and understand how heat and thirst and a cleverer enemy can undo the proudest army on Earth.

**The Berth.** Galilee: the kibbutz guesthouses and boutique hotels around the Sea of Galilee (Tiberias, Ginosar); the Scots Hotel on the lakeshore; the cool of the Galilean hills above the lake.

**The Galley.** Galilee: St. Peter's fish from the lake; Galilean and Druze cooking in the hill villages; fresh labneh and olives and the produce of the north; a table by the Sea of Galilee at sunset where so much sacred history converges.

> I shall not wipe away these tears by killing those who no longer fight.
> *attributed to Saladin, on the fall of Jerusalem*

### Stop 6. Krak des Chevaliers

**Waypoint:** western Syria

Where the mightiest castle of the age still stands. On a high spur dominating the gap between the Syrian coast and the interior stands Krak des Chevaliers, the greatest and best-preserved of all Crusader castles, held by the Knights Hospitaller from 1142 and rebuilt by them into a concentric masterpiece of stone, two rings of walls and towers stocked to withstand a five-year siege. T. E. Lawrence, who studied it as a young man, called it perhaps the finest castle in the world, and it is: a thing of brutal beauty, defying a dozen sieges, never taken by storm. It fell at last in 1271 not to assault but to a forged order of surrender, when its garrison had dwindled to a remnant before the armies of the Mamluk Sultan Baibars. The castle survived nine centuries nearly intact, only to be damaged in the Syrian civil war that began in 2011; its future, like Syria's, is uncertain, and travel there must be weighed with great care. Picture, if you cannot stand there, the great hall and the echoing vaults, and the small band who held the finest castle in the world.

**The Berth.** Western Syria: travel to Syria requires careful checking of current safety and access; the castle has at times been closed or restricted. When conditions allow, the Homs and coastal region provides the nearest base; verify everything first.

**The Galley.** Syrian: among the great cuisines of the world, the meze, kibbeh, and grilled meats; the sweets of Homs and Hama; the citrus and olives of the coast; the legendary hospitality of a country that has suffered greatly.

> Perhaps the best preserved and most wholly admirable castle in the world.
> *T. E. Lawrence, on Krak des Chevaliers*

### Stop 7. Acre

**Waypoint:** Akko, Israel

Where the Crusader world made its last stand. The great port of Acre, on a promontory of the northern coast, was the chief city and final capital of the Crusader Kingdom, taken by Richard the Lionheart after a brutal two-year siege in 1191 and held for a century as the last great Christian foothold in the Holy Land. When it fell at last to the Mamluks in 1291, after savage street fighting and the slaughter or enslavement of those who could not flee by sea, the Crusader Levant was finished; the surviving knights took ship for Cyprus, and two centuries of Crusading came to an end in the rubble of Acre. Beneath the Ottoman city, archaeologists have uncovered the vast, vaulted Hospitaller fortress nearly intact, the great refectory and the knights' halls and the secret tunnel to the sea, one of the finest Crusader complexes anywhere. Walk the Hospitaller halls below and the sea walls above, and stand where the long Crusader dream guttered out at the water's edge.

**The Berth.** Akko (Acre): boutique hotels in the restored Ottoman old city within the sea walls; the Efendi Hotel in two restored palaces; or base in nearby Haifa for the range and the gardens of the Baha'i shrine.

**The Galley.** Akko: superb hummus (Said and Hummus Akko are institutions); the fresh fish of the harbor; Galilean-Arab cooking; knafeh; the markets of the old city; a seafood dinner on the harbor within the medieval walls.

> The sea was full of ships, and the shore was full of those who could not reach them.
> *after the chroniclers of the fall of Acre, 1291*

### Stop 8. Rhodes & Malta

**Waypoint:** Greece & Malta

Where the Knights survived their own defeat. Driven from the Holy Land in 1291, the Knights Hospitaller did not disband; they reinvented themselves as a sea power. From 1310 they ruled the Greek island of Rhodes, fortifying its harbor city into one of the great walled towns of the Mediterranean, until the Ottomans drove them out after an epic siege in 1522. Then, granted the rocky island of Malta, they made their final and most famous stand: in the Great Siege of 1565 a few hundred knights and the Maltese held out against a vast Ottoman armada, a victory that rang through Europe, and afterward built the fortress-city of Valletta, named for their grand master. The Order endures even now, as the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, having returned, after all the centuries of war, to its first purpose: the care of the sick and the poor. Walk the walls of Rhodes or the golden streets of Valletta, and trace how a defeated order outlived its cause and became, again, a work of mercy.

**The Berth.** Rhodes: hotels within the medieval walled town. Valletta, Malta: the boutique hotels of the golden Baroque capital (the Phoenicia by the gate; the restored palazzi within the walls), one of the Mediterranean's loveliest small cities.

**The Galley.** Maltese: rabbit stew (fenkata), the national dish; pastizzi and ftira; the fish and the Mediterranean produce; Gozitan wine. Rhodes: Greek island cooking, fresh seafood, and the long taverna evening by the harbor.

> Not for ourselves alone, but for the sick and the poor.
> *the enduring motto of the Order of St. John*

### Stop 9. The Temple Church

**Waypoint:** London, England

Where the Templars are remembered, and the legend lives. Off Fleet Street in London, hidden among the lawyers' courts of the Inns of Court, stands the Temple Church, built by the Knights Templar and consecrated in 1185, its round nave modeled on the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The Templars, founded around 1119 to protect pilgrims on the roads of the Holy Land, grew into the most powerful and richest of the military orders, pioneers of medieval banking, until in 1307 the king of France, Philip the Fair, deep in their debt, had them arrested, tortured into false confessions, and burned, in one of history's great judicial crimes. Their last grand master, Jacques de Molay, is said to have cursed king and pope from the flames; both were dead within the year. Stand in the round nave that echoes the Sepulchre, among the worn stone effigies of Templar knights, and consider how the hunters of heretics were themselves destroyed as heretics in the end.

**The Berth.** London: the grand hotels of the city and the West End (the Savoy and the Waldorf are near; the Rosewood on High Holborn); or the legal quarter's quiet corners around the Inns of Court themselves.

**The Galley.** The City of London: the historic chophouses and pubs (the Olde Cheshire Cheese on Fleet Street, rebuilt 1667); a proper roast; the old legal-quarter taverns where the barristers still lunch.

> God knows who has sinned; misfortune will soon befall those who have wrongly condemned us.
> *Jacques de Molay, last Grand Master of the Templars, 1314*

### Stop 10. The Holy Sepulchre, Again

**Waypoint:** Jerusalem, where it began and ends

Where the pilgrim returns, and the reckoning is made. The trail ends where the Crusaders' own ended: back at the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, the goal of every Crusader vow. Two centuries of war, of hundreds of thousands dead, of cities sacked and faiths embittered, won and then lost this single church, and in the end Jerusalem returned to Muslim rule, where, by the truce Richard and Saladin struck, Christian pilgrims could come and pray as they always had. That is the hardest lesson of the Crusades, and the truest: that the holy places were never closed to the peaceful, and that the wars to seize them achieved, after all the blood, only what mercy and patience would have granted for free. Three faiths still hold this small city sacred and still, mostly, share it. Stand once more in the Sepulchre, listen to the Greek and Latin and Armenian chant overlapping under the dome, and end the pilgrimage not in triumph or defeat, but in the long, hard hope of peace.

**The Berth.** Jerusalem: the American Colony, long a meeting-ground of peoples; the pilgrim hospices of the Old City (the Austrian, the Lutheran); a simple room within the walls, to wake to the bells and the call to prayer and the shofar in their turns.

**The Galley.** Jerusalem: the shared table of the city, hummus and falafel and the maqluba and the kebab claimed by all and made by each; a last meal in the Old City; the bread broken, as it should be, by people of every faith at once.

> Jerusalem is a port city on the shore of eternity.
> *Yehuda Amichai*

---

## Pilgrimage XV. The Long Quarrel

Year-round destinations along the longest war in European history, the struggle between the crowns of England and France that ran from 1337 to 1453, a hundred and sixteen years across five generations of kings, fought for the throne of France and decided at last in France's favor. This trail follows the war's arc across northern France, the Loire, and the southwest, and back to England: the great English victories of the longbow at Crécy, Poitiers, and Agincourt; the turning of the tide by a teenage peasant girl who heard the voices of saints and is now one herself; and the final French triumph at Castillon, where gunpowder ended the age of the armored knight and, with it, the Middle Ages. It is a journey through cathedral and battlefield, through the birth of two nations from a single dynastic quarrel, and through the brief, blazing life of Joan of Arc, the most extraordinary figure of the medieval world. Best traveled spring through autumn, the French countryside at its kindest. Two voices contend the whole way, 'Dieu et mon droit' and 'Montjoie Saint-Denis.' Walk between them.

> We few, we happy few, we band of brothers.
> *Henry V, before Agincourt, in Shakespeare*

### Stop 1. Crécy

**Waypoint:** Picardy, northern France

Where the longbow changed warfare forever. On 26 August 1346, on a gentle slope of farmland in Picardy, King Edward III of England, cornered with a smaller, exhausted army, chose his ground and waited. When the flower of French chivalry under Philip VI charged, the massed English and Welsh longbowmen loosed arrows so thick that chroniclers said they darkened the sky, and the French knights and their Genoese crossbowmen were cut down in their thousands before they could close. Crécy was the first great battle of the war and a thunderclap across Europe: it announced that the armored mounted knight, the master of the battlefield for three centuries, could be destroyed by common men with bows of yew, and that the age of feudal chivalry was ending. The blind King John of Bohemia, fighting for France, had his knights tie their horses to his so he could die sword in hand in the press; his ostrich-feather badge and motto, it is said, the Black Prince took for his own. Walk the quiet ridge, today only fields, and imagine the sky going dark.

**The Berth.** Picardy: the regional inns and chambres d'hôtes around Abbeville and the Baie de Somme; or base in the cathedral city of Amiens, half an hour south, for the grand Gothic and the finest restaurants.

**The Galley.** Picard cooking: the ficelle picarde (ham-and-mushroom crêpe); duck and game from the Somme marshes; gâteau battu; the seafood of the Baie de Somme; a glass of cider or northern beer in a village café.

> The arrows fell so thick and fast that it seemed as if it snowed.
> *Jean Froissart, Chronicles*

### Stop 2. Calais

**Waypoint:** the Channel coast, France

Where six burghers offered their lives. After Crécy, Edward III marched on the port of Calais and besieged it for eleven months until, in 1347, it surrendered. The famous story, carved by Rodin into one of the greatest sculptures in the world, is of the Burghers of Calais: six leading citizens who, to save the starving town, walked out barefoot in sackcloth with nooses round their necks and the keys of the city in their hands, offering their lives to the English king, and were spared only at the pleading of his pregnant queen, Philippa. Calais would remain an English possession for over two centuries, the last toehold of the old French empire, not lost until 1558, when Queen Mary I said the word would be found engraved on her heart. Rodin's bronze of the burghers, gaunt and despairing, stands before the town hall, the original of a work cast for cities around the world. Stand before the six doomed men and read the oldest lesson of war, that it is the civilians who pay.

**The Berth.** Calais: the practical hotels of the ferry port; or, far better, base down the coast in Boulogne-sur-Mer or in the elegant resort town of Le Touquet for the seafood and the sands.

**The Galley.** The catch of the Channel: moules-frites, fresh herring and mackerel, the fish of Boulogne (France's largest fishing port); welsh (the local rarebit) in a Calais estaminet; northern beer and genièvre.

> I would the noble citizens of Calais might be spared.
> *Queen Philippa of Hainault, to her husband, 1347*

### Stop 3. Poitiers

**Waypoint:** Nouvelle-Aquitaine, France

Where a king of France was taken prisoner. On 19 September 1356, near Poitiers, Edward the Black Prince, son of Edward III and the very model of the chivalric warrior, won perhaps the most stunning English victory of the war. Outnumbered, the English archers and dismounted men-at-arms broke wave after wave of French attacks, and when it was over they had captured King John II of France himself, along with much of his nobility. The king was carried off to honorable captivity in London, where he was feasted and treated as a royal guest while France was bled white for his colossal ransom; he died there, in the end, having voluntarily returned when a hostage broke parole, a strange medieval point of honor. The victory led to the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360, the high-water mark of English fortune. Poitiers itself is a city of astonishing Romanesque churches, Notre-Dame-la- Grande above all. Walk the old town, then drive out to the battlefield country to the southeast where the king of France was led away in chains.

**The Berth.** Poitiers: the Mercure and boutique hotels of the old town; or stay in the surrounding Vienne countryside in a restored manor; Futuroscope nearby for those traveling with children.

**The Galley.** Poitevin: the goat cheeses (chabichou du Poitou); farci poitevin; broyé du Poitou; the freshwater fish; the wines and the Cognac of the neighboring Charente, an easy detour to the south.

> It is the fortune of war: today on me, tomorrow on you.
> *the chivalric saying of the age*

### Stop 4. Agincourt

**Waypoint:** Azincourt, Pas-de-Calais, France

Where Henry V won against all odds. On Saint Crispin's Day, 25 October 1415, in a muddy, narrow field between two woods near the village of Azincourt, King Henry V of England, his small army sick with dysentery and trapped far from safety, faced a French host several times its size. The French men-at-arms, packed into the narrow ground and bogged to their knees in the mud of a ploughed field after rain, were funneled onto the English line and slaughtered by the longbowmen, who, when their arrows were spent, fell on the floundering knights with mallets and daggers. The French lost the cream of their nobility; the English lost a few hundred. Shakespeare made of it the supreme English myth, Henry's St Crispin's Day speech the most quoted battle oration in the language. The modern visitor center at Azincourt tells the story honestly from both sides. Walk the field between the woods, picture it ankle-deep in October mud, and understand how terrain and weather, not valor alone, decide battles.

**The Berth.** Pas-de-Calais: the village inns around Azincourt and Hesdin; the country hotels of the Sept Vallées; or base in Montreuil-sur-Mer, the walled hill town where Hugo set part of Les Misérables.

**The Galley.** Northern French country cooking: the potjevleesch and carbonnade of the region; maroilles cheese; the famous restaurant tradition of Montreuil-sur-Mer; tarte au sucre and a northern ale.

> We few, we happy few; for he that sheds his blood with me shall be my brother.
> *Henry V, in Shakespeare's Henry V*

### Stop 5. Domrémy

**Waypoint:** Lorraine, eastern France

Where the Maid was born. In the small village of Domrémy, on the marches of Lorraine, a farmer's daughter named Jeanne was born around 1412, and there, at about thirteen, in her father's garden, she began to hear the voices of Saint Michael, Saint Catherine, and Saint Margaret, telling her that she must drive the English from France and see the dauphin crowned. That a teenage peasant girl who could not read, from a village on the edge of nowhere, would within three years lead the armies of France, lift the siege of Orléans, and crown a king, is the most improbable true story in the whole of medieval history. Her birthplace, a modest stone cottage, still stands and is preserved as a museum; beside it rises the basilica of Bois-Chenu on the hill where she heard the voices, and the church where she was baptized. This is where the turning of the entire war began, in the faith of a child. Stand in the small dark cottage where she was born, and consider what belief can do.

**The Berth.** Lorraine: the inns of the Vosges and the Meuse valley; base in Nancy, the exquisite ducal city with its golden Place Stanislas, an hour east, or in Domrémy's quiet countryside.

**The Galley.** Lorraine: the quiche lorraine in its homeland; the mirabelle plum in every form (tart, eau-de-vie); potée lorraine; the macarons of Nancy; bergamotes and the pâtisserie of the ducal city.

> I am not afraid; I was born to do this.
> *Joan of Arc*

### Stop 6. Orléans

**Waypoint:** the Loire, France

Where the tide turned. By 1429 the English and their Burgundian allies held most of northern France, and the city of Orléans on the Loire, the gateway to the still-unconquered south, had been under siege for months and was near to falling; with it would have fallen the last hope of the dauphin Charles. Then came Joan, seventeen years old, in white armor, having convinced the desperate prince to give her troops. In nine days, against the judgment of his captains, she lifted the siege, storming the English forts around the city and turning a war that France was losing into one it would win. Orléans has honored her ever since: the Fêtes de Jeanne d'Arc each late April and early May, marking the anniversary of the deliverance, are among the oldest continuous civic festivals in France, nearly six centuries unbroken, with a young local woman chosen each year to ride through the city as the Maid. Cross the Loire bridge she fought to take, and stand in the cathedral of Sainte-Croix where she gave thanks. A city saved still says her name.

**The Berth.** Orléans: the boutique hotels of the restored old town near the cathedral; or move down the Loire to the great châteaux country and stay near Chambord, Cheverny, or Chenonceau, a short drive south.

**The Galley.** Loire Valley: the freshwater fish (sandre, brochet) in beurre blanc; Orléans' famous vinegar and mustard; rillettes and andouillette; the great white wines of the Loire, Sancerre, Vouvray, Muscadet, the length of the river.

> Go forward bravely. Fear nothing. God will give the victory.
> *Joan of Arc, at Orléans*

### Stop 7. Reims Cathedral

**Waypoint:** Champagne, France

Where the king was crowned and the prophecy fulfilled. The great Gothic cathedral of Notre-Dame de Reims was, for a thousand years, the place where the kings of France were anointed and crowned, the sacred heart of French kingship. After Orléans, Joan's whole purpose was to bring the dauphin across enemy country to Reims to be crowned and made the true king, and on 17 July 1429, having swept the English from the Loire at Patay and marched boldly through hostile territory, she stood beside Charles VII at the altar as he was anointed with the holy oil, her banner held among the great ones, because, she said, it had borne the burden and deserved the honor. It was the summit of her life and the making of a king. The cathedral, a wonder of high Gothic with its smiling angel and glorious west front, was savagely shelled in the First World War and lovingly rebuilt, with later windows by Chagall. Stand where a shepherd girl saw a king crowned, and raise, afterward, a glass of the wine these hills invented.

**The Berth.** Reims: the grand Domaine Les Crayères, the great Champagne-country château-hotel; the boutique hotels of the cathedral quarter; or stay among the vineyards toward Épernay, the capital of Champagne.

**The Galley.** Champagne, of course, in its homeland, the great houses (Taittinger, Veuve Clicquot, Pommery) open for tasting; the biscuit rose de Reims; jambon de Reims; the Michelin tables of Les Crayères; chalk-cellar dinners deep under the city.

> Hold the banner high; it has borne the burden, let it have the honor.
> *Joan of Arc, at the coronation*

### Stop 8. Rouen

**Waypoint:** Normandy, France

Where the Maid was burned. Captured at Compiègne in 1430 and sold to the English, Joan of Arc was brought to Rouen, the capital of English-held Normandy, and put on trial for heresy by a church court doing the occupiers' bidding. For months the nineteen-year-old, alone and unschooled, faced a tribunal of learned clerics and answered them with a shrewdness and courage that survives, word for word, in the trial record, one of the most moving documents of the Middle Ages. On 30 May 1431 she was burned alive in the old market square of Rouen; an English soldier who had cursed her is said to have wept that they had burned a saint. Twenty-five years later her conviction was annulled; in 1920 she was canonized. The modern church of Sainte-Jeanne-d'Arc, its roof shaped like the flames, marks the spot of her death in the Place du Vieux-Marché. Stand on the spot of the fire, and feel the weight of a judicial murder.

**The Berth.** Rouen: the boutique hotels of the medieval old town beneath the cathedral; the Hôtel de Bourgtheroulde in a Renaissance mansion; or the Normandy countryside and the Seine valley around the city.

**The Galley.** Norman: duck à la rouennaise; the cheeses (Camembert, Livarot, Pont-l'Évêque); the cream and butter and apples of Normandy; cider and Calvados; the seafood of the nearby coast at Honfleur and Dieppe.

> If I am not in God's grace, may God put me there; and if I am, may God keep me there.
> *Joan of Arc, at her trial, Rouen*

### Stop 9. Castillon

**Waypoint:** Gascony, near Bordeaux, France

Where the war, and the Middle Ages, ended. On 17 July 1453, near the small town of Castillon in the English-held wine country east of Bordeaux, the last battle of the Hundred Years' War was fought, and it ended an age. The veteran English commander John Talbot, Earl of Shrewsbury, the terror of France for a generation, charged a fortified French camp, not knowing that the French had ringed it with three hundred cannon. The massed artillery tore his army to pieces; Talbot, an old man, was killed when a cannonball felled his horse and pinned him. It was the first battle in European history decided by field artillery, and the gun had now done to the mounted knight and the longbowman alike what the longbow had once done to chivalry. With Castillon the English lost Gascony, held since Eleanor of Aquitaine, and the war was over: France had won, and England kept only Calais. The age of gunpowder and the nation-state had begun. The battlefield is marked, and each summer a great reenactment is staged.

**The Berth.** Near Bordeaux: stay in the wine country of Saint-Émilion, minutes away, among the greatest vineyards on Earth; or in Bordeaux itself, the grand 18th-century city, half an hour west.

**The Galley.** Bordeaux and Gascony: the great red wines of Saint-Émilion and the Médoc; entrecôte à la bordelaise; lamprey, duck confit and foie gras of the southwest; canelés; the oysters of Arcachon, an easy drive to the coast.

> Wars begin with the young dying for the old; this one ended a whole world of war.
> *the historian's reflection on Castillon*

### Stop 10. Westminster & Canterbury

**Waypoint:** England

Where the English kings of the war lie, and the war is remembered. The trail ends across the Channel, in England, where the protagonists of the war sleep. In Westminster Abbey lies Henry V, the victor of Agincourt, beneath a chantry chapel high above the shrine of Edward the Confessor, his battered funeral achievements, the helm and saddle and shield carried at his funeral, long kept above the tomb. In Canterbury Cathedral, in the loveliest tomb of the age, lies Edward the Black Prince, the hero of Poitiers, his gilt-bronze effigy in full armor, his real helm and gauntlets and surcoat hung above him for six centuries, with his own chosen humble epitaph reminding the passer-by that all glory ends in dust. Here the English remember a war they spent a century winning and then lost, that helped forge them into a nation by turning their kings' eyes at last away from France and toward the sea and the world beyond. Stand at the Black Prince's tomb, read the French verses he chose, and end the pilgrimage where the longest war's ambition came, in the end, to rest.

**The Berth.** London: the grand hotels near Westminster (the Goring, the Corinthia). Canterbury: the cathedral-quarter inns and the historic Falstaff; or the Kentish countryside of the Pilgrims' Way.

**The Galley.** English: a proper roast and a pint near Westminster; Kentish ale, oysters from Whitstable, and apples from the Garden of England near Canterbury; afternoon tea; the gastropubs of the North Downs along the old Pilgrims' Way.

> Such as thou art, sometime was I. Such as I am, such shalt thou be.
> *the epitaph of the Black Prince, Canterbury Cathedral*

---

## Pilgrimage XVI. The Shot Heard Round the World

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of the American Revolution, from the first shots at Lexington Green in April 1775 through the British surrender at Yorktown in October 1781, anchored to eight battlefields, two capitals, and one estate where the war was fought and won. The Sestercentennial commemoration period (2025-2033) is in full swing: the 250th anniversary of Saratoga falls on October 7, within this calendar year, and is the year's central commemoration. Best timed for Patriots' Day (the third Monday of April, falling exactly on the April 19 anniversary), the Saratoga 250th in October, or the Christmas-night Washington's Crossing reenactment on the Delaware. Two trips, six days each: New England and Saratoga in spring or early fall, the Mid-Atlantic through Virginia in autumn.

> These are the times that try men's souls.
> *Thomas Paine, The American Crisis, December 1776*

### Stop 1. Boston & the Freedom Trail

**Waypoint:** Boston, Massachusetts

Where the revolution was born. Before a single shot was fired, the Revolution was made in Boston, in arguments and anger and the slow boil of a decade of resistance, and no city holds more of its memory. The 2.5-mile Freedom Trail, a red line set into the pavement, threads the sacred sites: the Old South Meeting House where the Tea Party was planned, the Old State House and the cobbled circle marking the Boston Massacre of 1770, Faneuil Hall the cradle of liberty, and the Old North Church where the two lanterns hung, one if by land, two if by sea, that sent Paul Revere riding into legend. Across the river rises the granite obelisk of Bunker Hill, where in June 1775 raw colonial militia twice threw back the finest army in the world and bled it white before yielding the ground, proving that the redcoats could be fought. Walk the red line from the Common to the harbor, climb the Bunker Hill monument for the view, and stand where a colonial grievance hardened into a war for a nation.

**The Berth.** Boston: the grand Omni Parker House, America's longest continuously operating hotel; the Liberty in a converted jail; or the boutique hotels of Beacon Hill and the Back Bay near the Common and the trail's start.

**The Galley.** Boston: clam chowder and oysters at the Union Oyster House, open since 1826; lobster rolls and scrod; Italian feasting in the North End near the Old North Church; a pint in a Beacon Hill tavern where the Sons of Liberty once plotted.

> The die is now cast; the colonies must either submit or triumph.
> *King George III, 1774*

### Stop 2. Lexington Green & Concord's North Bridge

**Waypoint:** Massachusetts

Where it started, on the morning of April 19, 1775. British regulars marching from Boston to seize colonial gunpowder met 77 minutemen on Lexington Green at dawn; eight Americans were killed in the brief skirmish, the first deaths of the war. By midday, hundreds of militia at Concord's North Bridge had pushed the regulars back across the river, killing three, the 'shot heard round the world' Emerson named in his 1837 hymn. Both sites are within Minute Man National Historical Park; the road between them is walkable. The Patriots' Day reenactments, the third Monday of April, falling exactly on the April 19 anniversary, start before sunrise on the Green and conclude at the North Bridge by mid-morning. Eat at the Colonial Inn in Concord afterward, where the militia gathered on the morning of the alarm. Walk the half-mile Battle Road trace between the two sites, and stand on the Green at dawn where the first volley of the Revolution was fired.

**The Berth.** Stay in Boston (25 km east): Boston Harbor Hotel; The Liberty; XV Beacon. Or in Concord: The Colonial Inn since 1716.

**The Galley.** Concord: The Colonial Inn dining room; 80 Thoreau for the modern. Boston: Neptune Oyster; Mamma Maria; Townsman; Mike's Pastry.

> Stand your ground. Don't fire unless fired upon, but if they mean to have a war, let it begin here.
> *Captain John Parker, to his minutemen on Lexington Green, 1775*

### Stop 3. Independence Hall & the Liberty Bell

**Waypoint:** Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

Where independence was declared. The Declaration of Independence was approved here on July 2 and signed through the summer of 1776; the Constitution was drafted in the same room in the summer of 1787. Free timed-entry tickets are required May through September. The Liberty Bell, with its famous crack, sits in its own pavilion across the street. Walk Old City, Christ Church (where Washington, Franklin, and Adams worshipped), Carpenter's Hall (First Continental Congress, 1774), the Betsy Ross House. Eat at the Reading Terminal Market; settle the South Philly cheesesteak question yourself (Pat's vs. Geno's; locals will tell you Tony Luke's beats both).

**The Berth.** The Rittenhouse on Rittenhouse Square; The Logan in Logan Square; or The Notary Hotel in the converted City Hall annex.

**The Galley.** Vetri Cucina for the Italian Michelin; Zahav for the canonical modern Israeli (Solomonov); Reading Terminal Market for the everyday; Pat's or Geno's for the cheesesteak debate.

> We must all hang together, or assuredly we shall all hang separately.
> *Benjamin Franklin, at the signing of the Declaration, 1776*

### Stop 4. Trenton & Princeton

**Waypoint:** New Jersey

Where Washington saved the war over ten days from late December 1776 through early January 1777, after a brutal year of retreats. On Christmas night, his army crossed the ice-clogged Delaware in Durham boats, marched nine miles in a sleet storm, and surprised the Hessian garrison at Trenton at dawn, capturing nearly 900 prisoners against five American casualties. A week later he beat a British force at Princeton. The Washington's Crossing reenactment of the Delaware crossing, every December 25 (FIXED, weather permitting), draws thousands of spectators; the Trenton and Princeton battlefields are both National Historic Landmarks within an hour of New York City.

**The Berth.** Stay in Princeton (15 minutes north): Nassau Inn; or in Philadelphia (60 minutes south): The Rittenhouse; Hotel Monaco.

**The Galley.** Princeton: Witherspoon Grill; Mistral. Philadelphia: Vetri Cucina; Zahav; Reading Terminal Market; Pat's or Geno's.

> The summer soldier and the sunshine patriot will, in this crisis, shrink from the service of their country.
> *Thomas Paine, The American Crisis, read to the troops before Trenton*

### Stop 5. Saratoga National Historical Park

**Waypoint:** New York

Where the war turned and France joined in. General John Burgoyne's British army, advancing south from Canada to split the colonies in two, was surrounded at Saratoga and surrendered on October 17, 1777, the first time a full British army had ever surrendered in the field. The diplomatic consequence was the French alliance, signed February 1778, which brought the navy and troops that ultimately won the war. The 250th anniversary on October 7, date of the decisive Battle of Bemis Heights, is the year's central Sestercentennial commemoration. The battlefield is large and drivable, with a 9.5-mile auto tour route and walking trails to each engagement; the Schuyler House and Saratoga Monument anchor the surrounding park.

**The Berth.** Saratoga Springs (20 minutes from the battlefield): the historic Adelphi Hotel on Broadway; the Gideon Putnam in the spa state park; or the Victorian inns of the old spa town.

**The Galley.** Saratoga Springs: farm-to-table dining on Broadway; Hattie's and the Wishing Well for the classics; the Saratoga chip, born here; a meal in the old racing town around the battlefield drive.

> While the people are virtuous they cannot be subdued.
> *Samuel Adams*

### Stop 6. Valley Forge National Historical Park

**Waypoint:** Pennsylvania

Where Washington's army wintered from December 1777 to June 1778, the 'crucible of the Revolution.' Of the 12,000 troops who arrived at the encampment, roughly 2,000 died of disease, exposure, and malnutrition before spring. Yet it was here that the Prussian volunteer Friedrich von Steuben drilled the surviving ragtag force into a disciplined Continental Army on the snowy parade grounds, using a manual the U.S. Army would use through the War of 1812. Reconstructed log huts, the Washington's Headquarters house, a 6-mile loop drive past every major encampment site. Visit in late winter to feel the cold the army felt, or in early summer for the wildflowers across the same fields.

**The Berth.** Stay in King of Prussia (10 minutes east): Sheraton Valley Forge; or Philadelphia (50 minutes east): The Rittenhouse; Hotel Monaco.

**The Galley.** Philadelphia: Vetri Cucina; Zahav; Reading Terminal Market; Pat's or Geno's. King of Prussia: Maggiano's for the casual Italian.

> What we obtain too cheap, we esteem too lightly.
> *Thomas Paine, The American Crisis*

### Stop 7. The Southern Campaign

**Waypoint:** the Carolina backcountry

Where the war was won the hard way. After Charleston fell to the British in May 1780, the war's center shifted south into a savage backcountry conflict, part regular war and part neighbor-against-neighbor civil war, fought across the pine forests and red-clay hills of the Carolinas. Here the tide turned in a string of patriot victories now preserved as quiet national battlefields: at Kings Mountain in October 1780, frontier militia destroyed a Loyalist force in an hour, a fight Jefferson called the turn of the tide; at Cowpens in January 1781, the brilliant Daniel Morgan trapped and shattered the dreaded Banastre Tarleton in a double envelopment studied at West Point to this day; and at Guilford Courthouse in March 1781, Nathanael Greene so bled Cornwallis in victory that the British general abandoned the Carolinas and marched north to his doom in Virginia. Walk these uncrowded fields, the most underappreciated ground of the whole war, and grasp how patience and the land itself defeated an empire.

**The Berth.** The Carolina Upstate: base in Greenville or Spartanburg, South Carolina, near Cowpens and Kings Mountain; or in Greensboro, North Carolina, beside the Guilford Courthouse park; country inns through the rolling backcountry between.

**The Galley.** Carolina barbecue country: whole-hog pork with the vinegar-pepper sauce of the Carolinas; fried catfish and hush puppies; shrimp and grits toward the coast; sweet tea and banana pudding; the great pitmasters of the Upstate.

> The turn of the tide of success.
> *Thomas Jefferson, on the Battle of Kings Mountain*

### Stop 8. The Battle of the Capes

**Waypoint:** the mouth of the Chesapeake, Virginia

Where the sea sealed the victory on land. The Revolution's most decisive battle was fought not by Americans at all, but by the French and British navies off the Virginia capes on 5 September 1781, and almost no one remembers it. As Washington and Rochambeau marched south to trap Cornwallis at Yorktown, everything depended on who controlled the Chesapeake: if the Royal Navy got through, the British army could be supplied or evacuated by sea, and the siege would fail. Instead the French fleet under the Comte de Grasse fought off the British relief squadron and held the bay, slamming the door of the sea behind Cornwallis and sealing his fate. Without this French naval victory, there is no Yorktown and perhaps no United States. The waters are best seen today from the beaches and lighthouses of Cape Henry and the Virginia shore, or from the bridge- tunnel that crosses the bay. Stand at the edge of the Chesapeake, look out to where the fleets maneuvered, and remember the battle at sea that won the war on land.

**The Berth.** Coastal Virginia: the historic Cavalier in Virginia Beach; the inns of Williamsburg, a short drive from both the capes and Yorktown; or Norfolk on the harbor for the great naval city and its museums.

**The Galley.** Tidewater Virginia: Chesapeake blue crab and oysters; she-crab soup; Virginia ham and peanuts; the seafood houses of the bay; a crab feast on a waterfront deck at the mouth of the river that decided the war.

> You will have seen that the world has been turned upside down.
> *attributed to the British at Yorktown*

### Stop 9. Yorktown Battlefield

**Waypoint:** Virginia

Where it ended, on October 19, 1781. Cornwallis's army, trapped between Washington's combined American-French force on land and the French fleet of Admiral de Grasse blocking the Chesapeake, surrendered after a three-week siege. British fife and drums played 'The World Turned Upside Down' as Cornwallis's troops marched out to lay down their arms in defeat. The reconstructed siege lines, the Surrender Field, and the Moore House (where the articles of capitulation were negotiated) are all walkable. Combine with Colonial Williamsburg 12 miles away, a living-history town with reenactors and the largest concentration of restored 18th-century buildings anywhere, and historic Jamestown 10 miles further. Yorktown Day on October 19 is the annual commemoration; the 250th falls in 2031.

**The Berth.** Richmond: The Jefferson Hotel since 1895; Quirk Hotel for the design-set. Williamsburg: Williamsburg Inn. Charlottesville: Keswick Hall; The Clifton.

**The Galley.** Richmond: L'Opossum for canonical modern Southern; Heritage in The Fan. Williamsburg: The Trellis; The Cheese Shop. Charlottesville: The Local; Tavola for Italian.

> Oh God, it is all over.
> *Lord North, British Prime Minister, on hearing of Yorktown*

### Stop 10. Mount Vernon

**Waypoint:** Virginia

Where Washington came home at last. His home on the Potomac River, sixteen miles south of Washington, DC, and the natural resting place at the end of the trail.
