The mansion (built 1758-1778), the working blacksmith shop, the wharf where shad were caught and exported, the slave quarters, interpreted with increasing honesty in recent decades. George and Martha Washington are buried in the family tomb on the grounds. The reconstructed Distillery & Gristmill three miles up the road is operating; the rye whiskey is good. Open every day of the year. End the trail here, by the river. The country is what was made.

**The Berth.** Stay in Old Town Alexandria (15 minutes north): Morrison House; The Alexandrian; or DC (30 minutes north): The Hay-Adams.

**The Galley.** Old Town Alexandria: Vermilion; Restaurant Eve; The Wharf for seafood. DC: Minibar; Old Ebbitt Grill; Rasika.

> I had rather be on my farm than be emperor of the world.
> *George Washington, at Mount Vernon*

---

## Pilgrimage XVII. The Last Full Measure

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of the American Civil War, from John Brown's raid at Harpers Ferry in October 1859 through Lee's surrender at Appomattox in April 1865 and its coda at Ford's Theatre five days later, anchored to eight battlefields, plantations, and memorials where the war's meaning was made and remade. The 160th-anniversary commemorations are underway; the battlefields are best visited outside the July-August heat. Best timed for Gettysburg's Dedication Day on November 19 (when Lincoln's Address is re-delivered annually), the April 9 Appomattox anniversary, or the September 17 anniversary at Antietam. Three trips, four to five days each: Maryland-to-Pennsylvania for the Eastern Theater, the Charleston-to-Appomattox arc, and the Mississippi River route through Vicksburg and Louisiana.

> With malice toward none, with charity for all.
> *Abraham Lincoln, Second Inaugural, 1865*

### Stop 1. Harpers Ferry

**Waypoint:** West Virginia

Where the war began in spirit, eighteen months before the first shots. On October 16, 1859, the abolitionist John Brown led twenty-one men in a raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, intending to arm an enslaved insurrection across the South. The raid was crushed within 36 hours by a Marine detachment commanded by Colonel Robert E. Lee; Brown was tried in nearby Charles Town, hanged on December 2, and became a Northern martyr. The raid radicalized both sides and made disunion inevitable. Today the lower town is a National Historical Park where Brown's Fort (the engine house he defended), the armory grounds, and the dramatic confluence of the Potomac and Shenandoah rivers are all walkable in a long afternoon. The town changed hands eight times during the war.

**The Berth.** Stay in Charles Town, WV (10 minutes west); or in Frederick, MD (40 minutes east): Hotel Frederick.

**The Galley.** Harpers Ferry village: The Anvil Restaurant for the canonical Civil-War-era American; Battle Grounds Bakery & Coffee. Frederick: Volt; Family Meal; Brewer's Alley.

> I, John Brown, am now quite certain that the crimes of this guilty land will never be purged away but with blood.
> *John Brown, on the day of his execution, 1859*

### Stop 2. Fort Sumter & Charleston

**Waypoint:** South Carolina

Where the war began literally: at 4:30 a.m. on April 12, 1861, Confederate batteries on the Charleston shore opened fire on the federal garrison in Fort Sumter; the fort surrendered after 34 hours of bombardment. The fort sits on a man-made island in the harbor, accessed by ferry from Liberty Square; allow a full half-day for the round trip and tour. Charleston itself was the heart of the secessionist movement and one of the wealthiest cities in the antebellum South, much of that wealth built on the nearly half a million enslaved Africans who passed through its port. The International African American Museum (opened 2023), built directly above Gadsden's Wharf where roughly 40% of all enslaved Africans brought to North America first set foot on land, is the essential modern context. Eat shrimp and grits at Husk.

**The Berth.** The Spectator Hotel; Hotel Bennett on King Street; The Dewberry; Charleston Place; or Wentworth Mansion for the boutique.

**The Galley.** FIG (Mike Lata) for the canonical Lowcountry; Husk for the heritage; The Ordinary for the seafood; Hominy Grill for breakfast; Rodney Scott's BBQ for the whole-hog.

> We are not enemies, but friends. We must not be enemies.
> *Abraham Lincoln, First Inaugural Address, 1861*

### Stop 3. Manassas

**Waypoint:** Virginia

Where the nation learned the war would be terrible. On 21 July 1861, near a sluggish Virginia creek called Bull Run beside the railroad junction at Manassas, two armies of green volunteers blundered into the first major battle of the Civil War, while Washington picnickers drove out in carriages to watch the show. There was no show. By afternoon the Union attack had broken on Henry Hill, where a Virginia brigade stood firm and its commander, Thomas Jackson, earned the name Stonewall, and the Federal army fled back to the capital in a panicked rout among the overturned picnic baskets. The illusion of a quick and glorious war died that day; both sides now knew it would be long and bloody beyond imagining. Much of the field is preserved as Manassas National Battlefield Park, with the Henry House, the Stone House, and the statue of Jackson on his horse. Walk Henry Hill where the long agony began, and remember how cheaply the war was first imagined.

**The Berth.** Northern Virginia: the inns and hotels of old-town Manassas and Centreville; or base in Washington, DC, forty minutes east, within reach of the war's great monuments and the Eastern Theater battlefields.

**The Galley.** Northern Virginia: Southern country cooking in the old railroad towns; Virginia ham and biscuits; the farm-to-table tables of the Piedmont; barbecue and brunswick stew; local Virginia wine from the nearby vineyards.

> There is Jackson standing like a stone wall. Rally behind the Virginians!
> *attributed to General Barnard Bee, at Bull Run, 1861*

### Stop 4. Antietam National Battlefield

**Waypoint:** Maryland

Where the bloodiest day in American history was fought: September 17, 1862. Twelve hours of combat outside Sharpsburg produced 22,717 casualties, more than the total American casualties from the Revolution, the War of 1812, and the Mexican War combined. The Sunken Road (Bloody Lane), the Cornfield, and Burnside Bridge each have their own walking tours within the park. Tactically inconclusive, the battle was strategically decisive: the Confederate retreat gave Lincoln the political opening to issue the Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation five days later, transforming the war's purpose from Union to Union and Liberation. Less commercial than Gettysburg, more sobering. The September 17 anniversary draws living-history events.

**The Berth.** Stay in Frederick, MD (30 minutes east): Hotel Frederick; or in Hagerstown: Plaza Hotel and Suites.

**The Galley.** Frederick: Volt; Family Meal; Brewer's Alley. Hagerstown: 28 South for the modern American.

> In giving freedom to the slave, we assure freedom to the free.
> *Abraham Lincoln, 1862*

### Stop 5. Gettysburg National Military Park

**Waypoint:** Pennsylvania

Where the tide of the Confederacy crested and broke. The largest battle ever fought in North America and the war's turning point. Three days, July 1-3, 1863, 51,000 casualties. The Confederate high tide reached the stone wall on Cemetery Ridge during Pickett's Charge on the third afternoon, then receded; Lee retreated south the next day and never invaded the North again. The battlefield's preservation is unmatched, over 1,300 monuments across 6,000 acres, a 26-mile self-guided drive, with the Round Tops, Devil's Den, the Wheatfield, and Cemetery Ridge each yielding their own walks. Lincoln's Gettysburg Address was delivered at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery on November 19, 1863, 272 words, two minutes, the most-quoted speech in American history. Visit on Dedication Day (Nov 19) for the annual address re-delivery.

**The Berth.** Federal Pointe Inn in the borough; The Gettysburg Hotel since 1797 on Lincoln Square; or the Inn at Lincoln Square.

**The Galley.** 1776 American Bistro; The Pub & Restaurant on Lincoln Square; Dobbin House Tavern in the 1776 stone building; The Lincoln Diner for breakfast.

> That government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.
> *Abraham Lincoln, the Gettysburg Address, 1863*

### Stop 6. Vicksburg National Military Park

**Waypoint:** Mississippi

Where the Confederacy was split in two. The Confederacy's last stronghold on the Mississippi River, surrendered to Grant on July 4, 1863, one day after Lee's defeat at Gettysburg. The 47-day siege starved Vicksburg's military and civilian population alike; the loss split the Confederacy in half and gave the Union complete control of the river. The 16-mile auto tour through the park follows the original siege lines; the USS Cairo, a Union ironclad sunk in the Yazoo River, raised in 1965, now displayed under a protective canopy with most of its original timbers, is the unexpected highlight. The town refused to celebrate the Fourth of July for 81 years. Pair with the Mississippi Delta Blues Trail already on this calendar, Highway 61 connects them.

**The Berth.** Anchuca Historic Mansion & Inn for the converted Greek Revival; Cedar Grove Mansion Inn; or 10 South Rooftop Bar & Grill's adjacent property.

**The Galley.** Walnut Hills for the canonical Mississippi round-table service; 10 South for the rooftop view of the river; Rusty's Riverfront Grill for the catfish.

> Find out where your enemy is, get at him as soon as you can, strike him as hard as you can, and keep moving on.
> *Ulysses S. Grant*

### Stop 7. Andersonville

**Waypoint:** Georgia

Where the war showed its cruelest face. In a clearing of the Georgia pine woods, the Confederate prison camp known to history as Andersonville, officially Camp Sumter, opened in February 1864 and in fourteen months became a place of almost unimaginable suffering. Built for ten thousand, it held some forty-five thousand Union prisoners behind a stockade with a single foul creek for water and sewer alike, and a line called the Deadline that guards would shoot a man for crossing. Nearly thirteen thousand died of disease, exposure, and starvation, their bodies laid in trenches that are now the white-stoned ranks of the national cemetery. The camp's commandant, Henry Wirz, was hanged after the war, the only Confederate executed for war crimes, though many believe he was a scapegoat for a system that had run out of everything. Clara Barton came to help name the graves. Today the site holds the National Prisoner of War Museum, honoring captives of every American war. Walk the silent stockade ground and the cemetery rows, and grasp what war does past the battlefield.

**The Berth.** Southwest Georgia: the bed-and-breakfasts of nearby Americus, including a historic inn or two; the small-town inns of the region; or base in Macon, an hour northeast, for the larger city's antebellum streets.

**The Galley.** South Georgia country cooking: fried chicken and field peas; pulled-pork barbecue and Brunswick stew; cornbread and collard greens; sweet tea on a porch in the Georgia heat.

> It is going to be an awful place; thousands will die, no doubt.
> *John L. Ransom, Andersonville Diary*

### Stop 8. Whitney Plantation

**Waypoint:** St. John the Baptist Parish, Louisiana

Where the war's true cause is remembered. The only major plantation museum in the United States interpreted entirely from the perspective of the enslaved, opened to the public in 2014 after fifteen years of restoration by New Orleans attorney John Cummings, who privately funded the project. The 1790 plantation grew indigo, then sugar; over its first century, hundreds of enslaved Africans lived, worked, and died on its grounds. The memorials on site, the Wall of Honor with the names of the 107,000 enslaved people of antebellum Louisiana, the children's memorial, the Field of Angels, make the war's central cause unforgettable. An hour upriver from New Orleans on the Old River Road. The single most important Civil War-era site in the lower Mississippi. Pair with RÉVEILLON SEASON in New Orleans (December, already on calendar) or with the new orleans jazz & heritage festival (Apr-May).

**The Berth.** River Road, Louisiana: base in New Orleans (45 minutes downriver) at the Hotel Monteleone or the Pontchartrain; or the historic inns of the plantation country along the river.

**The Galley.** Louisiana River Road and New Orleans: gumbo, jambalaya, and boudin; the Creole and Cajun tables of the river parishes; café au lait and beignets in the city; a po'boy on the way downriver.

> No man can put a chain about the ankle of his fellow man without at last finding the other end fastened about his own neck.
> *Frederick Douglass*

### Stop 9. Appomattox Court House

**Waypoint:** Virginia

Where the war ended with grace. Appomattox Court House National Historical Park preserves the quiet Virginia village where, on 9 April 1865, Robert E. Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to Ulysses S. Grant in the parlor of Wilmer McLean's house, the symbolic end of the Civil War. The story holds a strange perfection: McLean had moved his family here from Manassas to escape the fighting, and so, as he put it, the war began in his front yard and ended in his front parlor. Grant's terms were famously generous, a deliberate act of healing: officers kept their sidearms and their horses, the men were paroled to return home, and the starving Confederates were fed from Union supplies. As the defeated army marched past to lay down its arms, a Union general called his troops to attention in salute, and the gesture was returned. The reconstructed McLean House and the courthouse anchor a small but deeply moving park. Visit on April 9, stand in the parlor where the killing stopped, and consider how a war ends.

**The Berth.** Central Virginia: the inns of Lynchburg and the Appomattox area; or historic Charlottesville within reach, near Monticello; country bed-and-breakfasts among the rolling Virginia farmland.

**The Galley.** Virginia: country ham and red-eye gravy; fried chicken and biscuits; peanut soup and Brunswick stew; the farm tables of the Piedmont; a glass of Virginia wine from the Monticello vineyards.

> Let us have peace.
> *Ulysses S. Grant*

### Stop 10. Ford's Theatre & the Lincoln Memorial

**Waypoint:** Washington, DC

Where the president was struck down at the hour of victory. Five days after Appomattox, on Good Friday, April 14, 1865, John Wilkes Booth shot Lincoln in the back of the head during the third act of Our American Cousin at Ford's Theatre on Tenth Street. Lincoln died at 7:22 the following morning in the back bedroom of the Petersen House across the street, where he had been carried. Both buildings are National Historic Sites, joint-ticketed, walkable in two hours. Fifty-seven years later, his memorial, the seated figure by Daniel Chester French, with the Gettysburg Address engraved on the south wall and the Second Inaugural on the north, was completed on the Mall. The natural ending of the trail. Stand at the foot of the statue and read the Second Inaugural in full. 'With malice toward none, with charity for all.'

**The Berth.** The Hay-Adams across from the White House; Riggs in the converted bank in Penn Quarter; or the Eaton DC for the design-set option.

**The Galley.** Minibar by José Andrés for the two-Michelin-star; Old Ebbitt Grill near the White House since 1856; Rasika in Penn Quarter for the modern Indian; Ben's Chili Bowl on U Street for the half-smoke.

> Now he belongs to the ages.
> *Edwin Stanton, at Lincoln's deathbed, 1865*

---

## Pilgrimage XVIII. The Eagle's Shadow

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of Napoleon Bonaparte and the Napoleonic Wars, from his birth on Corsica in 1769 through his death on St Helena in 1821, anchored to the battlefields, palaces, and exile islands where the empire was won and lost. The shape is unique: it begins on a Mediterranean island, sweeps through central Europe to its ultimate triumph at Austerlitz, collapses across Germany and France, and ends on the most remote inhabited rock in the South Atlantic. Best timed for the Battle of the Nations reenactment in Leipzig (mid-October), the Waterloo reenactment on the closest weekend to June 18, or the Austerlitz reenactment on December 2 (the FIXED anniversary, also Napoleon's coronation date). Three trips: a French swing (Corsica + Paris + Fontainebleau), a Central European loop (Austerlitz + Leipzig + Waterloo), and the two island exiles (Elba and St Helena, the latter genuinely remote).

> From the sublime to the ridiculous is only a step.
> *Napoleon Bonaparte*

### Stop 1. Ajaccio

**Waypoint:** Corsica, France

Where it began. Napoleon Bonaparte was born on August 15, 1769, in the Maison Bonaparte on Rue Saint-Charles in the old town of Ajaccio, fifteen months after Genoa sold Corsica to France, technically making him a Corsican by family and a Frenchman by accident of timing. The family home is now a national museum with the original furnishings, his cradle, and the genealogical archive. The Cathedral of Ajaccio where he was baptized is two blocks away. Ajaccio itself is a quietly beautiful Mediterranean port with strong food (Corsican charcuterie, brocciu cheese, fiadone) and the Maquis country, the rugged scrub he played in as a child, beginning at the city limits. Best May, June, or September.

**The Berth.** Ajaccio: the seafront Hôtel Les Mouettes in a 19th-century villa; the Palazzu u Domu in the old town; or a coastal hotel along the Gulf of Ajaccio. Inland: the granite village inns of the Corsican interior.

**The Galley.** Corsican: charcuterie (figatellu, lonzu, coppa) from the Maquis-fed pigs; brocciu cheese in everything; fiadone and canistrelli; chestnut-flour dishes; the seafood of the gulf and a glass of Patrimonio wine.

> I was born when Corsica was dying.
> *Napoleon Bonaparte, on his birth in Ajaccio*

### Stop 2. Paris

**Waypoint:** Les Invalides, the Arc de Triomphe & the Vendôme Column

Where the emperor reigned and now lies. Three monuments, walking distance apart in the 1st and 7th arrondissements: the Arc de Triomphe, commissioned by Napoleon in 1806 to honor the Grande Armée and completed fifteen years after his death; the Vendôme Column, cast in 1810 from the bronze of 1,200 cannons captured at Austerlitz, with reliefs spiraling up the shaft like Trajan's; and Les Invalides, the great gilded-dome veterans' hospital where Napoleon's body, repatriated from St Helena in 1840 (nineteen years after his death), lies in a porphyry sarcophagus on the lower level of the Église du Dôme, surrounded by the tombs of his marshals. Allow a full day. Pair with any Paris-anchored event already on this calendar.

**The Berth.** Hôtel de Crillon on Place de la Concorde; Le Meurice; the Lutetia on the Left Bank; or the Hôtel des Grands Boulevards in the 2nd for the small-budget option.

**The Galley.** Le Comptoir du Relais for canonical bistro; Septime in the 11th; L'Arpège (Alain Passard); Frenchie Bar à Vins after the show; Du Pain et des Idées for the breakfast escargot.

> Glory is fleeting, but obscurity is forever.
> *Napoleon Bonaparte*

### Stop 3. Austerlitz

**Waypoint:** Czech Republic

Where Napoleon won his masterpiece. On December 2, 1805, the first anniversary of his coronation as Emperor, Napoleon defeated the combined Russian and Austrian armies on the rolling fields outside the Moravian town of Slavkov u Brna ('Austerlitz' in German). 'The Battle of the Three Emperors,' for the three monarchs present (Napoleon, Tsar Alexander I, Emperor Francis II of the Holy Roman Empire), is taught in every staff college on Earth as the textbook example of the offensive-defensive double trap. The Pratzen Heights are walkable; the Cairn of Peace on the central knoll, completed in 1912 by an Austrian peace movement, is the principal monument. The Austerlitz Castle nearby served as the Russian-Austrian headquarters and now houses a battle museum. December 2 brings annual reenactments in period uniform across the original ground.

**The Berth.** Prague: Augustine, Aria Hotel, or the Carlo IV. In Brno: The Barceló Brno Palace or Grandezza Hotel Luxury Palace.

**The Galley.** Prague: Field; La Degustation Bohême Bourgeoise; U Kroka for canonical svíčková; Lokál for the pilsner-and-pork institution. Brno: Pavillon for the modern Czech.

> Soldiers, I am pleased with you. You have decked your eagles with immortal glory.
> *Napoleon Bonaparte, proclamation after Austerlitz, 1805*

### Stop 4. Trafalgar & HMS Victory

**Waypoint:** Portsmouth, England, and Cape Trafalgar, Spain

Where the sea was lost, and the invasion died. Six weeks before Austerlitz, on 21 October 1805, off Cape Trafalgar on the Atlantic coast of Spain, the British fleet under Admiral Lord Nelson destroyed the combined French and Spanish fleet and ended forever Napoleon's hope of invading England. Nelson, who signaled his fleet that England expects that every man will do his duty, was shot by a sniper on his own quarterdeck at the height of the battle and died as victory was won, becoming Britain's greatest naval hero in the moment of his death. So long as Britain ruled the sea, Napoleon could never be wholly master of Europe, and Trafalgar sealed that fact for a century. Nelson's flagship, HMS Victory, survives in dry dock at Portsmouth, the world's oldest commissioned warship, and you can walk her decks and stand on the very plaque where he fell. Pace the quarterdeck of the Victory where Nelson died, then look out from the Spanish cape to the sea that kept Britain free.

**The Berth.** Portsmouth: the waterfront hotels by the Historic Dockyard and the Spinnaker Tower; or for the Spanish cape, the white towns of the Costa de la Luz, Vejer de la Frontera and Conil, near Cape Trafalgar itself.

**The Galley.** English naval port: fish and chips on the Portsmouth quay; a pint of ale in an old sailors' pub; or on the Spanish side, the fried fish and sherry of Cádiz, the bluefin tuna of the Trafalgar coast, gazpacho in the heat.

> England expects that every man will do his duty.
> *Admiral Lord Nelson, at Trafalgar*

### Stop 5. Borodino & the Road to Moscow

**Waypoint:** near Mozhaysk, Russia

Where the empire began to die. In June 1812 Napoleon led the largest army Europe had ever seen, some six hundred thousand men, across the Niemen into Russia, certain of a swift victory. Instead the Russians fell back for months, burning their own land behind them, until the veteran Kutuzov at last turned to fight a hundred and twenty kilometers west of Moscow. The Battle of Borodino, on 7 September 1812, was the bloodiest single day of the entire Napoleonic Wars: some seventy thousand men fell in fifteen hours of cannon fire that witnesses said rolled like unbroken thunder. Napoleon won the field but not the war. He entered a Moscow emptied of its people and set ablaze, found no one to surrender to, and began too late the winter retreat that destroyed the Grande Armée and the empire with it. The Borodino field is preserved with its monuments, museum, and great autumn reenactment. Walk the redoubts where the empire crested and broke, and feel how far it is to Moscow, and how far back.

**The Berth.** Moscow region: base in Moscow itself, two hours east, for its incomparable museums and the 1812 panorama; or the simple inns and guesthouses near Mozhaysk and the Borodino field for the early-morning quiet of the battlefield.

**The Galley.** Russian: borscht and beef stroganoff; blini with sour cream; pelmeni dumplings; black bread and pickles; a glass of vodka against the cold, the same cold that broke an empire on the long road home.

> Of all my battles, the most terrible was the one before Moscow.
> *Napoleon Bonaparte, on Borodino*

### Stop 6. Leipzig

**Waypoint:** Battle of the Nations, Germany

Where the nations turned on the emperor. The largest battle fought in Europe before the First World War: from October 16 to 19, 1813, six hundred thousand men of seven nations clashed across the fields southeast of Leipzig. Napoleon's outnumbered army, the survivors of the catastrophic 1812 invasion of Russia, where the Grande Armée of 600,000 had been reduced to fewer than 30,000 by Russian winter, scorched-earth tactics, and the bloody draw at Borodino on September 7, was finally crushed by the combined coalition forces here. The Völkerschlachtdenkmal (Monument to the Battle of the Nations), completed in 1913 on the centenary, is a 91-meter Wagnerian colossus visible from the autobahn miles away, climb the 364 steps for the view across the battlefield. The Forum 1813 museum at its base is excellent. The annual reenactment in mid-October draws thousands of period-uniformed soldiers from across Europe.

**The Berth.** Berlin: Hotel Adlon Kempinski; Soho House Berlin; 25hours Bikini. Munich: Bayerischer Hof. Hamburg: The Fontenay. Frankfurt: Roomers.

**The Galley.** Berlin: Markthalle Neun; Mustafa's Gemüse Kebap; Lode & Stijn. Munich: Tantris; Hofbräuhaus; Schneider Bräuhaus. Hamburg: Fischmarkt; Bullerei. Frankfurt: Adolf Wagner; Lafleur.

> In war, the moral is to the physical as three to one.
> *Napoleon Bonaparte*

### Stop 7. Château de Fontainebleau

**Waypoint:** France

Where the empire first ended. After the Allied armies entered Paris on March 31, 1814, Napoleon retreated seventy kilometers south to his favorite palace and signed his unconditional abdication on April 6 in the Salon Rouge. On April 20, in the Cour des Adieux (the White Horse Courtyard), he made his famous farewell to the Old Guard, kissing the eagle of the regimental standard before departing for exile on Elba. The palace itself has been a royal residence since the 12th century and was Napoleon's preferred home; both the Salon Rouge (with the original abdication-table) and his apartments are preserved. Easy day trip from Paris by rail, one hour from Gare de Lyon.

**The Berth.** Paris: Hôtel de Crillon, Le Meurice, Lutetia. Provence: La Bastide de Gordes; Hotel Crillon le Brave. Burgundy: Le Cep in Beaune; Loire: Domaine des Hauts de Loire.

**The Galley.** Paris: Le Comptoir du Relais; Septime; L'Arpège; Frenchie. Provence: La Mirande in Avignon; Baumanière. Burgundy: Lameloise in Chagny; Loire: Le Choiseul in Amboise.

> Soldiers of my Old Guard, I bid you farewell. For twenty years you have been my constant companions on the road to honour and glory.
> *Napoleon Bonaparte, farewell to the Old Guard, Fontainebleau, 1814*

### Stop 8. Elba

**Waypoint:** Tuscany, Italy

Where the emperor was first exiled, and escaped. His first exile ran from May 4, 1814 to February 26, 1815. The Allied powers granted Napoleon sovereignty over the small Tuscan island of Elba and an annual income of two million francs; he ruled it as Emperor of Elba for 300 days, reformed its mining operations, built roads, and personally redesigned the gardens at the Villa San Martino. From the Villa dei Mulini in Portoferraio, his official residence, now a museum preserved with the original furnishings, he could see the Italian mainland and his native Corsica on a clear day, which helped fuel his return. He sailed for France on the brig L'Inconstant on February 26, 1815, beginning the Hundred Days. The island today is a quiet Tuscan archipelago destination, ferry from Piombino, beaches, vineyards, the two Napoleon villas. Pair with palio di siena (July or August, already on calendar); Tuscany makes a natural extended trip.

**The Berth.** Rome: Hotel de Russie; Hassler. Florence: Hotel Savoy; J.K. Place. Milan: Bulgari Milano. Venice: Aman Venice; Cipriani.

**The Galley.** Rome: Roscioli; Felice a Testaccio; Da Cesare al Casaletto. Florence: Enoteca Pinchiorri; Sostanza; All'Antico Vinaio. Milan: Trussardi alla Scala; Trattoria Milanese. Venice: Alle Testiere; Antiche Carampane.

> Impossible is a word to be found only in the dictionary of fools.
> *Napoleon Bonaparte*

### Stop 9. Waterloo Battlefield

**Waypoint:** Belgium

Where it ended, on Sunday, June 18, 1815. After his return from Elba in March, the rapid reconstitution of an army, and a brilliant initial campaign in early June, Napoleon met the combined Anglo-Allied force under Wellington and the Prussian army under Blücher on the rolling farmland twenty kilometers south of Brussels. Twelve hours of combat, 50,000 casualties, the Old Guard's failed final charge at La Haye Sainte, and the empire was over. The Lion's Mound, a 43-meter artificial hill topped by a cast-iron lion, completed in 1826, is the visitor anchor; climb the 226 steps for the view down across the entire battlefield. The Hougoumont farmhouse complex, the Anglo-Allied right anchor where the British Guards held all day, has been restored and is the most evocative single building on the field. The annual reenactment on the weekend closest to June 18 is the largest in Europe.

**The Berth.** Brussels: Hotel Amigo near the Grand-Place; Steigenberger Wiltcher's; or the boutique Vintage Hotel. Bruges: Hotel Dukes' Palace; Relais Bourgondisch Cruyce.

**The Galley.** Brussels: Comme Chez Soi for the canonical Belgian since 1926; Bon Bon for Christophe Hardiquest's Michelin two-star; Fin de Siècle for the bistronomy. Bruges: De Karmeliet; Park Restaurant for the canonical.

> It has been a damned nice thing — the nearest run thing you ever saw in your life.
> *the Duke of Wellington, on Waterloo*

### Stop 10. St Helena

**Waypoint:** South Atlantic

Where the emperor died, alone at the end of the world. His final exile, and where his body lay for nineteen years before its return to Paris. After Waterloo, Napoleon surrendered to a British warship and was transported four thousand miles to St Helena, a small volcanic island halfway between Africa and South America, chosen specifically for its remoteness. He lived at Longwood House (still preserved as French national property by treaty) for five and a half years and died there on May 5, 1821, at the age of 51, likely of stomach cancer, though arsenic-poisoning theories persist. His original tomb in the Sane Valley is empty; his body was repatriated to Paris in 1840 and now rests at Les Invalides. St Helena was reachable only by Royal Mail ship until the airport finally opened in 2017; even now, flights run from Johannesburg only once a week. The most remote stop in this calendar, and the natural ending of the trail. The pilgrimage doesn't end at the tomb in Paris. It ends here, where he actually died.

**The Berth.** St Helena: Mantis St Helena in Jamestown is the only international-standard hotel on the island. Book with the RMS or air arrival.

**The Galley.** Mantis St Helena restaurant; Anne's Place for the local fish-and-chips and tuna fishcakes; the Consulate Hotel for the heritage dining room.

> What a romance my life has been.
> *Napoleon Bonaparte, at St Helena*

---

## Pilgrimage XIX. In Flanders Fields

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of the First World War, from the assassination in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914, that triggered four years of industrial slaughter, through to the railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne where the Armistice was signed at 5:10 a.m. on November 11, 1918. Anchored to the principal battlefields and memorials of the Western Front (Ypres, the Somme, Verdun, Vimy, Meuse-Argonne) plus the Gallipoli peninsula in Türkiye and the Sarajevo street corner where it all began. Best timed for Armistice Day (November 11, FIXED, the most-observed commemoration across Europe), Anzac Day (April 25, FIXED, with dawn services at Gallipoli and across the former British Empire), or for the daily Last Post ceremony at the Menin Gate in Ypres, performed at 8 p.m. every evening since 1928. Two trips: a Western Front circuit of seven to ten days (Belgium, northern France, the Meuse), and a separate journey to Sarajevo and Gallipoli that pairs with a longer Balkans-and-Türkiye itinerary.

> In Flanders fields the poppies blow, between the crosses, row on row.
> *John McCrae, In Flanders Fields, 1915*

### Stop 1. Sarajevo

**Waypoint:** Bosnia and Herzegovina

Where two pistol shots set the world on fire. On the morning of June 28, 1914, a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb named Gavrilo Princip stepped out of Schiller's delicatessen on the corner of Obala Kulina Bana and Zelenih Beretki and fired two pistol shots into Archduke Franz Ferdinand's open touring car as it reversed through a wrong turn. The Archduke and his wife Sophie were both dead within ten minutes. Within five weeks, every great power of Europe was at war. The corner today is marked by a small plaque and the Sarajevo Museum 1878-1918 in the building that was Schiller's; the Latin Bridge over the Miljacka river is twenty meters away. Sarajevo itself is one of the most quietly haunting cities in Europe, Ottoman, Habsburg, and Yugoslav strata layered on top of each other, the scars of the 1992-1996 siege still visible on every façade. Eat nevapi at Željo. Pair with a longer Balkans trip.

**The Berth.** Sarajevo: Hotel Europe on Vladislava Skarića (the heritage 1882 dame); Hotel Bristol Sarajevo; or Boutique Hotel Aziza in the historic Vratnik.

**The Galley.** Sarajevo: Mrkva ćevabdžinica for the canonical ćevapi (10 pieces in a somun bun); Aščinica Hadži Zikina Kuća for the slow-cooked Bosnian; Inat Kuća (the Spite House) on Obala Kulina Bana for the historic atmosphere.

> The lamps are going out all over Europe; we shall not see them lit again in our lifetime.
> *Sir Edward Grey, on the eve of war, 1914*

### Stop 2. Ypres

**Waypoint:** Flanders, Belgium

Where half a million of the Empire's dead lie. The British and Commonwealth sector for nearly the entire war: roughly half a million men of the British Empire died in the salient outside Ypres (now Ieper) between 1914 and 1918. The medieval town was reduced to dust and rebuilt brick by brick after the war. The Menin Gate Memorial, completed in 1927, lists the names of 54,000 Commonwealth soldiers missing without graves; the Last Post ceremony has been performed beneath the gate every evening at 8 p.m. since 1928, interrupted only during the German occupation. Tyne Cot Cemetery, ten kilometers east, is the largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the world, 11,961 graves and 35,000 further names on the Memorial to the Missing for those who fell in the Passchendaele offensive of 1917. The In Flanders Fields Museum in the rebuilt Cloth Hall (Lakenhallen) is essential context. Stay in Ypres at least one night to attend the 8 p.m. Last Post ceremony, unbroken since 1928, and stand beneath the Menin Gate as the bugles sound for the missing.

**The Berth.** Brussels: Hotel Amigo near the Grand-Place; Steigenberger Wiltcher's; or the boutique Vintage Hotel. Bruges: Hotel Dukes' Palace; Relais Bourgondisch Cruyce.

**The Galley.** Brussels: Comme Chez Soi for the canonical Belgian since 1926; Bon Bon for Christophe Hardiquest's Michelin two-star; Fin de Siècle for the bistronomy. Bruges: De Karmeliet; Park Restaurant for the canonical.

> ...some corner of a foreign field that is for ever England.
> *Rupert Brooke, The Soldier, 1914*

### Stop 3. Tyne Cot & Passchendaele

**Waypoint:** Zonnebeke, Flanders, Belgium

Where the largest field of the Commonwealth dead lies. A few miles northeast of Ypres, on the gentle rise the soldiers called Passchendaele, lies Tyne Cot, the largest Commonwealth war cemetery in the world, where nearly twelve thousand headstones stand in white ranks across the slope and the names of another thirty-five thousand men with no known grave are carved on the memorial wall behind them. The Third Battle of Ypres in the autumn of 1917, Passchendaele in common memory, was the war at its most pitiless: months of attritional assault across a shell-churned bog where the rain never stopped and wounded men drowned in the mud of the craters, half a million casualties on both sides for a few miles of ruined ground that was abandoned the following spring. The village that gave the battle its name is rebuilt and quiet now, the fields green again, which is somehow the hardest thing of all. Walk the white rows at Tyne Cot in the Flanders silence, read the ages on the stones, and try to comprehend the arithmetic.

**The Berth.** Ypres (Ieper): the boutique hotels of the rebuilt medieval town around the Cloth Hall; the country inns of the Salient; or a room near the Menin Gate to walk to the nightly Last Post.

**The Galley.** Flemish: the beef-and-beer stew carbonnade; moules-frites; Belgian fries with mayonnaise; the Trappist and abbey ales of Flanders; Belgian chocolate; a quiet meal in Ypres after the evening ceremony.

> I died in hell. They called it Passchendaele.
> *Siegfried Sassoon*

### Stop 4. Verdun

**Waypoint:** Lorraine, France

Where France bled and would not break. The longest battle of the war and the symbol of French national sacrifice. From February 21 to December 18, 1916, French and German forces fought across a few square miles of the Meuse hills outside Verdun, producing roughly 700,000 casualties on both sides. Nine villages within the battle zone were destroyed and never rebuilt, they are still designated 'mort pour la France' on French maps. The Douaumont Ossuary, completed in 1932, contains the unidentified remains of 130,000 French and German soldiers in 46 sealed alcoves, visible through small windows around the lower exterior. Fort Douaumont, the largest of the Verdun fortresses, fell to German troops on the fourth day of the battle and was retaken by France eight months later, its scarred concrete and steel cupolas can be entered. The Verdun Memorial Museum in Fleury reopened in 2016 with modernized exhibits. Pair with the Somme, they are 200 kilometers apart.

**The Berth.** Verdun: the hotels of the town on the Meuse (the Hostellerie du Coq Hardi); or base in Metz or Nancy, the great cities of Lorraine, an hour or so away, for the wider region.

**The Galley.** Lorraine: the quiche lorraine in its homeland; the Verdun dragée (sugared almond) made here since the Middle Ages; potée lorraine; mirabelle plums; a quiet meal in the town after the battlefields.

> Ils ne passeront pas — They shall not pass.
> *the French cry at Verdun, 1916*

### Stop 5. The Somme

**Waypoint:** Picardy, northern France

Where twenty thousand fell in a single morning. On the morning of 1 July 1916, after a week-long bombardment they believed had destroyed the German defenses, the British infantry climbed from their trenches and walked in long lines toward the enemy, and were cut down in their thousands by machine guns the shelling had never reached: nearly twenty thousand British soldiers killed and forty thousand wounded in a single day, the worst in the history of the British Army, and the battle ground on for four more months. The Somme is now a landscape of quiet memorials among the wheat. At Thiepval, Lutyens' vast brick arch bears the names of more than seventy-two thousand men with no known grave. At Beaumont-Hamel, the preserved trenches and the bronze caribou remember the Newfoundland Regiment, ninety percent of them fallen in half an hour. At the great Lochnagar Crater, a mine blast still gapes in the chalk. Stand at Thiepval beneath the names without end, and grasp what the word Somme has meant for a century.

**The Berth.** The Somme: base in the market town of Albert, with its golden basilica and its 1916 museum; the country hotels and chambres d'hotes of Picardy among the battlefields and cemeteries.

**The Galley.** Picard: the ficelle picarde; duck and pate; the rustic cooking of the Somme valley; local cider and beer; a simple lunch in Albert between visits to the silent fields.

> The Somme. The whole of human history seemed to have died there.
> *after the soldiers of the Somme*

### Stop 6. Vimy Ridge

**Waypoint:** Pas-de-Calais, France

Where Canada came of age. The Canadian National Vimy Memorial, designed by Walter Allward, completed in 1936, sits on the dominating ridge captured by all four Canadian divisions fighting together for the first time across Easter Monday morning, April 9, 1917. The twin white pylons, thirty meters tall in Croatian Seget limestone, can be seen from twenty kilometers across the Pas-de-Calais plain; twenty allegorical figures around the base include the famous Canada Bereft mourning her dead at the front of the monument. The names of 11,285 Canadian soldiers killed in France with no known grave are inscribed on the memorial walls. The preserved trenches and underground tunnels of the Canadian and German front lines are open to the public, with student guides from Canadian universities staffing the visitor center. Combine with Notre-Dame-de-Lorette National Cemetery, the largest French military cemetery in the world, 40,000 graves, six kilometers away.

**The Berth.** Paris: Hôtel de Crillon, Le Meurice, Lutetia. Provence: La Bastide de Gordes; Hotel Crillon le Brave. Burgundy: Le Cep in Beaune; Loire: Domaine des Hauts de Loire.

**The Galley.** Paris: Le Comptoir du Relais; Septime; L'Arpège; Frenchie. Provence: La Mirande in Avignon; Baumanière. Burgundy: Lameloise in Chagny; Loire: Le Choiseul in Amboise.

> In those few minutes I witnessed the birth of a nation.
> *Brigadier-General Alexander Ross, on Vimy Ridge*

### Stop 7. Caporetto

**Waypoint:** the Soca valley, Slovenia

Where the war was fought among rock and ice. Far from Flanders, along the turquoise Soca river in what is now western Slovenia, Italy and Austria-Hungary fought a dozen brutal battles up and down the Isonzo Front between 1915 and 1917, a war waged among rock and ice at altitude, where as many men died of avalanche and cold as of bullets. It climaxed in October 1917 at the Battle of Caporetto, the modern Kobarid, when a German-Austrian assault using new infiltration tactics shattered the Italian line and sent the army reeling sixty miles in retreat, one of the great routs of the war. A young American ambulance driver named Ernest Hemingway served on this front and drew from it A Farewell to Arms, whose retreat from Caporetto is among the finest war writing ever made. The superb Kobarid Museum tells the story without victors, and the Walk of Peace threads the old front through stunning mountain country. Walk the Soca valley where the river runs impossibly blue, and find the war that the West forgot.

**The Berth.** The Soca valley: the boutique hotels and guesthouses of Kobarid and Bovec; alpine lodges among the Julian Alps; or Lake Bled and Ljubljana within reach for the wider Slovenian journey.

**The Galley.** Soca valley: the Kobarid cheese dumplings (kobariski struklji); fresh trout from the river; Slovenian and Friulian alpine cooking; the wines of the Goriska Brda hills; a streamside lunch in one of the valley's celebrated restaurants.

> I was always embarrassed by the words sacred, glorious, and sacrifice.
> *Ernest Hemingway, A Farewell to Arms*

### Stop 8. Gallipoli

**Waypoint:** Çanakkale Province, Türkiye

Where two young nations were forged in the surf. The failed Allied amphibious campaign that defined Australian and New Zealand military identity. From April 25, 1915 to January 9, 1916, British, French, Australian, New Zealand, and Indian troops attempted to force the Dardanelles strait and knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war by capturing Constantinople; the Turkish defense, organized by a young officer named Mustafa Kemal, later Atatürk, held the high ground and turned the campaign into eight months of stalemate. Roughly 130,000 men died on the peninsula. Anzac Cove, where the Australian and New Zealand troops landed in the dawn surf, is now Anzac Koyu; the Lone Pine and Chunuk Bair memorials sit on the heights above. The Anzac Day dawn service on April 25, FIXED, the morning of the original landing, draws thousands of pilgrims from Australia and New Zealand annually and books out a year ahead. Ferry from Çanakkale on the Asian shore.

**The Berth.** Istanbul: Çırağan Palace Kempinski on the Bosphorus; the Pera Palace in Beyoğlu; the Sumahan on the Asian shore. Cappadocia: Argos in Cappadocia.

**The Galley.** Istanbul: Mikla on the rooftop of the Marmara Pera; Pandeli in the Spice Bazaar; Karaköy Lokantası; Çiya Sofrası in Kadıköy. Anatolia: Asitane in Edirnekapı for the Ottoman court cuisine.

> Those heroes that shed their blood now lie in the soil of a friendly country; rest in peace.
> *Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, to the Anzac mothers, 1934*

### Stop 9. Meuse-Argonne American Cemetery

**Waypoint:** Romagne-sous-Montfaucon, France

Where America paid its heaviest price. The deadliest American campaign of the First World War, and still one of the deadliest American military operations in history. The Meuse-Argonne Offensive ran from September 26 to November 11, 1918, six weeks ending with the armistice itself. Twenty-six thousand, two hundred seventy-seven American soldiers were killed in 47 days. The Meuse-Argonne American Cemetery at Romagne-sous-Montfaucon contains 14,246 graves arranged in eight plots radiating from a central reflecting pool, the largest American military cemetery in Europe. The American Battle Monuments Commission staffs the visitor center and runs guided walks across engagement sites in the surrounding Argonne Forest. Combine with Verdun, sixty kilometers south.

**The Berth.** Paris: Hôtel de Crillon, Le Meurice, Lutetia. Provence: La Bastide de Gordes; Hotel Crillon le Brave. Burgundy: Le Cep in Beaune; Loire: Domaine des Hauts de Loire.

**The Galley.** Paris: Le Comptoir du Relais; Septime; L'Arpège; Frenchie. Provence: La Mirande in Avignon; Baumanière. Burgundy: Lameloise in Chagny; Loire: Le Choiseul in Amboise.

> I have a rendezvous with Death at some disputed barricade.
> *Alan Seeger, American volunteer killed in France, 1916*

### Stop 10. Compiègne Forest

**Waypoint:** Picardy, France

Where it ended. At 5:10 in the morning of November 11, 1918, in a railway carriage of the French commander Marshal Foch parked in a forest clearing 80 kilometers north of Paris, German envoys signed the Armistice, to take effect six hours later, on the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month. The Clairière de l'Armistice in the Forest of Compiègne preserves the original siding, with a stone marker on the spot where the carriage stood and an Armistice Museum housing a faithful replica of the carriage itself (the original was taken to Berlin in 1940 by Hitler, who staged the French WWII surrender in the same carriage on the same spot, and destroyed by the SS at the end of the war). The marble slab in the center of the clearing is inscribed: 'Here on the eleventh of November 1918 succumbed the criminal pride of the German Empire, vanquished by the free peoples it had set out to enslave.' Visit any time, but ideally on November 11. From here, the trail extends naturally to the Imperial War Museum in London for a final day of context.

**The Berth.** Compiègne: the hotels of the elegant town by its great royal château; or base in Paris (80 kilometers south, an hour by rail) for the wider approach to the armistice clearing.

**The Galley.** Picardy and the Oise: the ficelle picarde; the game and forest cooking of the Compiègne woods; the patisseries of the old town; a quiet lunch before the drive out to the Clairière.

> The war that will end war.
> *H.G. Wells, 1914*

---

## Pilgrimage XX. A World in Flames

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of the Second World War, from the German naval bombardment of Westerplatte at 4:48 a.m. on September 1, 1939 that opened the war in Europe, through to the surrender of Japan aboard the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay on September 2, 1945 that closed it on the other side of the Earth. Anchored to the war's principal fronts (Poland, the Netherlands, Normandy, the Ardennes, Berlin, the Pacific), to its central moral horror (Auschwitz-Birkenau and the Holocaust memorials at Anne Frank House and Berlin), and to its two American endpoints (Pearl Harbor and Hiroshima). Best timed for the D-Day anniversary on June 6 (FIXED, with heads of state in Normandy), the Pearl Harbor anniversary on December 7, the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Ceremony on August 6 at 8:15 a.m., or International Holocaust Remembrance Day on January 27 (the date Auschwitz was liberated by the Red Army in 1945). Three trips, six to ten days each: a Polish-German circuit (Westerplatte + Auschwitz + Berlin), a Western Front circuit (Anne Frank + Normandy + Bastogne), and a Pacific journey (Pearl Harbor + Hiroshima, with the USS Missouri at anchor in Tokyo Bay where the surrender was signed on September 2, 1945).

> We have nothing to fear but fear itself.
> *Franklin D. Roosevelt, First Inaugural, 1933*

### Stop 1. Westerplatte & Gdańsk

**Waypoint:** Poland

Where the war began. At 4:48 a.m. on September 1, 1939, the German battleship Schleswig-Holstein, anchored on a 'goodwill' visit in the Free City of Danzig harbor, opened fire on the Polish military transit depot at Westerplatte, the first shots of the Second World War in Europe. The Polish garrison of 182 men, expected to hold for twelve hours, held out for seven days against air and naval bombardment, German marines, and panzers. The peninsula today is a memorial park with the surviving guardhouse ruins, the 25-meter Monument to the Coast Defenders (1966), and original brick walls still scarred with shell impacts. Combine with the European Solidarity Centre at the nearby Gdansk Shipyard, where the war's other historical bookend, the 1980-1989 collapse of communism, was set in motion. Eat pierogi at Pierogarnia Mandu in the old town.

**The Berth.** Warsaw: Hotel Bristol on Krakowskie Przedmieście; H15 Boutique Hotel; Raffles Europejski. Kraków: Stary Hotel; Hotel Copernicus.

**The Galley.** Warsaw: Atelier Amaro for the Michelin-starred Polish; Bibenda for the modern; pierogi at Pierogarnia Mandu. Kraków: Bottiglieria 1881; Pod Aniołami for canonical Polish.

> Nigdy więcej wojny — never again war.
> *inscription, Westerplatte Memorial, Gdańsk*

### Stop 2. Auschwitz-Birkenau

**Waypoint:** Oświęcim, Poland

Where the Holocaust reached its darkest depth. The central site of the Holocaust and the moral center of any honest pilgrimage of the Second World War. Of the approximately six million Jews murdered by Nazi Germany and its collaborators, roughly 1.1 million were killed at Auschwitz-Birkenau between 1942 and 1945, alongside roughly 100,000 non-Jewish victims (Polish political prisoners, Soviet POWs, Roma and Sinti, others). The original camp (Auschwitz I) preserves the brick barracks and the Arbeit Macht Frei gate; Birkenau, two kilometers away, preserves the rail spur, the unloading ramp, the brick chimneys of the destroyed gas chambers, and the wooden barracks of the women's camp. Free entry; pre-booking required and fills weeks ahead. Plan a full day. Take the guided tour. Stand at the end of the rail spur where the selections happened. The most morally serious place to stand in modern Europe.

**The Berth.** Warsaw: Hotel Bristol on Krakowskie Przedmieście; H15 Boutique Hotel; Raffles Europejski. Kraków: Stary Hotel; Hotel Copernicus.

**The Galley.** Warsaw: Atelier Amaro for the Michelin-starred Polish; Bibenda for the modern; pierogi at Pierogarnia Mandu. Kraków: Bottiglieria 1881; Pod Aniołami for canonical Polish.

> For the dead and the living, we must bear witness.
> *Elie Wiesel*

### Stop 3. Anne Frank House

**Waypoint:** Amsterdam, the Netherlands

Where a girl wrote hope into hiding. The Achterhuis, the 'Secret Annex' behind the rotating bookcase at Prinsengracht 263, where Anne Frank, her parents Otto and Edith, her sister Margot, and four others hid from July 1942 until they were betrayed and arrested on August 4, 1944. Anne died at Bergen-Belsen in February 1945, two months before British troops liberated the camp; she was fifteen. The annex is preserved exactly as the Gestapo left it on the day of the arrest, Otto, the only one of the eight to survive, requested the rooms be left bare. Anne's diary, hidden in the office below by family friend Miep Gies during the arrest and recovered after the war, is now the most-read first-person account of the Holocaust on Earth. Timed-entry tickets release exactly six weeks ahead and sell out within an hour. Pair with a visit to Westerbork transit camp ninety minutes east, where Anne and 102,000 other Dutch Jews were held before deportation.

**The Berth.** The Hoxton on the Herengracht; or Pulitzer Amsterdam in the canal-house compound; or Sir Adam in the A'DAM Tower for the design-set view.

**The Galley.** De Kas in the greenhouse; Restaurant De Compagnon in the Red Light District for old Dutch; Mata Hari for Indonesian rijsttafel; Café de Klos for ribs.

> In spite of everything, I still believe that people are really good at heart.
> *Anne Frank, diary, July 15, 1944*

### Stop 4. Stalingrad

**Waypoint:** Volgograd, Russia

Where the tide of the war turned. On the banks of the Volga, in the city that then bore Stalin's name, was fought the largest and bloodiest battle in human history. From the late summer of 1942 into the bitter February of 1943, German and Soviet armies tore at each other through the rubble of the city in a struggle so savage that men fought room by room and floor by floor for a single ruined house, and a soldier's life at the front was measured in hours. When the encircled German Sixth Army finally surrendered, some two million men on both sides had been killed, wounded, or captured, and the myth of German invincibility was broken. From Stalingrad onward, the Wehrmacht was in retreat, and the road led back to Berlin. Above the city now rises Mamayev Kurgan, the hill where the fighting was fiercest, crowned by the colossal statue The Motherland Calls, a woman with a sword raised against the sky; the hill itself is a grave for tens of thousands. Climb to the Motherland through the solemn Hall of Military Glory, and grasp the true scale of the war in the East.

**The Berth.** Volgograd: the riverside hotels along the Volga embankment; the comfortable hotels of the rebuilt city center; or a simple guesthouse from which to walk the vast memorial complex at dawn before the crowds.

**The Galley.** Russian and Volga fare: borscht and solyanka soup; pelmeni and blini; grilled river fish from the Volga; black bread, pickles, and honey cake; a glass of kvass or vodka in a city that knows the cost of survival.

> For us there is no land beyond the Volga.
> *the Soviet defenders of Stalingrad, 1942*

### Stop 5. Normandy D-Day Beaches

**Waypoint:** France

Where the liberation of Europe began. The largest amphibious operation in history. On the morning of June 6, 1944, D-Day, 156,000 Allied troops landed across five beaches on a 50-mile stretch of the Norman coast: Utah and Omaha (American), Gold and Sword (British), Juno (Canadian), supported by 13,000 paratroopers, 6,939 ships, and 11,590 aircraft. The Normandy American Cemetery at Colleville-sur-Mer, perched on the bluff above Omaha Beach, holds 9,388 white marble crosses and Stars of David in perfectly aligned ranks; the visitor center opened in 2007 is among the best in Europe. Pointe du Hoc, where US Army Rangers scaled a 100-foot cliff under fire to silence German guns, is preserved with the original shell craters and bunkers intact. The reconstructed Mulberry Harbor at Arromanches, the prefabricated artificial port the British towed across the Channel piece by piece, is still partially visible at low tide. Plan three days; the Mémorial de Caen is the regional museum anchor. The June 6 anniversary draws heads of state and surviving veterans annually.

**The Berth.** Normandy: the seaside hotels of Bayeux (steps from the tapestry and the beaches); Deauville and Honfleur on the coast; or a restored manor in the Calvados countryside.

**The Galley.** Norman: the oysters and mussels of the coast; Camembert, Livarot, and Pont-l'Évêque; the cream, butter, and apples of the bocage; cider and Calvados; a seafood lunch at Port-en-Bessin.

> You are about to embark upon the Great Crusade.
> *Dwight D. Eisenhower, Order of the Day, June 6, 1944*

### Stop 6. Bastogne

**Waypoint:** Ardennes, Belgium

Where the surrounded answered 'NUTS!'. The Battle of the Bulge, Hitler's last great offensive in the West, opened December 16, 1944. Nineteen German divisions punched through the thin American line in the Ardennes Forest in deep snow and fog, hoping to drive 200 kilometers to Antwerp. The 101st Airborne Division, surrounded at the road junction of Bastogne, refused to surrender, when the German commander demanded capitulation on December 22, the acting American commander General Anthony McAuliffe wrote 'NUTS!' on a piece of paper and sent it back. Patton's Third Army wheeled ninety degrees through impossible weather and broke the siege the day after Christmas. The Mardasson Memorial, a five-pointed star fifty meters across, dedicated to the 76,890 American soldiers killed, wounded, captured, or missing in the Bulge, sits on the rise outside town. The Bastogne War Museum at its base reopened in 2014 with immersive exhibits. Visit in winter to feel what they felt; the snow comes back every year.

**The Berth.** Brussels: Hotel Amigo near the Grand-Place; Steigenberger Wiltcher's; or the boutique Vintage Hotel. Bruges: Hotel Dukes' Palace; Relais Bourgondisch Cruyce.

**The Galley.** Brussels: Comme Chez Soi for the canonical Belgian since 1926; Bon Bon for Christophe Hardiquest's Michelin two-star; Fin de Siècle for the bistronomy. Bruges: De Karmeliet; Park Restaurant for the canonical.

> NUTS!
> *Brig. Gen. Anthony McAuliffe, reply to the German surrender demand, Dec 22, 1944*

### Stop 7. Berlin

**Waypoint:** Reichstag, Brandenburg Gate & Holocaust Memorial, Germany

Where the Reich began and ended. The Reichstag, the German parliament Hitler had burned in 1933 to seize emergency powers, is where the Soviet Red Army raised its flag at 10:40 p.m. on April 30, 1945, the iconic photograph staged in the rooftop ruins two days later. The Brandenburg Gate, two hundred meters away, was Berlin's symbolic east-west boundary throughout the Cold War. The Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe, Peter Eisenman's 2,711 concrete stelae across two and a half acres immediately south of the gate, completed 2005, is the German nation's principal Holocaust memorial. Topography of Terror sits on the excavated foundations of the former Gestapo and SS headquarters on Niederkirchnerstraße. Hitler's bunker, where he killed himself on April 30, 1945, is unmarked except for an information board in a parking lot at the corner of Gertrud-Kolmar-Straße and An der Kolonnade. All within walking distance. Allow two days.

**The Berth.** Hotel Adlon Kempinski on Unter den Linden facing the Brandenburg Gate; or Soho House Berlin in Mitte; or 25hours Hotel Bikini for the budget-modern in West Berlin.

**The Galley.** Markthalle Neun in Kreuzberg for Street Food Thursday; Mustafa's Gemüse Kebap on Mehringdamm; Lode & Stijn in Neukölln; Curry 36 for Currywurst at 2 a.m.

> The dark curse of Hitler will be lifted from our age.
> *Winston Churchill, 1940*

### Stop 8. Pearl Harbor & the USS Arizona Memorial

**Waypoint:** Oahu, Hawaii

Where the United States entered the war. At 7:48 a.m. on Sunday, December 7, 1941, 353 Japanese aircraft attacked the US Pacific Fleet at anchor in Pearl Harbor; in 110 minutes they sank or damaged eight battleships, killed 2,403 Americans, and pulled the United States into the Second World War. The USS Arizona, sunk by a single bomb that detonated her forward magazine, lies on the harbor floor with 1,177 of her crew still entombed in the wreck below; she is the central memorial site. The 1962 white concrete memorial bridge spans the hull just below the surface; the launch from the visitor center is free but timed-entry. Oil still seeps from the wreck at a rate of roughly a quart a day, the so-called 'black tears of the Arizona.'

**The Berth.** Honolulu/Waikiki: The Royal Hawaiian; Halekulani; The Kahala Resort east of Waikiki for the quieter beach.

**The Galley.** Alan Wong's; Helena's Hawaiian Food since 1946; Leonard's Bakery for malasadas; Marukame Udon on Kuhio.

> Yesterday, December 7, 1941 — a date which will live in infamy.
> *Franklin D. Roosevelt, address to Congress, December 8, 1941*

### Stop 9. USS Missouri

**Waypoint:** Ford Island, Pearl Harbor

Where it was signed. Across the harbor from the Arizona, the USS Missouri, the Iowa-class battleship aboard which the Japanese instrument of surrender was received at 9:04 a.m. on September 2, 1945, has been preserved as a museum ship since 1999. The signing took place on the starboard veranda deck; the bronze plaque marks the exact spot where the foreign minister Mamoru Shigemitsu and General Yoshijirō Umezu signed for Japan and General Douglas MacArthur signed for the Allied Powers. The two American endpoints of the war, the harbor's first day and its last, lie two miles apart. Plan a full day for both.

**The Berth.** Honolulu: The Royal Hawaiian; Halekulani; The Kahala Resort.

**The Galley.** Alan Wong's; Helena's Hawaiian Food; Leonard's Bakery; Marukame Udon.

> These proceedings are closed.
> *Gen. Douglas MacArthur, closing the surrender ceremony, September 2, 1945*

### Stop 10. Hiroshima Peace Memorial

**Waypoint:** Japan

Where it ended. At 8:15 a.m. on Monday, August 6, 1945, the B-29 Enola Gay released a uranium-235 bomb codenamed Little Boy over the city of Hiroshima; the bomb detonated 580 meters above the Shima Hospital, the first nuclear weapon ever used against human beings. The blast killed roughly 80,000 people instantly; another 60,000 died of injuries and radiation by year's end. The Genbaku Dome, the skeletal remains of the Hiroshima Prefectural Industrial Promotion Hall, 160 meters from the hypocenter, the only structure in the area to remain partially standing, has been preserved exactly as it was at 8:15 a.m., UNESCO-listed since 1996. The Peace Memorial Park surrounding it includes the Children's Peace Monument (Sadako Sasaki and the thousand origami cranes), the Cenotaph for the A-bomb Victims, and the Peace Memorial Museum (renovated 2019, harrowing). The Peace Memorial Ceremony on the August 6 anniversary at 8:15 a.m. is the central observance. Pair with hanami in late March-early April when cherry blossoms line the Motoyasu River below the dome. The natural ending of the trail, and of the war.

**The Berth.** Tokyo: Aman Tokyo; Park Hyatt Shinjuku; Hoshinoya Tokyo. Kyoto: Tawaraya; Aman Kyoto. Osaka: Conrad Osaka.

**The Galley.** Tokyo: Sukiyabashi Jiro; Den; Narisawa; Toyosu market sushi. Kyoto: Kikunoi; Hyotei; Den Shinsen. Osaka: Mizuno for okonomiyaki; Hashi for tempura.

> Rest in peace, for the error shall not be repeated.
> *inscription, Cenotaph for the A-bomb Victims, Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park*

---

## Pilgrimage XXI. The War That Came Home

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of the Vietnam War, from the August 2-4, 1964 Gulf of Tonkin incident that escalated direct American involvement, through to the fall of Saigon on April 30, 1975 that closed the war on the other side of the Earth. Anchored to the war's principal fronts on the ground (the DMZ, Khe Sanh, Huế, the Củ Chi tunnels), to its central moral weight (Mỹ Lai), to its political endpoints (Hanoi and Saigon), and to its American endpoint (the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Wall in Washington). Best timed for the April 30 anniversary in Vietnam (Reunification Day, FIXED, when Ho Chi Minh City fills the streets), the Memorial Day weekend at the Wall (last Monday of May, the canonical American observance), or Veterans Day on November 11. Two trips: a Vietnamese arc of ten to twelve days running south from Hanoi through the Central Highlands to Ho Chi Minh City, and a separate one-day pilgrimage to the Wall. Vietnamese visa required for US citizens; the Vietnamese people, fifty years on, are among the warmest hosts in Asia.

> We had to destroy the village in order to save it.
> *attributed to a U.S. Army major, quoted by Peter Arnett, AP, Feb 1968*

### Stop 1. Hỏa Lò Prison

**Waypoint:** the Hanoi Hilton, Hanoi

Where the captured airmen were held. The colonial-era French prison in central Hanoi held 591 American airmen between 1964 and 1973, including future Senator John McCain (shot down October 26, 1967, held for five and a half years), Admiral James Stockdale, and Congressman Sam Johnson. The Vietnamese had used the same prison to hold Vietnamese nationalists under French rule, the irony was not lost on either side. The Americans called it the Hanoi Hilton with the bitter humor of men who knew exactly what it was. Today two-thirds of the site has been demolished for an office tower; the surviving wing is a museum that emphasizes the French colonial torture chambers and treats the American POW period unevenly. McCain's flight suit and helmet are displayed in a glass case. Visit early; visit briefly; visit honestly.

**The Berth.** Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi (the colonial grand-dame, where Graham Greene wrote The Quiet American in 1951); Capella Hanoi; or the boutique Apricot Hotel on Hoàn Kiếm Lake.

**The Galley.** Phở Gia Truyền on Bát Đàn for the canonical phở bò; Bún chả Hương Liên (the Obama-Bourdain table in 2016); Chả Cá Lã Vọng for the heritage turmeric fish; bia hơi anywhere on Tạ Hiện after sundown.

> The thing they carried was their own bodies, and the dread of their own death.
> *Tim O'Brien, The Things They Carried*

### Stop 2. Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum & the Old Quarter

**Waypoint:** Hanoi

Where the founder of the nation lies. The granite mausoleum on Ba Đình Square holds Hồ Chí Minh's embalmed body in a glass case, modeled on Lenin's in Moscow and maintained by Russian preservationists who fly in annually. Hồ died on September 2, 1969, six years before the fall of Saigon he had spent forty years working toward; his wish, recorded in his will, was to be cremated and his ashes scattered across the three regions of Vietnam, but the Party overruled him. The mausoleum is open mornings only; silence is enforced; hands out of pockets; no cameras. Beside it stands the modest stilt house where he actually lived from 1958, two rooms, a bed, a bookshelf, no concessions to power. Walk afterward through the Old Quarter's thirty-six guild streets (Hàng Bạc the silver street, Hàng Mã the votive-paper street, Hàng Bông the cotton street), continuously inhabited for a thousand years, the city the French never quite controlled and the Americans never reached.

**The Berth.** Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi (the colonial grand-dame, where Graham Greene wrote The Quiet American in 1951); Capella Hanoi; or the boutique Apricot Hotel on Hoàn Kiếm Lake.

**The Galley.** Phở Gia Truyền on Bát Đàn for the canonical phở bò; Bún chả Hương Liên (the Obama-Bourdain table in 2016); Chả Cá Lã Vọng for the heritage turmeric fish; bia hơi anywhere on Tạ Hiện after sundown.

> Nothing is more precious than independence and freedom.
> *Hồ Chí Minh, July 17, 1966*

### Stop 3. Điện Biên Phủ

**Waypoint:** northwest Vietnam, near the Lao border

Where French colonial rule in Indochina ended. From March 13 to May 7, 1954, the Việt Minh under General Võ Nguyên Giáp besieged twelve French strongpoints in the valley floor, having dragged disassembled artillery up the surrounding ridges on bicycles and human backs over months of jungle terrain, then reassembled the guns on the heights and rained fire down. The French garrison surrendered on May 7; the next day the Geneva Conference opened, partitioned Vietnam at the 17th parallel, and the United States began the long slide into the war it had just watched France lose. The battlefield is preserved with the original French command bunker (where Colonel de Castries surrendered) intact, the Vietnamese artillery positions on the ridges, the Eliane and Dominique hilltops, and the A1 Hill cemetery. A long day's drive from Hanoi, or a short flight; the ridges are worth the journey, the geometry of how the war was won becomes obvious from the heights.

**The Berth.** Điện Biên Phủ: Mường Thanh Holiday Hotel for the practical proximity. Or return to Hanoi (Sofitel Metropole, Capella).

**The Galley.** Local Thái ethnic-minority cooking: thắng cố (offal stew), pa pỉnh tộp (grilled river fish stuffed with herbs), sticky rice in bamboo. Or back in Hanoi for the canonical northern bowl.

> You can kill ten of our men for every one we kill of yours. But even at those odds, you will lose and we will win.
> *Hồ Chí Minh to the French, 1946*

### Stop 4. The DMZ & Khe Sanh

**Waypoint:** Quảng Trị Province, the 17th Parallel

Where the country was cut in two. The Demilitarized Zone divided North and South Vietnam from the 1954 Geneva Accords until reunification in 1976, a five-mile-wide buffer along the Bến Hải River that became the most heavily fortified frontier on Earth and the war's central geographic obsession. The Hiền Lương Bridge across the river, the actual line, is preserved with the original checkpoints; the loudspeaker arrays on both banks (each side broadcast propaganda at higher volume than the other until the war ended) are still in place. Twenty miles south, the US Marine combat base at Khe Sanh, besieged by 20,000 PAVN troops from January 21 to July 9, 1968, ran in parallel with Tet and was for two months the focus of Lyndon Johnson's White House anxieties. The remnant runway, command bunkers, and an open-air museum of recovered ordnance sit on the original plateau. The Vinh Mốc tunnels north of the river, where an entire fishing village lived underground for six years to survive the bombing, are the day's third essential stop.

**The Berth.** Huế: Azerai La Residence (the 1930 Art Deco former French Résident Supérieur's mansion on the Perfume River); Pilgrimage Village Boutique; or Vedana Lagoon for the resort.

**The Galley.** Huế imperial cuisine: bún bò Huế at Bún Bò Huế Bà Tuyết; bánh khoái at Lạc Thiện; the seven-course imperial dinner at Y Thảo Garden; cơm hến at any riverbank stand.

> Hue cleansed me. Khe Sanh cleansed me. Heroic Khe Sanh.
> *Michael Herr, Dispatches*

### Stop 5. The Ho Chi Minh Trail

**Waypoint:** the Truong Son Mountains, central Vietnam

Where the artery that won the war ran. It was never a single road but a vast, shifting web of jungle paths, truck tracks, river crossings, and hidden depots, sixteen thousand kilometers of it, threading down the spine of the Truong Son range and looping through Laos and Cambodia to carry men and weapons and rice from the North to the battlefields of the South. Begun in 1959 and pounded for years by the heaviest aerial bombardment in history, the trail was rebuilt faster than it could be destroyed by armies of porters, bicycle convoys, and truck drivers, tens of thousands of whom died along it, many of them young volunteers far from home. Without it the war the North fought could not have been fought at all. Today a paved mountain highway traces its route through breathtaking, lonely country; you can cross the Da Krong Bridge, walk the rows of the Truong Son National Martyrs' Cemetery, and stand among the karst giants of Phong Nha-Ke Bang. Drive the Truong Son road, and grasp what a people will carry to be free.

**The Berth.** Central Vietnam: the riverside guesthouses and cave-country lodges of Phong Nha; the hotels of Dong Hoi on the coast; or simple inns in the mountain towns along the Truong Son road, waking to mist in the high valleys.

**The Galley.** Central Vietnamese mountain fare: the fiery beef noodle soup bun bo Hue; banh khoai and savory pancakes; grilled river fish and forest greens; sticky rice in bamboo; strong Vietnamese coffee from the highland plantations.

> Born in the North to die in the South.
> *a saying of the trail's soldiers*

### Stop 6. Huế & the Citadel

**Waypoint:** Central Vietnam, on the Perfume River

Where the imperial city fell in the Tet Offensive. The former imperial capital of Vietnam, seat of the Nguyễn dynasty from 1802 to 1945. On January 31, 1968, NVA and Việt Cộng forces seized the Citadel and held the city for twenty-six days; in the house-to-house fight to retake it, US Marines and ARVN troops reduced large portions of the 19th-century walled imperial city to rubble. The 1968 massacre of an estimated 2,800 to 6,000 Vietnamese civilians by retreating Communist forces, the bodies buried in mass graves discovered over the following months, is the South's central remembered atrocity of the war, and is the rough counterweight that any honest accounting of Mỹ Lai must reckon with. The Citadel and the Imperial City (the Forbidden Purple City within it) were UNESCO-listed in 1993 and have been under careful restoration ever since; some buildings remain in their 1968 state as memorials. Cross the Perfume River by sampan at sunset; eat the bún bò; spend two days.

**The Berth.** Huế: Azerai La Residence (the 1930 Art Deco former French Résident Supérieur's mansion on the Perfume River); Pilgrimage Village Boutique; or Vedana Lagoon for the resort.

**The Galley.** Huế imperial cuisine: bún bò Huế at Bún Bò Huế Bà Tuyết; bánh khoái at Lạc Thiện; the seven-course imperial dinner at Y Thảo Garden; cơm hến at any riverbank stand.

> The sorrow of war inside a soldier's heart was in a strange way similar to the sorrow of love.
> *Bảo Ninh, The Sorrow of War*

### Stop 7. Mỹ Lai Memorial

**Waypoint:** Sơn Mỹ village, Quảng Ngãi Province

Where the war's conscience must be faced. On the morning of March 16, 1968, a company of US soldiers from Charlie Company, 1st Battalion, 20th Infantry, entered the hamlet of Sơn Mỹ on a search-and-destroy mission and over the next four hours murdered between 347 and 504 unarmed Vietnamese civilians, mostly women, children, and elderly men. The killings were stopped by Warrant Officer Hugh Thompson, a helicopter pilot who landed his aircraft between the soldiers and a group of surviving villagers, ordered his door gunner to fire on American troops if they continued, and evacuated eleven civilians to safety. The story was suppressed for twenty months until Seymour Hersh broke it in November 1969; of the 26 soldiers charged, only Lieutenant William Calley was convicted. The memorial museum at Sơn Mỹ preserves the irrigation ditch where most of the victims were shot, marks each family's home with a name plaque, and lists every victim's age. Children two days old. Men ninety-three years old. A place every American who visits the country should stand at least once.

**The Berth.** Hội An (60 km north): Anantara Hội An Resort; Four Seasons Resort The Nam Hai; or Hotel Royal Hội An for the heritage in the old town.

**The Galley.** Hội An: cao lầu at Trung Bắc since 1955; bánh mì at Bánh Mì Phượng (the Bourdain-anointed); white rose dumplings at Bông Hồng Trắng; mì Quảng at any market stand.

> You can never do enough, and yet you must do everything you can.
> *Hugh Thompson, on returning to Mỹ Lai for the 30th anniversary, 1998*

### Stop 8. Củ Chi Tunnels

**Waypoint:** 70 km northwest of Ho Chi Minh City

Where a whole war was fought underground. Two hundred and fifty kilometers of hand-dug tunnels in three layers beneath the red earth of Củ Chi District, the underground infrastructure of the Viet Cong's war in the South. Dug initially against the French in the 1940s and continuously extended through the 1960s, the system held field hospitals, command centers, ammunition dumps, kitchens (with chimneys that vented the smoke kilometers away through dispersed outlets), sleeping quarters, and an entire civilian population that lived underground for years. The Củ Chi tunnels became the operational base for the 1968 Tet Offensive against Saigon, twenty-five miles to the southeast. Two sections (Bến Đình and Bến Dược) are open to visitors; both have widened a sample of the original tunnels (originally 60 cm high and 80 cm wide, designed to be too small for American soldiers to follow) and you can crawl forty meters of the wider version, which is still claustrophobic enough to require commitment. The site treats the war from the Vietnamese point of view, which is both the point and a reasonable thing for Americans to listen to for an afternoon.

**The Berth.** Ho Chi Minh City: Park Hyatt Saigon on Lam Sơn Square; The Reverie Saigon; or the heritage Hôtel Continental Saigon (Graham Greene's Saigon residence while writing The Quiet American).

**The Galley.** Cục Gạch Quán for the heritage Vietnamese in a restored 1940s villa; Anan Saigon for the Michelin Vietnamese-American; phở at Phở Hòa Pasteur since 1968; bánh xèo at Bánh Xèo 46A.

> The guerrilla wins if he does not lose. The conventional army loses if it does not win.
> *Henry Kissinger, Foreign Affairs, January 1969*

### Stop 9. War Remnants Museum & Reunification Palace

**Waypoint:** Ho Chi Minh City (Saigon)

Where the Vietnamese half of the trail closes. The two essential Saigon stops, two kilometers apart, that together close the Vietnamese half of the trail. The War Remnants Museum (until 1995 called the Museum of American War Crimes) holds the photojournalism of Tim Page, Eddie Adams, Nick Ut, and the Magnum photographers who covered the war, alongside captured American hardware, an unflinching Agent Orange exhibition, and the tiger cages from Côn Đảo prison. The Reunification Palace, three blocks east, is preserved in its April 30, 1975 condition: the day a North Vietnamese T-54 tank, number 843, crashed through the front gates at 11:30 a.m., the photograph that ended the war. The tank is parked on the lawn. The president's office is unchanged. The basement war room with its 1960s radios is unchanged. Stand on the lawn beside the tank and recognize that you are standing inside the photograph.

**The Berth.** Ho Chi Minh City: Park Hyatt Saigon on Lam Sơn Square; The Reverie Saigon; or the heritage Hôtel Continental Saigon (Graham Greene's Saigon residence while writing The Quiet American).

**The Galley.** Cục Gạch Quán for the heritage Vietnamese in a restored 1940s villa; Anan Saigon for the Michelin Vietnamese-American; phở at Phở Hòa Pasteur since 1968; bánh xèo at Bánh Xèo 46A.

> We were wrong, terribly wrong. We owe it to future generations to explain why.
> *Robert S. McNamara, In Retrospect: The Tragedy and Lessons of Vietnam, 1995*

### Stop 10. The Vietnam Veterans Memorial

**Waypoint:** the Wall, the National Mall, Washington, D.C.

Where the trail comes home, and the names begin. Maya Lin's two black granite walls, 246 feet long, meeting at a 125-degree angle and sunk into the earth of the National Mall, list the names of 58,318 American service members killed or missing in the war, inscribed in chronological order from the first death (US Army Special Forces Captain Harry Cramer, October 21, 1957) to the last (Marine Lance Corporal Darwin Judge, April 29, 1975, killed at the Defense Attaché compound the day before the fall of Saigon). Lin designed the memorial as a 21-year-old Yale undergraduate; the design was controversial when it opened on November 13, 1982, and is now understood to be among the great American monuments. The polished granite reflects the face of every visitor, so the dead and the living are in the same plane. Find the name. Touch the name.
