Leave whatever you brought; the Park Service archives every offering. Memorial Day weekend is the canonical American moment to be here; November 11 is the quieter one.

**The Berth.** Washington, D.C.: The Hay-Adams across Lafayette Square from the White House; the Jefferson Hotel on 16th Street; or the boutique Riggs Washington on Pennsylvania Avenue.

**The Galley.** Rasika for the canonical modern Indian; Komi (Peter Chang) for the omakase; Maydan for the wood-fire Middle Eastern; Ben's Chili Bowl on U Street for the half-smoke since 1958.

> How do you ask a man to be the last man to die for a mistake?
> *John Kerry, testimony to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, April 22, 1971*

---

## Pilgrimage XXII. A Short Life and a Merry One

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of the Golden Age of Piracy, the brief, blazing window from roughly 1690 to 1726 when a few thousand outlaws on stolen ships briefly terrorized the shipping lanes of the Atlantic and the Caribbean and lodged themselves permanently in the world's imagination. Anchored to the pirate republics where the age was born (Port Royal, Nassau, Tortuga), to the colonial ports they raided and were hanged in (Charleston, Bridgetown), to the two authenticated wreck sites where the archaeology is real (the Whydah off Cape Cod, the Queen Anne's Revenge off Beaufort), to the Indian Ocean haven at the far end of the world (Île Sainte-Marie, Madagascar), and to the London dock where the age was finally hanged out of existence. Best timed for Gasparilla in Tampa (late January), Pirates Week in the Cayman Islands (November), or any of the Caribbean pirate festivals already on this calendar. Two or three trips: a Caribbean-and- Atlantic-seaboard ring, a separate Indian Ocean leg for the determined, and a single day in London. The Jolly Roger flew for barely a generation. This is where it flew.

> They villify us, the scoundrels do, when there is only this difference, they rob the poor under the cover of law, and we plunder the rich under the protection of our own courage.
> *Black Sam Bellamy, 1717, as recorded by Captain Charles Johnson*

### Stop 1. Port Royal

**Waypoint:** Jamaica

Where the wickedest city on Earth once stood. Through the 1660s and 1670s Port Royal was the richest and most debauched town in the New World, the headquarters of the buccaneers who raided the Spanish Main under loose English license, Henry Morgan chief among them, and a town said to hold one tavern for every ten residents. On June 7, 1692, a massive earthquake and the tsunami that followed dropped two-thirds of the city into Kingston Harbour in a matter of minutes, killing some two thousand people and ending the buccaneer capital in an afternoon, an event the surviving Puritans of the age read as plain divine judgment. Today a small fishing village sits on the surviving spit; Fort Charles (where a young Horatio Nelson later served) still stands, with its tilted 'Giddy House' artillery store knocked permanently off-plumb by the 1907 earthquake. The sunken city beneath the harbour is a protected archaeological site, one of the few submerged 17th-century towns anywhere on Earth. Stand on the fort wall and look at the water. The city is still down there.

**The Berth.** Kingston: The Spanish Court Hotel in New Kingston; the historic Liguanea Club; or the boutique R Hotel. Or out at Port Antonio: Trident Hotel; Geejam.

**The Galley.** Jerk at Scotchies in Kingston; the seafood at Gloria's in Port Royal itself (the fried fish and festival within sight of the sunken city); patties at Tastee; rum at any bar that will pour you a Wray & Nephew overproof.

> They refresh themselves at one island or another; here they careen their vessels, while some hunt and others cruise for prizes.
> *Alexandre Exquemelin, The Buccaneers of America, 1678*

### Stop 2. Nassau & New Providence

**Waypoint:** the Bahamas

Where the pirates ran their own republic. After Port Royal sank, the action moved to Nassau, a lawless harbor town on New Providence Island deep enough to shelter pirate sloops but too shallow for the Royal Navy's warships, ideal geography for outlawry. From roughly 1706 to 1718 it was governed by no nation but by a loose pirate council, Benjamin Hornigold, Henry Jennings, Charles Vane, Calico Jack Rackham, Anne Bonny, Mary Read, and a young protégé named Edward Teach who would become Blackbeard all worked out of Nassau in these years. The party ended in July 1718 when Woodes Rogers, a former privateer turned royal governor, sailed in with a king's pardon in one hand and a noose in the other under the motto Expulsis Piratis, Restituta Commercia, 'pirates expelled, commerce restored,' still the Bahamian national motto today. Most of the old town burned long ago, but the Pirates of Nassau museum on King Street reconstructs the Republic, and Fort Montagu (1741) and the Queen's Staircase remain. The harbor is the same harbor.

**The Berth.** Nassau: The Ocean Club, A Four Seasons Resort on Paradise Island (the old Huntington estate); Rosewood at Baha Mar; or the boutique Graycliff Hotel in a 1740 colonial mansion on West Hill Street.

**The Galley.** Conch everything at Arawak Cay's 'Fish Fry' (cracked conch, conch salad, conch fritters); the heritage dinner and cigar cellar at Graycliff; fresh grouper at any shack on Potter's Cay under the bridge.

> Damnation seize my soul if I give you quarters, or take any from you.
> *Edward 'Blackbeard' Teach, attributed*

### Stop 3. Ocracoke Inlet

**Waypoint:** the Outer Banks, North Carolina

Where Blackbeard died. By the autumn of 1718 Edward Teach had taken a royal pardon, settled near Bath, North Carolina, and then quietly returned to raiding from a base at Ocracoke Inlet on the Outer Banks. The governor of Virginia, Alexander Spotswood, dispatched two commandeered sloops under Lieutenant Robert Maynard of the Royal Navy. They cornered Blackbeard at Ocracoke on the morning of November 22, 1718. In the hand-to-hand fighting on Maynard's deck Blackbeard took, by the surgeon's later count, five musket-ball wounds and some twenty cuts before he fell; Maynard had his head cut off and hung from the bowsprit, and the channel around the inlet is called Teach's Hole to this day. Ocracoke is now a tiny, beautiful village reachable only by ferry, all wild beach and live oaks and the second-oldest working lighthouse in America (1823). Order a plate of fried oysters, walk to Teach's Hole at dusk, and consider that the most famous pirate who ever lived died in four feet of water within sight of where you are standing.

**The Berth.** Ocracoke: The Castle on Silver Lake; Blackbeard's Lodge (since 1936, the island's oldest hotel); or the cottages at The Cove. Off-season the island nearly empties.

**The Galley.** Oysters and fish at Howard's Pub; the local catch at Dajio; figs and seafood at The Flying Melon; Ocracoke fig cake anywhere it appears.

> Such a day; rum all out. Our company somewhat sober. A damned confusion amongst us!
> *from Blackbeard's journal, as quoted by Charles Johnson, 1724*

### Stop 4. Charleston

**Waypoint:** South Carolina

Where the pirates were blockaded, then hanged. In May 1718 Blackbeard blockaded Charleston harbor for nearly a week with the Queen Anne's Revenge and three other vessels, seizing ships and hostages until the city paid a ransom, of all things, a chest of medicine. That same year the tide turned: Colonel William Rhett captured the 'Gentleman Pirate' Stede Bonnet at the Battle of Cape Fear River, and in the late autumn of 1718 Bonnet and some twenty-nine of his men were hanged at White Point, the tip of the Charleston peninsula now called the Battery, and buried in the marsh below the low-water mark. The Old Exchange and Provost Dungeon on East Bay Street held pirates awaiting trial; you can stand in the cellar where Bonnet was confined. Charleston today is one of the most beautiful preserved colonial cities in America, the pastel single houses, the Battery promenade, the church spires, but the genteel surface sits directly on top of the gallows ground.

**The Berth.** Charleston: The Charleston Place; the boutique Zero George; The Dewberry in the old federal building; or Wentworth Mansion in the 1886 Second Empire house.

**The Galley.** FIG (Mike Lata) for the canonical Lowcountry; Husk for the heritage; The Ordinary for the seafood; Hominy Grill for breakfast; Rodney Scott's BBQ for the whole-hog.

> A merry life and a short one shall be my motto.
> *Bartholomew 'Black Bart' Roberts*

### Stop 5. Tortuga & the Côte de Fer

**Waypoint:** Île de la Tortue, Haiti

Where Caribbean piracy was born. The small turtle-shaped island off the north coast of Hispaniola, Tortuga, was through the mid-1600s the original buccaneer stronghold, a base for the boucaniers (French hunters who smoked meat on wooden frames called boucans, and gave the word buccaneer to the language) who turned to raiding Spanish shipping. From Tortuga came the first generation of the legend: the Brethren of the Coast, the privateer-pirate confederation that produced Henry Morgan and François l'Olonnais and that fed directly into the Port Royal years. The island is today a quiet, hard-to-reach part of Haiti with little tourist infrastructure, and the security situation on the Haitian mainland should be checked carefully before any attempt; for most travelers this stop is best understood from the water or appreciated as the origin point it was. Where it can be reached, the ruins of the French fort and the old harbor at Basse-Terre remain. The Brethren began here.

**The Berth.** This stop is logistically difficult and security-dependent. The practical base for the region is the Dominican Republic side: Casas del XVI in Santo Domingo's colonial zone; or Amanera on the north coast.

**The Galley.** Dominican mangú and la bandera in Santo Domingo's Zona Colonial; fresh fish at the Samaná peninsula; Haitian griot and pikliz where it can be safely found.

> We are gentlemen of fortune, and our trade is the sea.
> *the Brethren of the Coast, traditional*

### Stop 6. Île Sainte-Marie

**Waypoint:** Nosy Boraha, Madagascar

Where the pirates fled to the far side of the world. The long thin island off the east coast of Madagascar, called Île Sainte-Marie by the French and Nosy Boraha in Malagasy, was from the 1690s the great Indian Ocean base for pirates working the rich Red Sea and Mughal trade routes, a deep sheltered bay far beyond the reach of any European navy. Captain Kidd, Henry Every (whose 1695 capture of the Mughal treasure ship Ganj-i-Sawai was the single richest pirate haul of the age), Thomas Tew, and the semi-legendary pirate utopia of 'Libertalia' all attach to this coast. In the shallow water of the Baie des Forbans, Pirate Bay, lie several 18th-century wrecks, and on a tiny islet sits one of the only dedicated pirate cemeteries on Earth, weathered headstones leaning under the palms, a few carved with a skull and crossbones. Reachable by short flight or ferry from the mainland; the whales migrate past from July to September.

**The Berth.** Île Sainte-Marie: Princesse Bora Lodge & Spa on the beach (the whale-watching base); Libertalia Boutique Hotel; or the simple bungalows at Masoandro Lodge.

**The Galley.** Malagasy seafood: grilled zebu skewers, fresh crab and crayfish, coconut-and- vanilla everything (the island is in the heart of Madagascar's vanilla country); the catch of the day at any beach gargotte; THB beer cold.

> In an honest service there is thin commons, low wages, and hard labour; in this, plenty and satiety, pleasure and ease, liberty and power.
> *Bartholomew Roberts, on why men turned pirate*

### Stop 7. The Whydah Wreck & Cape Cod

**Waypoint:** Wellfleet, Massachusetts

Where the only proven pirate treasure was found. The Whydah Gally was a state-of-the-art London-built slave ship captured in early 1717 in the Windward Passage by Black Sam Bellamy, the 'Prince of Pirates,' who refit her as his flagship; for a few weeks Bellamy was, by some reckonings, the richest pirate in history, his hold packed with the plunder of over fifty ships. On April 26, 1717, a violent nor'easter drove the overloaded Whydah onto the sandbars off Wellfleet at midnight; she capsized and sank in minutes, taking Bellamy and all but two of his 146 men. The wreck was found in 1984 by Barry Clifford, 500 yards off Marconi Beach under fifteen feet of water and decades of sand, the ship's bell ('THE WHYDAH GALLY 1716') the proof. The artifacts, gold, cannon, and a child's leather shoe and leg bone (John King, the eleven-year-old pirate), are at the Whydah Pirate Museum in West Yarmouth, with an active conservation lab on site. The treasure is still out there, four miles of it, under the sand.

**The Berth.** Cape Cod: Wequassett Resort in Harwich; Chatham Bars Inn; or the boutique Captain's House Inn in Chatham. Provincetown: Crowne Pointe; Land's End Inn.

**The Galley.** Lobster rolls and fried clams at the Friendly Fisherman in Eastham; oysters at Wellfleet itself (the best on the East Coast); the Brewster Fish House; PB Boulangerie Bistro in Wellfleet for the morning.

> We are men who declared war on the whole world.
> *Black Sam Bellamy, to a captured captain, 1717*

### Stop 8. The Queen Anne's Revenge & Beaufort

**Waypoint:** Beaufort, North Carolina

Where Blackbeard's flagship lies. The Queen Anne's Revenge was a French slave ship, La Concorde, that Edward Teach captured in 1717 and armed with forty guns to become the most feared vessel in the Atlantic. In June 1718, weeks after the Charleston blockade, Blackbeard ran her aground on the bar at Beaufort Inlet (then Topsail Inlet) and abandoned her, an act some contemporaries called deliberate, a way to break up a fleet that had grown too large to share. The wreck was located in 1996 by the salvage firm Intersal and confirmed, after fifteen years of careful excavation, as categorically the Queen Anne's Revenge. More than three hundred conserved artifacts, cannon, the ship's bell, a complete apothecary kit, gold dust, navigational dividers, are on free display at the North Carolina Maritime Museum in Beaufort, with the conservation lab in Greenville still working the wreck three centuries on. Beaufort itself is a perfectly preserved colonial seaport of white clapboard houses; the old burying ground holds graves from the period. The ship is two miles offshore, twenty feet down.

**The Berth.** Beaufort: the Beaufort Hotel on Front Street; the Inlet Inn on the waterfront; or the historic Pecan Tree Inn in an 1866 house. Or nearby Atlantic Beach for the shore.

**The Galley.** The seafood at the Beaufort Grocery Co.; fresh catch at Aqua; shrimp and grits at the Front Street Grill at Stillwater; hush puppies anywhere on the water.

> If they have no good chaplain, they should not be cast away for that.
> *Edward 'Blackbeard' Teach, on his crew, attributed*

### Stop 9. Bridgetown & Speightstown

**Waypoint:** Barbados

Where the gentleman pirate set sail. Barbados was the wealthiest English colony in the 17th-century Caribbean, the first stop of the transatlantic trade winds and so the funnel through which sugar, enslaved people, and treasure flowed, which made its shipping lanes prime hunting. Stede Bonnet, the 'Gentleman Pirate,' was a wealthy Barbados plantation owner who, by the contemporary account, took up piracy to escape an unhappy marriage, bought his own ship rather than stealing one (unheard of), and sailed off in 1717 to a career that ended on the Charleston gallows. Bridgetown's careenage, the inner harbor where ships were heeled over and scraped, is now a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the Barbados Museum at the Garrison holds the colonial-maritime record. The island today is calm, prosperous, and beautiful, the place to end the Atlantic leg with a rum punch where the rum trade was born, Mount Gay has distilled here since 1703, older than the United States and most of the pirates.

**The Berth.** Barbados: Sandy Lane on the west coast for the grand; the boutique Little Good Harbour in Saint Peter near Speightstown; or the historic Cobblers Cove.

**The Galley.** The Friday-night fish fry at Oistins (marlin, flying fish, the national dish); Brown Sugar for canonical Bajan; The Cliff for the dramatic; a Mount Gay tour and tasting at the Bridgetown distillery.

> Take heart, lads. We have done a great deal of mischief, and it is a pity we should not enjoy it.
> *attributed to a Barbados pirate, the Brethren years*

### Stop 10. Execution Dock & Wapping

**Waypoint:** London, England

Where the age was hanged. For four hundred years the Admiralty hanged pirates at Execution Dock, a spot on the Thames foreshore at Wapping in the East End, just below the high-water mark, because piracy was a crime of the sea and so fell under Admiralty rather than common-law jurisdiction. The condemned were brought along the river from Marshalsea prison, allowed a quart of ale at a tavern on the way, and hanged on a shortened rope that produced a slow strangling death, the 'Marshal's dance'; bodies were left chained until three tides had washed over them. Captain William Kidd was hanged here on May 23, 1701 (the rope broke on the first attempt; they hanged him again), and his tarred body was gibbeted downriver at Tilbury Point as a warning to sailors entering the port. The spot is marked near the Prospect of Whitby (a pub on the site since 1520, with a replica gibbet over the water). Stand on the foreshore at low tide, look at the river, and recognize that the Golden Age that began at Port Royal ended here, on this mud, at the end of a rope.

**The Berth.** London: The Tower Hotel by Tower Bridge for the proximity; the boutique Town Hall Hotel in Bethnal Green; or the Hoxton, Shoreditch for the East End.

**The Galley.** The Prospect of Whitby and the Town of Ramsgate for the historic riverside pints; St. JOHN in Smithfield for the canonical nose-to-tail; the Grapes in Limehouse (part-owned by Ian McKellen) for the Thames-side dinner.

> I have lain long enough; it is time to be gone.
> *attributed to Captain William Kidd at the gallows, May 23, 1701*

---

## Pilgrimage XXIII. The Pilgrimage of the Palate

Year-round destinations along the world's defining wine and food traditions, eight stops anchored to the regions where European tradition was made (Burgundy, Champagne, the Italian food triangle, San Sebastián, Lyon) and the regions where it has been most ambitiously rewritten (Tokyo, Mexico City, Napa). Three trips, five to seven days each: a French wine-and-food circuit (Burgundy + Champagne + Lyon, with a side to San Sebastián); an Italian arc through Emilia-Romagna, ideally on the SAGRA TRAIL in autumn; and an intercontinental Pacific-American leg (Tokyo + Mexico City + Napa). Best paired with the existing food and wine events on this calendar, HOSPICES DE BEAUNE in Burgundy (Nov 21), SAN SEBASTIÁN GASTRONOMIKA (September), TERRA MADRE / SALONE DEL GUSTO in Turin (September), and DIA DE LOS MUERTOS in Oaxaca (Nov 1-2). Reservations at the temples (Etxebarri, Osteria Francescana, Sukiyabashi Jiro, The French Laundry, Pujol) need to be made three to six months ahead.

> Tell me what you eat, and I will tell you what you are.
> *Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin, Physiology of Taste, 1825*

### Stop 1. Beaune & La Côte d'Or

**Waypoint:** Burgundy, France

Where the holy grail of wine is grown. Beaune sits at the heart of the Côte d'Or, the fifty-kilometer escarpment of limestone vineyards running south from Dijon to Santenay, where roughly 3,300 climats (named individual parcels) produce some of the most expensive and most argued-about wines on Earth. The Romanée-Conti monopole, 1.8 hectares, eighteen barrels a year, sits halfway down. Walk the Sentier des Grands Crus footpath through the named vineyards of Vosne-Romanée and Chambolle-Musigny. The Marché aux Vins in Beaune, in the 15th-century cellars beneath the Église des Cordeliers, runs daily tastings of fifteen wines for the price of a museum ticket. Charolais beef in red-wine sauce, escargots de Bourgogne, gougères, époisses cheese with Marc de Bourgogne. Pair with hospices de beaune (Nov 21, already on calendar). Three days minimum.

**The Berth.** Paris: Hôtel de Crillon, Le Meurice, Lutetia. Provence: La Bastide de Gordes; Hotel Crillon le Brave. Burgundy: Le Cep in Beaune; Loire: Domaine des Hauts de Loire.

**The Galley.** Paris: Le Comptoir du Relais; Septime; L'Arpège; Frenchie. Provence: La Mirande in Avignon; Baumanière. Burgundy: Lameloise in Chagny; Loire: Le Choiseul in Amboise.

> Good food is the foundation of genuine happiness.
> *Auguste Escoffier*

### Stop 2. Reims & Épernay

**Waypoint:** Champagne, France

Where the wine of celebration is made. In chalk cellars cut by Roman quarry workers in the 3rd century. Reims is the historical and cultural capital, its cathedral was the coronation site of every French king from Clovis in 496 to Charles X in 1825 (UNESCO-listed). The crayères beneath the city, also UNESCO, run for hundreds of kilometers; the great houses (Veuve Clicquot, Pommery, Taittinger, Krug, Ruinart, Mumm) all offer cellar tours and tastings. Forty kilometers south, Épernay's Avenue de Champagne is the most expensive street in the world by the value of the liquid stored beneath it, Moët & Chandon, Perrier-Jouët, Pol Roger, Dom Pérignon all stacked along three kilometers. Eat at the city's bouchons rémois and at the Michelin-starred Le Foch. Best in late spring or in September during the harvest.

**The Berth.** Paris: Hôtel de Crillon, Le Meurice, Lutetia. Provence: La Bastide de Gordes; Hotel Crillon le Brave. Burgundy: Le Cep in Beaune; Loire: Domaine des Hauts de Loire.

**The Galley.** Paris: Le Comptoir du Relais; Septime; L'Arpège; Frenchie. Provence: La Mirande in Avignon; Baumanière. Burgundy: Lameloise in Chagny; Loire: Le Choiseul in Amboise.

> I drink Champagne when I'm happy and when I'm sad. Otherwise I never touch it — unless I'm thirsty.
> *Lily Bollinger, of Champagne Bollinger*

### Stop 3. San Sebastián

**Waypoint:** Spanish Basque Country

Where the stars and the pintxos cluster thickest. Per capita, the densest concentration of Michelin three-star restaurants on Earth, and below that, in the cobbled Parte Vieja old town, the most thrilling pintxo culture anywhere. Walk the bars from late afternoon: La Cuchara de San Telmo for foie gras and pig-cheek; Borda Berri for risotto carbonara and rabbit ravioli; Bar Néstor for chuletón and tortilla (the ten-minute appearance windows for which are a religion); Atari for txakoli and txangurro. Then the temples: Arzak (three stars since 1989), Akelarre on its cliff above the Atlantic, Mugaritz in the hills inland. Twenty minutes east in the Basque mountains, Asador Etxebarri, Bittor Arginzoniz's wood-fire grill restaurant, is widely regarded the best restaurant in the world. Pair with SAN SEBASTIÁN GASTRONOMIKA (September, already on calendar). Three days, properly fueled.

**The Berth.** Hotel María Cristina since 1912; Hotel de Londres y de Inglaterra on La Concha; Akelare Hotel above the Atlantic.

**The Galley.** Arzak (Juan Mari and Elena Arzak); Akelaŕe (Pedro Subijana); Mugaritz (Andoni Aduriz); the Parte Vieja pintxo bars: La Cuchara de San Telmo, Borda Berri, Bar Sport.

> First we eat, then we do everything else.
> *M.F.K. Fisher*

### Stop 4. Bologna, Modena & Parma

**Waypoint:** Emilia-Romagna, Italy

Where Italy's food triangle meets. Three medieval cities within an hour of each other across the Po Plain, each devoted to its own gastronomic patrimony. Bologna, 'la Grassa,' the fat one, is the source of ragù bolognese, tortellini in brodo, mortadella, and the daily pasta-rolling sfogline you can watch through windows in the Quadrilatero medieval food market. Eat at Trattoria di Via Serra; walk the porticoes (UNESCO-listed) afterward. Modena, forty kilometers north, is the home of Aceto Balsamico Tradizionale (twelve years aged minimum, by law) and of Massimo Bottura's Osteria Francescana, number-one in the world twice; book three months ahead. Parma, an hour west of Modena, is the home of Prosciutto di Parma and Parmigiano Reggiano (visit a working caseificio at 6 a.m. for the morning wheel-cutting). Lambrusco, the local sparkling red, with everything. Pair with terra madre / salone del gusto in Turin (September, already on calendar).

**The Berth.** Rome: Hotel de Russie; Hassler. Florence: Hotel Savoy; J.K. Place. Milan: Bulgari Milano. Venice: Aman Venice; Cipriani.

**The Galley.** Rome: Roscioli; Felice a Testaccio; Da Cesare al Casaletto. Florence: Enoteca Pinchiorri; Sostanza; All'Antico Vinaio. Milan: Trussardi alla Scala; Trattoria Milanese. Venice: Alle Testiere; Antiche Carampane.

> The discovery of a new dish does more for the happiness of mankind than the discovery of a star.
> *Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin*

### Stop 5. Piedmont: Alba & the Langhe

**Waypoint:** northwestern Italy

Where the truffle and the great red wine were born. In the misty, vine-combed hills of the Langhe, south of Turin, lies the deepest treasure-house of Italian gastronomy. Here, around the town of Alba each autumn, dogs hunt the legendary white truffle of Alba, the most precious and intoxicating ingredient on earth, shaved raw and fragrant over a plate of fresh tajarin pasta or a soft fried egg. Here too, on the steep Nebbiolo slopes of villages whose names ring like a litany, Barolo and Barbaresco, are made the kings and queens of Italian wine, dark, perfumed, and ageless. And here, in the nearby town of Bra, the Slow Food movement was founded in 1986 as a stand against the fast and the industrial, a defense of place, patience, and pleasure that has reshaped how the world thinks about eating. The whole region is a UNESCO landscape of cellars and trattorie. Come in October for the Alba truffle fair, eat slowly as the movement teaches, and taste the patient soul of Italy.

**The Berth.** The Langhe: a wine estate among the Barolo vineyards; the elegant small hotels of Alba and Barbaresco; or a restored farmhouse (cascina) in the hills, waking to mist over the Nebbiolo rows.

**The Galley.** Piedmontese: tajarin and agnolotti del plin; the white truffle of Alba in season; vitello tonnato; bagna cauda; Castelmagno cheese; and the great reds, Barolo, Barbaresco, and a glass of Moscato d'Asti to finish.

> Good, clean, and fair: this is the food the world deserves.
> *the credo of the Slow Food movement, Bra*

### Stop 6. Lyon

**Waypoint:** France

Where France crowned its gastronomic capital. Officially declared so by Curnonsky in 1934, and few have argued since. Lyon's bouchons, small, slightly raucous workers' restaurants, several certified by the city, serving the canon of Lyonnais cooking unchanged for a century, are the heart of the experience. Café des Fédérations, Daniel et Denise, Chez Hugon, Le Garet all serve the same essential menu: salade lyonnaise (frisée, lardons, poached egg, mustard vinaigrette), quenelles de brochet in Nantua sauce, andouillette tirée à la ficelle, tarte aux pralines roses. Eat at least once at L'Auberge du Pont de Collonges, Paul Bocuse's mothership just north of town, three Michelin stars from 1965 until his death in 2018, still iconic. The Halles Paul Bocuse market on Cours Lafayette is the city's gastronomic temple. Tarte tatin and the morning quenelle at Boulangerie Jocteur next door.

**The Berth.** Paris: Hôtel de Crillon, Le Meurice, Lutetia. Provence: La Bastide de Gordes; Hotel Crillon le Brave. Burgundy: Le Cep in Beaune; Loire: Domaine des Hauts de Loire.

**The Galley.** Paris: Le Comptoir du Relais; Septime; L'Arpège; Frenchie. Provence: La Mirande in Avignon; Baumanière. Burgundy: Lameloise in Chagny; Loire: Le Choiseul in Amboise.

> Make food simple, and let things taste of what they are.
> *Curnonsky, the Prince of Gastronomy*

### Stop 7. Tokyo & Toyosu Market

**Waypoint:** Japan

Where more Michelin stars shine than anywhere on Earth. Over two hundred, and at the high end, the most exacting omakase culture anywhere. The Toyosu Wholesale Market, successor to Tsukiji since 2018, is open to the public from 5 a.m.; the tuna auction at 5:30 a.m. is the early-morning obligatory ritual, followed by sushi breakfast at one of the small counters inside the market itself. The temples are mostly tiny ten-seat counters: Sushi Saito, Sushi Yoshitake, Sukiyabashi Jiro (the Ginza basement of Jiro Dreams of Sushi). They book six months out via concierge. The wider scene matters as much: tonkatsu at Butagumi, soba at Kanda Yabu, yakitori at Birdland, ramen at Tsuta or Nakiryu (both Michelin-starred for under a thousand yen a bowl), kaiseki at Ryugin or Kohaku. Three days minimum. Pair with gion matsuri in Kyoto (July, already on calendar) for an extended Japanese gastronomic trip.

**The Berth.** Aman Tokyo in Otemachi for the panoramic onsen; the Park Hyatt Shinjuku of Lost in Translation; the Hoshinoya Tokyo for the modern ryokan in Marunouchi.

**The Galley.** Sukiyabashi Jiro (booking three months ahead); Den (Zaiyu Hasegawa); Narisawa; Tsukiji and Toyosu for the dawn-market sushi; tonkatsu at Maisen in Aoyama; ramen at Afuri.

> Good food is very often, even most often, simple food.
> *Anthony Bourdain*

### Stop 8. Bangkok

**Waypoint:** Thailand

Where the streets are the greatest kitchen on Earth. No city eats like Bangkok. Again and again ranked the finest food city in the world, the Thai capital turns its streets into one endless, sizzling, fragrant kitchen: charcoal smoke and wok-fire, the thud of the som-tam pestle, the perfume of lemongrass and chili and palm sugar drifting from ten thousand carts. The genius of Thai food is balance, the simultaneous hit of sweet, sour, salty, hot, and savory in a single mouthful, and nowhere is it pursued with such joyful intensity. In the lantern-lit lanes of Yaowarat, the old Chinatown, the night belongs to the vendors; on Sukhumvit's side streets, boat noodles and grilled satay; in a humble shophouse, a crab omelette so good it earned a Michelin star for the street cook Jay Fai. Here the highest art and the cheapest plastic stool meet on equal terms. Pull up a stool on a steaming Bangkok night, point at what smells best, and eat your way through the most democratic great cuisine in the world.

**The Berth.** Bangkok: the legendary riverside Mandarin Oriental, a temple of service since 1876; the grand old Peninsula across the Chao Phraya; or the design hotels of Sukhumvit, steps from the night markets.

**The Galley.** Thai: pad thai and pad see ew; green and massaman curry; som tam and larb; tom yum goong; boat noodles in Yaowarat; mango sticky rice to finish; and a Michelin-starred crab omelette at Jay Fai for the pilgrimage's splurge.

> The secret of Thai food is balance: sweet, sour, salty, hot, all at once.
> *the wisdom of the Thai kitchen*

### Stop 9. Mexico City

**Waypoint:** Mexico

Where the Americas' food capital is having its moment. Mexico City is arguably the most exciting food city in the world right now. The historical depth, pre-Columbian corn cuisine layered with three centuries of Spanish, Asian, and Lebanese influence, gives it a complexity nowhere else has. The street canon: tacos al pastor at El Vilsito or El Califa (the trompo arrives in the late afternoon), tacos de canasta from a basket on a bicycle at lunch, quesadillas with squash blossoms in any market. The high end: Pujol, Enrique Olvera's mole madre, aged for over three thousand days now and counting; Quintonil; Sud777; Contramar for fried fish and tuna tostadas at the long lunch. Mezcal at Bósforo or La Botica. Pair with DÍA de muertos in Oaxaca (Nov 1-2, already on calendar) and the feria nacional del mole for a multi-stop Mexican gastronomic trip.

**The Berth.** Las Alcobas in Polanco; Four Seasons on Reforma; Casa Habita in Roma Norte; or Downtown México in the Centro Histórico for the converted-palace stay.

**The Galley.** Pujol (Enrique Olvera); Quintonil; Sud 777; Contramar for the Pacific seafood lunch; Lalo! and Rosetta in Roma; Café de Tacuba for canonical chocolate and tamales.

> Food is our common ground, a universal experience.
> *James Beard*

### Stop 10. Napa Valley

**Waypoint:** California

Where America answered Bordeaux. Thirty miles long, five miles wide at its widest, the floor of an inland lake bed sheltered from Pacific fog by the Mayacamas mountains. The Cabernet Sauvignon vines on the valley floor and benchlands have produced, since the 1976 Judgment of Paris, the only New World wines the great châteaux of Bordeaux take seriously as peers. The Robert Mondavi Winery (1966) anchors the south end; Opus One (the Mondavi-Rothschild collaboration) sits across the road; Stag's Leap, Screaming Eagle, Harlan Estate, and Dominus stretch up the valley. At the table: The French Laundry in Yountville, Thomas Keller's nine-course tasting menu, three Michelin stars since 2007, is the ritual splurge of American fine dining; Bouchon, also in Yountville, is the more accessible bistro from the same kitchen. Drive Highway 29 north to St. Helena and Calistoga; the small-production Cabernet Franc and old-vine Zinfandel beyond the famous bottles are the wines worth seeking out.

**The Berth.** Auberge du Soleil in Rutherford on the hillside; Meadowood; Bardessono in Yountville; or Cottages of Napa Valley for the budget-classic.

**The Galley.** The French Laundry (Thomas Keller), book three months ahead; Bouchon for the bistro; SingleThread in Healdsburg for the Sonoma equivalent; Oxbow Public Market in downtown Napa for the lunch graze.

> You don't have to cook fancy or complicated masterpieces, just good food from fresh ingredients.
> *Julia Child*

---

## Pilgrimage XXIV. The Fame That Never Dies

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of the Viking Age, from the raid on the Lindisfarne monastery on June 8, 793, that announced the Vikings to a horrified Christian Europe, through to King Harald Hardrada's defeat at Stamford Bridge on September 25, 1066, that closed the era. Anchored to the great Viking-Age trading and political centers of Norway, Sweden, Denmark, and the North Atlantic outposts in Iceland and L'Anse aux Meadows. This calendar already lists 30+ Viking festivals across the year, Up Helly Aa, Jorvik, Lofotr, Trelleborg, Birka, Catoira, Ribe, Foteviken, that bring the period to life on real ground. The trail below is the year-round permanent infrastructure: the museums, the ship halls, the runestones, the actual archaeological sites where the period happened. Three trips, four to seven days each: a Northumbria-and-North-Sea crossing prelude (Lindisfarne + Jorvik York), the Scandinavian core circuit (Oslo + Stockholm + Copenhagen + Denmark's Jelling), and the North Atlantic outposts (Iceland and Newfoundland, for the determined).

> From the fury of the Northmen, deliver us, O Lord.
> *9th-century European prayer*

### Stop 1. Lindisfarne

**Waypoint:** Northumbria, UK

Where it began. On June 8, 793, a Viking raiding party fell on the monastery of Lindisfarne, the spiritual heart of Northumbrian Christianity, founded by Saint Aidan in 635, slaughtering or carrying off the monks and looting the precious metalwork that had drawn them. The raid sent a single horrified report racing through the courts of Christian Europe (Alcuin of York: 'never before has such a terror appeared in Britain as we have now suffered from a pagan race'); within a generation, Viking raiding had spread along every coast of the British Isles and into Francia. The island today is tide-locked: a paved causeway, submerged at high tide, connects to the mainland twice daily, check the safe-crossing tide tables. The 12th-century Norman priory ruins occupy the site of the original monastery; the Lindisfarne Heritage Centre (rebuilt 2019) covers the raid in detail. Pair with Jorvik in York 90 minutes south.

**The Berth.** London anchored: The Connaught, The Beaumont, The Zetter Townhouse, or the Hoxton. Country: Heckfield Place, The Pig hotels, or Soho Farmhouse.

**The Galley.** London: St. JOHN, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers in Marlow; L'Enclume in Cumbria; or the canonical local gastropub.

> Never before has such terror appeared in Britain as we have now suffered from a pagan race.
> *Alcuin of York, on the raid of 793*

### Stop 2. Jorvik Viking Centre & York

**Waypoint:** Yorkshire, UK

Where the Norse ruled northern England. York's purpose-built Viking museum on Coppergate, built atop the 1976-81 archaeological excavation of Jorvik, the Norse-controlled York that ruled northern England from 866 to 954. The reconstructed time-ride glides past sound, smell, and 800-figure recreation of the 10th-century city; the gallery above holds the original recovered artifacts (the Coppergate Helmet, the leather shoes, the silver hoard). The Jorvik Viking Festival in mid-February is the year's anchor, strongman contests, longship rowing on the Ouse, the boat-burning finale on the riverbank. York Minster, Clifford's Tower, and the medieval city walls fill the rest of the day.

**The Berth.** Grays Court, the boutique inside the city walls; The Grand York on Station Rise; or Hotel Du Vin York in the converted 19th-century engineer's mess.

**The Galley.** Skosh on Micklegate for the small-plate seasonal; The Star Inn the City for the Yorkshire restaurant on the river; Bettys Café Tea Rooms on St Helen's Square for the canonical Yorkshire tea.

> A guest must depart again on his way; no man can stay forever.
> *the Hávamál*

### Stop 3. Dublin & the National Museum

**Waypoint:** Ireland

Where the Vikings built a capital in Ireland. The Norse founded Dublin in 841 as a longphort, a fortified ship-camp on the black pool (dubh linn) where the Poddle meets the Liffey, and it grew into the greatest Viking town in the western seas, a hub of the slave and silver trade with tendrils reaching to Iceland, Spain, and Byzantium. For three centuries Norse kings ruled here, until Brian Boru broke their power at the Battle of Clontarf in 1014. The Wood Quay excavations of the 1970s uncovered the timber houses, wharves, and workshops of the Viking city beneath the modern streets, the richest urban Viking dig in Europe, and its finds, the swords, the decorated combs, the runic inscriptions, the great hoards of Hiberno-Norse silver, fill the Viking gallery of the National Museum of Ireland on Kildare Street. Walk Wood Quay along the Liffey where the longships once beached, then stand among the recovered treasures and grasp how far these northern sailors reached.

**The Berth.** Dublin: The Shelbourne on St Stephen's Green, the grande dame; The Merrion in a row of Georgian townhouses; or the Wilder for the boutique stay near the green.

**The Galley.** Dublin: Chapter One for the Michelin Irish; the seafood at Klaw; oysters and stout at the Lord Edward; a proper pint of Guinness drawn slow at Kehoe's or the Long Hall.

> Cattle die, kinsmen die, the self must also die; but the fame of a dead man's deeds never dies.
> *the Hávamál, the Sayings of the High One*

### Stop 4. Viking Ship Museum & Historical Museum

**Waypoint:** Oslo, Norway

Where the great longships were raised from the earth. The two essential anchors of any Viking pilgrimage in Norway. The Viking Ship Museum on the Bygdøy peninsula displays three actual Viking-Age ship burials excavated from the Oslo Fjord region, the Oseberg ship (820 CE, the most ornate, with elaborate animal-head prow carvings; buried with two women, one likely a queen), the Gokstad ship (890 CE, the largest at 23.8 meters, the warship), and the Tune ship (the smallest and most damaged). The museum is currently being rebuilt as the Museum of the Viking Age (reopening planned soon, confirm status before booking). The Historical Museum in central Oslo holds the surviving Viking gold and silver hoards plus the Oseberg grave goods (textiles, sled, wagon, the carved 'Buddha bucket'). Together: a complete day.

**The Berth.** Oslo: The Thief on Tjuvholmen; Grand Hotel on Karl Johans gate; or Amerikalinjen in the converted shipping-line headquarters. Bergen: Opus XVI in the heritage building near Bryggen.

**The Galley.** Oslo: Maaemo for the three-Michelin-star New Nordic; Statholdergaarden in the historic stadthouse; Mathallen Oslo for the food-hall graze. Bergen: Lysverket for the modern Norwegian.

> When faring on journeys, ward yourself well.
> *the Hávamál*

### Stop 5. Trondheim & Nidaros Cathedral

**Waypoint:** Norway

Where Norway's saint-king lies. The medieval capital of Norway, founded in 997 by King Olaf Tryggvason at the mouth of the Nidelva river, the political heart of the Viking-Age kingdom for two centuries. Nidaros Cathedral, begun 1070 over the burial site of Saint Olaf (King Olaf II Haraldsson, killed at the Battle of Stiklestad in 1030, canonized in 1031), is the northernmost medieval cathedral in the world and Norway's coronation church; Saint Olaf's relics drew pilgrims from across northern Europe along the Pilgrim's Way (the St. Olav Ways) until the Reformation. The modern Pilgrim's Way has been revived since 1997, walked routes from Oslo (640 km) and Selånger in Sweden to Nidaros, with marked stages and pilgrim hostels. Pair with the Trøndelag region's strong Viking-Age heritage.

**The Berth.** Oslo: The Thief on Tjuvholmen; Grand Hotel on Karl Johans gate; or Amerikalinjen in the converted shipping-line headquarters. Bergen: Opus XVI in the heritage building near Bryggen.

**The Galley.** Oslo: Maaemo for the three-Michelin-star New Nordic; Statholdergaarden in the historic stadthouse; Mathallen Oslo for the food-hall graze. Bergen: Lysverket for the modern Norwegian.

> Better to fight and fall than to live without hope.
> *the Völsunga Saga*

### Stop 6. Birka, Hovgården & Stockholm's Historiska

**Waypoint:** Sweden

Where Sweden's first town traded with the world. The Viking-Age port of Birka on Björkö island in Lake Mälaren, Sweden's first town, the major Scandinavian trading hub from c.750 to 975, UNESCO-listed alongside the royal estate of Hovgården on neighboring Adelsö. The Birka Viking Village permanent reconstruction operates as a year-round museum; ferry from Stockholm city center, two-hour day trip. Pair with the Historiska Museet in central Stockholm, the Swedish History Museum holds the largest Viking-Age artifact collection on Earth, including the spectacular Gold Room (silver hoards, the Vendel Period helmets that pre-figure Viking design, and the Mälsåker treasure). The birka viking festival in early August, the foteviken viking market in late July, and alsnu vikingadagar in early May are all on this calendar.

**The Berth.** Stockholm: Grand Hôtel on Blasieholmskajen; Ett Hem in Lärkstaden for the boutique; or At Six in Brunkeberg.

**The Galley.** Frantzén for the three-Michelin-star; Aira on Djurgården for the Nordic seasonal; Tradition for canonical husmanskost; Östermalms Saluhall for the hall lunch.

> A wayfarer should not walk unarmed, but have his weapons to hand.
> *the Hávamál*

### Stop 7. Roskilde Viking Ship Museum & the Jelling Stones

**Waypoint:** Denmark

Where Denmark was born a Christian kingdom. Two anchors of the Danish Viking world. The Roskilde Viking Ship Museum on the Roskilde Fjord 30 km west of Copenhagen displays the Skuldelev Ships, five Viking vessels (a longship, a knarr trader, a coastal trader, a ferry, and the Skuldelev 5 warship) deliberately scuttled around 1070 to block the fjord against attackers, raised in 1962, painstakingly reassembled from waterlogged fragments. The museum's outdoor boatyard builds full-scale sailing replicas; in summer you can sail one. The Jelling Stones in central Jutland, two hours west, are the runic 'birth certificate of Denmark', King Gorm's smaller stone (c.950) and his son Harald Bluetooth's larger stone (c.965) declaring Harald 'won for himself all Denmark and Norway, and made the Danes Christian.' UNESCO-listed. Together they bracket the moment Denmark became a unified Christian kingdom.

**The Berth.** Copenhagen: Hotel d'Angleterre on Kongens Nytorv; Hotel Sanders in the historic block; or Nimb at Tivoli for the festival proximity.

**The Galley.** Geranium for the three-Michelin-star; Restaurant Barr on the harbour; Apollo Bar at Charlottenborg for the natural-wine bistro; smørrebrød at Schønnemann for the canonical lunch.

> King Harald won for himself all Denmark and Norway, and made the Danes Christian.
> *the great Jelling Stone of Harald Bluetooth, c. 965*

### Stop 8. Hedeby

**Waypoint:** Schleswig, Germany

Where the Baltic met the North Sea. The largest Viking-Age trading city in Northern Europe, UNESCO-listed since 2018 (jointly with the Danevirke earthwork that defended its southern approaches). At its peak around 900, Hedeby held perhaps 1,500-2,000 inhabitants and connected the Baltic to the North Sea via the short overland route between the Schlei fjord and the Eider river, a key choke-point on the trade route between the Frankish empire and the Viking world. Sacked by King Harald Hardrada around 1050 (a Norwegian Viking destroying a Danish-Viking city, the period's late, complicated politics), abandoned soon after, never rebuilt; the site is now a vast preserved earthwork ring of ramparts on a quiet meadow. The Wikinger Museum Haithabu reconstructs the harbor and seven longhouses. Pair with the haithabhu spring viking market in mid-April, already on calendar.

**The Berth.** Berlin: Hotel Adlon Kempinski; Soho House Berlin; 25hours Bikini. Munich: Bayerischer Hof. Hamburg: The Fontenay. Frankfurt: Roomers.

**The Galley.** Berlin: Markthalle Neun; Mustafa's Gemüse Kebap; Lode & Stijn. Munich: Tantris; Hofbräuhaus; Schneider Bräuhaus. Hamburg: Fischmarkt; Bullerei. Frankfurt: Adolf Wagner; Lafleur.

> No better burden a man can bear on the road than a store of common sense.
> *the Hávamál*

### Stop 9. Reykjavík & the Þingvellir National Park

**Waypoint:** Iceland

Where the world's oldest parliament first met. The first North Atlantic Viking colony, settled by Norwegian Norsemen led by Ingólfr Arnarson around 874 CE, and home to the Alþingi, the world's oldest continuously functioning parliamentary assembly, founded in 930 at Þingvellir. The Þingvellir plain, a UNESCO site where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge surfaces between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates, was the convening ground every June for the assembled chieftains and free farmers; you can walk the Almannagjá rift between the continental plates and stand at the Lögberg (Law Rock) where laws were proclaimed annually. In Reykjavík, the Settlement Exhibition (Landnámssýningin) is built around an actual 10th-century Viking longhouse foundation discovered in 2001 during construction, preserved in situ beneath the modern museum. Pair with a longer Iceland circuit (Golden Circle, South Coast).

**The Berth.** Reykjavík: The Reykjavik Edition on Austurbakki; Tower Suites at Hotel Reykjavík Saga; or Hotel Borg on Austurvöllur for the heritage. North/East: Hotel Húsafell or Sigló Hótel in Siglufjörður.

**The Galley.** Reykjavík: Dill for the Michelin-starred New Nordic; Matur og Drykkur in the harbour for canonical Icelandic; Bæjarins Beztu Pylsur for the lamb hot dog. Around the Ring Road: hotel restaurants and roadside lamb soup.

> With law shall our land be built up, but with lawlessness laid waste.
> *Njáll, in Njáls saga*

### Stop 10. L'Anse aux Meadows

**Waypoint:** Newfoundland, Canada

Where the Vikings reached the New World. The 11th-century Norse settlement at the northern tip of Newfoundland, UNESCO-listed since 1978, the only confirmed pre-Columbian Viking site in North America, occupied briefly around 1000 CE by Norse Greenlanders led likely by Leif Erikson and his brother Thorvald (the Vinland of the Vinland Sagas). Eight reconstructed turf-and-timber buildings on the actual archaeological site; the visitor center frames the discovery (by Norwegian explorer Helge Ingstad and archaeologist Anne Stine in 1960) as the moment Indigenous oral history and Norse saga literature converged on a single piece of physical evidence. The most remote stop in this trail and the geographic westernmost point the Vikings ever reached. Best June-September. Fly into Deer Lake, then drive 5 hours north up the Viking Trail (Highway 430).

**The Berth.** Fogo Island Inn, one of the most distinctive hotels in the world, on the rocks of Fogo Island. Or in St John's: Alt Hotel St John's or The Capital Hotel.

**The Galley.** Fogo Island Inn dining room for the foraged-and-fished tasting menu; in St John's: Raymonds for the modern Canadian; Mallard Cottage on the harbour for the brunch; Chinched Bistro for the meaty seasonal.

> Leif the Lucky found a new land to the west, with wild grapes and self-sown wheat, and called it Vinland.
> *after the Saga of the Greenlanders*

## Pilgrimage XXV. The Glory That Was Greece

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of ancient Greece, from the Bronze Age citadels of the Mycenaean world (Homer's Iliad, c.1250 BCE) and the Minoan palaces of Crete (an even earlier non-Greek Aegean civilization) through the foundational moments of Classical Greece: the 490 BCE victory at Marathon and the 480 BCE last stand at Thermopylae, the philosophical and democratic flowering at Athens, the religious authority of the Delphic Oracle, and the pan-Hellenic athletic gathering at Olympia. Already paired on calendar with the ATHENS & EPIDAURUS FESTIVAL (June-August), the surviving tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripides performed in their original 4th-century BCE theater on the Argolid, and with the Acropolis & Parthenon already in the Monuments section. Three trips, five to seven days each: a mainland leg (Athens + Marathon + Thermopylae + Delphi), a Peloponnese circuit (Olympia + Mycenae/Epidaurus + Sparta/Mystras), and a Crete-and-Anatolia bookend pairing the Minoan and Trojan ends of the Greek imagination (Knossos + Troy). Best April-May or September-October to avoid Aegean

> Come back with your shield, or upon it.
> *Spartan mothers to their sons, per Plutarch*

### Stop 1. Athens

**Waypoint:** the Acropolis, the Agora & the Pnyx

Where democracy and philosophy were born. The cultural and political center of Classical Greece, the city of Pericles, Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. The Acropolis is the iconic anchor: the Parthenon (447-432 BCE, Iktinos and Kallikrates with Phidias as artistic director), the Erechtheion with its Caryatid Porch, the Temple of Athena Nike. Below on the north slope, the Ancient Agora was the political and commercial heart of the polis, the rebuilt Stoa of Attalos houses the Agora Museum; the Temple of Hephaestus (449 BCE) is the best-preserved Classical Greek temple anywhere in Greece. The Pnyx, a small rocky hill 400 meters southwest of the Acropolis, was the meeting place of the Athenian Ekklesia where direct democracy was practiced from 508 BCE; the speakers' platform (bema) is still visible. Pair with the new Acropolis Museum at the foot of the south slope, the National Archaeological Museum (Mycenaean gold, the Antikythera Mechanism), and the ATHENS & epidaurus festival July-August, already on calendar.

**The Berth.** Athens: Hotel Grande Bretagne on Syntagma; AthensWas in Plaka for the Acropolis-view boutique; Electra Metropolis for the rooftop view.

**The Galley.** Athens: Spondi for the Michelin canonical; Diporto in the central market for the canonical kafeneio; Karamanlidika for the deli-restaurant; To Kafenio in Plaka.

> Our constitution is called a democracy because power is in the hands not of a minority but of the whole people.
> *Pericles, Funeral Oration, via Thucydides*

### Stop 2. Cape Sounion

**Waypoint:** the southern tip of Attica

Where a king leapt into the sea, and gave it his name. On a high white cliff at the very end of the Attica peninsula, where the land of Athens runs out into the blue, stands the Temple of Poseidon, built in the fifth century BCE of gleaming local marble, fifteen of its slender Doric columns still rising sixty meters above the waves. To this headland, the myth says, old King Aegeus came day after day to watch the horizon for the ship of his son Theseus, returning from Crete and the Minotaur; the two had agreed on white sails for victory. Theseus triumphed but forgot to change his black sails of mourning, and Aegeus, seeing them, threw himself in despair from this cliff into the water, which has been called the Aegean Sea ever after. For ancient sailors the temple was the first and last sight of home; for the poet Byron it was so beautiful he carved his name in a column, where it remains. Come for the sunset, when the marble turns to gold above the wine-dark sea, and feel the place where myth and horizon meet.

**The Berth.** The Athens Riviera: the seaside resorts and hotels of the Sounion coast, some looking straight up at the temple; the elegant suburbs of Vouliagmeni and Glyfada on the way; or stay in Athens and come for the evening.

**The Galley.** Aegean seaside: the day's catch grilled simply with lemon and oil at a taverna below the cape; grilled octopus and fried calamari; a Greek salad with island feta; ouzo or a cold white wine as the sun goes down over the water.

> Place me on Sunium's marbled steep, where nothing, save the waves and I, may hear our mutual murmurs sweep.
> *Lord Byron, on Cape Sounion*

### Stop 3. Marathon Battlefield & the Athenian Tumulus

**Waypoint:** 30 km northeast of Athens

Where 10,000 Greeks turned back an empire. Miltiades defeated a Persian invasion force three times their size in September 490 BCE. The Athenian Tumulus, the surviving 12-meter burial mound of the 192 Athenian dead, still stands at the edge of the field; the Persian dead (estimated 6,400) were buried in a separate mound nearby. After the battle, the runner Pheidippides covered the 42 km from Marathon to Athens to deliver the news ('nenikēkamen', 'we have won') and collapsed dead from exhaustion, the origin of the marathon-distance footrace, formalized at the 1896 Athens Olympics over the same route. The Marathon Run Museum and the modern Marathon Race Start (the Athens Classic Marathon, second Sunday of November) anchor the village. Half-day trip from Athens.

**The Berth.** Stay in Athens (40 minutes south): Hotel Grande Bretagne; AthensWas; Electra Metropolis.

**The Galley.** Athens: Spondi; Diporto; Karamanlidika.

> Rejoice! We have won.
> *Pheidippides, the run from Marathon, 490 BCE*

### Stop 4. Thermopylae & the Leonidas Monument

**Waypoint:** 180 km northwest of Athens on the road to Lamia

Where the 300 made their stand. At the narrow coastal pass, King Leonidas I of Sparta and his 300 Spartans (plus 700 Thespians and 6,000 other Greek allies) held off Xerxes's Persian army for three days in August 480 BCE before being outflanked and annihilated. The pass has silted up over 2,500 years; the original Aegean shoreline is now 5 km inland, but the hot springs that gave the pass its name still flow at the modern site. The Leonidas Monument (1955) stands across the highway from the original battlefield, inscribed with Leonidas's reply to Xerxes's demand to surrender his weapons: 'Molōn labe' (Molon labe, 'Come and take them'). The Simonides epitaph from the burial mound, 'Go tell the Spartans, stranger passing by, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie', is reproduced beside it. The new Thermopylae Battle Centre (2010) provides historical context with a high-resolution model of the engagement. Pair with Delphi, an hour east through the mountains.

**The Berth.** Stay in Athens (90 minutes south): Hotel Grande Bretagne; AthensWas; Electra Metropolis.

**The Galley.** Athens: Spondi; Diporto; Karamanlidika; Funky Gourmet when open.

> Go tell the Spartans, stranger passing by, that here, obedient to their laws, we lie.
> *the epitaph of Simonides at Thermopylae*

### Stop 5. Delphi

**Waypoint:** the Oracle of Apollo & the Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia

Where the Greeks set the center of the world. The seat of the Pythian Oracle, UNESCO-listed since 1987, the most-consulted oracle in the Mediterranean for over a thousand years. The Greeks believed the Omphalos (a carved stone navel preserved in the on-site museum) marked the literal center of the Earth, identified by Zeus when he released two eagles from opposite ends of the world and they met above Delphi. The Sacred Way climbs Mount Parnassus past the rebuilt Athenian Treasury (490 BCE, dedicated after Marathon), the Temple of Apollo (where the Pythia delivered her oracular utterances over a chasm reportedly releasing intoxicating vapors), the theater, and the stadium where the Pythian Games were held every four years. The separate Sanctuary of Athena Pronaia below the main site holds the iconic Tholos, the most-photographed Doric rotunda in Greece. Pair with Mount Parnassus (skiing December-March, hiking June-September). Best April-May or September-October.

**The Berth.** Amalia Hotel Delphi at the foot of Mount Parnassus; Hotel Leto in central Delphi; or Pan Hotel for the budget choice.

**The Galley.** Taverna Vakhos in central Delphi for the canonical Phocian moussaka and lamb; Taverna Iniochos for the modern Greek; To Patriko Mas for the meze.

> Know thyself.
> *the Delphic maxim, inscribed at the Temple of Apollo*

### Stop 6. Olympia

**Waypoint:** the Sacred Grove & the Origin of the Games

Where the Games began. UNESCO-listed since 1989, the site of the original Olympic Games, held every four years from 776 BCE through 393 CE, a continuous 1,169-year run, the longest of any institution in classical antiquity. The Sacred Grove (the Altis) holds the ruins of the Temple of Zeus (which originally housed Phidias's 13-meter chryselephantine Statue of Zeus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, lost to fire and looting after 426 CE), the Temple of Hera, the Workshop of Phidias (where the statue was sculpted), and the Stadium that held 45,000 spectators. The starting line of the original stadium (192 meters, the standard Greek stade) is preserved, you can run it. The Altar of Hera at the western end is where the modern Olympic Torch is lit by parabolic mirror in a ceremony staged in costume by actresses in the role of priestesses, before each Olympic Games (most recently February 2026 for the Milan-Cortina Winter Games). Pair with the Olympia Archaeological Museum across the road for the Hermes of Praxiteles.

**The Berth.** Hotel Antonios in central Ancient Olympia; Best Western Europa Hotel; or Olympia Diana Hotel for the small-budget choice.

**The Galley.** Taverna Pasxalia for canonical Peloponnesian; Taverna Symposium for the modern Greek; The Aegli Café for the morning frappé.

> Water is best, and gold shines like fire blazing in the night.
> *Pindar, Olympian Ode 1*

### Stop 7. Mycenae & Epidaurus

**Waypoint:** the Argolid Peninsula

Where Agamemnon ruled and the theater still sings. Two of the great archaeological sites of the Peloponnese, 90 minutes apart and easily paired in a single day or overnight from Nafplio. Mycenae (UNESCO-listed) is the Bronze Age citadel of the Atreid dynasty, Agamemnon's capital, the Greek heart of the Iliad. The Lion Gate (1250 BCE) is the oldest monumental sculpture in Europe; the Cyclopean walls, the Treasury of Atreus (the tholos beehive tomb that prefigured the Pantheon's dome by 1,500 years), and the surviving foundations of the megaron palace remain. Heinrich Schliemann excavated the site in 1876 and pulled the gold 'Mask of Agamemnon' from Grave Circle A (now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens). Epidaurus (UNESCO-listed) was the great healing sanctuary of Asclepius and holds the most perfectly preserved 4th-century BCE theater in Greece, 14,000 seats with acoustics so refined a coin dropped on the orkhestra is audible from the top row. Already paired with the ATHENS & epidaurus festival on calendar (June-August).

**The Berth.** Stay in Nafplio (20 minutes south): Nafplia Palace; Amphitryon Hotel; or Aetoma Hotel for the boutique.

**The Galley.** Nafplio: To Omorfo Tavernaki for canonical Argolid; Bouboulina's; To Skouma for the seafood; Antica Gelateria di Roma for the Italian gelato in the square.

> Sing, goddess, the rage of Achilles, son of Peleus.
> *Homer, the opening of the Iliad*

### Stop 8. Sparta & Mystras

**Waypoint:** the Eurotas Valley

Where the warrior city left almost no trace. Modern Sparta sits in the broad valley of the Eurotas river, beautiful agricultural land, but archaeologically thin, exactly as Thucydides predicted in the 5th century BCE: that future generations would find here 'no temples or buildings of magnificence.' The surviving ancient sites are sparse: the Menelaion (the sanctuary of Menelaus and Helen, with sweeping valley views), the partially excavated Acropolis, and the foundations of the theater. The modern Leonidas statue at the north end of town and the ceremonial Tomb of Leonidas (the actual remains were lost) carry the symbolic weight. Eight kilometers west, the UNESCO-listed Byzantine fortified city of Mystras compensates for the Spartan austerity, climbing the Taygetos foothills in tiers of medieval churches, palaces, and monasteries from the 13th through 15th centuries; Constantine XI Palaiologos, the last Byzantine emperor, was crowned here in 1449 before the fall of Constantinople. Pair with the surrounding Mani peninsula, tower-houses, isolated coastal villages, and the mythological entrance to the underworld at the Caves of Diros.

**The Berth.** Sparta Inn in central Sparta; Lakonia Hotel; or stay in Mystras itself: Pyrgos Mystra Hotel.

**The Galley.** Sparta: Diporto for canonical Laconian; Stou Vrettou for the local meze. Mystras: Taverna Marmara for the village taverna.

> Future ages would never guess, from her ruins, how great the power of Sparta had been.
> *after Thucydides, on Sparta*

### Stop 9. Knossos & the Heraklion Archaeological Museum

**Waypoint:** Crete

Where the labyrinth and the Minotaur were dreamed. UNESCO-listed, the Bronze Age palace complex of the Minoan civilization, the pre-Greek Aegean civilization that flourished from c.3000 to 1450 BCE, named by Sir Arthur Evans (who excavated and controversially reconstructed the site between 1900 and 1931) after the legendary King Minos. The Throne Room holds the oldest throne in Europe; the bull-leaping frescoes, the snake goddesses, and the mythological labyrinth are all here. Evans's reinforced-concrete reconstructions are aesthetically polarizing but allow you to read the spaces in three dimensions. The Heraklion Archaeological Museum, a 20-minute drive away in the city, holds all the original finds, the Bull-Leaping Fresco, the Phaistos Disc (the undeciphered clay disc of Minoan symbols, c.1700 BCE), the figurine snake goddesses, the gold Bee Pendant. Combine with Phaistos and Malia (other Minoan palaces on the same island) for a full Minoan circuit. Best April-May or September-November.

**The Berth.** Heraklion: GDM Megaron Hotel; Lato Boutique Hotel. Crete coast: Domes of Elounda; Blue Palace.

**The Galley.** Heraklion: Peskesi for canonical Cretan; Karnayio for the seafood. Crete coast: the local taverna in any village for the dakos and cretan cheese.

> I hope for nothing. I fear nothing. I am free.
> *Nikos Kazantzakis, his epitaph in Heraklion, Crete*

### Stop 10. Troy

**Waypoint:** Çanakkale Province, Türkiye

Where Homer's war was found in the earth. UNESCO-listed since 1998, the site Heinrich Schliemann excavated 1870-1890 on the strength of nothing more than his obsessive reading of Homer, and was vindicated by uncovering nine layers of city stacked atop each other on the mound of Hisarlik. Troy VII (c.1180 BCE) is the layer most likely corresponding to the Homeric Trojan War; Troy II is the layer Schliemann incorrectly identified as Priam's city, and from which he removed the gold 'Treasure of Priam' (most of it lost in WWII Berlin, now contested between several museums). The site is austere, foundations, walls, the surviving section of the legendary Walls of Troy still standing after over 3,000 years, but Homer's text overlays everything you walk through. The kitsch wooden horse replica at the entrance is the ritual photograph; the actual film prop sits on the Çanakkale waterfront. The Troy Museum 200 meters from the archaeological site (opened 2018) is superb. Just 50 km south of Gallipoli, pair with anzac day at Gallipoli, April 25 (already on calendar) for a paired ancient-and-modern war pilgrimage.

**The Berth.** Istanbul: Çırağan Palace Kempinski on the Bosphorus; the Pera Palace in Beyoğlu; the Sumahan on the Asian shore. Cappadocia: Argos in Cappadocia.

**The Galley.** Istanbul: Mikla on the rooftop of the Marmara Pera; Pandeli in the Spice Bazaar; Karaköy Lokantası; Çiya Sofrası in Kadıköy. Anatolia: Asitane in Edirnekapı for the Ottoman court cuisine.

> There will come a day when sacred Troy shall perish.
> *Homer, the Iliad*
