## Pilgrimage XXVI. The Grandeur That Was Rome

Year-round destinations along the historical and geographic arc of the Roman world, from the mythological 753 BCE founding of Rome through the unification of the Mediterranean basin under Augustus (27 BCE) to the gradual fragmentation of the Western Empire by 476 CE. The Roman achievement was the most successful imperial project in Western history; its surviving infrastructure, roads, aqueducts, theaters, baths, amphitheaters, walls, defined the urban template of every European city for the next two thousand years and underwrites the Western legal, linguistic, and architectural inheritance. Already paired on calendar with the Colosseum, Forum, and Pantheon (Monuments section), with Pompeii (Monuments section), with Volubilis in Morocco (Monuments section, Roman Mauretania), and naturally adjacent to the Greek & Spartan Pilgrimage that precedes it (Greek civilization providing the cultural and philosophical material that Rome systematized and exported across three continents). Three trips, five to seven days each: the Italian core (Rome + Pompeii + Tivoli/Ostia), the northern frontier (Hadrian's Wall + Trier + Provence), and the Mediterranean rim (Ephesus + Carthage + Volubilis), the three continents Rome stitched into a single political imagination.

> All roads lead to Rome.
> *medieval European proverb*

### Stop 1. Rome

**Waypoint:** the Forum, Capitoline, Aurelian Walls & Appian Way

Where the empire was governed and remembered. The Roman Forum (Foro Romano) was the political, religious, and commercial heart of the Republic and early Empire. The Capitoline Museums (founded 1471, the world's oldest public museum, set in the Michelangelo-designed Piazza del Campidoglio) hold the Capitoline She-Wolf, the colossal head and hand of Constantine, and the original equestrian Marcus Aurelius (the Piazza version is a copy). The Aurelian Walls (271-275 CE) define the late-imperial city perimeter, 19 km of brick-faced concrete still encircle the historic center. Walk a kilometer of the original basalt Appian Way (the queen of roads, begun 312 BCE) past the Tomb of Cecilia Metella to the Catacombs of San Callisto, the underground Christian burial galleries that ran for 20 km beneath the surface. The Trastevere neighborhood across the Tiber holds the medieval continuity: cacio e pepe at Da Enzo, the Basilica of Santa Maria in Trastevere (3rd century, oldest church dedicated to the Virgin Mary). Allow at least three days for Rome alone.

**The Berth.** Hotel de Russie on Via del Babuino with the secret garden; Hotel Hassler at the top of the Spanish Steps; or G-Rough on Piazza Navona for the design-set boutique.

**The Galley.** Roscioli on Via dei Giubbonari for cacio e pepe and the Saturday-afternoon salumi tasting; Felice a Testaccio for Tonnarelli; Trattoria Da Cesare al Casaletto for fritti; Bonci Pizzarium for pizza al taglio near the Vatican.

> Romans, remember to rule the peoples with your power.
> *Virgil, the Aeneid*

### Stop 2. Pompeii, Herculaneum & Vesuvius

**Waypoint:** Bay of Naples

Where a city was frozen in an afternoon. Already covered in this calendar's Monuments section, Pompeii is the best-preserved snapshot of any Roman city, frozen by the August 24, 79 CE eruption of Vesuvius (some scholars now argue for an October 24 date based on charred fruit and brazier remains; either way, the chronology is clear). The trail expands the experience: pair Pompeii with Herculaneum 6 km west on the bay, the smaller, wealthier sister-city buried in a different way (volcanic mud sealed organic material; Herculaneum's wooden beams, papyrus scrolls, and even bread loaves survive). The Villa of the Papyri at Herculaneum yielded a library of carbonized scrolls now being deciphered with synchrotron imaging, first Greek philosophical text fully recovered from the Vesuvius scrolls was published in 2024. Climb Vesuvius itself (1,281 m, 30-minute walk from the parking area at 1,000 m, dormant but actively monitored). The Naples National Archaeological Museum holds the original frescoes and mosaics removed from both sites, the Alexander Mosaic from the House of the Faun and the Gabinetto Segreto erotic-art collection are essential.

**The Berth.** Grand Hotel Vesuvio on the Lungomare; Romeo Hotel in the Porto; or Hotel Excelsior facing Castel dell'Ovo.

**The Galley.** L'Antica Pizzeria da Michele for the Margherita; Sorbillo on Via dei Tribunali; Trattoria Nennella in the Spanish Quarters; sfogliatella from Pintauro on Via Toledo.

> Ashes were already falling, but not yet thickly; I looked back, and a dense cloud loomed behind us.
> *Pliny the Younger, on the eruption of Vesuvius*

### Stop 3. Hadrian's Villa & Ostia Antica

**Waypoint:** outside Rome

Where an emperor dreamed and a port city worked. Two contrasting Roman experiences within an hour of central Rome. Hadrian's Villa (UNESCO-listed) at Tivoli, 30 km east, was the emperor's enormous private retreat (118-138 CE), 120 hectares of palaces, libraries, baths, two theaters, a monumental swimming pool (the Canopus, modeled on a temple complex in Egypt that Hadrian had visited), and a private island villa (the Maritime Theatre) where the emperor went to be alone. The site was looted across the Renaissance and the Grand Tour, and many of the great Roman bronzes and marbles in European museums originated here. Pair with the nearby Villa d'Este (1572 Renaissance gardens with 51 fountains). Ostia Antica, 30 km southwest of Rome at the original Tiber mouth, is what Pompeii would look like if it had been a port, a complete Roman commercial city with apartment blocks (insulae) up to four stories, a forum, baths, an amphitheater, and the well-preserved Mithraeum of the Imperial Palace. Allow a half-day for each.

**The Berth.** Hotel de Russie on Via del Babuino with the secret garden; Hotel Hassler at the top of the Spanish Steps; or G-Rough on Piazza Navona for the design-set boutique.

**The Galley.** Roscioli on Via dei Giubbonari for cacio e pepe and the Saturday-afternoon salumi tasting; Felice a Testaccio for Tonnarelli; Trattoria Da Cesare al Casaletto for fritti; Bonci Pizzarium for pizza al taglio near the Vatican.

> Little soul, gentle and wandering, guest and companion of the body.
> *the Emperor Hadrian, his dying lines*

### Stop 4. Hadrian's Wall, Vindolanda & the Northern Frontier

**Waypoint:** England

Where Rome drew its northern edge. The frontier of the empire, UNESCO-listed since 1987 (as part of the broader Frontiers of the Roman Empire site). The 117-km wall built between 122 and 128 CE under Emperor Hadrian, from the Solway Firth on the west to the Tyne river on the east, with 80 milecastles, 16 forts, and the deep ditch of the Vallum still visible across Northumberland's open moors. The most evocative stretches run between Sycamore Gap (made famous by the now-felled tree at the dip in the wall, cut down overnight on 27 September 2023) and Housesteads Roman Fort. Vindolanda, the auxiliary fort just south of the Wall, has yielded over 1,800 wooden writing tablets, the actual letters of Roman soldiers, including a birthday party invitation from one officer's wife to another (the earliest surviving handwriting by a woman in Latin, c.100 CE), all on display at the on-site Vindolanda Museum. Walk the National Trail (84 miles, Wallsend to Bowness-on-Solway) end to end in 6-7 days, or sample sections from Hexham. Best April-October.

**The Berth.** London: The Connaught, The Beaumont, The Zetter Townhouse, or The Hoxton. Country: Heckfield Place, The Newt in Somerset, or Soho Farmhouse.

**The Galley.** London: St. JOHN, Sketch, Padella, Quo Vadis. Country: The Hand & Flowers (Tom Kerridge), L'Enclume in Cumbria, or any local gastropub Sunday roast.

> I shall expect you, sister. Farewell, my dearest soul.
> *the Vindolanda birthday invitation, c. 100 CE*

### Stop 5. Trier

**Waypoint:** Roman Capital of Gaul, Germany

Where emperors ruled north of the Alps. The largest Roman city north of the Alps, UNESCO-listed since 1986. Founded by Augustus in 16 BCE as Augusta Treverorum, Trier served as imperial residence to Diocletian, Constantine, and Valentinian, and at its peak in the 4th century was one of the four capitals of the Tetrarchy. The Porta Nigra (170 CE) is the largest surviving Roman city gate in the world, named for the basalt-blackened sandstone. The Aula Palatina (Constantine's Basilica, 310 CE) is the largest single-room Roman structure surviving anywhere, 67 meters long, now a Lutheran church. The Imperial Baths (Kaiserthermen) and the smaller Forum Baths cover several hectares; the Roman amphitheater seated 18,000; the Roman Bridge (144 CE) still carries traffic across the Mosel. The Rheinisches Landesmuseum holds the Neumagen Wine Ship sculpture and the Trier Gold Hoard. Pair with the Mosel Valley wine region for a longer trip.

**The Berth.** Berlin: Hotel Adlon Kempinski; Soho House Berlin; 25hours Bikini. Munich: Bayerischer Hof. Hamburg: The Fontenay. Frankfurt: Roomers.

**The Galley.** Berlin: Markthalle Neun; Mustafa's Gemüse Kebap; Lode & Stijn. Munich: Tantris; Hofbräuhaus; Schneider Bräuhaus. Hamburg: Fischmarkt; Bullerei. Frankfurt: Adolf Wagner; Lafleur.

> Hail to thee, Treveri, city that feeds, clothes, and arms the empire.
> *after Ausonius, poet of Roman Trier*

### Stop 6. Nîmes, Pont du Gard & Arles

**Waypoint:** Provence, France

Where Rome left its mark on Provence. The Roman trio of southern France, all UNESCO-listed. Nîmes preserves the Maison Carrée (built c.16-20 BCE by Marcus Agrippa, dedicated to Augustus's grandsons Gaius and Lucius Caesar, the only Roman temple in the world surviving completely intact, the model for Thomas Jefferson's Virginia State Capitol; UNESCO-listed September 2023) and the 1st-century CE amphitheater (24,000 seats, still hosting bullfights and concerts). The Pont du Gard, 25 km northeast, is the highest surviving Roman aqueduct bridge, three tiers, 49 meters above the Gardon river, built mid-1st century CE to carry water 50 km from Uzès to Nîmes (the channel still drains by gravity along its original 1-in-3,000 gradient). Arles, an hour east, anchored Roman Provence with its own amphitheater (still hosting Camargue bullfights), the cryptoportiques beneath the forum, the necropolis of Alyscamps that Van Gogh painted, and the Musée de l'Arles antique. The whole region was Roman from 121 BCE. Best April-October.

**The Berth.** Provence: a mas (farmhouse) in the Alpilles near Saint-Rémy; the hotels of old Nîmes or Arles; or the elegant Avignon and Uzès within easy reach of all three Roman sites.

**The Galley.** Provençal: the bull-meat gardiane of the Camargue with Camargue red rice; tapenade, brandade de Nîmes, and aïoli; the rosés of the Rhône; a long lunch in a shaded Arles square.

> I have raised a monument more lasting than bronze.
> *Horace, Odes*

### Stop 7. Mérida

**Waypoint:** Augusta Emerita, Spain

Where Rome's legionnaires retired. UNESCO-listed since 1993, the most spectacular Roman city in Spain, Augusta Emerita, founded by Augustus in 25 BCE as a settlement for legionnaires retired from the Cantabrian Wars (the name means 'colony of the retirees'). The Roman Theatre (16-15 BCE), with 6,000 seats and an intact stage backdrop of marble columns, hosts the annual Mérida Classical Theatre Festival every July-August (the oldest theater festival in Spain, performances of Aeschylus, Sophocles, Plautus, and Seneca staged on the original Roman stage). The adjoining amphitheater, the Roman Circus, the Casa del Mitreo with its Cosmological Mosaic, the Aqueduct of the Miraculous, and the Roman Bridge over the Guadiana (792 meters, the longest surviving Roman bridge anywhere) complete the complex. The Museo Nacional de Arte Romano (Rafael Moneo, 1986) is the best Roman museum in Spain. Pair with Cáceres (UNESCO-listed medieval city) and Trujillo to the north for an Extremadura circuit. 3 hours southwest of Madrid by train.

**The Berth.** Madrid: The Westin Palace; The Ritz; NH Collection on Atocha. Barcelona: Hotel Casa Fuster; El Palace. San Sebastián: Hotel María Cristina.

**The Galley.** Madrid: Casa Lucio; Sobrino de Botín; DiverXO. Barcelona: Disfrutar; Tickets; Bar Cañete; Quimet i Quimet. San Sebastián: Arzak; Akelaŕe; pintxo bars in the Parte Vieja.

> As is a tale, so is life: not how long it is, but how good it is, is what matters.
> *Seneca, born in Roman Spain*

### Stop 8. Carthage & El Djem

**Waypoint:** Tunisia

Where Rome destroyed its great rival, then rebuilt it. Two of the great Roman sites in North Africa, both UNESCO-listed. Carthage, 15 km northeast of Tunis, was destroyed by Rome in 146 BCE at the end of the Third Punic War (Cato the Elder's 'Carthago delenda est' finally satisfied), then refounded as Colonia Julia Carthago by Julius Caesar in 44 BCE and expanded under Augustus until it became, by the 2nd century CE, the second-largest city in the western Roman Empire after Rome itself. The Antonine Baths (the largest Roman thermal complex outside Rome), the Punic Quarter on the Byrsa Hill, and the Tophet (the contested Carthaginian sacrificial site) survive across the modern suburb. El Djem, 200 km south, holds the third-largest Roman amphitheater in the world (after the Colosseum and Capua), a 35,000-seat 3rd-century CE arena rising from a wheat plain, its honey-colored stone visible from kilometers away. The Bardo National Museum in Tunis holds the world's greatest collection of Roman mosaics. Best October-April.

**The Berth.** Dar El Jeld in Tunis medina for the converted-palace stay; or La Villa Bleue in Sidi Bou Said for the cliff-top boutique.

**The Galley.** Dar El Jeld restaurant for the canonical Tunisian palace dinner; Le Golfe in La Marsa for the seafood; Café des Nattes in Sidi Bou Said for mint tea with pine nuts; brik à l'œuf at any street vendor.

> Carthago delenda est — Carthage must be destroyed.
> *Cato the Elder, to the Roman Senate*

### Stop 9. Split: Diocletian's Palace

**Waypoint:** the Dalmatian coast, Croatia

Where a Roman emperor retired to grow cabbages. When Diocletian abdicated in 305 CE, the only Roman emperor ever to step down willingly, he built himself a vast fortified palace on the Adriatic shore near his birthplace at Salona, and lived out his days there among his gardens. The palace was so enormous, some four hectares behind walls and sixteen towers, that the entire medieval town of Split later grew up inside it, and lives inside it still: shops and apartments and cafés are built into the imperial walls, the emperor's mausoleum became the cathedral, and his Temple of Jupiter became a baptistery. The colonnaded Peristyle court, the vast subterranean cellars (a favourite location for film and television crews), and the Golden Gate all survive. UNESCO-listed since 1979. Walk the Peristyle at dusk, when the white limestone glows, and grasp that you are standing inside a living Roman palace seventeen centuries old.

**The Berth.** Split: the Palace Judita Heritage Hotel inside the walls; Hotel Park near the Bačvice beach; or Vestibul Palace built into the Roman fabric itself.

**The Galley.** Dalmatian: black risotto and grilled Adriatic fish; pašticada (slow-braised beef) with gnocchi; Pag cheese and prosciutto; the wines of Hvar and Korčula; a konoba supper in the old town.

> Were you to see the cabbages I have planted with my own hands, you would not ask me to resume power.
> *attributed to the Emperor Diocletian, in his retirement at Split*

### Stop 10. Ephesus & Aphrodisias

**Waypoint:** Türkiye

Where Rome ruled the Greek East. The pair of great Roman cities in Asia Minor (Anatolia), both UNESCO-listed. Ephesus on the Aegean coast 70 km south of İzmir was the capital of the Roman province of Asia and one of the four largest cities in the empire by the 1st century CE. The Library of Celsus (135 CE) is the most-photographed Roman ruin outside Italy; the Great Theatre (24,000 seats, where Saint Paul reportedly preached against Artemis worship in Acts 19), the Temple of Hadrian, and the marble-paved Curetes Way connect them. The Terrace Houses, the surviving frescoed interiors of the Ephesian elite, are essential. Aphrodisias, 230 km inland, was the imperial-era marble-sculpture capital of the eastern empire, the site quarried its own white-and-gray marble (the Aphrodisian school of sculptors supplied much of imperial Rome); the on-site museum holds 200+ original Roman portrait sculptures, and the perfectly preserved 30,000-seat Stadium is the most intact ancient stadium anywhere. Pair with the surrounding Pamukkale travertines. Best April-May or September-October.

**The Berth.** Istanbul: Çırağan Palace Kempinski on the Bosphorus; the Pera Palace in Beyoğlu; the Sumahan on the Asian shore. Cappadocia: Argos in Cappadocia.

**The Galley.** Istanbul: Mikla on the rooftop of the Marmara Pera; Pandeli in the Spice Bazaar; Karaköy Lokantası; Çiya Sofrası in Kadıköy. Anatolia: Asitane in Edirnekapı for the Ottoman court cuisine.

> No man ever steps in the same river twice.
> *Heraclitus of Ephesus*

## Pilgrimage XXVII. Where Glory Is Won

Year-round destinations along the calendar of the great recurring sporting spectacles, the modern pilgrimage that draws devotees from across the world on a fixed and sacred date, where the venue is the relic and the match is the rite. This is the secular festival raised to the scale of a faith: the millions who travel each year to a final, a major, a classic, gathering in their colors as pilgrims once gathered for the holy days. Anchored to the root of it all at ancient Olympia, where the games began as a religious act, and to the nine modern cathedrals that the sporting world circles back to, year on year, generation on generation. Each stop is fixed to its own season; the trail is a lifetime's calendar, not a single trip. Book years ahead for the great finals, dress in your team's colors, and understand that the stadium roar at the decisive moment is, for the believer, indistinguishable from prayer. The flame is lit, the anthem plays, the crowd rises as one.

> The most important thing is not to win but to take part.
> *the Olympic Creed, after Pierre de Coubertin*

### Stop 1. Olympia & the Olympic Games

**Waypoint:** the Peloponnese, Greece

Where the games began as worship. In the sanctuary of Olympia, in the western Peloponnese, the ancient Greeks gathered every four years from 776 BCE for almost twelve centuries to compete in honor of Zeus, in games so sacred that the warring city-states laid down their arms for an Olympic truce to let the athletes and pilgrims pass. The first recorded victor was Koroibos, a cook from nearby Elis, who won the stadion sprint; the four-year interval, the Olympiad, became the unit by which the Greek world measured time. Here stood the colossal gold-and-ivory statue of Zeus, one of the Seven Wonders. The ruins remain, the temple of Zeus and the original stadium, where you can still run a length of the track the first Olympians ran. The modern Games, revived in Athens in 1896, light their flame here at the temple of Hera before every Olympiad and carry it around the world. Run the length of the ancient stadion. This is where sport began as a sacred thing, and never entirely stopped being one.

**The Berth.** Olympia: the Aldemar Olympian Village and the Europa Hotel near the site. Or base on the Peloponnese coast and combine with the Greek & Spartan Pilgrimage already on this calendar.

**The Galley.** Peloponnesian Greek: grilled fish and lamb; Kalamata olives and olive oil; horiatiki salad; loukoumades; the wines of the Peloponnese; a long taverna lunch under the plane trees after the morning at the ruins.

> Ask not for victory, ask for courage; for if you endure, you bring honor to us all.
> *the Olympic ideal, after Pindar*

### Stop 2. Wimbledon

**Waypoint:** London, England

Where tennis keeps its cathedral. The Championships at the All England Lawn Tennis Club in the London suburb of Wimbledon, first played in 1877, are the oldest and most prestigious tennis tournament in the world, and the last of the four majors still played on grass, the surface from which the game itself was born. Everything at Wimbledon is ritual: the strict all-white dress code for players, the strawberries and cream eaten by the ton, the Pimm's, the royal box, the ivy on the walls, the grass cut precisely to eight millimeters for its low and lightning-fast bounce. The queue, capital Q, is itself an institution, fans camping overnight on the grass for a chance at a Centre Court ticket. To sit on Centre Court for the final fortnight of June into July, the green so vivid it seems lit from within, and watch the best in the world on the lawn where Borg and Navratilova and Federer wrote their legends, is the tennis pilgrim's highest day. Eat the strawberries. Stand for the champion.

**The Berth.** London: the Cannizaro House on Wimbledon Common for the proximity; the Hotel du Vin Cannizaro House; or stay central in London (the Goring, the Connaught) and take the District line out to SW19.

**The Galley.** Strawberries and cream and a jug of Pimm's, the only correct Wimbledon meal; in Wimbledon Village, the Ivy Café and Côte; back in London, the full range of one of the world's great restaurant cities.

> You cannot be serious.
> *John McEnroe, Wimbledon, 1981*

### Stop 3. Augusta & the Masters

**Waypoint:** Georgia, USA

Where golf takes its most beautiful walk. The Masters Tournament, played every April at the Augusta National Golf Club in Georgia, is the most coveted title in the sport and the one major that returns to the same hallowed course year after year, so that every blade of the place is known and loved: Amen Corner, the treacherous 11th, 12th, and 13th; the azaleas and dogwoods in full bloom; Rae's Creek; the Hogan and Nelson bridges; the green jacket awarded to the champion and kept at the club. The traditions are fierce and unbroken: the par-3 contest, the Champions Dinner, the honorary starters, the patrons (never 'fans' or 'spectators') who may not run, may not bring a phone, and pay a pittance for a pimento cheese sandwich. The course is so manicured and the broadcast so controlled that Augusta in April looks less like a sporting venue than like Eden with a flagstick. Walk Amen Corner on a Sunday afternoon with the leaders coming through. The azaleas, the green, the hush, then the roar.

**The Berth.** Augusta: tickets and lodging are famously scarce; many rent private homes for Masters week. The Partridge Inn is the local landmark; chains fill early; some base in Atlanta (two and a half hours) for the range.

**The Galley.** The Augusta National pimento cheese and egg-salad sandwiches, an institution at a dollar and a half; in town, Augusta's Southern cooking, fried green tomatoes, shrimp and grits, peach cobbler; sweet tea on every porch.

> The Masters is the only tournament I ever knew where you choke when you drive through the front gate.
> *Gary Player*

### Stop 4. The Tour de France

**Waypoint:** France, on the roads and the cols

Where a whole country becomes the stadium. The Tour de France, first run in 1903, is the greatest bicycle race on Earth and the largest annual sporting event of any kind, three weeks each July covering some 3,500 kilometers around France and its mountains, watched live and free along the roadsides by twelve million people who wait all day, sometimes all week camped on a mountainside, for the riders to pass in a few thrilling seconds. The pilgrim's stops are the great climbs: the bare moonscape of Mont Ventoux; the twenty-one switchbacks of Alpe d'Huez, each named for a stage winner, where the crowds press so close the riders pass through a tunnel of roaring bodies; the Col du Tourmalet in the Pyrenees. The race ends on the Champs-Élysées in Paris, the peloton sweeping under the Arc de Triomphe in the gold evening light. Ride a col yourself the morning before the race comes through, then find a corner of the mountain, and wait with the crowd for the leaders. The roar moves up the mountain toward you like weather.

**The Berth.** On the route: book a year ahead in the mountain towns (Bourg d'Oisans below Alpe d'Huez; the Pyrenean spa towns). In Paris for the finish: the grand hotels off the Champs-Élysées, or any room with a Metro to the avenue.

**The Galley.** Roadside and regional: the charcuterie, cheese, and bread of a French picnic on a mountainside; the cooking of whichever region the race crosses; in Paris, the final-night celebration in any bistro off the Champs-Élysées.

> The Tour is the closest thing we have to a moving cathedral.
> *the cycling tradition*

### Stop 5. The Monaco Grand Prix

**Waypoint:** Monte Carlo, Monaco

Where the cars thread between the barriers. The crown jewel of motor racing, run through the streets of Monte Carlo since 1929 and part of the Formula One World Championship since its first season in 1950, the Monaco Grand Prix is the most glamorous and most coveted race on the calendar, the slowest and tightest circuit in Formula One and the hardest to win, where the cars graze the Fairmont hairpin, plunge through the harborfront tunnel, and brush the Armco with no margin at all. To win at Monaco is one leg of motorsport's unofficial Triple Crown, alongside the Le Mans 24 Hours and the Indianapolis 500. Ayrton Senna, the greatest of all around these streets, won here six times, five of them in a row. There is no overtaking and no room for error, which is precisely the point. Watch from the rocks above the harbor as the field comes screaming out of the tunnel into the light.

**The Berth.** Monaco: the Hotel de Paris and the Hermitage in Monte Carlo for the grand (and the trackside balconies); nearby Nice and the Riviera for the more affordable, with the train down to the principality on race day.

**The Galley.** Monégasque and Niçoise: barbagiuan, socca, the salade niçoise; the grand dining rooms of the Hotel de Paris; a harborfront table where the yachts are moored; the Riviera seafood up and down the coast.

> Once you no longer go for a gap that exists, you are no longer a racing driver.
> *Ayrton Senna*

### Stop 6. The Kentucky Derby

**Waypoint:** Louisville, Kentucky, USA

Where the most exciting two minutes in sport are run. On the first Saturday in May at Churchill Downs in Louisville since 1875, the Kentucky Derby is the oldest continuously held major sporting event in America and the first jewel of thoroughbred racing's Triple Crown. The race itself is barely two minutes long, but the day around it is an institution: the twin spires of the grandstand, the mint juleps in souvenir glasses, the broad-brimmed hats, the singing of 'My Old Kentucky Home' as the horses come onto the track, and the blanket of four hundred red roses laid over the winner, the Run for the Roses. The infield is a riotous party; Millionaires' Row is a parade of finery. Behind it all stands the deep horse culture of the Kentucky bluegrass, the breeding farms where the great bloodlines are kept. Wear the hat. Hold the julep. Sing along, and when the gate opens, lose your voice for the two minutes that the whole year of the bluegrass points toward.

**The Berth.** Louisville: the historic Brown Hotel (home of the Hot Brown); the Seelbach, of Gatsby fame; the Galt House on the river. Derby week books out a year ahead across the whole city.

**The Galley.** The Brown Hotel's Hot Brown (the open-faced turkey-and-Mornay institution); burgoo and beaten biscuits; the mint julep, of course; bourbon everything, with the great distilleries of the Kentucky Bourbon Trail an easy drive away.

> And they're off!
> *the call of the Kentucky Derby*

### Stop 7. The Maracanã & the World Cup

**Waypoint:** Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

Where the beautiful game keeps its temple. No sport gathers humanity like football, and no country worships it like Brazil, where the Estádio do Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro is the spiritual home of the world's game. Built for the 1950 World Cup, it held a crowd of nearly two hundred thousand for the final, where Uruguay's victory over Brazil, the Maracanazo, became a national trauma still spoken of in hushed tones. It was here that Pelé scored his thousandth goal, here that the 2014 World Cup and the 2016 Olympic football finals were played. The World Cup itself, held every four years since 1930, is the most watched event on Earth, half the planet tuning in to the final; to be in the host country during the tournament is to feel an entire world briefly united around a single ball. Stand on the Maracanã terraces when a goal goes in and the sound is a physical force. Football is not a matter of life and death here. It is, as the saying goes, far more important than that.

**The Berth.** Rio de Janeiro: the storied Copacabana Palace on the beach; the Fasano in Ipanema; or a guesthouse in Santa Teresa on the hill. Book far ahead for any World Cup or Olympic year.

**The Galley.** Brazilian: the churrascaria rodízio of endless grilled meats; feijoada, the national bean-and-pork stew, on a Saturday; açaí and pão de queijo; a caipirinha on the Copacabana sand as the sun goes down.

> Football is the ballet of the masses.
> *the Brazilian tradition, after Dmitri Shostakovich*

### Stop 8. The Boston Marathon

**Waypoint:** Massachusetts, USA

Where the people make their pilgrimage on foot. The marathon is itself an act of devotion, 26.2 miles run in memory of the Greek messenger Pheidippides, who ran from Marathon to Athens to bring word of victory and died upon delivering it. The Boston Marathon, first run in 1897 and the oldest annual marathon in the world, is the one every amateur runner dreams of, the one you cannot buy your way into but must qualify for by time, run each Patriots' Day in April from rural Hopkinton to Copley Square in Boston. The course is a pilgrim's road: the Wellesley 'scream tunnel' of college students, the brutal Heartbreak Hill at mile twenty, the right on Hereford and left on Boylston to the finish. After the 2013 bombing, 'Boston Strong' made the race a symbol of a city's defiance. To run Boston, or to stand at the finish on Boylston Street and cheer the strangers home for hours, is to witness ordinary people doing a heroic thing. Cheer for the back of the pack. They have come the furthest.

**The Berth.** Boston: the Fairmont Copley Plaza and the Lenox near the finish line; the Eliot in the Back Bay; book Marathon weekend (Patriots' Day, mid-April) far in advance, the whole city fills.

**The Galley.** New England: clam chowder and a lobster roll at Neptune Oyster; the Union Oyster House, America's oldest restaurant; the carbo-loading pasta dinners the night before; Italian in the North End on Hanover Street.

> The miracle isn't that I finished. The miracle is that I had the courage to start.
> *John Bingham, on the marathon*

### Stop 9. Lord's

**Waypoint:** London, England

Where cricket comes home. Lord's Cricket Ground in St John's Wood, London, opened on its present site in 1814 and home to the Marylebone Cricket Club, which wrote and still guards the Laws of the game, is universally called the Home of Cricket, the most revered ground in a sport followed by more than a billion people across the Commonwealth and the Indian subcontinent. To play a Test at Lord's, to walk down the steps of the Long Room through the members in their egg-and-bacon ties and out onto the turf, to get your name on the honours board for a century or a five-wicket haul, is the ambition of every cricketer alive. The ground holds the old Father Time weathervane, the modern spaceship of the Media Centre, the famous slope across the pitch, and the small museum that keeps the Ashes urn, the tiny terracotta trophy that England and Australia have contested since 1882. Sit in the stands through a long summer's day of a Test match, the slow and subtle rhythm of the oldest team game, and understand why its devotees call it not a sport but a religion.

**The Berth.** London: the Lord's-adjacent boutique hotels of St John's Wood and Maida Vale; the Landmark in nearby Marylebone; or central London with a short Tube ride to St John's Wood on the Jubilee line.

**The Galley.** A long day at the cricket runs on Champagne and smoked salmon in the stands, or a pork pie and a pint; in St John's Wood and Marylebone, the gastropubs and the restaurants of the Marylebone High Street; afternoon tea, the cricket-day ritual.

> Cricket is a game which the English, not being a spiritual people, have invented in order to give themselves some conception of eternity.
> *attributed to the English game*

### Stop 10. The Super Bowl

**Waypoint:** the United States, a different city each year

Where America keeps its high holy day of sport. The Super Bowl, the championship of the National Football League played on the first Sunday of February, is the most watched television broadcast in the United States every single year and has become a secular national holiday in all but name, a day of gathering, feasting, and shared ritual observed by families and strangers alike whether they follow the game or not. Unlike the other stops on this trail, it has no fixed temple: it moves to a different host city and stadium each year, so the pilgrimage is to the event rather than the place. Around the game has grown a whole liturgy, the multimillion-dollar advertisements watched as keenly as the play, the halftime show that is itself one of the largest concerts on Earth, the parties, the prop bets, the rivers of wings and nachos and beer. It is the modern festival in its purest form: a nation pausing together on a winter Sunday to watch, eat, and belong. End the pilgrimage here, in the present, at the spectacle that proves the old festival impulse is alive and roaring still.

**The Berth.** The host city changes yearly (recent and coming Super Bowls have been in New Orleans, Las Vegas, and the great domed stadiums of the Sun Belt); book the moment the host is announced, as the whole city fills for the week.

**The Galley.** The Super Bowl spread is the meal: wings, nachos, chili, ribs, seven-layer dip, and cold beer, eaten in front of the television; in the host city, the local specialties become part of the week-long festival around the game.

> Winning isn't everything, but wanting to win is.
> *Vince Lombardi*

---

## Pilgrimage XXVIII. I Am Haunted by Waters

Year-round destinations along the great waters of the angling world, the rivers, flats, and seas that serious fishers dream of casting at least once before they die. Angling is among the oldest of the contemplative pursuits, and certain waters have become true pilgrimage sites, spoken of with the reverence other travelers reserve for cathedrals: the chalkstream where the dry fly was born, the Montana river that Maclean made scripture, the Gulf Stream where Hemingway chased marlin, the tropical flats where the saltwater fly fisher hunts on foot through ankle-deep water for fish that vanish like ghosts. Anchored to the species, the method, and the literature of the sport, this is a trail measured less in fish landed than in mornings on the water. Each stop is fixed to its own run and season; the angler's calendar is the trail. Match the hatch, mind the tide, and remember Walton's counsel that the point was never only the catching. Tight lines, and study to be quiet.

> We may say of angling as Dr. Boteler said of strawberries: Doubtless God could have made a better berry, but doubtless God never did.
> *Izaak Walton, The Compleat Angler, 1653*

### Stop 1. The River Test

**Waypoint:** Hampshire, England

Where fly fishing was born. The River Test, rising in the hamlet of Ashe and winding thirty-nine miles of crystalline Hampshire chalkstream to the sea, is the cradle of modern fly fishing and the most revered trout water on Earth. Here, on these gin-clear, weed-waving, gravel-bottomed waters, Frederic Halford codified the dry fly in the 1880s, while fifteen miles east on the Itchen, G.E.M. Skues invented nymph fishing and the two gentlemen feuded for a generation over the soul of the sport. Two hundred years earlier Izaak Walton fished these valleys and wrote The Compleat Angler, the second-most reprinted book in the English language after the Bible; he lies in Winchester Cathedral, in a chapel with a stained-glass window dedicated to anglers. The fishing is by invitation, beat, and river keeper, the most exclusive in the world, dry fly only by tradition, casting to a rising wild brown trout you can see. Fish the mayfly hatch in late May, 'Duffers' Fortnight,' when the great green drakes come off and even the biggest fish lose their caution. Cast upstream, to a rising fish, and wait.

**The Berth.** Hampshire: the Greyhound on the Test in Stockbridge (the angler's inn on the river); Lainston House near Winchester; the Pig hotels of the county. The fly shop is Robjent's in Stockbridge.

**The Galley.** The Greyhound's river-caught and estate fare; potted trout and a pint of Hampshire ale; the chalk-valley pubs; afternoon tea after a morning on the beat; Winchester's restaurants near the cathedral and Walton's tomb.

> Study to be quiet.
> *Izaak Walton, The Compleat Angler*

### Stop 2. The Big Blackfoot River

**Waypoint:** Montana, USA

Where fly fishing became scripture. The Big Blackfoot River runs west out of the Bob Marshall Wilderness through canyon walls of moss-covered cliff and ponderosa pine, a classic Montana freestone of emerald pools, boulder pocket water, and long riffled runs full of wild cutthroat, rainbow, and brown trout. It is the river Norman Maclean made immortal in A River Runs Through It, the 1976 novella that begins 'In our family, there was no clear line between religion and fly fishing' and ends 'I am haunted by waters,' the book that, more than any other, gave American fly fishing its soul, and after the 1992 film, its crowds. The great salmonfly hatch comes off in late June, when trout the size of a forearm rise for the big bugs and the fishing is as thrilling as the sport gets. Float it in a drift boat, or wade the runs, casting attractor dries to willing trout under the cliffs. Fish it at dawn or in the evening light, when the canyon glows and the river, as Maclean wrote, has trout in it, but also runs over the words.

**The Berth.** Montana: the historic lodges and guest ranches around Missoula and Ovando; the Resort at Paws Up on the Blackfoot for the grand; cabins and the classic Montana fishing-town motels. Fly shops in Missoula outfit the river.

**The Galley.** Montana: bison and trout; a steak and a Moose Drool brown ale in a Missoula saloon; the breakfast at a fishing-town diner before dawn on the water; huckleberry everything in season; a streamside lunch from the drift boat.

> Eventually, all things merge into one, and a river runs through it.
> *Norman Maclean, A River Runs Through It*

### Stop 3. The River Spey

**Waypoint:** the Scottish Highlands

Where the Atlantic salmon comes home. The River Spey, running fast and cold out of the Cairngorms through the heart of Speyside whisky country to the North Sea, is one of the great salmon rivers of Scotland and gave its name to the Spey cast, the rolling two-handed technique developed here in the 19th century to throw long lines on big water with no room for a backcast. To swing a fly through a famous pool for a fresh-run Atlantic salmon, the fish of a thousand casts, silver from the sea and bound upriver to spawn, is the classic pursuit of the game-fishing world, fished by ghillie and beat as on the English chalkstreams, in tweed against the Highland cold. The salmon runs vary through the season from spring fish to the autumn run. Between casts the angler stands in the current of one of the most beautiful valleys in Britain, a distillery very likely just downstream. Swing the fly, and when the line comes tight on a fresh salmon, you understand the obsession of centuries.

**The Berth.** Speyside: the grand sporting hotels and fishing lodges of the valley; Craigellachie Hotel; the Dowans; estate lodges let with the beats. The whisky distilleries of Speyside line the river for the evening dram.

**The Galley.** Scottish: the salmon, of course, and Highland game and beef; cullen skink and cranachan; a dram of Speyside single malt (Macallan, Glenfiddich, and a dozen more are neighbors) by the fire after a cold day on the water.

> There is certainly something in angling that tends to produce a serenity of the mind.
> *Washington Irving*

### Stop 4. The Florida Keys

**Waypoint:** Florida, USA

Where the saltwater fly fisher hunts on foot. The shallow turquoise flats of the Florida Keys, from Islamorada down to Key West, are the birthplace and capital of saltwater fly fishing, where the angler poles a skiff or wades across ankle-deep water hunting by sight for three great gamefish: the bonefish, the gray ghost of the flats that vanishes the instant it sees you; the permit, the most maddeningly difficult fish in the sea to take on a fly; and the tarpon, the silver king, a hundred-plus pounds of prehistoric muscle that rolls on the surface, eats the fly, and then cartwheels into the air shaking its head. To take all three in a day is the fabled grand slam, the saltwater fly fisher's holy grail. This is hunting as much as fishing: long hours of poling and watching, the guide on the platform calling the fish by the clock face, then one shot, one cast, at a moving target. The tarpon migration peaks in spring. Stand on the bow, line stripped and ready, and wait for the guide to say the word.

**The Berth.** The Keys: the historic Cheeca Lodge in Islamorada (the anglers' headquarters); the Moorings Village; the Ocean Reef Club. Key West for the southern end. The fly shops of Islamorada are the saltwater nerve center.

**The Galley.** The Keys: fresh hogfish, yellowtail snapper, stone crab in season; conch fritters and key lime pie; a cold beer at a dockside fish house at sunset; Hemingway's haunts in Key West, Sloppy Joe's and the rest.

> The flats are a chessboard, and the fish always moves first.
> *the saltwater angling tradition*

### Stop 5. The Gulf Stream off Cuba

**Waypoint:** Havana & Cojímar, Cuba

Where the old man fished. Out of the little fishing village of Cojímar, east of Havana, Ernest Hemingway kept his boat Pilar and fished the deep blue Gulf Stream for marlin through the 1930s and 40s, and from those waters and those fishermen he drew The Old Man and the Sea, the 1952 novella of an old Cuban fisherman, Santiago, and the great marlin that wins him the Nobel Prize and breaks his heart. The Gulf Stream here runs close to shore, deep and fast and full of life, and the big blue and white marlin, the wahoo, the tuna, and the dorado still cross it; the Hemingway Billfish Tournament, which the writer founded in 1950 and once fished against Fidel Castro, runs out of Havana to this day. Visit the Pilar, preserved at Hemingway's hilltop home Finca Vigía outside the city. Then go out into the stream at dawn, where the flying fish scatter and a marlin is rising below, and fish the water that made the most famous fishing story ever written.

**The Berth.** Havana: the Hotel Nacional de Cuba on the Malecón (the grand old dame); the restored hotels of Old Havana; a casa particular for the local immersion. Cojímar and the eastern beaches for the proximity to the stream.

**The Galley.** Cuban: ropa vieja, the fresh catch grilled simply, rice and beans, tostones; a daiquiri at El Floridita and a mojito at La Bodeguita del Medio, both Hemingway's bars; strong Cuban coffee and a cigar to close the evening.

> But man is not made for defeat. A man can be destroyed but not defeated.
> *Ernest Hemingway, The Old Man and the Sea*

### Stop 6. The Skeena & the Steelhead Rivers

**Waypoint:** British Columbia, Canada

Where the steelhead runs through the rainforest. In the wild river systems of northern British Columbia, the Skeena and its legendary tributaries, the Bulkley, the Babine, the Kispiox, run the largest and most coveted steelhead on Earth, the sea-run rainbow trout that, like salmon, is born in the river, goes to the ocean for years, and returns enormous and chrome- bright to spawn. The steelhead is the great prize of the swung fly, fished two-handed on big water, and the angler may cast for days for a single grab; the takes, when they come, are violent, and the fish are the size of a leg. This is fishing in true wilderness, the rivers running through temperate rainforest and grizzly country, the autumn cottonwoods turning gold, the mountains white above. The fall run is the classic season. There is a purity to steelheading that its devotees describe in almost religious terms: the long swing, the endless hope, the rare and electric reward. Wade in, make the cast, mend the line, and let the fly swing all the way around.

**The Berth.** British Columbia: the storied steelhead lodges of the Skeena watershed (the Babine, the Bulkley); wilderness camps reached by float plane or jet boat; the fishing towns of Smithers and Terrace as base camps.

**The Galley.** The lodge table: wild salmon and game, hearty wilderness cooking after a cold day's wading; a dram by the woodstove; the spare provisions of a remote camp where the fishing, not the dining, is the point.

> Steelhead fishing is the art of staying hopeful longer than is reasonable.
> *the steelheading tradition*

### Stop 7. The Rivers of Patagonia

**Waypoint:** Argentina & Chile

Where the trout found a paradise at the bottom of the world. When British and European settlers stocked the rivers and lakes of Patagonia with brown and rainbow trout a century ago, they created, at the bottom of the world, one of the greatest trout fisheries on Earth. Across the vast wild country of southern Argentina and Chile, the Limay, the Chimehuín, the Malleo, and a hundred lesser-known rivers run clear and cold off the Andes through steppe and southern beech forest, holding wild trout grown large and strong in waters that see few anglers. This is also the realm of the golden dorado, the savage golden-scaled predator of the subtropical rivers to the north, all teeth and muscle and acrobatics, increasingly the prize of the adventurous fly fisher. The seasons are reversed: the southern summer, December to March, is the high season, the perfect escape from the northern winter. Wade the gin-clear rivers under the Andes, the condors overhead and not another soul in sight, and cast to wild trout in some of the last and least-fished great water on the planet.

**The Berth.** Patagonia: the great estancia lodges of Argentine and Chilean Patagonia (Jurassic Lake for monster rainbows; the Chimehuín lodges); wilderness fishing camps; the mountain towns of Bariloche and San Martín de los Andes as bases.

**The Galley.** Argentine: the asado, whole lamb and beef over open fire; Malbec from Mendoza; empanadas and dulce de leche; the trout itself, fresh from the river; the long late Patagonian dinner under the southern stars.

> The fish you release is a gift to another angler, and a gift to yourself in the future.
> *Lee Wulff*

### Stop 8. The South Island

**Waypoint:** New Zealand

Where the water is clearest and the wild trout largest. The rivers of New Zealand's South Island run through some of the most beautiful and unspoiled country on Earth, and hold, in water so clear it seems not to exist, the largest wild brown trout most anglers will ever stalk. This is sight-fishing of the highest and most demanding order: the angler and guide walk miles of river spotting individual fish, often a single great trout holding in a clear run, then make one careful cast, because the second chance rarely comes. The fish are few, large, and educated, and the fishing is more hunting than angling. The landscape is the Lord of the Rings country of snow peaks, beech forest, and impossibly turquoise glacial rivers, fished from helicopter-accessed backcountry to roadside water. The southern summer, November to April, is the season. Walk the river slowly with your eyes down, spot the shadow that is a five-pound trout, and make the cast count.

**The Berth.** New Zealand: the luxury lodges of the South Island (Owen River Lodge, Cedar Lodge, Poronui on the North Island); backcountry huts and helicopter-accessed camps; the small fishing towns of the Southern Alps.

**The Galley.** New Zealand: lamb and venison; green-lipped mussels and crayfish; Central Otago Pinot Noir and Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc; the catch from sea and river; a backcountry barbecue after a long day's walking and wading.

> Many men go fishing all of their lives without knowing that it is not fish they are after.
> *Henry David Thoreau*

### Stop 9. The Salmon Runs of Alaska

**Waypoint:** Bristol Bay & the Alaskan rivers

Where the rivers run silver with fish. Each summer, in one of the greatest wildlife events on Earth, tens of millions of Pacific salmon, five species of them, return from the ocean to spawn in the rivers of Alaska, turning the water itself silver with their numbers. Bristol Bay hosts the largest sockeye salmon run on the planet; the rivers of the Bristol Bay watershed, the Naknek, the Kvichak, the Alagnak, and the wild waters of Katmai and the Alaska Peninsula, offer fishing of an abundance found almost nowhere else, for all five salmon, for enormous rainbow trout that grow fat on salmon eggs and flesh, for arctic char and grayling. And where the salmon run, the brown bears gather; to fish an Alaskan river is to share it with the largest land predators in North America, fishing the same water for the same fish. This is fishing at the scale of the wild itself. Fly in to a remote lodge or float a river through the tundra, and cast into water boiling with more fish than you have ever seen.

**The Berth.** Alaska: the fly-in wilderness lodges of Bristol Bay and Katmai (Tikchik, Crystal Creek, Royal Coachman); tented float-trip camps; the bush-plane access that is part of the Alaskan fishing experience.

**The Galley.** Alaska: wild salmon every way, fresh-caught and grilled on the riverbank; halibut and king crab; the hearty lodge table; sourdough; the simple pleasure of eating the fish you caught an hour before, in the country it came from.

> Time spent fishing is not deducted from one's lifespan.
> *the angler's proverb*

### Stop 10. Home Water

**Waypoint:** wherever you learned

Where every angler's pilgrimage truly begins and ends. After the great rivers and the famous flats, the trail returns to the smallest and most important water of all: home water, the pond, creek, lake, or stretch of river where you first learned to fish, and to which the angler returns all their life. It may be a chalkstream or a farm pond, a tidal flat or a mountain brook; what matters is that you know it, season by season, year by year, until you read it like a face. The great fishing writers understood that the famous destinations are pilgrimages precisely because they send you home again changed, to see your own water with new eyes. John Gierach spent a career writing about ordinary trout in ordinary creeks and made it sing. Walton fished modest rivers and wrote of contentment. End the pilgrimage not at some far paradise but at the bank where you began, on an evening when the fish are rising and there is nowhere else you would rather be, and understand at last that the fishing was never really about the fish.

**The Berth.** Home: your own bed, the night before an early start; the familiar tackle by the door; the coffee in the dark kitchen; the drive to the water you have driven a hundred times. This is the one stop on the trail that needs no booking.

**The Galley.** Home: a sandwich in your vest pocket; coffee from a thermos on the bank; the fish, if you keep one, cooked simply in your own kitchen; or, just as good, the meal that tastes better for a day spent outdoors doing the thing you love.

> Many of us probably would be better fishermen if we did not spend so much time watching and waiting for the world to become perfect.
> *Norman Maclean, A River Runs Through It*

---

## Pilgrimage XXIX. The Cradle and the Dawn

Year-round destinations along the great wild places of Africa, the last continent where the largest land animals on Earth still roam in their millions across landscapes that have scarcely changed since our own species first stood up and walked out of them. The word safari is simply Swahili for 'journey,' and the safari is a pilgrimage in the oldest sense: a return to the country that made us, where the human animal remembers what it is to be one creature among many on an open plain at dawn. This trail crosses East and Southern Africa, from the migration plains of the Serengeti to the deltas of Botswana, the gorilla forests of Rwanda, and the desert edges of Namibia, to see the Big Five and the great migration, the predator and the prey, the dawn and the dusk when the wild is most awake. The dry season, broadly May to October, concentrates the game at the water. Rise before light, go slowly, keep silent, and let the oldest landscape on Earth do the rest. Twende, polepole: let us go, slowly.

> The earth has music for those who listen, and Africa plays it loudest at dawn.
> *the safari tradition*

### Stop 1. The Serengeti & the Masai Mara

**Waypoint:** Tanzania & Kenya

Where the great herds still run to the horizon. Across the endless short-grass plains of the Serengeti in Tanzania and the Masai Mara in Kenya moves the Great Migration, more than 1.5 million wildebeest and several hundred thousand zebra and gazelle in an endless circuit following the rains, the largest overland migration of mammals left on the planet. Serengeti is Maa for 'the endless plain,' and that is exactly what it is, a horizon of grass with nothing to break it but a lone acacia and the herds. The most dramatic moments are the river crossings, the herds plunging in their thousands through the crocodile-filled Mara River between July and October; the calving on the southern plains in February draws every predator for miles. This is the landscape our own species evolved to walk, home to some 3,000 lions, and to stand in it among the herds at dawn is to feel something older than memory switch on. There is no sound on Earth like a lion calling across a plain you cannot see the edge of.

**The Berth.** Serengeti: the mobile tented camps that follow the migration (Serengeti Under Canvas; Sanctuary Kichakani); Singita Grumeti for the grand. Masai Mara: Angama Mara on the escarpment; Cottar's 1920s Camp.

**The Galley.** Camp dining is full-board and often superb: bush breakfasts laid out on the plain, sundowners at dusk; Tanzanian nyama choma and ugali; Swahili coastal flavors; strong coffee before the dawn drive.

> In the end we will conserve only what we love, and we will love only what we understand.
> *Baba Dioum, Senegalese conservationist*

### Stop 2. The Ngorongoro Crater

**Waypoint:** Tanzania

Where a whole world lives inside a volcano. The Ngorongoro Crater is the largest intact volcanic caldera on Earth, a collapsed volcano twenty kilometers across, its six-hundred-meter walls enclosing a self-contained world of grassland, soda lake, forest, and swamp on the crater floor, home to one of the densest concentrations of wildlife anywhere in Africa. Some twenty-five thousand large animals live within the crater, and because they cannot easily leave, a game drive on the floor delivers the Big Five, lion, leopard, elephant, buffalo, and the critically endangered black rhino, often in a single morning. Descend the steep track from the misty rim at dawn into the bowl below, where the light comes up over the wall and the lake turns pink with flamingos and the lions are still on their kills. Nearby lies Olduvai Gorge, where the Leakeys found the fossils that rewrote the story of human origins, a reminder that this is, quite literally, the cradle of humankind. The crater is busy; go early, go quiet, and stay all day.

**The Berth.** Ngorongoro: the dramatic &Beyond Ngorongoro Crater Lodge on the rim (the grand); the Ngorongoro Sopa and Serena lodges; or lodges in the Karatu highlands below for the gardens and the cool.

**The Galley.** Tanzanian highland fare: the lodge tables with crater views; roasted meats and fresh garden vegetables from the fertile Karatu farms; Tanzanian Arabica coffee grown on the volcanic slopes; a packed bush lunch on the crater floor.

> Out of Africa always something new.
> *Pliny the Elder, quoted by Karen Blixen*

### Stop 3. The Okavango Delta

**Waypoint:** Botswana

Where a river vanishes into the desert and the wild comes to drink. The Okavango is one of the strangest and most beautiful wildernesses on Earth: a great inland delta where the Okavango River, instead of running to the sea, spreads out and dies in the sands of the Kalahari, flooding each year into a vast labyrinth of channels, lagoons, and palm islands that draws all the wildlife of the dry country to the water. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, it is safari country like no other, explored as much by water as by land: glide in silence through the reed channels in a mokoro, the traditional dugout canoe poled by a guide standing in the stern, past hippos yawning and elephants crossing and the lily-trotters stepping over the floating leaves. The delta holds lion, leopard, and one of Africa's last strongholds of the endangered African wild dog. Lie back in the mokoro as the guide poles you through the papyrus at sunset, the water mirror-still, and understand why this is the safari that other safari-goers dream about.

**The Berth.** Okavango: the legendary water-and-land camps of the private concessions (Mombo, Vumbura, Jao, Duba Plains); fly-in by light aircraft over the delta, itself an unforgettable sight; Botswana's low-volume, high-cost model keeps it pristine.

**The Galley.** Camp dining at the high end of the safari world: candlelit dinners under the stars, fresh and inventive cooking flown in; bush brunches on an island; sundowners on a mokoro in the channels; the boma fire and the night sounds.

> The delta breathes once a year, and all of Africa comes to its water.
> *the Okavango tradition*

### Stop 4. Sabi Sands & Kruger

**Waypoint:** South Africa

Where the leopard drapes the evening branches. Along the western boundary of South Africa's vast Kruger National Park lie the private reserves of the Greater Kruger, the Sabi Sands above all, where the fences have come down so the game moves freely between them, and where decades of careful habituation have made this the finest place on Earth to see the leopard, the most beautiful and elusive of the great cats, draped along a branch in the golden evening light. Kruger itself, one of the oldest and largest national parks in Africa, is the great democratic safari, self-driveable and open to all, two million hectares of bushveld holding the full African bestiary. The private reserves offer what the park cannot: off-road tracking, expert ranger-and-tracker teams reading the dust for a leopard's pug marks, and the night drive, when the spotlight finds eyes in the dark and the nocturnal Africa wakes. This is where many travelers see their first lion, their first leopard, their first elephant up close. Sit with a leopard at dusk as it wakes and begins to hunt.

**The Berth.** Sabi Sands: the storied lodges (Londolozi, Singita, MalaMala, Sabi Sabi), among the best in Africa. Kruger itself: the SANParks rest camps for the self-drive classic, a great and affordable African tradition.

**The Galley.** South African: the braai (barbecue) and boerewors; venison and bobotie; the lodge fine dining paired with Cape wines; biltong for the game drive; rusks and coffee before dawn; the communal boma dinner around the fire.

> The leopard does not change his spots, nor would we wish him to.
> *the bushveld tradition*

### Stop 5. Victoria Falls

**Waypoint:** Zambia & Zimbabwe, on the Zambezi

Where the great Zambezi falls into thunder. The Smoke That Thunders, where the river plunges over a mile-wide basalt lip and falls more than a hundred meters into a narrow gorge, it throws up a column of spray visible from forty kilometers away, which gave the falls their African name, Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the Smoke That Thunders.' Twice the height of Niagara and, by the combined measure of width and height, the largest sheet of falling water in the world, it is one of the natural wonders of the Earth and the great pause in any Southern African safari, the place where the wildlife journey meets pure spectacle. Walk the rainforest path along the lip in your raincoat as the spray soaks you through and the rainbows arc in the gorge below; or, for the bold, swim to the very edge in the Devil's Pool when the water is low. The town is Africa's adventure capital, with rafting, microlights, and the historic bridge to leap from. Stand at the edge of the chasm where the whole river disappears into thunder and mist, and feel the ground itself shake.

**The Berth.** Victoria Falls: the colonial-grand Victoria Falls Hotel (1904) on the Zimbabwe side, with its lawns facing the bridge; the Royal Livingstone on the Zambian bank, where the river slides past the terrace toward the edge.

**The Galley.** High tea on the lawn of the Victoria Falls Hotel, a colonial ritual; the Zambezi riverboat sunset cruise with sundowners; game meats and Zimbabwean and Zambian cooking; fresh bream from the river.

> Scenes so lovely must have been gazed upon by angels in their flight.
> *David Livingstone, on first seeing the falls*

### Stop 6. The Mountain Gorillas

**Waypoint:** Volcanoes National Park, Rwanda

Where we may sit an hour with our closest wild kin. High in the misty bamboo and Hagenia forests of the Virunga volcanoes, on the borders of Rwanda, Uganda, and the Congo, live the last mountain gorillas on Earth, fewer than a thousand of them, brought back from the edge of extinction by the work that Dian Fossey gave her life to. In Rwanda's Volcanoes National Park, small groups of trekkers climb for hours through dense, dripping forest behind expert guides, following the trackers to a habituated gorilla family, and are granted exactly one hour in their presence. To sit a few meters from a silverback the size of a small car, calmly stripping celery while his family dozes and the young tumble around him, to meet the eyes of an animal that shares almost all our DNA and see that someone is home behind them, is among the most moving encounters available anywhere. The permits are costly and limited by design, and every dollar guards the forest. Trek in the mist, sit, and carry it with you forever.

**The Berth.** Volcanoes NP: the extraordinary lodges that have risen near the park (Singita Kwitonda, Bisate, One&Only Gorilla's Nest, Sabyinyo Silver Lodge); base in Kigali the night before, an easy and surprisingly lovely city.

**The Galley.** Rwandan: fresh highland produce and tilapia from the lakes; the famous Rwandan coffee, among the world's best, grown on the volcanic slopes; the lodge tables; a hot meal and a fire after a cold, wet, triumphant trek.

> When you realize the value of all life, you dwell less on what is past and concentrate on the preservation of the future.
> *Dian Fossey*

### Stop 7. South Luangwa

**Waypoint:** Zambia

Where the walking safari was born. In the Luangwa Valley of eastern Zambia, a tail of the Great Rift, the meandering Luangwa River and its oxbow lagoons sustain one of the richest concentrations of wildlife in Africa, vast herds of elephant and buffalo, prides of lion, and a famous density of leopard. But South Luangwa's true distinction is that it is the birthplace of the walking safari: here, in the 1950s and 60s, the legendary conservationist Norman Carr pioneered the idea of exploring the bush on foot rather than from a vehicle, and nowhere are the guides better at it. To walk in single file behind an armed ranger and a guide who reads every track and broken twig and pile of dung, to approach the game on its own terms with your own senses fully awake, the smell of wild sage, the alarm call of a baboon, is to experience Africa as no game drive can deliver. This is the safari stripped to its essence, the human animal back on foot in the country that made it. Walk softly. The bush rewards the quiet.

**The Berth.** South Luangwa: the owner-run bushcamps that pioneered the walking safari (the Norman Carr camps, Tafika, Chinzombo, Tena Tena); intimate, remote, and among the most authentic safari experiences left in Africa.

**The Galley.** Bushcamp dining: hearty and personal, often around a single table with the guides; fresh-baked bread from a camp oven; the riverbank breakfast after the morning walk; sundowners on a sandbank as the hippos grunt.

> The bush is not a place you look at. It is a place that looks back at you.
> *the walking-safari tradition*

### Stop 8. Etosha & the Namib

**Waypoint:** Namibia

Where the desert keeps its own wildlife. Namibia is the great exception, a safari in a desert, where the wildlife has adapted to one of the driest inhabited places on Earth. In Etosha National Park, the game gathers around the waterholes at the edge of a vast white salt pan so large it can be seen from space, and the white dust coats the elephants until they become the famous 'ghost elephants,' pale as bone against the glare. To the west, in Damaraland and the Skeleton Coast, live the desert-adapted elephant and the desert black rhino, animals that have learned to survive where almost nothing else can, walking enormous distances between scarce water. And in the south rise the dunes of Sossusvlei, the highest in the world, blood-orange against a hard blue sky, where dead camel-thorn trees stand black on the white clay pan of Deadvlei, eight hundred years dead and too dry to rot. This is the most photogenic country in Africa. Climb a dune at dawn, and watch the light pour down the sand like something being born.

**The Berth.** Namibia: the desert lodges of the great spaces (Hoanib Skeleton Coast Camp, Sossusvlei Desert Lodge, Onguma at Etosha); the self-drive routes that make Namibia one of Africa's great road trips through empty, surreal country.

**The Galley.** Namibian: game meats (oryx, kudu, springbok); the German colonial legacy of good bread, beer, and apfelstrudel in Swakopmund; fresh oysters from Walvis Bay; a braai under a sky thick with stars in the clearest air on the continent.

> The desert tells a different story every time one ventures into it.
> *Robyn Davidson*

### Stop 9. The Chobe Elephants

**Waypoint:** Botswana, on the Chobe River

Where the elephants gather in their thousands. Along the Chobe River in northern Botswana lives the largest concentration of elephants on the continent, part of a population of well over a hundred thousand, the greatest surviving herd of the largest land animal on Earth. In the dry season they come down to the river in their hundreds to drink, bathe, swim, and play, crossing the channels in long files with the calves swimming between the adults, often at the golden end of the day. The classic Chobe experience is the river safari: a boat lets you drift quietly alongside the herds at water level, close enough to hear them drink and rumble to one another in the deep infrasound that carries for miles, while hippo, crocodile, buffalo, and a wealth of birds crowd the same water. There is no better place to simply sit with elephants, to watch a creature of such intelligence and tenderness and memory go about its life. Drift with the herd at sunset, cut the engine, and let them fill the whole evening.

**The Berth.** Chobe: the riverfront lodges of Kasane (the Chobe Game Lodge, where Taylor and Burton honeymooned); the houseboats that drift the river; an easy combination with Victoria Falls, an hour and a half away.

**The Galley.** Riverside lodge dining overlooking the Chobe; the sunset cruise with drinks among the elephants; Botswanan beef, some of the finest in Africa; fresh bream from the river; the boma buffet and the fireside night.

> Elephants are the keepers of the wild. Where they walk, the land remembers.
> *the Chobe tradition*

### Stop 10. The Last Light

**Waypoint:** anywhere the sun goes down over the bush

Where every safari ends, and stays with you. After the migration and the crater, the delta and the desert, every safari comes down at last to the same thing: the sundowner, the oldest ritual of the bush, when the vehicle stops on a rise or a riverbank as the sun drops, the guide pours a drink, and everyone falls silent to watch the African sky catch fire. It is in that hour, the light going from gold to blood to violet, the herds turning to silhouette, the stars pricking through and the night sounds beginning, that the safari does its deepest work, reminding the traveler that they are an animal on a living planet, that this immense and breathing wild is the true and original home of all of us, and that it is, right now, in our hands to keep. The old explorers caught a fever here they could never shake. Now you have it too. Watch the last light go, and know that part of you will always be listening for the lion in the dark. This is where the longest journey home begins.

**The Berth.** Wherever you are when the sun goes down: the last camp of the trip, the fire lit, the bags not yet packed; or already home, lying awake, hearing the whoop of a hyena that is four thousand miles and a whole world away. The bush does not let you go.

**The Galley.** The sundowner itself: a gin and tonic on the bonnet of a Land Rover, biltong and nuts, as the sun sets; and later, the last dinner under the stars, when no one wants to speak of leaving, and Africa holds you one more night.

> Once you have been to Africa, you will never be wholly at home anywhere else again.
> *after Karen Blixen, Out of Africa Colophon The Pilgrimages is Book the Second of Calendar For Life. Twenty-nine historical and literary trails, two hundred and ninety stops, drawn from the year-round armature beneath the festival calendar. The text is set in Liberation Serif. The ornaments are diamond, fleuron, and four-pointed star. The borders are antique gold over parchment. The road is the pilgrimage. Anonymous — Outside of Time Z.P.*
